New Brunswick is weaving AI into its K-12 curriculum, drawing praise — and pushback
'Tsunami of AI use' already in schools, says researcher, and education system needs to catch up
In a Moncton middle school this week, students entered a virtual dungeon, tasked with escaping from the dragon within while learning about cybersecurity.
After, some moved on to designing a visual presentation, while others tapped through colourful screens to read and answer questions for a unit about food. A few more programmed tiny robots.
Artificial intelligence tools were part of the activities, as the Grade 7 students worked under the watchful eyes of their teacher.
For the last few years, the Anglophone East School District has been exploring bringing AI into its classrooms, but now more New Brunswick schools are joining them, after the Department of Education added learning about AI into its updated anglophone K-12 curriculum.
The move comes as some international school systems recently set strict prohibitions around AI, with Norway banning most student use of generative AI through Grade 7, and the two largest U.S. school boards (New York and Los Angeles) restricting student use.
Amid wide, ongoing calls for more consistency and clarity teaching students when, how and if AI should be used, some are calling for more deliberation and pushing back against the technology in classrooms right now, especially for younger learners.
New Brunswick's approach
The curriculum update in New Brunswick basically fleshes out its digital literacy curriculum to incorporate AI in a structured way, according to André Côté, executive director of public policy think tank The Dais at Toronto Metropolitan University.
It's an important first step he hopes other provincial and territorial peers will soon follow, given that our education systems generally haven't moved urgently enough to address the "tsunami of AI use that has washed into schools," he said.
New Brunswick has "mindfully integrated" AI so educators can teach students in an age-appropriate way and to consider the technology with a critical eye, says Jordan Smith, Anglophone East's tech, innovation and AI subject coordinator.
That means students in kindergarten through Grade 2 start to learn basic digital literacy concepts via classroom discussions, says Smith, a former elementary teacher. They will talk about how they feel during and after using technology, for instance, or noticing that information from digital sources or tools isn't always correct.
As students get older, they start practising on digital devices like tablet computers, but AI in the curriculum doesn't mean primary students using chatbots, she said.
Smith noted that any school use of AI tools must adhere to platform age restrictions and, of Anglophone East's nine approved platforms, about half are listed as for students 13+ (younger students require parental consent) and a third are for teachers alone.
Along with the Microsoft chatbot Copilot (accessible to Grade 9 and up), that approved list includes visual design platform Canva, music-maker Suno and chatbot Gemini Notebook that works from user uploads (for educator use).
In high school, a student might input their interests into Copilot to generate potential book choices for an independent study, she shared as an example, or use it to analyze the intro to an essay they're writing. Students learn to consider any use or interaction with AI critically, Smith emphasized, and use it as support but not a shortcut for their own work.
Smith also said teachers are getting professional development on multiple fronts, with educators in her district trained at periodic professional development sessions and supported in class by a roving team of tech coaches. The province has also released learning modules about AI for teachers.
New Brunswick's anglophone curriculum update incorporates safe and ethical AI use in schools and development of AI literacy, Education Minister Claire Johnson told CBC News in a statement Friday, noting similar work is ongoing on the francophone side.
Integration, however, doesn't displace "fundamentals of literacy and numeracy," she said, nor the importance of teacher judgement for learning.
This is a learning journey schools and families are on together, according to Anglophone East Superintendent Randolph MacLean. "It's very much a Rubik's Cube that we're all working on at the same time — and we don't have all the sides figured out yet," he said.
However, "introduction of any new piece of technology, any new curriculum ... these are not done rapidly or without thought."
Digital consent forms for using AI tools have already gone home this year, MacLean added, so if parents don't want their kids engaging with AI, they don't.
"We've had very few parents who have pushed back on us, but the ones who have, [we] engage in the conversation. It's not an us-versus-them," he said.
Calling for a pause
There's been a renewed wave of parental concern over tech use in classrooms today, with some highlighting AI amid broader alarm bells over the breakneck pace of AI development.
Generative AI made its public debut less than four years ago and research remains early about its impacts on learning, but many parents are concerned "things were going too fast," said Ben Humphreys, father of a seven-year-old and co-founder of Vancouver group Parents for AI Caution in Schools.
- B.C. schools are bringing AI into classrooms, but some parents worry it will harm critical thinking
- In the age of AI, how do we teach young people to think critically?
Many also don't want kids serving as test subjects for new technology without oversight, he added. "Is the tool there just because it's a tool that is popular right now or does it help students learn?"
Along with worrying about the social development of kids befriending AI chatbots, Humphreys is wary of student overreliance on AI stunting cognition and wants schools to take a pause right now.
"Having that time in school where they can learn to think for themselves and figure out what they feel about the world, to learn ... determination to really push through tasks even when it's difficult — that's something that I'm worried will go away."
Many educators have similar concerns, according to Canadian Teachers' Federation president Clint Johnston, whose national alliance represents more than 370,000 elementary and secondary teachers.
"Slow down, give proper support and training to educators," many of whom feel unprepared, Johnston said from Ottawa.
"Right now it's this presumption that [AI] will be pervasive and therefore everyone needs to be using it all the time."
More policy, guidance needed
A recent KPMG Canada survey of 1,009 Canadians over 17 attending or teaching at secondary or post-secondary schools on their use of AI found that students' use is dramatically overshadowing that of educators.
"Students are absolutely using it, educators are starting to ... but we're not on the same page in terms of what it shouldn't be used for and how it should," said Rob Clayton, KPMG Canada's national education leader.
Both student and teacher respondents indicated we're not teaching responsible AI use adequately or enough, he said. Clayton thinks part of the disconnect "comes down to a lack of clear policy and guidance" from above.
Change "really does need to start at the top," Dais executive director Côté said, noting that ministries of education should be moving in unison: sharing successes "at a pan-Canadian level" and leveraging AI in education best practices and research from global organizations like the OECD and UNESCO.
He also wants to see movement to tackle thornier issues, including evaluating teaching, learning and assessment against the backdrop of AI and the multitude of risks facing students, from cognitive offloading to data privacy and online safety.
"This is a really generational and systemic change that we're experiencing and it can't just be dealt with at the classroom level."

In March, the Federal Communications Commission banned new consumer internet routers manufactured outside the US, citing national security concerns. The ban doesn’t affect any routers already in American homes or currently on sale in the US, but all new routers aimed at the consumer market will need to be approved. That has inevitably included some of the best new routers to come out in the past six months.
While the headline is that foreign-made consumer routers are banned, manufacturers can apply for exemptions, and some have been approved. There's no need to throw out your router, and you'll still find plenty of mesh systems on the store shelves. But what does this mean for you?
Updated September 2026: I added the news that Conditional Approval has been granted to several more companies, the biggest being Asus.
Why Are Foreign-Made Routers Banned?
“Malicious actors have exploited security gaps in foreign-made routers to attack American households, disrupt networks, enable espionage, and facilitate intellectual property theft,” the FCC wrote. “Foreign-made routers were also involved in the Volt, Flax, and Salt Typhoon cyberattacks targeting vital US infrastructure.”
Foreign-made consumer routers were added to the Covered List, which details equipment and services “deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States.”
Bogdan Botezatu, director of Threat Research at cybersecurity firm Bitdefender, says this ban is a step to harden the cybersecurity readiness of US households, given ongoing geopolitical tensions.
“Consumer routers sit at the edge of every home network, which makes them an attractive target and a strategic risk if compromised at scale,” he says. Asked whether he thinks the risk is real, Botezatu says yes, though there’s no easy way to prove intent. “[Internet of Things] devices, including routers, are a weak point across the internet.”
Which Routers Are Banned?
The ban only affects the sale of new Wi-Fi routers and mobile Wi-Fi or hotspot devices aimed at consumer households. The ban does not apply to existing FCC-approved routers on sale in the US or to phones with hotspot features. Previously purchased routers already in use in homes across the country are also fine and aren't part of the ban, according to the FCC’s FAQ. These routers can continue to be sold, used, and updated with new firmware, at least until January 1, 2029.
Any new router manufactured outside the US now requires FCC approval before it can be imported, marketed, or sold in the US. This includes routers from US companies manufactured overseas, which is the vast majority of the market right now.
What Does Foreign-Made Mean?
This is decidedly murky. The ban is concerned with “consumer-grade” routers and could include any designed or manufactured outside the US or manufactured by companies that are not completely US-owned and operated. All the major players in the market, including Netgear, TP-Link, Asus, Amazon’s Eero, Google’s Nest, Synology, Linksys, and Ubiquiti, fall under the definition. As do most, if not all, of the routers supplied by internet service providers in the US.
Just like the recent federal drone ban, or the even more recent robot vacuum ban, the router ban only applies to new devices, but manufacturers can apply for Conditional Approval from the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security.
What Is Conditional Approval?
There are three main elements to securing a Conditional Approval in the official guidelines:
- Corporate Structure: This must disclose the ownership, board membership, and “any foreign government ownership, control, influence, financing, or material support.”
- Manufacturing and Supply Chain Disclosure: Router manufacturers must submit detailed reports that break down where every major stage of production happens, covering manufacturing, assembly, design, and development. That means listing every component in every router or hotspot they manufacture and explaining where it comes from.
- US Manufacturing and Onshoring Plan: This must include “A detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States for the router for which the applicant is seeking Conditional Approval" to qualify for FCC authorization, along with details about any existing US manufacturing and quarterly status updates on progress.
Companies that receive Conditional Approval can continue to sell and update existing devices and release new routers, mesh systems, and mobile hot spots for 18 months. This includes firmware and other software updates for existing and new devices. All new devices are subject to the regular FCC approval process.
Companies With Conditional Approval
So far, several companies have been granted Conditional Approval. Here’s the FCC list.
- Netgear, a popular US manufacturer of Orbi mesh systems and Nighthawk routers, has been granted a Conditional Approval until October 1, 2027.
- Eero, Amazon’s mesh router brand, was granted a Conditional Approval until October 31, 2027.
- Asus, popular maker of many routers and mesh systems, was granted a Conditional Approval until March 6, 2028.
- Arcadyan, which makes routers for AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, was granted a Conditional Approval until December 12, 2027.
Other companies that have been granted Conditional Approvals so far include Zyxel, Gryphon, SpaceX, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, and Sagemcom.
Outside the guidelines, the Department of Defense, Department of Homeland Security, and FCC have not released any further information on why certain companies have been granted Conditional Approvals. None of these companies has released any detailed information on how they secured a Conditional Approval or about plans for US-based manufacturing.
The Consumer Technology Association (CTA) has appealed via this FCC filing for greater clarity and clearer guidelines. It also raised concerns about software patching and component updates.
What About Software Updates?
While the FCC initially published a waiver covering software and firmware updates until March 1, 2027, it has now extended that waiver “at least until January 1, 2029.”
What happens after that date is not clear. The fear was that companies that failed to secure Conditional Approval before the original deadline would not only be unable to sell new routers but also unable to update existing routers.
“The biggest practical security risk with routers is not only who made them, but whether they remain patched. Routers sit at the edge of homes, businesses, and critical networks. When they stop receiving updates, known vulnerabilities remain exposed, attackers gain durable footholds, and consumers are left with equipment they cannot realistically secure on their own," says Matt Wyckhouse, Founder and CEO of Finite State. “The original restriction risked creating exactly that problem: millions of deployed routers frozen in time, unable to receive security fixes. I appreciate the FCC recognizing that preventing updates could unintentionally make Americans less safe."
The majority of routers compromised and used in cyberattacks are older (end-of-life) devices that no longer receive security updates.
What About Foreign-Made Components?
Due to the vagaries of international supply chains, it is very common for router manufacturers to substitute certain components in existing devices. How this fits with the router ban is unclear, but companies are clearly worried enough about it that the CTA has asked the administration to consider “additional waivers of Class I permissive change rules for changes that do not materially change the security posture of the device, for example, routine parts substitutions that do not materially affect the device’s RF characteristics.”
Well, the FCC provides some clarification in its FAQ (“covered” here means banned):
“Non-'covered' devices do not become ‘covered’ simply because they contain a 'covered' component part, unless the 'covered' component part is a modular transmitter under the FCC’s rules,” it says. “Therefore, a router produced in the United States is not considered ‘covered’ equipment solely because it contains one or more foreign-made components.”
Manufacturers importing components from China but assembling them in the US will presumably be OK, though it’s far from clear. “Applicants will need to be able to have sufficient evidence that the routers were not produced in a foreign country to make this certification, but there is no specific documentation or evidence required,” according to the FCC.
Netgear Has Approval
Netgear published a letter from its CEO to announce its Conditional Approval. While it is a US-founded and headquartered company, Netgear’s routers are manufactured abroad, mostly in Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, and Taiwan. The company has moved away from China in recent years. Netgear has been lobbying the government on “cybersecurity and strategic competition with China.”
“We commend the administration and the FCC for their action toward a safer digital future for Americans,” a Netgear spokesperson tells WIRED. “Home routers and mesh systems are critical to national security and consumer protection, and today’s decision is a step forward.”
Netgear is a publicly traded company on Nasdaq, mostly owned by institutional investors, including BlackRock and Vanguard. The company’s stock rose on news of the ban.
Will TP-Link Be Banned?
Since all of its routers are made overseas, TP-Link must apply for Conditional Approval or spin up manufacturing in the US to sell any new routers. Estimates vary, but TP-Link’s US consumer router market share is somewhere around 35 percent, with Netgear and Asus accounting for another 25 percent or so.
The US Commerce, Defense, and Justice departments have reportedly been investigating and considering a ban on TP-Link routers for more than a year over concerns about the company’s links to China. No ban has been enacted until now, but Texas attorney general Ken Paxton sued TP-Link in February, claiming the company allows the Chinese Communist Party to access American consumers’ devices. Detractors have also criticized perceived predatory pricing, claiming TP-Link flooded the US market with a wide range of affordable routers to establish dominance.
TP-Link has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and claims it has divested from its Chinese roots and is now headquartered in the US with the bulk of manufacturing in Vietnam. TP-Link’s cofounder and CEO, Jeffrey Chao, recently applied for permanent US residency through President Trump’s Gold Card program, according to the Times of India.
“Virtually all routers are made outside the United States, including those produced by US-based companies like TP-Link, which manufactures its products in Vietnam,” a spokesperson from TP-Link tells WIRED. “It appears that the entire router industry will be impacted by the FCC’s announcement concerning new devices not previously authorized by the FCC.”
TP-Link is a privately owned company and not publicly listed on any stock exchange. Chao and his wife, Hillary, are listed as the company's sole owners.
Asus Has Approval
Asus primarily makes its routers in Taiwan, though it has production facilities in China and works with several third-party manufacturers. Recent tariff pressures led the company to branch out to Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, Mexico, and the Czech Republic, but the bulk of its routers still come from Taiwan or China.
Asus posted after securing Conditional Approval in September, 2026, stating, “We are honored to announce to users worldwide that ASUS has successfully passed the U.S. FCC’s rigorous cybersecurity review for consumer networking equipment, receiving official conditional approval and being listed as a Trusted Consumer Router Vendor.”
Asus is listed on the Taiwanese Stock Exchange and is mostly owned by public shareholders. The ban doesn’t appear to have impacted its stock price.
Are Any Routers Manufactured in the US?
The only routers I know of that are manufactured in the US are some Starlink Wi-Fi routers, which are primarily made in Texas. Starlink is part of Elon Musk's SpaceX company, but many of the components in these routers come from East Asia.
Botezatu says what matters more than geography is the security model behind the product. Companies that invest in “long-term firmware support, vulnerability management, and built-in protection layers” offer stronger security.
How Will the Router Ban Impact Ordinary Folks?
It’s not entirely clear, but it probably won’t have a huge immediate impact. There is already a wide range of Wi-Fi 7 routers and mesh systems on the market that will continue to be sold—they enable speeds well in excess of what most people need at home. Whether companies spin up manufacturing in the US or find other ways to satisfy government agencies that their wares are not a security risk, the result is likely to be higher prices for consumers.
"This ruling has the potential to significantly disrupt the US consumer router market," Brandon Butler, a research manager of Network Infrastructure and Services at IDC, tells WIRED. “In the near term, much will depend on how quickly conditional waivers are processed. Most vendors are likely to pursue them, but any delays could constrain supply and create upward pressure on pricing.”
If you haven't upgraded to the latest Wi-Fi 7 standard, now might be a good time to do it. But it's worth keeping in mind what you're buying. Botezatu says consumers should “stick with reputable manufacturers that have a track record of issuing updates and maintaining their devices. Check that your router is still supported and running the latest firmware.”
When current stocks run low, the ban could have a serious impact on the router market in the US. Not only will spinning up US manufacturing take years and increase costs, but the ban is also likely to limit choice in the market, as smaller companies may struggle with the compliance burden, and chipset vendors and OEMs, turned off by a slowdown and unpredictability in the market, may deprioritize the US, according to a Global Electronics Association report.
Unanswered Questions
The ban does leave several unanswered questions. Why is it being applied only to consumer routers? Why are some manufacturers being granted Conditional Approvals and not others? Why are the foreign-made routers currently on sale and in our homes deemed safe? What happens when the software update waiver runs out? The FCC did not address these questions.

2 workers die after falling from 19th floor at Gurugram construction site: Cops
The deceased were Dilkhush, a resident of Bihar’s Katihar, and Vasudev from West Bengal, police said
Two construction workers died after falling from the 19th floor of an under-construction project in Gurugram’s Sector 113 on Friday, police said on Saturday.
The deceased were Dilkhush, a resident of Bihar’s Katihar, and Vasudev from West Bengal, police said.
According to police, Vasudev fell to the ground and died immediately, while Dilkhush got caught on a floor in between and was critically injured. He was rushed to a private hospital, where he died during treatment on Saturday.
Deep Dive
Sandeep Turan, public relations officer of Gurugram police, said the exact circumstances leading to the accident would become clear during the investigation.

On September 10, two days after researcher Jacob Coxon, who had recently quit his job at Anthropic, sounded the alarm about the industry potentially bringing about the end of humanity, the New York City Democratic Socialists of America posted a carousel of images on Instagram. The first slide was a drawing of an ouroboros—a dragon eating its own tail—set against a hot pink background. “AI alarmism and AI hype are the same story: both keep your attention on a science-fiction future to distract you from the real harms experienced in the present,” the image reads.
The post was authored by the NYC DSA’s Tech Action Working Group, which focuses on tech regulation issues for the chapter, the largest in the country. It garnered more than 25,000 likes on Instagram. But not everyone agreed with the post: “Horrible and dangerous take,” one comment reads. “Sometimes sounding the alarm is justified.”
As politicians scramble to understand AI safety, an ideological split is opening on the American left. Among the questions it’s centered on is whether to believe tech companies’ claims that their products are so powerful that they could end the world.
Some on the left question the value in elevating theoretical concerns about AI over actual harms. They believe repeating claims promoted by the frontier labs about the dangers of AI empowers the AI companies, turning attention away from regulating the current harms of the technology and toward an impossible future.
“AI has become the latest tool of capitalist exploitation. The damage that unregulated and misused AI is already causing is clear across the country,” Alan Dang, a member of Tech Action, tells WIRED. “As socialists, we don’t trust these corporations to craft their own regulations.”
But others are following the direction of Senator Bernie Sanders, the unofficial leader of the American left, who has enthusiastically taken up the AI safety issue, asserting that AI has the potential to eliminate humanity. They say that it’s possible to address all harms from AI—both those happening now and those that could happen in the future—at once.
“The same people concerned about frontier governance and the development of superintelligence are also addressing those current harms,” says Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI issues. “We should address all these other important factors. Those frontier AI abilities are true and increasing in power. They are not fake or hype.”
Over the past year, Sanders dove head-first into the world of AI safety, bringing conversations that were previously happening in Bay Area circles to Washington and his large populist base. The 85-year-old was early to both opposing data centers—a massive organizing pole for the left this year—and speaking out about AI’s potential harms, from job loss to existential dangers. His data center moratorium bill, released in March, explicitly linked pausing construction with the need to pass federal regulation to protect “the future of humanity.”
Sanders’s positioning on this issue has put him in some unusual alliances, most notably with Steve Bannon, President Donald Trump’s former adviser and a right-wing populist podcast host. It has also seemingly inspired a raft of messaging from left-wing candidates running for office across the country, many of whom have been tying broader concerns around AI to the furor over data centers. On September 9, a day before the New York DSA post, six candidates affiliated with the Working Families Party, including four backed by Sanders, released statements on the need for Washington to regulate AI to prevent existential threats to humanity.
This has come with both public and private criticism. AI researcher and tech industry critic Timnit Gebru has accused Sanders and others on the left of “taking their cues from literal doomsday eugenicist cults,” referring to the effective altruist and rationalist philosophies, which underpin AI safety conversations in Silicon Valley. And Sanders’s moves have inspired some private agita within certain left-wing circles.
“Some of us are looking at Bernie and saying, what happened?” one NYC DSA member with a tech background tells WIRED.
Rumman Chowdhury, CEO and founder of the nonprofit Humane Intelligence, understands the concerns expressed by the DSA working group. Chowdhury, who formerly led the machine learning ethics, transparency, and accountability team at Twitter, thinks that all the attention that the AI safety discourse is generating will ultimately be beneficial to frontier labs.
“[The companies] grab all the attention, time, energy, and money by spouting really extreme perspectives. But then they actually backtrack to where we sit, all while they discount all of our expertise,” she says. “I think it's hard for normal people to think of how the mind of a venture capitalist works and these investors work. The scarier and more fantastic these CEOs make these companies seem, the more investors want in on it.”
For AI companies—particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, which aim to go public in the coming years—the attention and scrutiny on their products now could also be a boon in the long run. “Part of IPOing is sharing a lot of diligence documentation on risks and how risks have been addressed,” says Chowdhury. “This way, they can say, there is a full regulatory regime that they are part of establishing in this industry to guard against the worst risks, and that we have all established exactly what the ‘worst risks’ are.”
Pragathi Barusubramanian is a member of the NYC DSA’s Tech Action working group and a leader in the group’s anti-data center organizing, which netted a major win earlier this year by helping New York pass a one-year moratorium. Barusubramanian feels there may be a disconnect in the conversation around what exactly constitutes the most pressing AI-related harms to regulate. “When it comes down to what's happening on the ground,” they say, the conversation about existential risk “doesn’t come up at all.” Instead, they say, “there's an understanding that AI and data center companies don't have our interests at heart.”
McCoy, who is advising several Congressional candidates on AI, asserts that there is no real divide between actual leaders on the left on the issue. McCoy noted that several members of the DSA, including New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, have come out with recent statements about Coxon’s warnings and the Hugging Face hack.
McCoy says Gebru and similarly-minded critics are “marginal, unrepresentative, and also, frankly, picking an unnecessary distinction. It’s yes and. We should address harms like surveillance and Flock cameras, and other important factors. These do not come in any way at the expense of governing frontier AI capabilities.”
Phil Aroneanu, executive director of Irreplaceable, a left-leaning pro-AI safety organization, says that his time working as a climate activist has informed his approach to the AI regulation question. He believes that addressing both AI’s immediate and existing harms as well as future threats is both needed and possible. (McCoy helped found Irreplaceable with an initial seed fund from the Center for AI Safety.)
“This very similar intersection between the direct impact of fossil fuel extraction, people's homes getting flooded out because of climate-change-fueled storms, and then the broader movement focusing on the longer-term issue of risks and emissions,” he says.
Sanders and New York representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez don’t appear to be on the exact same page, either. While she cosponsored Sanders’ data center moratorium legislation, including the language around AI threatening humanity in her own House version of the bill, she has not participated in the high-profile AI safety discussions that he has been present for. While Sanders has called AI “the most transformational technology in the history of the world,” much of Ocasio-Cortez’s language around AI thus far has focused on data centers and the harms to jobs the technology could create, and worries that the industry is creating a bubble.
When asked by a reporter about AI safety last week, Ocasio-Cortez threaded a careful line, saying that “two things can be true at once,” noting AI “can be very dangerous when pursued without any guardrails,” and warning that “we could be seeing an economic bubble collide with a technological frontier.”
As the safety conversation quickly coalesces in Washington and in statehouses around the country, the ultimate question for the left is not whether to support AI regulation, but what regulations the movement should put its time and resources behind. Dang told WIRED that the DSA Tech Working Group supports “comprehensive AI and tech regulation at the federal, state, and city level, addressing frontier model regulation while also fighting back against the ways that corporate AI is already being used.”
A convention resolution currently before the DSA, meanwhile, proposes organizational support for Sanders and representative Greg Casar’s bill to ban superintelligence altogether—hardly something the frontier labs would agree on. And any ideological concerns within the DSA itself may not matter too much when voters get a say. A Politico poll released Wednesday shows that two in three Americans think that there is at least some risk that AI could “destroy humanity.”
Barusubramanian says that, if nothing else, they’re “happy that everyone is talking about AI now.”

9 years of talks, 2 nations, one deal: India, Pakistan signed Indus Waters Treaty on this day in 1960
India put the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance after the April 2025 terror attack in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir, which claimed 26 lives.
On this day in 1960, ink met paper to seal the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), which was signed by India and Pakistan with the World Bank and its then-president, Eugene Black, playing the role of a mediator in the nine years of negotiations.
Former US President Dwight Eisenhower hailed it as "one bright spot... in a very depressing world picture."
However, India put the water-sharing framework in abeyance after the April 2025 terror attack in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir, which claimed 26 lives.
Also Read | Pact born out of Partition: The Indus Waters Treaty, why India rejects The Hague tribunal & its ruling
Indus Waters Treaty - World Bank's role as mediator
Following the 1947 partition, the Indus Basin river system, supporting millions of people, was abruptly cleaved between India and Pakistan. As the negotiations between the two countries went on for years, Eugene Black approached the leaders of both nations, offering mediation and other services, according to the World Bank.
India and Pakistan signed the treaty, with then Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru representing India and President Field Marshal Mohammad Ayub Khan for Pakistan.
Inaugural meetings were held in the US on May 6, 1952, and over the next eight years, negotiations continued on various aspects. The result was the signing of the Indus Waters Treaty on September 19, 1960, it added.
The Indus is the westernmost river system in the subcontinent, according to the Central Water Commission's Indus Basin Organisation. Its tributaries include: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Satluj.
The blueprint of Indus Waters Treaty
The World Bank notes that under the framework, to which the World Bank is a co-signatory, the river system was divided:
The eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej): Allocated to India.
The western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab): Allocated to Pakistan.
Access to rivers: The eastern rivers were allocated for India's unrestricted use, while the western rivers were allocated for Pakistan's unrestricted use, subject to specified rights and obligations, as HT reported earlier. Neither country is completely restricted from using the rivers allocated to the other.
Role of World Bank:
As a signatory to the Treaty, the role of the World Bank is limited and procedural, it added.
Its role related to "differences" and "disputes" is limited to the designation of individuals to carry out certain duties in the context of Neutral Expert or Court of Arbitration proceedings.
Also Read | President Murmu on Indus Water Treaty suspension: ‘Decisive step in interest of nation, farmers’
Islamabad, in 2016, asked the World Bank to set up an ad hoc Court of Arbitration to look into two hydroelectric power projects, Kishenganga and Ratle.
India countered by demanding the appointment of a Neutral Expert.
Notably, the Treaty does not empower the Bank to choose which procedure takes precedence. Here's what happened after that:
- Then-World Bank Group President Jim Yong Kim declared a pause in December 2016.
- In March 2022, the World Bank decided to resume the process of appointing a Neutral Expert and a Chairman for the Court of Arbitration.
- In November 2022, the World Bank held two separate hand-over meetings with the Neutral Expert and the Chairman of the Court of Arbitration.
Also Read | India rejects Court of Arbitration's Indus Waters Treaty award: ‘Illegally constituted, has no jurisdiction’
What happened to the Indus Waters Treaty?
Following the Pahalgam terror attack, India placed the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance as part of a series of actions against Islamabad.
New Delhi linked the attack to terror networks operating out of Pakistan.
India on August 31 rejected the Permanent Court of Arbitration's order setting aside its decision to suspend the Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan, saying the "illegally-constituted" body has no jurisdiction to comment on New Delhi's sovereign decisions.
The ministry of external affairs (MEA), in a statement, said India's decision to hold the IWT in abeyance remains in force.
"Today, the illegally constituted so-called Court of Arbitration (CoA) has issued what it termed as an award concerning Interim Measures and Status of the Indus Waters Treaty," it said.
"This so called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body," the MEA added.
“This so-called Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India’s sovereign decisions. Its pronouncements, now or in the future, will have no effect on India’s actions in connection with the projects being undertaken by India,” the ministry continued.
India has stepped up work on several hydropower projects in Jammu and Kashmir, which Pakistan had opposed under the provisions of the 1960 agreement.

Senegal job an 'absolute dream' for new boss Vieira
- Published
Patrick Vieira says it is "an honour" to become Senegal head coach, with the decision to take the job "one from the heart".
The 50-year-old was born in the West African nation but subsequently represented France as a player, winning the 1998 World Cup and the 2000 European Championship with Les Bleus.
The former Arsenal midfielder spoke of his "immense pride" to begin his first international job, following stints with New York City, Nice, Crystal Palace, Strasbourg and Genoa, at his unveiling by the Teranga Lions on Friday.
"Being head coach of the Senegal national team is an absolute dream," he told a news conference in Dakar.
"I was born here, my parents were born here, and it really is a homecoming.
"From the very first meetings I had with the [Senegal football federation] president, I accepted this challenge straight away, because there was also an exceptional generation of players.
"I realise the expectations of the people - all 20 million Senegalese. And I know that with the experience I have, with the determination I have, I'll be able to see this project through."
- Vieira named new Senegal head coach 
  - Published18 August
Taking over after the dismissal of Pape Thiaw, Vieira inherits a Senegal side which exited the 2026 World Cup in dramatic fashion in the last 32, throwing away a 2-0 lead after 85 minutes against Belgium before losing 3-2 following extra time.
Before that the Teranga Lions claimed the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) title with a 1-0 extra-time win over Morocco in January.
However, the ultimate destination of the trophy will be decided by the Court of Arbitration for Sport after a walk-off by some Senegal players and staff protesting against a penalty decision in the final resulted in the trophy being handed to the North African hosts instead in March.
"Today, Senegal is among the major nations in world football," Vieira said.
"Senegal's objectives aren't what they were 10 or 15 years ago. On the back of its recent results, Senegal has moved forward, has reached new levels.
"The demand for results has also stepped up. We need to lay solid foundations."
Vieira plans to build a side with "a very precise structure" which can play with "intensity and aggression".
"What matters to me isn't starting again from scratch," he added.
"It's about respecting what the federation has put in place over the last few years and building the next stage, opening a new chapter.
"A new chapter meaning my job isn't to tear everything down, it isn't to throw everything out of the window.
"It's about keeping this team's strength: its identity, its unity, its ability to suffer together.
"To make this project work, I'll need the whole nation united. I'll work heart and soul to restore the team's pride."
Starting with two away trips
Vieira has been thrust straight into competitive action in qualifiers for the 2027 Afcon with two fixtures in this international window, two more in November and the final two rounds in March 2027.
His stint in charge was due to begin with a home match against Mozambique on Friday, 25 September but the fixture has been reversed as Dakar is in the midst of preparations for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
"Of course, I'd have preferred to play the first match here in Dakar but unfortunately, with the federation, we all felt the best decision was to postpone the match and go and play in Mozambique," Vieira explained.
"Those are difficulties we're going to accept and deal with."
Senegal will be without several notable names for the trip to Maputo and the subsequent away game against Ethiopia on 29 September.
Long-time number one Edouard Mendy, 34, has retired from Teranga Lions duty and Vieira said talismanic forward Sadio Mane will be absent with "a bit of a physical issue".
Despite previous speculation that Mane, also 34, could follow Mendy into retirement, Vieira said the former Liverpool and Bayern Munich man will "surely" be part of his next selection, fitness permitting.
Right-back Krepin Diatta has been left out because he is currently without a club, while forward Ismaila Sarr, who is yet to feature for Crystal Palace this season because of transfer speculation and a groin injury, is also absent.
'No doubt' about his managerial ability
Vieira's career as a player was trophy-laden but he has found the same kind of success hard to come by as a manager.
He departed Palace in March 2023 with a record of 22 wins from 74 games in all competitions and, after a season at Strasbourg, has been out of work since being sacked by Genoa in November last year with the Italian club bottom of the table.
He had guided them to safety in Serie A in the 2024-25 campaign but was then dismissed after six defeats in nine league games at the start of last season.
"When you talk about my coaching career, or a certain amount of experience, I've always been someone who stays positive," Vieira said.
"That means you learn, and there are always positive things to take from it. I'm a better coach today than I was in my last spell at Genoa, because that experience helped me grow and made me realise certain things.
"Given the experience I have as a manager, I've got no doubt about my ability to meet the expectations of fans."
Vieira was warmly received when he arrived in Dakar on Thursday evening, with video clips posted on social media showing him holding a Senegal flag aloft while shaking hands with a throng of fans gathered at the capital's airport.
"I couldn't have been given a warmer welcome. I saw the supporters' enthusiasm and I thank them for it.
"Taking charge of this national team isn't just a new stage in my career - it's coming back home."

Markets regulator SEBI has greenlit the proposed listing of audio OTT startup Kuku Technologies months after it filed its draft IPO documents confidentially. As per its latest update, it had issued its observation letter for Kuku’s offer documents last Friday (September 11). In SEBI parlance, the observation letter signals the regulator has given its go-ahead to a company to proceed with its public issue. Kuku filed its confidential DRHP with the SEBI in June. As per sources, the IPO’s size could be in the range of ₹2,500-3,500 Cr ($261-366 Mn) and could potentially value it at ₹15,000 Cr (about $1.8 Bn). The IPO will consist of a fresh issue of shares as well as an offer-for-sale component. Kuku plans to deploy the capital to upgrade its tech, AI infrastructure, content production and fuel geographic expansion. Founded in 2018 by Lal Chand Bisu, Vikas Goyal and Vinod Meena, Kuku offers audiobooks, podcasts, and original audio shows via its Kuku FM brand, while also operating microdrama platform Kuku TV and microlearning platform Guru. The startup’s content library spans more than 20,000 titles across seven languages and multiple genres including drama, finance, and well-being. It claims to have more than 1 Cr listeners and creators on its platform and 400 Mn app downloads across its portfolio. Kuku has raised over $156 Mn to date from the likes of Fundamentum Partnership, Krafton, Vertex Ventures, IFC, 3one4 Capital, among others. Its most recent $85 Mn Series C funding round, in October 2025, was led by Granite Asia. Earlier this year, it even roped in former Indian cricket team captain Mahendra Singh Dhoni as an investor and as the brand ambassador for Kuku TV. Driven by increasing smart phone penetration and affordable internet access, the market for microdramas is expected to grow to $6.5 Bn by 2033 from $1.5 Bn currently. Kuku competes with the likes of Pocket FM, Flick TV, ReelSaga and Miniplix, as well as OTT majors like Amazon, JioHotstar and Zee5, in this segment.

Nagoya – IOC President Kirsty Coventry called the shipping container-style huts for Asian Games athletes “beautiful” on Sunday — but conceded they were “a little tighter” than similar accommodation at the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics earlier this year.
Asia’s biggest sporting spectacle, which opened on Saturday in Nagoya, has split with past Games by having no traditional athletes’ village.
To save costs, the more than 17,000 Asian Games participants will stay in temporary huts, hotels and a cruise ship.
Some countries have criticized the wooden cabins as too small, with beds that are too short.
But after touring the lodgings, Coventry said she could not understand the negativity.
“We had similar cabins in Milan-Cortina and the athletes were very happy,“ said the Zimbabwean former Olympic champion swimmer. “And the cabins here are really nice.
“They’re a little tighter. So, you know, if you want something negative, it’s a little smaller.
“But I don’t think it’s a negative thing. I love the village.”
About 2,000 participants are staying in the lodgings by the water in Nagoya.
“The cabins are quiet, they’re very cool,” Coventry said. “The air conditioning is working well.
“The flooring and the walls are beautiful. It’s better than some of the villages I’ve stayed in.
“So I think to be very fair to Japan and to the organizing committee, I was really impressed.
“I had only been reading everything that had been said. And I was expecting something completely different to when I walked in.”
Asked if she would happily see the temporary cabins and also a cruise ship serve as accommodation at the Olympics, she said she had not been to the vessel.
But she pointed to the accommodation at the Milano Cortina Games, and said those “very closely” resembled the ones in Nagoya.
“It’s not a new concept,” she added.
“And it is a concept that I think, for me, when we talk about an athlete experience, being an athlete ... as soon as I go in, I’m not necessarily concerned about the look.”

It always creates apprehension because the sight is somewhat gory, but a nosebleed, in general, isn’t a cause for major concern. Occurring mostly in the under 10s and the over 45s, nosebleeds are very common: about 60% of the population is estimated to experience one in their lifetime. They can occur in one or both nostrils, but usually affect one. The medical term for a nosebleed is epistaxis.
How do they occur?
Our noses are lined with a moist, delicate tissue, the nasal mucosa. This lining cleans the air that we breathe in, and also warms and moistens the air. The mucosa is made of many tiny blood vessels, lying to close to the surface. These blood vessels can easily be irritated, injured and broken. When they break, they cause a nosebleed.
There are two types of nosebleeds: anterior and posterior. An anterior nosebleed, which is the most common type, starts at the front of the nose. These types of nosebleeds can mostly be treated at home. A posterior nosebleed takes place place deep at the back the nose, may cause heavier bleeding and could result in blood going down the back of the throat. This type of nosebleed requires medical attention.
Why do they occur?
Common causes include the inside of the nose becoming dry, usually due to a change in temperature, picking the nose, or blowing the nose too hard.
When the air is very dry, it causes the nasal mucosa, which is meant to be moist, to dry out, making it prone to crusting and bleeding. Dry air can occur in hot places with low humidity, areas of high altitude and in air-conditioned or heated spaces. People with upper respiratory infections, sinus infections, allergies or other ailments such as rhinitis may also sneeze, cough or blow their nose frequently, making them more prone to bleeds. The frequent use of medications such as antihistamines, nasal sprays or blood thinners, could also make people vulnerable to nosebleeds, as could breathing in strong fumes.
Nosebleeds can also occur due to injuries to the nose, the insertion of objects into the nose, a deviated septum, recreational drug use as well as less common causes such as having blood disorders, alcohol use, nasal polyps or tumours.
Being pregnant may also increase the chances of nosebleeds.
When to see a doctor
In general, nosebleeds aren’t serious and can be treated at home. In some circumstances, however, it is best to consult a medical professional. You should see a doctor if: the nosebleed has followed an injury or accident; if there is heavy bleeding or the bleeding lasts longer than 30 minutes; blood has been swallowed; if there is a feeling of weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness or if you have breathing difficulties, chest pain or a rapid heart rate. A doctor should also be consulted if the person with the nosebleed has other health issues such as a bleeding disorder, or high blood pressure, or if the person is a child under two years old.
How to stop a nosebleed
To stop a nosebleed, there are some first-aid measures that can be taken:
- Sit upright so the head is above the level of the heart, lean forward slightly
- Breathe through the mouth and gently blow the nose to clear it
- Use the thumb and index finger to pinch the both nostrils shut. Do this for 10 minutes.
- Use an icepack on the bridge of the nose at the same time as the pinching
- Check in 10 minutes, and if the bleeding has not stopped, repeat the pinching for another 10 minutes
- Once the bleeding has stopped, lean forward and clean the nose with lukewarm water
- See a doctor immediately if the bleeding does not stop in 30 minutes
Preventing nosebleeds
Using a humidifier in the house especially in dry air conditions, trimming children’s fingernails, managing allergies, using a nasal saline spray or petroleum jelly to keep the inner lining of the nose moist and avoiding smoke exposure can all help prevent nosebleeds.

On Sept. 9, 2026, just under a year after the assassination of Charlie Kirk, the conservative commentator and co-founder of Turning Point USA, people posted an image online suggesting Kirk was just the latest victim in a stretch of political violence committed by Democrats.
According to the image, Democrats had killed or attempted to kill four U.S. presidents — Abraham Lincoln, John F. Kennedy, Ronald Reagan and Donald Trump — as well as U.S. Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., and Kirk.
Snopes readers contacted us, asking for an investigation of the claim.
It's demonstrably false. We found no publicly available evidence suggesting that any of the seven assassins or attempted assassins were registered Democrats.
Before examining the claim in full, it's worth noting a few things about its framing.
Framing
First: The post neatly aligns with a conservative talking point suggesting political violence in the United States comes from the left. Donald Trump has famously used dramatic language such as "far-left" and "radical" to describe the entirety of the Democratic Party. He designated antifa, a loosely organized network of left-wing activists, a terrorist organization in September 2025, and announced a task force against "Radical Left Terrorism" in July 2026. The repeated description of the Democratic Party as "far-left" without proof of its factual accuracy has become relatively commonplace in conservative spaces, and this post is an excellent example of that rhetorical framework.
While reputable evidence has consistently shown that the amount of left-wing political violence has grown in recent years, it still pales in comparison to political violence from the right. 
Second: The political figures mentioned in the post span 150 years of history, and across that time, the two main political parties in the United States slowly realigned their positions. This is a deeply thorny topic with much nuance, but as a basic overview:
Historically, both the Republicans and the Democrats had progressive and conservative blocs. In the wake of the Great Depression, for instance, a broad group of voters called the New Deal coalition elected Franklin D. Roosevelt as president. That coalition was made up of the conservative, rural South (the Democratic Party's traditional stronghold after the Civil War) and more-progressive, working-class and minority voters in urban cities. But Roosevelt's progressive policies greatly influenced the trajectory of the party, and as new politicians attempted to follow in his footsteps, they alienated the rural South's conservative Democrats (sometimes called the Dixiecrats) who supported policies of segregation.
In a tactic later called the Southern Strategy, Republicans began catering to the conservative voters who felt left behind by the national Democrats' support of civil rights. The strategy worked. Once-Democratic strongholds slowly began electing Republicans, first at the national level during Richard Nixon and Reagan's presidencies, and then at the state and local level in the 1990s.
So while the claim implies that the Democratic Party is the party of the left, that has not always been the case. Painting such a large organization as an unchanging monolith over time does not allow for the nuance this discussion deserves.
Third: The post cherry-picks four of the most famous assassination victims in American history as its martyrs. It lists Lincoln and Kennedy, but there are two other, lesser-known presidents who were assassinated — James Garfield and William McKinley. McKinley was shot by an anarchist, which would ostensibly help convey the post's message.
The inclusion of Robert F. Kennedy, Martin Luther King Jr. and Charlie Kirk, none of whom were presidents, also raises the question of why figures like Malcolm X, Huey Long or Harvey Milk aren't on the list. And by mentioning Reagan and Trump, the list expands to attempted assassinations. Theodore Roosevelt was famously shot in the chest while giving a speech, and he isn't included either. There have been enough presidential assassination attempts that Stephen Sondheim wrote a musical about it, but none of those failed attempts is mentioned in the image.
Finally, and this bears repeating: People with normal political views generally do not attempt to assassinate people. Attempting to scrutinize their views in order to place them on some sort of political compass chart is an exercise in futility.
Political views of the assassins
The seven people on the list and their assassins, attempted assassins and alleged assassins are:
- Abraham Lincoln, assassinated by John Wilkes Booth
- John F. Kennedy, assassinated by Lee Harvey Oswald
- Martin Luther King Jr., assassinated by James Earl Ray
- Robert F. Kennedy, assassinated by Sirhan Sirhan
- Ronald Reagan, assassination attempted by John Hinckley Jr.
- Donald Trump, assassination attempted by Thomas Crooks
- Charlie Kirk, assassination allegedly by Tyler Robinson (trial pending)
(There are countless conspiracy theories surrounding assassinations, and of these seven, about Kennedy and King in particular. The cases for and against such theories have been well documented in other places, but the claim does not make any such assumptions. Thus, we examine Oswald and Ray).
In sum, there is no evidence suggesting any of the assassins, attempted assassins or alleged assassins were registered Democrats. Three — Oswald, Sirhan and Robinson — could reasonably be said to have held at least some left-wing views, but none ever registered as a Democrat. (Furthermore, Sirhan is not a U.S. citizen and therefore could not have voted.)
John Wilkes Booth was registered with the anti-immigrant Know-Nothing Party in the 1850s, according to Factcheck.org. He certainly hated Lincoln's Republican Party, given his defense of slavery and the Confederate States of America, but Snopes found no evidence he was a registered Democrat.
Lee Harvey Oswald became disaffected by America and began expressing pro-Soviet views after dropping out of high school to join the Marines in 1956, according to Britannica. He left the Marines in 1959 and moved to the Soviet Union for a few years before returning to America in 1962. Given that, it's relatively safe to conclude that at least some of Oswald's views were left-wing. However, there is no evidence he was a registered Democrat.
James Earl Ray held racist views throughout his life, according to interviews with people close to him, and he appeared to be involved with the American Independent Party in 1968, a third-party organized for the segregationist former governor of Alabama, George Wallace, as he ran for president. Wallace was a Democrat, we should note — but there is no such evidence for Ray.
Sirhan Sirhan was born in Palestine and immigrated to the U.S. in his youth. He openly admitted to shooting Robert F. Kennedy "for [his] country," as he was vocally opposed to the nation of Israel, while Kennedy had publicly stated support for Israel during his 1968 presidential campaign. Sirhan's stance on Israel does align with modern left-wing beliefs in the U.S., but using that as evidence that he holds left-wing political beliefs (much less is a Democrat) is complicated by the fact he was born in Palestine — his motivation seems to lie on an entirely separate axis. Regardless, because he is not a U.S. citizen, he is not eligible to vote in elections. As such, there is no evidence suggesting he is or was a Democrat.
John Hinckley Jr. infamously shot Ronald Reagan in an attempt to impress the actress Jodie Foster. Reagan survived, and Hinckley was found not guilty by reason of insanity. He was released from the mental hospital to his mother's care in 2016. Hinckley was a member of the National Socialist Party of America — a neo-Nazi group — for one year, according to The Washington Post, but was expelled in 1979 because he was "too extremist and violent." Given that Hinckley requested (and was denied) ballots several times while he was living at the mental hospital, it is perfectly reasonable to suspect he may be registered to vote. Hinckley now lives in Virginia, but that state does not make its voter registration public and therefore it is unclear whether he votes and if so, for what party. In posts on X, Hinckley has suggested that he is anti-communist and apolitical, despite reportedly founding a political party in 2022.
Thomas Crooks, Trump's would-be assassin, does not have clear politics. Snopes previously reported that he donated $15 to a Democratic PAC in 2021. We also reported that he was a registered Republican. Profiles of Crooks released after the shooting describe him as lonely and intelligent, and don't often mention politics. Reviews of his internet history suggest that Crooks searched for multiple political figures, including Democrats, when deciding on a target.
Tyler Robinson, who is alleged to have fatally shot Charlie Kirk, was supposedly a Republican who donated to Trump's campaign — two claims already debunked by Snopes. Though reports portray Robinson as growing up in a Republican family, his mother said he had become "pro-gay and trans-rights oriented," in the recent past and had begun dating his roommate, reportedly a transgender woman. Two of the bullets engraved on the scene contained messages generally associated with the left — "Hey fascist! Catch!," and "Bella Ciao, Bella Ciao, Bella Ciao, Ciao, Ciao," — though, as Kyle Chayka wrote in The New Yorker, all four in context "revealed less about his political affiliations than his fluency in deep internet culture. […] In isolation, the references are vague enough to be interpreted every which way." Regardless, he was not a registered Democrat either.

The Climate 100 List: Erin Brockovich on her fight against ‘secretive’ data centres
Erin Brockovich’s work in helping win a $333m environmental lawsuit in the 1990s spawned a hit film starring Julia Roberts – now, Brockovich tells David Callaway, her attention has turned to the burgeoning issue of data centres
It’s been more than 30 years since Erin Brockovich made history – and had a movie made after her – for standing against one of America’s largest power companies and winning a $333m groundwater pollution suit for a small California town. People still email her with environmental concerns.
This past spring she noticed a spike in emails from a small Pennsylvania county concerned about the sudden growth of a large AI data centre in their community. Data centres are giant warehouses full of powerful computers used to run digital services from movie streaming to online banking. There are more than 4,000 across the US, the most in the world. The UK and Germany are next with more than 500 each.
There are concerns about the huge amount of energy and water the new data centres will consume, as well as the wastewater they produce that is funnelled out back into the environment.
Following those emails, Brockovich – who is recognised on this year’s Independent Climate 100 list of changemakers and activists working to save the planet – quickly built out a digital map of data centres across the country and within 72 hours had received email complaints from every state in the US. That has now become a dozen countries.
“What they all have in common is the secrecy, the lack of transparency to people about what is going on,” Brockovich says. “People’s water bills are going up. Their electricity bills are going up. Even their property bills are going up. They are changing zoning laws. Some people say local councils are trying to claim their property by eminent domain to lay transmission wires and cables.”
The Brockovich Data Center Map currently shows more than 9,200 complaints, coming from all 50 states.
Texas has the most complaints, followed by Ohio and Virginia. The complaints are tied to 112 operating data centres, 143 under construction, and 128 under proposal at the last count. Out of a total of more than 4,000 data centres across the country.
Brockovich, 66, is now at the centre of one of the most rapidly developing environmental issues in America; one that even threatens to upend the country’s midterm elections for Congress in November. “It’s bipartisan. It affects everybody,” she said. “Politics is definitely going to be involved.”
After months of growing anger, many city councils are starting to get the message. More than 500 moratoriums on new data centres are now in place, one of them declared by New York state governor Kathy Hochul. Some of the city councils trying to pause projects are being hit with multimillion lawsuits from the tech companies, however, Brockovich says. That makes it even harder for them to stand up.
Brockovich adds she has nothing against AI, arguing that the "genie is out of the bottle" on the new technology. She acknowledges she even uses it to get information from the tech and AI companies who rarely comment on their intentions beyond their growth plans. But she says the speed with which companies are building these massive operations is something every community should be concerned about.
Many of the data centres are being built in drought-restricted areas, meaning the threat to water rights and access is even more acute. The construction comes as AI companies – from Open AI to Meta and Google and Elon Musk's SpaceX – are racing to develop the technology, as investors throw money at them on the stock market and the administration of Donald Trump pushes them to achieve dominance before China does.
"I don't understand what the sudden rush is," Brockovich says. "It's as if these companies believe there is some sort of window that is going to close."
The phenomenon has been compared to the dot-com boom a quarter century ago, with many worried that it will also lead to a spectacular bust at some point, if the technology, and profits, don't develop as expected. As the AI arms race continues, many of these tech giants have resorted to using natural gas to power their data centres instead of cleaner, renewable energy, because gas is cheaper and more accessible.
Brockovich says her goals are to get companies and local governments to take a step back and assess what the actual environmental impact of building data centres might lead to before going forward.
For many people, climate change and global warming have always been vague terms, she says, which is why they probably never resonated in national politics before. But the data centres are "bringing it to life" for everybody.
"The stakes are too high for all of us," Brockovich adds. "People are mad enough. Maybe data centres are what unites us after all."

Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India, prompting authorities to investigate if they were trafficked into the country from south-east Asia.
The orangutans, native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra and known for their shaggy red fur, were found in Balasore district of Odisha state, thousands of kilometres away from their natural habitat.
Odisha’s environment minister, Ram Singh Khuntia, said wildlife investigators were trying to establish how the rare apes reached India.
“We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this,” Singh said.
International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites – a global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife.
The five babies were found by forest department officials who were patrolling in the Jaleswar range in Balasore district.
Officials believed the orangutans had been in the area for just a few days, and they have now been placed in quarantine at a zoological park in Odisha.
According to the World Wildlife Fund, about 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.
The Tapanuli orangutan (Pongo tapanuliensis), a third species, is classified as critically endangered, with fewer than 800 believed to survive in the wild.
In November, conservationists found the Tapanuli population had been reduced by 7% after severe flooding in Indonesia.
Between 33 and 54 Tapanuli orangutans were estimated to have been killed in widespread floods and landslides in North Sumatra province.
Previous research has suggested annual losses of 1% of the Tapanuli orangutan population would be sufficient to lead to eventual extinction.
The entire Tapanuli population dwells solely in the West Block of the Batang Toru, a forest threatened by mining, palm oil plantations and a large hydropower project.

Trump announces he’s forming an ‘AI Force’ similar to his ‘Space Force’
The move comes just days after his claim that concerns about artificial intelligence are a ‘hoax’
President Donald Trump announced Saturday that he’s forming a new “AI force” to oversee the development of artificial intelligence — just days after dismissing concerns about the potential threat posed by the cutting-edge technology as a “hoax” and saying he provided all the necessary guardrails.
In a social media post, the president said, “We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!”
“For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term,” he wrote. “To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”
Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he told Bloomberg he had “used up” his 130 days as a special government employee and was joining the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
In his post, Trump listed a series of other “hoaxes” he blamed on “Radical Left” Democrats and said “they are going straight at AI” after industry insiders went public with fears that it could lead to the end of humanity within the next 10 years, leading to calls for government regulation of the industry.
“And I, as President of the United States, will not stand by and let this happen,” Trump said. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP. We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!”
Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts quickly responded to Trump’s comments, saying on social media, “Congress cannot meet the pressing threat of AI by just forming another committee or continuing to have drawn-out discussions about it.”
“Let's actually pass some meaningful regulations on AI to protect people,” she added.

Sikh truck driver survives stabbing attack in rest stop bathroom
The attack came after deadly crashes involving Sikh truck drivers led to debate about commercial driver's licensing requirements
A violent attack against a truck driver at a rest stop in remote Wyoming has left the Sikh community on edge amid rising anti-immigrant vitriol against the community and its truck drivers in particular.
The Sikh victim was attacked from behind while in a restroom along the Interstate 80 Bitter Creek rest stop, midway between Cheyenne and Salt Lake City, according to court documents.
He suffered stabs to the neck and chest and over a dozen other cuts but survived.
Police were still investigating what prompted the Wyoming attack by a man who left the rest area driving a truck-trailer combination, Sweetwater County Sheriff's Department spokesperson Jeff Sheaman said.
“We have zero motive,” Sheaman said.
While police say the motive is unknown, the attack came after deadly crashes involving Sikh truck drivers led to debate about commercial driver's licensing requirements — sparking hatred toward Sikhs as a group, community leaders said.
Anti-Sikh sentiment has been especially severe on truck-driving forums, said one Sikh in the trucking industry, Harsimran Singh, CEO of Gillson Trucking in Stockton, California.
"I’ve been here for the last 25-plus years," Singh said. "I never felt this kind of hate before.”
The victim allegedly told police he was trying to use the restroom when he was attacked from behind. He pushed the attacker, he said, and didn't see the knife at first, according to the police affidavit filed in the case.
Within hours, police arrested Andrew Kris Bzdak in nearby Carbon County, Wyoming.
A family at the rest area who heard the attack allegedly followed Bzdak's truck back onto the highway and tipped off police to help find him, according to the affidavit.
Video taken from a truck at the rest area showed the victim walk casually into the restroom, followed by a man police said was Bzdak.
Soon after, Bzdak allegedly was recorded running from the restroom, followed by the stumbling, wounded victim who fell at least once, according to the affidavit.
Bzdak remained jailed on $1 million bond Friday in Rock Springs, on suspicion of attempted murder, a crime punishable in Wyoming by up to life in prison. An initial appearance was scheduled for Thursday.
A phone message left at an address for Bzdak in Catawissa, Pennsylvania, wasn't immediately returned, nor was a phone message for him at the jail and for his Wyoming public defender, Gary Arnell.
Despite no evident motive, the attack was unnerving for Sikhs, who number around 750,000 in the U.S. Many live in California.
Sikh men wear beards, uncut hair and turbans, and many work as truck drivers. Advocacy groups estimate that at least 150,000 Sikh truck drivers work in the U.S.
In August 2025, authorities said a Sikh truck driver's U-turn on a Florida turnpike caused a crash that killed three people. The crash prompted investigations as well as reports about Sikh truck drivers being harassed.
Then last October, a Sikh truck driver accused of being under the influence of drugs caused a fiery crash that killed three people, authorities said.
Both drivers were in the U.S. illegally, according to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which Singh, the trucking CEO, blamed for stirring anti-immigrant hatred with social media posts.
One such post, since taken down, showed a dark-skinned man with a beard that read, “Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh.” DHS officials have said the post referred specifically to the driver in the Florida crash. But Sikh community representatives pointed out that a large number of Sikhs — well over 100,000 in the U.S. and millions worldwide — have the last name Singh.
No matter what motivated the attack, the crime is difficult to separate from racism toward Sikhs, said Jasjit Singh, legal services director for the Sikh community group Jakara Movement and a representative of the victim.
“We were making noise about this,” Jasjit Singh said. “That is how the community feels. Until something really bad happens to us, nothing is going to really happen.”
The victim was headed home Friday after five days in a Casper hospital and hopes to drive his truck across Wyoming again, Jasjit Singh said.
But Harsimran Singh, the trucking CEO, also remained apprehensive.
“We are probably going to see more of this,” Harsimran Singh said. “I'm not surprised that it has happened.”
