When she finally claimed her semifinal match in the women’s teqball singles competition at the Asian Games on Saturday morning, Indonesia’s Sumaya fell to her knees and performed the sajdah in celebration. On the other side of the table, Quimcy Dsouza was bent over too, her hands on her knees as the result sank in.
Quimcy had won the first game comfortably, 12-7. She had led in the second. In the decider, she was up 7-3 before an extraordinary comeback saw the Indonesian win nine straight points to seal the tie. The 24-year-old from Mumbai had been within touching distance of a place in the final and of assuring India its first medal at Nagoya. Just like that, the chance was gone.
Quimcy might still medal on Sunday, when she competes for bronze in the women’s singles and mixed doubles. But what a difference a medal on Saturday, in the hours before the official opening ceremony of the Games, would have made. On Sunday, as the Games kick off in earnest, the sports cycle will move on to better-known sports and athletes at venues across town.
For nearly an hour at the Nagoya City Higashi Sports Center on Saturday, though, all eyes were on a sport making its Games debut and the Bengaluru-based engineer chasing an unlikely dream.
The stands at the Higashi centre were full of people, many curious about a sport that is a weird but fun cousin of table tennis, football and sepak takraw. They might have started out curious, but there was admiration for the athleticism on display. Dr. Dinshaw Pardiwala, knee specialist to some of India’s greatest sportspersons and Chief Medical Officer of the Indian contingent, was there. “Let’s go, Quimcy!” he yelled in encouragement from the stands.
Ultimately, though, it was not to be. You could see what the loss meant to Quimcy. She took time to compose herself before explaining how she felt.
“I’m feeling so bad I couldn’t make it to the finals but I’m happy that I even made it this far. I came here without a coach, without guidance or support. I just want India to know I gave it my all. I want India to know what teqball is,” she would say later.
Long-time dream
As a child growing up in Mumbai, Quimcy always dreamed she’d wear an India jersey. The daughter of a State-level footballer and hockey player, she initially thought that ambition would be fulfilled on the athletics track.
“I used to watch the Asian Games as a child and think I’d be running for India some day. I didn’t even know about teqball then,” she says.
The sport was still in its infancy in India when it came into Quimcy’s life by accident. She had moved from athletics to football, even representing Maharashtra at the nationals, when she suffered a ligament injury four years ago. As she lay in bed scrolling aimlessly on Instagram, she came across a video of Brazilian football legend Ronaldinho playing on a table.
That’s how the sport got its start.
“It came about as a way for footballers to have a less strenuous workout while still working on their ball handling ability,” says Nihar Shah, technical director of Teqball India.
Quimcy was instantly smitten.
“I knew I had to do this. The logo for teqball is in the shape of a ‘Q’. I thought right then that I was meant to play this game. I found out that there was a club in Mumbai where there was actually a place where there was a table,” she says.
The sport was still being figured out by players in India. Quimcy’s football background helped her pick it up faster, as it has for many of the players at these Asian Games. Sumaya, too, has a sepak takraw background, 12 years of it, which made overhead kicks against Quimcy easy to execute.
But Sumaya had another advantage: Indonesia had invested in teqball since its inclusion in the Asian Games programme.
“For the last two years I’ve been only playing and training teqball morning, afternoon and night,” she told reporters after her win.
That’s not the case for Quimcy. Like every other member of the Indian team here and like the 180-odd athletes registered as teqball players in India, she’s entirely self-funded.
“Everything that we make goes into the sport,” says Quimcy, who currently works as a test engineer at Decathlon in Bengaluru.
She’s largely self-taught too, learning simply through observation.
“Right from the start, when I’d go to international competitions, I’d look at what the other players were doing. I’d look at what new things they had introduced and how they performed. When we came back, we’d look at their videos, and train and adapt it to our style,” she says.
It’s all this that made the chance to compete in Nagoya so meaningful. Being part of an actual Indian team wasn’t just the fulfilment of a childhood dream but also the legitimising of her choice of sport and the struggles of her compatriots who played it.
“Until now we have paid money from own pockets in order to compete. This (Asian Games) is the first time everything was sponsored by IOA and team. That’s why it was so important. I only dreamed about this day. There’s so much joy because I’m not just carrying my dreams but the dreams of all my teammates as well,” she says.
She had nearly managed to make those dreams come true, winning both her group-stage matches against Japan and Cambodia before falling just short against the Indonesian in the semifinal.
But Quimcy isn’t ready to give up on her dreams just yet. She has already beaten Japan’s Yuina Sakamoto, whom she plays for bronze, in the group stage.
“I have two more chances for a medal. The goal still remains to take a medal for India. The fire still burns as much as it was before today’s match,” she says.

US President Donald Trump has signed a sweeping sanctions bill, taking aim at Russia's economy by punishing major purchasers of its oil and gas.
The bill, passed by the US House of Representatives earlier this week, gives Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.
At Trump's behest, the bill also extends to Iran's energy and weapons sectors.
The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.
The 48-page bill, formally titled the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, includes exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are working to lessen their dependency.
Additionally, the bill includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, a New York Democrat, previously described the legislation as "scorching sanctions" which would "throttle Putin's war machine".
Data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, or CREA, shows that China accounted for 50% of Russian crude exports between December 2022 and August 2026, followed by India at 37%.
Turkey and the European Union each accounted for 5% during the same time period, although Russian energy exports to the EU have been decreasing.
Senator Graham had long sought to push the Trump administration to do more to punish Russia for the war that followed its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The bill also received the support of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who thanked Trump for signing the "critically important legislation".
"The best way to honour Lindsey's memory will be to implement the provisions of this law fully and swiftly," he wrote on social media.
"Senator Graham never doubted for a second that America has enough strength to stand up to dictators and achieve results if it acts the right way."
Graham, 71, died on 11 July of an "aortic dissection" caused by cardiovascular disease shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv.
"He died doing the work he was born to do," Trump said at the time.
Prior to his death, he was widely considered one of Ukraine's fiercest allies on Capitol Hill, at a time when Republicans were bitterly divided over the extent of US involvement abroad and the amount of aid being given to Ukraine.

15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న ఉత్తర అరేబియా సముద్రంలో భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ నావికాదళాలకు చెందిన యుద్ధనౌకలు ఒకదానికొకటి ఢీకొన్నాయి. తమ నౌక సాధారణ నిఘా విధుల్లో ఉండగా పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక వేగంగా, ప్రమాదకరంగా దూసుకొచ్చిందని భారత్ పేర్కొంది. దీనిపై నిరసన తెలుపుతూ సెప్టెంబర్ 16న పాకిస్తాన్ దౌత్యాధికారికి భారత్ సమన్లు జారీ చేసింది. అయితే, పాకిస్తాన్ మాత్రం ఇందుకు భిన్నమైన వాదన వినిపించింది. తమ ‘SEASPARK-26’ నావికా విన్యాసాల్లో ఈ ఘటన జరిగిందని, భారత నౌక ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా తమ నౌక సమీపంలోకి వచ్చిందని ఆరోపించింది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, భారత, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఢీకొన్న దృశ్యాలంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఒకదానికొకటి ఢీకొన్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో 15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఢీకొన్న ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది కాదు. వాణిజ్య నౌక ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’కు భద్రతగా వెళ్తున్న సమయంలో 2011లో పాకిస్థాన్ నౌక పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్, భారత నౌక ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరిని ఢీకొన్న పాత సంఘటనకు సంబంధించిన వీడియో ఇది. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియోని 16 అక్టోబర్ 2014న “mix” అనే యూట్యూబ్ ఛానెల్లో అప్లోడ్ (ఆర్కైవ్) చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోలో పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక బాబర్ భారత నౌకతో పోటీ పడుతుందని పేర్కొనబడింది. ఏడెన్ అఖాతంలో (Gulf of Aden) ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’ అనే వాణిజ్య నౌకను రక్షించే సమయంలో తీసిన భారత, పాకిస్తాన్ నౌకల దృశ్యాలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుందని వివరణలో రాసి ఉంది. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియో సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నాటి ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది కాదని, అది దశాబ్దానికి పైగా పాతదని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
దీనికి సంబంధించిన మరింత సమాచారం కోసం ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతకగా, ఇదే ఘటన గురించి చెప్తున్నా 2011 నాటి NDTV వార్తా కథనం లభించింది. ఈ కథనం ప్రకారం, ఈ ఘటన 16 జూన్ 2011న జరిగింది. వాణిజ్య నౌక ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’కు భద్రతగా వెళ్తున్న సమయంలో, భారత నావికాదళానికి చెందిన ‘ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరి’ నౌకను దాటి వెళ్లే ప్రయత్నంలో పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌక ‘పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్’ దాని వెనుక భాగాన్ని ఢీకొట్టింది. సముద్రం అల్లకల్లోలంగా ఉన్న సమయంలో ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరికి అతి సమీపంలోకి వచ్చిన పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్ రాసుకుంటూ వెళ్లిందని, దీనివల్ల భారత నౌకలోని హెలికాప్టర్ డెక్కు నష్టం వాటిల్లిందని ఆ కథనం పేర్కొంది. నౌకలు ఢీకొన్న తర్వాత పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక సిబ్బంది సంబరాలు చేసుకుంటున్న దృశ్యాలను కూడా ఆ కథనం చూపించింది.
18 జూన్ 2011న భారత విదేశీ వ్యవహారాల మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ ఒక పత్రికా ప్రకటన విడుదల చేసి పాకిస్తాన్ తీరుపై నిరసన వ్యక్తం చేసింది. పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్ చేసిన ప్రమాదకరమైన విన్యాసాలు ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరి నౌక, దాని సిబ్బంది భద్రతను ప్రమాదంలో పడేశాయని అందులో పేర్కొంది. అంతేకాకుండా, పాకిస్తాన్ చర్యలు అంతర్జాతీయ సముద్ర భద్రతా నిబంధనలను, అలాగే సైనిక విన్యాసాలకు ముందస్తు సమాచారం ఇవ్వాలనే 1991 నాటి ఇండో-పాక్ ఒప్పందాన్ని ఉల్లంఘించాయని భారత్ స్పష్టం చేసింది.
చివరిగా, వైరల్ వీడియో 2011లో భారత్, పాకిస్థాన్ నౌకలు ఢీకొన్న పాత ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది.

Taipei – Taiwan’s labor minister traveled to China for an APEC ministerial meeting on Sunday, the first such trip by a senior Taiwanese government official since President Lai Ching-te took office two years ago.
China claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to take the self-ruled island by force if necessary.
Beijing has branded Lai — whose Democratic Progressive Party rejects China’s sovereignty claims over Taiwan — as an independence separatist and has halted formal communication with Taipei for a decade.
With China hosting this year’s APEC, there were concerns that Taiwan could be blocked from participating in the international forum.
Taiwanese Labor Minister Hung Sun-han took a 5:50 pm flight on Sunday to the eastern Chinese city of Nanjing, where he will attend meetings on Monday before returning home, his ministry said.
Chen Binhua, spokesman for China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, told a press briefing this month that Taiwan’s participation in APEC meetings and activities would be handled in accordance with the “one-China principle.”
Hung said this week that his visit to China would follow “the existing pattern” and be based on “the principle of parity and dignity.”
“APEC is a very important international, multilateral economic and trade forum for us,” Hung said.
The Taiwanese delegation will “share their experience and expertise in labor issues and human resources with other APEC member economies during the meeting, Hung said.
Hung did not have plans to travel to other Chinese cities during his trip, the Labor Ministry said.
Taiwan’s government said members of its delegation have already taken part in APEC meetings in various Chinese cities this year, including a May trip to Suzhou by then-top trade negotiator Yang Jen-ni.
These ministerial meetings will culminate in November at the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, where world leaders including Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump are expected to meet.
APEC represents 21 member economies and is one of the few international bodies in which Taiwan holds full membership.
Taiwanese presidents have over the years appointed special envoys to attend the flagship summit on their behalf.

The Asian Games are open with more athletes than the Summer Olympics and some unfamiliar sports
The opening ceremony of the Asian Games has marked the official start of the 16-day event
NAGOYA, Japan -- The opening ceremony of the Asian Games on Saturday marked the official start of the 16-day event — but in name only.
Facing a packed schedule, competition in basketball started on Sept. 10 — more than a week ago. The semifinals in men's basketball were on Friday, a day before the official opening.
Soccer has been going on for almost as long. The Summer Olympics typically start a few days early, but this multi-sport event pushes the envelope.
Welcome to the Asian Games, which feature at least 11,000 athletes. The 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris had about 10,700. The last Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, in 2023 had roughly 12,000.
Japanese organizers have yet to release an official athlete total from the 45 countries and regions contesting 43 sports. But it seems likely to reach the total in China of three years ago. Maybe more with a few new sports added.
The games feature the old-standby Olympic disciplines like track and field, swimming and soccer. But there are some Asian specialties, too: kurash, kabaddi, and sepaktakraw to name three.
Kurash is an ancient form of wrestling that originated in Uzbekistan. Kabaddi looks like a game of team tag with a physical edge. And sepaktakraw is a mix of volleyball and soccer.
Games organizers have also added mixed martial arts, padel and teqball to the menu — with esports also on the schedule — hence the time crunch.
Host Japan has the largest delegation with 933 athletes and China came with just over 800. China won 201 gold medals in the last games, followed by Japan (52) and South Korea (42). That pattern is expected to be repeated.
Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako headed the list of dignitaries. The president of the Olympic Council of Asia, Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani, elected earlier this year, was alongside.
“Tonight the eyes of Asia, and much of the world, turn to Japan,” Sheikh Joaan said in his address, which was followed by the Emperor officially opening the games.
The president of the International Olympic Committee, Kirsty Coventry, was also present.
The theme of the opening ceremony was the “Harmonic Heart Beat,” and the stage on the infield at the Nagoya City Stadium was in the shape of a large heart.
Afghanistan led off the traditional parade of athletes with Japan coming in last and, of course, receiving thunderous applause.
The Asian Games have been dotted with controversies in the leadup to the opening ceremony. This also happens in the rush to get ready for most Olympics.
First, there’s the issue of housing for athletes. Japanese organizers decided against building a dedicated athletes village. They opted instead to house an estimated 17,000 athletes and officials on a massive cruise ship, in hotels, and in wooden containers converted to lodging.
Japan officially spent $13 billion on the Tokyo Olympics, delayed until 2021 by the pandemic. A government audit suggested the figure was likely twice that large. So lavish spending was out this time.
Athletes have complained the beds and rooms are too small, some have reported the wooden huts have leaks, and logistics could be an issue with venues spread out around Nagoya.
This is Japan’s third largest metropolitan area with a population of about 9.5 million and located about 200 miles (350 kilometers) south of Tokyo.
Then the inevitable politics. On Friday, the day before the official opening, two incidents made headlines.
Organizers played the North Korean national anthem at a field hockey game between South Korea and Bangladesh. South Korea players stood at attention, bewildered the North Korean anthem was playing.
Many South Koreans are, in fact, unfamiliar with North Korea's anthem and did not know what they were hearing.
At about the same time, Taiwanese sports minister Lee Yang — a two-time Olympic gold medalist in badminton — was temporarily barred from a welcoming ceremony involving Taiwan, and other countries including North Korea, Palestine and India.
The Olympic Council of Asia attributed it to a misunderstanding but did not entirely clarify. Yang was eventually allowed to participate.
Taiwan competes in the Asian Games and the Olympics under the name of Chinese Taipei and without their flag due to China’s claim on the island off its east coast.

Israeli president pardons soldier convicted for killing wounded Palestinian
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has pardoned former Israeli soldier Elor Azaria, who was convicted of manslaughter for shooting a wounded Palestinian man in Hebron in 2016, erasing his criminal record, Haaretz reported on Saturday.
Azaria's pardon comes more than 10 years after he shot 21-year-old Abdel Fattah al-Sharif in the head after the Palestinian man was wounded by Israeli soldiers' fire.
Azaria welcomed the scraping of his criminal record by thanking God, his family, Katz and Herzog, saying to Channel 14 News that it was "a blessed week".
"Thank God we have reached this moment," he said.
"It is important that no fighter goes through what I went through," Azaria reportedly told Defence Minister Israel Katz during a phone call.

The killing, which was captured on camera by a Palestinian photographer working for Israeli human rights group B'Tselem, led to an uproar in Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories.
At the time, the Palestinian foreign ministry said the killing was an "extrajudicial execution", while the Israeli military said Azaria violated the army's ethics code.
Herzog's office said in a statement on Saturday that "Azaria bore the consequences of his actions" for many years, adding that the former Israeli soldier expressed remorse for the consequences of his actions and, therefore, it was justified to allow him "to turn a new page in his life".
The Israeli president said he was acting in the spirit of Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, one of the most important holidays in the Jewish calendar.
The decision, Herzog's statement said, was made "out of a belief in the importance of repair, reconciliation, and the ability to move forward".
However, according to Haaretz, Herzog acted against the advice of the Israeli military, as the army's chief, Eyal Zamir, said in a letter to the president that he was against pardoning, citing Azaria's lack of public remorse for the killing of al-Sharif.
Katz, who filed the pardon request to Herzog, welcomed the Israeli president's decision, calling it "a correct, humane, and fitting decision".
Azaria's pardon, Katz added, also sends an important message to Israeli soldiers and their family members: "We do not abandon soldiers and do not leave them behind."
The military said the young Palestinian man carried out a stabbing attack in the Tal Rumeida neighbourhood of Hebron.
Years of controversy
In 2017, Azaria was convicted in the manslaughter of al-Sharif and sentenced to 18 months in military prison, which the army's chief, Gadi Eisenkot, later reduced to 14 months.
Shortly after the killing, Azaria stood trial before a military court after Defence Minister Moshe Yaalon and Eisenkot condemned Azaria's actions.
Azaria's arrest led to right-wing demonstrations calling for the release of the soldier from custody, with politicians joining the calls to release him.
Three months after the incident in Hebron, amid government support for Azaria, Yaalon resigned, citing a lack of trust in Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the handling of the incident, with Azaria supporter Avigdor Liberman taking his place at the time.
Efforts to release Azaria started immediately after he was sentenced by the military court, with Liberman asking then-Israeli President Reuven Rivlin to pardon Azaria in 2017.
The minister said that Azaria was "an outstanding soldier".
Netanyahu joined the calls to pardon Azaria, but Rivlin rejected the request.
In May 2018, after serving a shortened sentence of nine months in prison, Azaria was released.
'A disgrace'
Yaalon, who later became one of Netanyahu's strongest political critics, condemned Herzog's latest decision.
In a post on X, Yaalon called the pardon "a disgrace" and accused Herzog of joining Netanyahu's attacks against former military chief Eisenkot, who is currently leading opinion polls ahead of elections in October.
Yaalon said that Azaria "did not claim he shot the terrorist because he felt his life was in danger, but rather 'because he deserved to die'", as he questioned Herzog's reasoning for pardoning Azaria.
Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir said he was thrilled with Herzog's decision, adding that "as someone who protested a decade ago on behalf of Elor Azaria", the pardoning of the former soldier "moves and delights me very much".
Ben Gvir said that if the rules of engagement were different in 2016, Azaria would not have been convicted, referring to the change the current Israeli far-right government has led in the military's rules of engagement in the past four years.
According to a recent report by B'Tselem, between October 2023 and June 2026, Israel killed 1,087 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, including 242 children and 21 women.
The group described Israeli policies in the Palestinian territories as "a sweeping Israeli assault that is systematically and at an accelerating pace dismantling the foundations of Palestinian existence".
According to the human rights group, Israeli soldiers, police officers and settlers receive "broad impunity" when it comes to harming Palestinians.
Between 2016 and 2024, the group said, 2,427 complaints were filed against soldiers, but investigations were opened in only 22.7 percent of cases, and indictments were filed in only 0.9 percent of cases.

An Islamic State group member was sentenced on Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization that took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 US service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the US military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.
A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the IS affiliate known as Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on 26 August 2021.
US troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah’s role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai international airport, prosecutors said.
Sharifullah, 28, received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that Donald Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress.
Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before the US district judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a “dedicated terrorist” who expressed no remorse for the “unfathomable” grief and suffering that he had caused.
Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of US service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children’s sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families.
Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps L/Cpl Jared Schmitz.
“They may have taken his life, but they’ll never take his legacy,” Mark Schmitz said. “A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for.”
Paula Knauss-Selph, whose son, army SSgt Ryan Knauss, was killed in the Abbey Gate bombing, said the family was “forever changed” by the attack.
“No justice will ever be enough to mend my broken heart,” she said.
Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers said he was never an ISKP leader and had not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.
“He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial,” defense attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors said in their sentencing memo that “from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to [ISKP], Sharifullah’s carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans.”
Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISKP. They deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport “resulted from” that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously decided that question.
According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to “catch and kill the crusaders” from the United States for invading his country after the attacks of September 11. They said Sharifullah was involved in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people.
Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the US.
A review by US Central Command found that the Abbey Gate bomber was Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an IS member who had been released from an Afghan prison by the Taliban. According to an FBI affidavit, Sharifullah recognized the alleged bomber as an operative he had known while incarcerated.

Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) swept the students' union election of the Delhi University on Saturday, with Yash Dabas being elected as the President of the Delhi University Students' Union (DUSU). Independent candidate Deepanshu Shokeen won the Vice President post as counting of votes for the student body elections concluded on Saturday.
In the presidential contest, ABVP’s Dabas polled 24,576 votes, defeating NSUI’s Vijai Shankar Meena by a margin of 2,053 votes. Shokeen won the vice-president’s post with 30,615 votes. He had contested as an independent after being denied an NSUI ticket. Track latest developments on DUSU polls

The win for the RSS-affiliated ABVP comes as a setback for Congress and its student wing – the NSUI – particularly after Gandhi's youth outreach campaign ‘Chhatro ki goonj’ over examination irregularities.

Dozens of suspected illegal miners die in Nigerian custody
- Published
Thirty-seven people accused of illegal mining in north-central Nigeria have died in custody, local officials said.
Police have set up an investigation into the deaths, which the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) blamed on an apparent disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report shared with AFP news agency suggested the group died because of overcrowding and poor ventilation inside the detention facility in the Nigerian state of Niger.
State governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called the deaths "sad and tragic" during a press conference on Thursday.
An NSCDC commander has been detained following the deaths, Bago added.
He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections scheduled for January.
Officials had arrested the group of young men on Tuesday for suspected illegal mining near Borgu, in the mineral-rich state of Niger. The region is known for small-scale gold mining.
Two days later, 37 people detained as part of the suspected unlawful operation were found dead inside the detention centre run by the NSCDC.
The NSCDC had earlier said the detainees were possibly victims of a diphtheria outbreak, a serious bacterial infection that can be fatal.
But the agency's national headquarters later said the cause had not been established and would require medical and laboratory tests.
"The NSCDC wishes to clarify that reports attributing the deaths to any specific disease remain subject to medical and laboratory confirmation," it added in a statement.
A survivor told the Associated Press news agency that about 65 people had been held in an overcrowded and poorly ventilated cell, suggesting the dead may have suffocated.
Some relatives of the deceased have disputed the official explanation of events, claiming to local media that they were deliberately killed.
One father told Nigerian media that his son had appeared healthy when relatives brought him food the day before his death and called for an independent post-mortem examination.
Another relative, whose 17-year-old brother was among those who died, said the family had visited him during his detention and questioned how a disease could have killed so many detainees without apparently affecting their guards.
Post-mortem examinations are expected to help establish what happened.
Niger's police chief ordered an immediate investigation into "the unfortunate death of suspected illegal miners while in the detention facility of the NSCDC", spokesman Wasiu Abiodun wrote in a statement.
The victim's bodies have since been taken to the general hospital in nearby Minna for examination.
The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state has been blamed for fuelling criminal gang violence, according to officials and experts.
Much of the gold in the region is trafficked through global supply chains, a 2024 SwissAid report found.

“DealShare is today an empty vessel with $90 Mn in cash.” That’s how an investor who is aware of the company’s financial status, describes the startup. Once valued at $1.7 Bn, this is what DealShare has been reduced to, and the company is actively looking for a potential acquirer, with many names reportedly close to acquiring it at a 95%-plus haircut. Truemeds is said to be one such suitor but the proposed acquisition is not a done deal yet, according to another investor aware of the development. Active discussions are ongoing, but Truemeds’ existing investors are not necessarily aligned with the deal. DealShare is also in talks with other potential buyers, the investors added. Captain Fresh is another name that had surfaced in connection with a possible acquisition but Inc42 has learnt that the company is not pursuing the transaction. The talks for an acquisition at a distressed valuation come after years of restructuring and attempts to find a viable business model for DealShare, which once enjoyed unicorn status. But as the company’s current situation shows, a lot of that was down to the timing of DealShare’s fundraising spree when VCs were investing at valuations that seemed unsustainable. Questions sent to DealShare, WestBridge and Truemeds didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story. For investors, that raises an old question related to distressed investments but with renewed urgency: what should be done with the roughly $90 Mn still sitting on DealShare’s balance sheet? The DealShare 2.0 Plan Tanks The first few years of DealShare’s existence were all about proving that its hybrid B2B and B2C model would be able to compete with the startups that were making inroads into B2B supply chain as well as ecommerce marketplaces. DealShare was pitched as the ecommerce and supply chain destination for consumers and small retailers or kiranas in Tier II, Tier III and beyond. By January 2022, it already had major investors on board and turned unicorn after raising $165 Mn from AlphaWave, Tiger Global and others. The startup raised its next round in rather quick time and was all set to enter the private label business towards the end of FY23. However, the business struggled to gain traction or show growth in the next year. Much of the money was spent in acquiring customers on both sides and by August 2023, DealShare exited the B2B vertical to focus only on B2C ecommerce operations. The company’s net loss crossed the ₹500 Cr mark in FY23 against a revenue of ₹1,963.5 Cr, despite raising more than $200 Mn in the previous year. After two years of struggle, where the company saw the departure of founders Vineet Rao, Sankar Bora and Sourjyendu Medda, DealShare was a shadow of the unicorn it once was. Towards the end of 2025, there emerged a new plan and a so-called DealShare 2.0 vision. Investors brought in Kamaldeep Singh, a former Big Bazaar executive, to run the company and build the next phase of DealShare. DealShare’s FY25 numbers also showed the strain. Revenue fell 13.4% YoY to ₹432.4 Cr, while net loss narrowed to ₹87.7 Cr from ₹167.7 Cr a year earlier. The idea behind this new DealShare was to return to the B2C value commerce, but with a different delivery model. While DealShare was never a quick commerce platform, with its reinvention it tried to reduce the delivery time to a two hour delivery. DealShare realised in comparison to 10-minute deliveries, standard fulfilment timelines would give the startup more room to curb delivery costs while continuing to serve customers looking for lower priced groceries and everyday products. As per sources the startup already had 40 dark stores and was doing about 25,000 - 30,000 orders a day. It focused primarily in cities such as Jaipur, Ghaziabad, Lucknow and Kolkata. The two-hour delivery timeline was a conscious choice. The startup did not want to spend heavily trying to match the delivery times of Blinkit and Zepto. “The 10-minute delivery model was not sustainable,” a source familiar with the operations at the time said, arguing that the economics of quick commerce made it difficult to generate profits after delivery and fulfilment costs. While DealShare did touch close to 38,000 orders a day at some point, another source added that gross margins in this business were around 5%-6%, leaving little to no margin for the company after subtracting costs. A separate industry source said DealShare’s online business faced high customer acquisition and fulfilment costs. “The new leadership had an offline retail background and lacked the technology, product and marketing know how needed to build an online-first business, which is why the company was forced to change tack again,” one of the sources said. By April 2026, DealShare had started cutting back its online operations, and turned to a physical store network as its next bet. The person familiar with the startup said the online business began going through changes from April onwards. At the same time, DealShare was expanding its physical store network, moving from around eight stores to 22. Sources said around 8-10 stores were profitable and that the offline business began generating revenue soon after opening. DealShare had plans to open more stores, including in markets such as Lucknow and Ajmer. Another industry source said DealShare had around 15-20 stores in Jaipur and was preparing to open another 15 stores in Lucknow and Kanpur. The stores were doing “decently well”, as per the source who has seen the numbers. The shift to offline, however, did not settle the question of what DealShare should become. The company considered several versions of the business, including an offline-only mode, retaining the online operation and an omnichannel setup where stores would fulfil online orders. “Multiple variations of AOPs (annual operating plan) and things were discussed, and nothing was sort of closed on by the board,” sources said. One person familiar with the discussions said the board, which was led by WestBridge and Alpha Wave was unable to agree on which business model to pursue. “The board was not able to decide on which way we should go forward with the organisation,” the person said. Investors Struggle To Agree On DealShare’s Future The majority institutional stakeholder in DealShare, WestBridge holds roughly 18.4% of the company, whereas Alpha Wave owns around 16.39% stake in the startup. For investors, the problem was not simply choosing between online and offline. It was finding a model that could make the remaining capital work. The startup had already spent years and hundreds of millions of dollars trying to build a growing business. This online vertical was struggling with low gross margins and high customer acquisition and fulfilment costs, while the newer offline business was still being tested. The indecision became harder to sustain with roughly $90 Mn, or around ₹800 - ₹900 Cr, still sitting on DealShare’s balance sheet, according to another investor familiar with the startup. One source said investors had been discussing how to salvage the remaining money for the startup. “The plan is to sell the startup off to someone who can take the money which we have in a bank account to fund their operations,” the person said. Sources told Inc42 that the talks between Truemeds and DealShare were primarily driven by WestBridge, which is a mutual investor in both the startups. That is where DealShare’s strategic uncertainty meets its acquisition talks. The strategy changes have also coincided with a steady churn in the organisation. Having come to steady the ship, new CEO Singh himself is on his way out. The person familiar with the startup said Singh is serving his notice period. CFO Ashish Shah is also close to the exit door. Besides this, several key employees have also left the startup. As per sources, the company has not carried out a blanket layoff, with employees leaving of their own accord. At the same time, DealShare’s online business has come to a complete halt. The startup began cutting back its online operations around April 2026 and eventually stopped fulfilment from its warehouses. The physical stores continue to operate, but the online business is now “next to zero,” according to the source. The app remains available and sources said around 30,000 users open the app every month, although many leave without placing an order. Roughly 22 DealShare stores are currently operational, but plans to add more stores in Lucknow and Kanpur have been put on hold. The result is a business that looks very different from the one investors were trying to build less than a year ago. The two hour delivery model has effectively been shut down, offline expansion has stopped and the management team brought in for DealShare 2.0 is changing again. Truemeds Talks Put The Cash In Focus The acquisition discussions with Truemeds come against this backdrop. Truemeds has emerged as the frontrunner, but the potential transaction is still subject to investor alignment, according to a person aware of the development. DealShare is also speaking with other potential parties. The roughly $90 Mn cash balance is likely to be a key part of any transaction, and sets the floor for the deal. 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

It’s the grand final for gunzels. But despite having one of the largest tram networks in the world, Melbourne’s Tramaroos finished second last at this year’s European TramDriver Championship, just ahead of London.
The event, held in Warsaw on Saturday, saw 26 teams compete across a series of demanding tasks, inspired – to varying degrees – by tram drivers’ day-to-day work.
In smooth stop and go, drivers travelled with a bowl of water attached to the front of the tram – with points deducted for every drop spilled. Other precision tasks involved speed control at 25 km/h, target braking, tram bowling, lateral distance, basketball, a perfect stop with the second door, and a reverse ride guided by whistle commands.
Daniel Bowen, a spokesperson for the Public Transport Users Association, said it was “an unusual event in the pantheon of world sports”.
“It’s pretty entertaining,” he said, and an opportunity to look for inspiration from great other tram systems around the world. “Everyone looked like they were having a great time.”
This year’s title went to Vendula Tmejová and Zdeněk Rychtář, from Prague, in the Czech Republic.
In 2022, Australia was the first ever non-European country chosen to participate. This year, Yarra Trams sent Ivan Cavanagh of Southbank depot and Claudia Barrientos from Kew depot to compete as the “Tramaroos”. Had they won, the trophy would have gone “straight to the pool room”, Cavanagh said.
“You would hope our team would do well but I’m sure there’s pretty stiff competition against you know the Europeans,” Bowen said. “Perhaps it’s a bit like Eurovision – it’s great to participate.”
Thousands of fans followed the spectacle live in Warsaw, with about 80,000 viewers worldwide watching the competition via livestream.
Melbourne is set to host the next event in 2027.
Bowen said it would be interesting to see if other Australian cities joined the competition, given recent extensions to light rail systems in Adelaide, Sydney, Canberra and the Gold Coast.
“Back in Melbourne, it’s a reminder that trams do form a vital part of the transport system. We do have the biggest tram network in the world, but there’s more to do in terms of accessibility and on-road priority and service frequency.”

No fire alarms or sprinklers at Pakistan neonatal unit where fire killed 14, report finds
- Published
An official inquiry into a Pakistan hospital fire that killed 14 babies last month has found the neonatal unit lacked fire alarms and sprinklers, while firefighters reported that escape routes were "locked or obstructed".
One firefighter, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC he had heard from other rescue workers that entering the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital in Islamabad was "extremely difficult".
"The doors were locked so they had to break through the windows to enter. Even after getting inside, the doors leading towards the ward were locked."
PIMS has not provided a comment on the report and its findings.
The firefighter said he arrived once the blaze had been put out.
It was "difficult for me to even describe what we saw," he said. "The medical equipment above [the babies] had melted and collapsed onto them."
The report from an investigative committee headed by a retired senior civil servant found "systemic and institutional failure" which meant what began as an electrical spark became a "catastrophe".
- At least 14 babies die in Pakistan hospital fire 
  - Published26 August
- Inside hospital after fire kills 14 babies in Pakistan 
  - Published26 August
For many inside the hospital on the morning of 26 August, the first warnings were shouts.
Abdul Ghafoor was in a nearby ward with his mother, who was a patient, when he heard someone warning that a fire had erupted. He went upstairs to see if he could help.
"The entire ward was filled with smoke, we could not see anything," he told the BBC.
CCTV from the corridor outside shows how quickly the fire spread. According to the report, the first indication that something was wrong came at 06:38 when a nurse can be seen running from the ward to get help, returning 20 seconds later with a security guard.
Another nurse, Razia Noreen, is then seen rushing into the ward, emerging seconds later with one of the babies who turned out to be the only one to survive.
Within a minute, the report says, dense smoke had obscured the camera.
Hivsa Walid, her newborn niece and sister-in-law were in the ward next door. Hours later she told the BBC that they had heard a loud commotion and then realised it was a fire when they saw smoke emerging from the unit where the babies were sleeping.
"In that moment, I couldn't understand what was going on. We just focused on getting downstairs and saving ourselves."
On the day of the fire, authorities suggested the fire had started from a spark in the ward's air conditioner.
The report agrees that this was the most probable source of the fire, due to an overheating electrical supply cable - although it remains unclear what exactly the electrical defect was.
The fire then spread quickly, igniting plastics, equipment and bins.
Several babies in the ward were on oxygen support, but the report says that while oxygen may have intensified the fire, there isn't evidence that it created a pathway for it to spread.
The air conditioning units had undergone maintenance, but the report says this is not the same as a safety check. Back in 2018, the hospital's air conditioning units had been approved to be replaced and upgraded, but eight years later this hadn't happened.
The report states that there was no functioning smoke detection, fire alarms or sprinkler system. It found no evidence that the staff in the unit had been trained or had ever rehearsed how to evacuate the ward of newborns, many of whom were premature or "medically fragile". It also found staff had not been trained on how to isolate the oxygen supply in the case of an emergency.
Several people described chaos and confusion in the hospital.
"There should have been fire extinguishers and protocols, but no one was doing anything," Walid said. "Everyone was just running."
Ghafoor said that he was part of a group of seven or eight who tried to find a way to relieve the thick smoke; they managed to break glass panels at the end of the corridor before firefighters arrived.
The emergency services weren't notified about the fire until 06:54, the report says, nearly 20 minutes after it first began. It says the first rescue workers arrived at 07:01.
Like the firefighter who spoke to the BBC, Ghafoor also said rescue staff struggled to get through some of the hospital's doors.
At the time, the hospital's executive director had told BBC News that the door to the newborns' ward was not locked, but guarded, because of previous incidents of baby abductions from government hospitals.
The report says that while "ordinary access restrictions may be legitimate for security purposes… they cannot render designated emergency routes inaccessible when needed."
The report also found that the hospital had received previous warnings about fire risks. A month before, a fire had broken out at its nursing hostel, raising issues with smoke detection, alarms and general fire preparedness.
It says that the hospital and its senior management "bear the principal institutional responsibility for failing to convert known risks, prior warnings and assigned duties into an effective safety system".
Pakistan's prime minister has directed the inquiry's short-term measures to be implemented within the next three months and ordered fire safety audits of public and private offices and buildings.
He has also suspended eight officials and asked for criminal proceedings to be initiated against them.

Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.
The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.
Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions at the Hotel Bamy – a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous.
The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received $7.5m as part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely.
The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo.
Advocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture, according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy.
Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off.
The two men who were tortured – Ahmed Soliman, 31, of Egypt, and Samson Birhane, 47, of Eritrea – have since been transferred to a prison in Malabo. Multiple witnesses recounted that the police officers shouted, “Where is the phone? Where is the phone!” as they beat the men, who had initially been accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel before they were pulled aside and arrested.
The beating, which occurred on 11 September, followed the release of a video first reported by Reuters showing conditions at the hotel and the violent behavior of the guards. The detainees had been using cellphones to communicate with lawyers and the media about the conditions they were facing.
In the video taken by Soliman, which lawyers shared with the Guardian, authorities are seen pointing guns at the deportees. A Cuban man asked the officer for the return of his confiscated mobile phone so he could contact relatives and a lawyer, but was ignored. When officers noticed Soliman filming the exchange with his mobile phone, multiple officers rushed at him and others standing nearby, pointed their guns, and told Soliman to remain on his knees with his hands up for 10-15 minutes.
In another video, Soliman was able to film authorities forcibly sending US deportees to Ethiopia, where they are likely to face torture. When deportees resisted going with authorities, officials gave them the option to “go back to their home country” or “go to prison”. At least 12 people have been returned by Equatorial Guinea to their home country, where they face persecution.
In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal asking Equatorial Guinea to halt plans to return deportees to their home countries and to comply with international human rights standards and avoid refoulement, or the expulsion of people to countries where they face persecution.
“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, who represents several of the deportees at Hotel Bamy. The US and Equatorial Guinea “must be held accountable for the atrocities they are committing”, she added.
In the week since Soliman and Birhane were beaten, police have also been searching the other detainees’ hotel rooms for cellphones, and have confiscated them. They have also barred lawyers from seeing the deportees. Authorities have told the 29 US deportees who remain at Hotel Bamy that they may never see Soliman or Birhane again, according to lawyers. One detainee who witnessed the beating said authorities treat them as if they are “blanks” who “don’t even exist”. Another detainee said an officer told her: “You will disappear from the earth. I am the law.”
Witnesses said they feared for the lives of Soliman and Birhane, who came to the US as children.
Soliman is a gay man from Egypt who had lived in Phoenix for most of his life. He had a green card, but lost status after he was convicted of drug possession. He served time for his crimes, and in October, a judge had determined he would face persecution and torture if he were to return to Egypt due to his sexuality.
Birhane had come to the US as a refugee when he was 13, but lost status after a conviction for robbery when he was in high school, in 1988. He was allowed to remain in the US after a judge ruled he faced torture in Eritrea, and had been regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement as required.
Lawyers for the deportees shared copies of multiple emails they had sent to the US embassy in Equatorial Guinea alerting them to threats and violence against those detained at Hotel Bamy, but those messages have gone unanswered, they said. In July, amid a lawsuit challenging conditions for deportees, the African Commission issued an urgent interim order instructing the government of Equatorial Guinea to refrain from deporting, transferring, or relocating deportees against their will.
The US Department of Homeland Security did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
A spokesperson for the state department said: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”
The agency did not respond to questions about whether it was aware of how Equatorial Guinea was treating US deportees, nor would it acknowledge whether any measures have been taken to intervene.
“As a general matter, we do not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments,” the spokesperson said.

Murder suspect who tried to surrender at police station was turned away by NYPD cop: report
Tiliek Shamel Thompson was later charged with with murder, assault, strangulation, child abandonment, and acting in a manner injurious to a child
A murder suspect accused of beating a New York City mother to death and leaving her body with her 7-year-old daughter allegedly walked out of an NYPD station after trying to surrender, according to his attorney and the New York Post.
Tiliek Shamel Thompson, 41, went to the 33rd Precinct stationhouse in Washington Heights around 5 a.m. on September 11, accompanied by his two cousins, as police investigated the killing of Lovay Williams, 27. However, he was not successfully taken into custody until September 12, when he was charged with murder, assault, strangulation and acting in manner injurious to a child.
Williams was found dead inside her apartment on 156th Street on September 6, suffering trauma to her face and neck, according to the Post. She was pronounced dead at the scene. Her 7-year-old daughter was also inside the apartment but was found unharmed. Williams and Thompson were dating, relatives told the Post.
Days later, Thompson and his cousins went to the station because they understood police were looking for him, his attorney, Neville Onielle Dexter Mitchell, told the Post.
“His two cousins said, ‘You’re looking for him,’” Mitchell said, according to the Post.
The officer working the desk allegedly responded, “I just came back from vacation. Nobody’s here,” Mitchell said.
However, an NYPD spokeswoman disputed that account to the Post after reviewing audio and video from the encounter. She said the family did not tell the officer that police were looking for Thompson and that the officer misunderstood the group’s reason for coming to the station.
The officer reportedly believed the three were members of Williams’ family and relayed that information to a sergeant. The officer's reference to being on vacation was meant to explain that he had been away when Williams was killed, according to the NYPD spokeswoman.
The officer then gave one of Thompson’s cousins a phone number for homicide detectives and allowed the group to leave.
Thompson, who police sources reportedly identified as a person of interest in Williams’ killing, later returned to police and successfully surrendered. He was charged with murder.
The NYPD has acknowledged that the encounter was mishandled, according to the Post.
The Independent has contacted the NYPD for comment.
The alleged handling of Thompson’s attempted surrender has drawn criticism from current and former NYPD officers, who said officers should have detained him or contacted homicide detectives even if investigators were not immediately available.
“If he went there and said he was there to turn himself in, they should have investigated,” a senior police officer told the Post on the condition of anonymity.
“I’d say you should hold the guy and investigate further,” the officer added. “Even if detectives aren’t there, you can call them. I’m sure they’d love to take a homicide collar.”
Former NYPD Detective Michael Alcazar similarly said officers should have contacted detectives working the overnight shift, known as nightwatch.
“You got a homicide suspect turning himself in, so you detain him until the squad gets there,” he said. “I’m not surprised if they turned him away. We’re scraping the bottom of the barrel.”
The incident comes as the NYPD works to increase its ranks after years of recruitment challenges. The department hired 4,056 new officers in 2025, the largest number hired in a single year, according to the Post. The NYPD also lowered some hiring requirements, including reducing the number of college credits required from 60 to 24.
