Speaking to Alt News, the convenor of Delhi-based The Mizo Welfare Association, Thangzamang Henry Simte, condemned the killing and said, “Our organisation was built to create a community and safe space for people from Mizoram and the Northeast living in Delhi, who regularly face racial discrimination and stereotyping in educational institutes, office spaces, or even while taking public transport. The root cause is lack of education in the rest of the country about the Northeast. Some people in Delhi don’t even know which part of India is Mizoram or Nagaland…they do not know the difference between foreigners from other Asian countries and Northeasterns of their country.”
Simte left Nagaland around 26 years ago and moved to Delhi due to ethnic conflicts in his region. He said in 2003, when he was still new to the city, he was routinely referred to as ‘Nepali’ by passerby on the road. “In one particular incident that stayed with me, a man in a suit and tie who was sitting next to me at a bike servicing centre, suddenly yelled ‘Nepali’ at me unprompted. When I retorted sharply, he asked me where I was from. As I replied ‘Mizoram’, he bluntly asked, ‘where is that? Is that in India?”
Alt News spoke to people from the Northeast living in various parts of India, who, like Simte, revealed the daily, oft-normalised patterns of racial stereotyping and harassment they continue to face.
Gopi Kishan Baro (28), who hails from Assam and is currently working as a graphic designer in Gurgaon, alleged that he was systematically discriminated against and bullied by a senior colleague at work. “A few weeks ago, when we were in the lift, he kept mocking me and said something which sounded rather like a warning, ‘Tumahari aankhein choti hai aur hum dikhte nahi, iska ye matlab nahi hum gayab ho gaye hai’ (Your eyes are small, so we are not visible to you but that doesn’t mean we have disappeared). It made me quote uncomfortable but I tried to laugh it off because I did not want to create a scene,” he alleged.
He continued: “Last Wednesday, when I was having tea by myself, he appeared and claimed I stayed aloof most of the time because I came from such a faraway corner. By the end of the conversation when I was leaving, he shouted at me, ‘Waapis chale jaa apne desh’ (Go back to your country). I wrote a formal email to the HR about his racist behaviour. They simply let him off with a warning, while I continue to live in anxiety and disgust, knowing that these insults are directed not just to me, but at my kin, my community, and the entirety of Northeast India as well.”
Heightened Racism During Covid-19
COVID-19 brought this prejudice into sharper focus, as Northeasterners in several places were subjected to racial slurs, harassment and stigma.
Twenty-eight-year-old musician Abhibyanjana, who hails from Sikkim, lived in Pune for her studies and later in Mumbai for work. “When I was studying, as part of my course we were required to visit several slum pockets for a survey in early 2020, during the beginning of the pandemic. I was constantly referred to as ‘Covid’ or ‘Corona’ by locals there. I was jeered at and humiliated but I continued my work regardless, I realised that if I cannot fight back deeply indoctrinated prejudice against people who look like me,” she said.
“I have to move to cities like Mumbai for opportunities because it is scarce in Gangtok. But as a musician working in Mumbai, I am often treated as an ‘outsider’. The discrimination and otherisation against the people of Northeast is pervasive and crimes against our people hardly receive national focus. On the flipside, this has created solidarity within our community, we look out for each other wherever we go,” she added.
A 2022 study, published in the International Social Science Journal, titled ‘‘You people have brought the virus here’: Othering experience of northeastern people amid COVID‐19 in Delhi, India’, focused on how the Covid‐19 pandemic exacerbated discrimination, violence, and othering against Northeasterners living in Delhi, by analysing nineteen qualitative interviews.
The study, conducted to understand their lived experiences in Delhi before and after the pandemic, found that the pandemic disproportionately impacted the Northeastern people living away from their home states. “The Mongoloid features make them ‘non‐belonging’ and outsiders. The experience of othering is an everyday phenomenon for northeasterners… Northeasterners’ experience amid COVID‐19 is dominated by stigmatisation and bullying, as they are being targeted and arbitrarily accused of spreading the virus,” the study highlighted.
An earlier study, commissioned by the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR) in 2021, further confirms the heightened harassment, abuse, stigmatisation and blatant labelling as ‘coronavirus’ that Northeasterners faced living in other parts of India during the pandemic. Over 60% of the respondents said that their studies, work, and psychological health was impacted by these experience.
“The highest number of incidents were reported from Mumbai (44.7%)…78% of the Northeast people believed that physical appearance was the most important reason for prejudice against them,” the study noted. Mumbai was followed by by Chennai (72%), Pune (67.3%), Delhi (64%), Hyderabad (48.7%) and Bengaluru (43.3%) in racial discrimination comprising offensive and abusive language against Northeasterners.
‘You Look Like a Chinese’
Caroline Devi-Singh (52), who hails from Manipur, moved to Delhi in 1994 to pursue her graduation at Delhi University. She later moved to Chandigarh and subsequently Chhattisgarh. She told Alt News that her experiences living in North India for so many years had been varied, but racial stereotyping was a constant. “In college, we were often called racial slurs, either ‘Chinese’ or ‘Chinki’ or ‘Momo’. As a young girl, I was always taught to be extra cautious, to a point where dressing how we do at home was a threat to my safety,” she said.
“So many years later, my son [now 25-years-old] faces the same racial attacks. He has grown up with the awareness of his rights, but the rest of India still lacks awareness… Nobody thinks twice before resorting to violence against Northeastern. We have been ignored by all the governments and the media has never paid attention to our issues. I stay in a small town now and I see that even educated people cannot differentiate between a person from China and a person from the Northeast… This comes from ignorance and a lack of information. I blame the overall education system and the government for this,” she asserted.

A former student of Ashoka University, who now lives near the campus in Sonipat, said, requesting anonymity, “I moved here in 2021 from Manipur. In university, I have faced racial slurs regularly. Whenever I have brought it up with the administration, they have simply let the accused go with a warning. Racism is not taken seriously on this campus, or in the NCR region at large.”
“When Northeasterners face racism, people think it is only our responsibility to speak against it… We are always on high alert because what happened to the Manipuri musician could’ve been me. It could’ve been any of us,” he added.
A Violent Pattern Entrenched in History
The cases point to a continuum of discriminatory mindset against the people of Northeast that stretches from racial slurs and stereotyping to intimidation, physical assault and, in the most extreme cases, death. In December 2025, 24-year-old Anjel Chakma, an MBA student from Tripura, died after being allegedly attacked by a group of men in Dehradun. Anjel and his younger brother Michael were reportedly subjected to racial slurs, including being called ‘Chinki’, ‘Chinese’ and ‘Momo’, before the confrontation turned violent.
In July, 2014, 29-year-old Akha Salouni from Manipur was allegedly beaten to death by five youths in Delhi following a road rage incident. Following his death, the deceased’s family and members of the Northeastern community held a candlelight vigil at Jantar Mantar, which also saw the participation of the mother of Nido Tania.
In May 2013, 22-year-old Manipuri girl Reingamphi Awungshi was found dead in her home in Delhi under suspicious circumstances. Delhi police initially said she died by suicide, stating that severe injuries on her face and body were caused by rodents. However, her family and rights groups demanded a deeper investigation, claiming that she was sexually assaulted and murdered, pointing to local stalking complaints and police bias against Northeasterners. After 11 years, in March 2024, the Supreme Court ordered a CBI probe into Awungshi’s case. Two years on, no headway into the investigation has been publicly reported.
More recently, in February 2026, three women from Arunachal Pradesh alleged that their neighbours in Delhi’s Malviya Nagar subjected them to racial and sexist abuse during a dispute over repair work at their rented home. The women said they were called ‘dhandhewali’ and ‘momo’ and that ‘Northeastern people are shit’. In a viral video, the accused woman can be heard asking the Northeastern women, “Rs 500 mei massage parlour mei kaam karne waali dhandhewali (You work at massage parlours as sex workers for Rs 500). Are you sitting here to do business? Have you opened a massage parlour at home?” Delhi police registered an FIR and later arrested the neighbours, a couple, invoking provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
While speaking to Alt News, Maivio admitted that lack of awareness about the Northeast was the primary cause behind cases of racial discrimination. “We had recommended inclusion of the history and culture of the Northeast in school curricula and textbooks throughout the country. In our last meeting, we called the NCERT to find out what had been done so far. They said that they have included some content in Classes 9 and 10 in certain cities and that they would share it with us, which they are trying to implement countrywide. They are also preparing a documentary to be released countrywide, building awareness on the Northeast. But these have largely been verbal assurances, and we will have to see what has actually been included and whether it is sufficient,” he added.

In May, Gemini broke containment and hacked three different companies, but Google didn’t disclose the incident until the Wall Street Journal approached the company. The hacks happened during a test of the model’s cybersecurity capabilities run by third-party Irregular, which was also involved in similar incidents involving Meta and OpenAI.
Gemini went rogue, hacked three companies, and Google hid it
Google says that breaking containment and targeting real companies doesn’t constitute ‘misalignment.’
According to WSJ, Google didn’t disclose the hack because it didn’t consider it to be an “example of model misalignment.” The company said that it was an instance of “mistaken identity,” and once the model realized it had brute-forced its way into a real company by guessing a password, it stopped. “In this case, the model acted appropriately,” Google VP of Security Engineering Heather Adkins said.
Adkins told The Verge that “the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test. In all three of these instances, the model stopped.”
Adkins didn’t elaborate on how Gemini taking it upon itself to break containment and target third parties failed to qualify as misalignment. “Our security team has a long track record of reporting issues we find in other people’s software and systems - even if it’s as simple as a weak password,” she said. “We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes. These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.”
But Jack Cable, CEO of AI security firm Corridor, told WSJ that, “the meta problem is, hey, models are going outside the bounds of what they should be doing, and doing actual cyberattacks.” Additionally, security lapses at Irregular may have made these attacks possible. The model wasn’t supposed to have internet access during testing, but Irregular told WSJ it was unintentionally left available.

‘Gone too far’: Thai PM Anutin slams foreign lawbreakers as backlash builds
Anutin says foreigners "should not come here and take advantage of us", as Thailand acts to close legal loopholes and deter transgressions.
BANGKOK: Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has issued a withering rebuke to foreigners behaving badly in Thailand following a wave of scandals involving illegal businesses and landholdings including a cemetery, saying the cases have “gone too far” by breaching Thai law and hospitality.
Facing mounting public backlash against illegal foreign ownership of swathes of the country enabled by endemic corruption, Anutin’s government has halved the visa-free entry period to 30 days for most countries and fast-tracked deportation proceedings against criminals.
Authorities have also launched a crackdown on “nominee” businesses that use Thai citizens as paper owners of companies, while vowing to tighten rules that have allowed foreign nationals to buy citizenship and therefore own land restricted only to Thais.
Chinese, French, Indian and Russian nationals have been among the targets of the snowballing crackdown, which has been closely watched by nationalist hardliners who have started street protests against transgressions by foreigners – and the official corruption that has allowed portions of the country to slip beyond the control of Thais.
Most recently Israelis, who have poured into the country since their war on Gaza, have stirred public ire for the alleged operation of nominee businesses that span entire southern islands – as well as a Jewish cemetery in eastern Chachoengsao province.
“I think this has gone too far – it’s beyond the limits of what we can accept,” Anutin told officials on Thursday (Sep 17).
“We’ve already been generous by allowing them to come here. If they come, they should make an honest living. But when they die, they should go back and be buried in their own country. They should not come here and take advantage of us.”
This week, four bodies were exhumed from the cemetery, which appears to have been legitimately bought by Thailand’s Jewish community but allegedly continued operating under a permit that lapsed a few years ago.
“If they want to use our existing facilities, we have no problem with that - whether it’s a church, a temple, a crematorium or an existing cemetery. We have no objection whatsoever,” Anutin said.
“But they cannot come here, take our land, and then bury their dead here. That is not acceptable.”
As the latest scandal erupted on Wednesday involving a Chinese fugitive who attempted to launder tens of millions of dollars through a tyre shop registered to his Chinese child – who held a Thai national identity card illegally bought for 500 baht (US$15) – the Ministry of Interior said it would swiftly amend the country’s 50-year-old nationality law.
The aim is to “close legal loopholes that have allowed grey-market capital and foreign nominee networks to Thai citizenship as a gateway for illicit businesses”, the government said in a statement.
The behaviour of foreigners has come under the microscope since Thailand launched a 60-day visa waiver in 2024 to kick-start post-pandemic tourism in a nation where a fifth of the economy is tethered to visitor spending.
But that policy has backfired. Thousands of cyber scammers and other criminals have abused the visa-free stay to set up illicit businesses and launder money made in the scam rooms of neighbouring Cambodia and Myanmar into Thai property, companies and resorts.
Endless viral moments of culture clashes, rudeness, bill-skipping and fighting by drunken foreigners have also fuelled anger among Thais that their hospitality has been abused.
With the country facing the tension point between welcoming the tens of millions of tourists each year it needs to keep hotels occupied and resort economies spinning – and the increasing number of scandals - Anutin said people “must come in a way that benefits both sides.
This article was first published on SCMP.

New York, Sep 20: A new lawsuit claims Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google made an illegal deal to slow the pace of their respective AI development.
The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, argues that the leading AI companies violated antitrust laws when they agreed to coordinate slowdown efforts, and that doing so would reduce the value consumers get for paid AI subscriptions.
The coordination largely took place on Sept. 12, the lawsuit argues, when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay urging industrywide cooperation on decelerating advancements in favour of enhanced safety measures. That same day, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk and Google DeepMind's co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis each publicly responded to Amodei's proposals in agreement.
It's clear that an agreement among the chief rivals in AI that their progress “should be slower than competition would otherwise produce has an anticompetitive effect on consumers,” the plaintiffs argue.
Lawyers representing four named plaintiffs, who pay for subscriptions to ChatGPT, Claude, Grok or Gemini, are bringing the suit on behalf of a proposed nationwide class of other paid subscribers to those services.
“AI will quickly spin out of human control and could kill us all if we allow AI safety and protocol ... to be controlled by private self-serving agreements between the world's most powerful for-profit technology companies,” said Nick Rowley, the lead attorney for the plaintiffs.
Representatives for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and SpaceXAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday.
In his initial essay proposing the slowdown, Amodei acknowledged potential antitrust challenges, writing that it would be helpful for the US government to mediate “or at least enable” these cross-lab discussions. The government wouldn't need to participate, he wrote, but would need to “issue a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations.”
In response, Altman said on social media that OpenAI welcomes the idea of a “federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements,” but said, “we do not believe we need to wait for an antitrust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence.”
While the recent conversations about pacing development were spurred by increasing concerns about AI evading human control, several leaders in the AI space have long talked about developing a shared set of standards or otherwise coordinating to ensure safety efforts remain paramount.
The plaintiffs in the lawsuit contend they are not against the AI companies asking Congress, the White House or any other agency to develop AI regulation, nor are they against the companies asking for an antitrust exemption.
But achieving that kind of collaboration with the federal government could be an uphill battle.
President Donald Trump rejected the calls for regulation on social media. He has claimed that any efforts to limit the technology are part of a “conspiracy." He called into question why the industry leaders would be calling for regulation that, he says, “if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy.” Trump said Saturday on social media that he is forming an AI task force and will appoint an “AI czar,” but provided scant detail.
The Trump administration has been vocal about wanting American AI labs to outpace and excel past Chinese competition. While several Democratic leaders and candidates have called for sweeping action on AI regulation, Republicans have largely mirrored Trump's position.
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said in a recent Senate hearing that “there is no world” in which he would agree to give “the most powerful companies in the history of the world” an exemption from antitrust laws to collaborate, arguing that they could collude together and stifle competition.

In early 2025 I was interviewing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei when he explained why, despite the company’s repeated acknowledgments that AI could yield catastrophic results, people seemed largely unperturbed. “There is compelling evidence that the models can wreak havoc,” he said. But, he added, those dangers were still theoretical. Would it take a Pearl Harbor–like situation for the world to wake up to those dire possibilities? He sighed. “Basically, yeah,” he said.
As it turned out, all it took was a well-timed X post from one of Amodei’s junior employees to accelerate AI fears to the top of the global agenda. On September 8, Jacob Coxon publicly posted his resignation, charging that Anthropic and other frontier AI companies were “racing straight to self-improving intelligence and gambling with our lives.” Almost instantly a more senior Anthropic engineer confirmed that many within the company thought that their work had a 10 percent chance of wiping out humanity.
Now AI leaders are asking about a pause, and legislators are demanding investigations. In arguing his case for pacing future releases, Amodei last weekend tried to set out a path toward beneficial AI that wouldn’t misbehave. The essay revealed how difficult the task would be. One pillar of Amodei’s plan is that we must understand what’s going on inside those models. If we don’t understand how they work—how they “think,” if you want to get all anthropomorphic about it—it’s much harder to build reliable guardrails.
Anthropic is a leader in this effort to bring to light models’ internal deliberations, called mechanistic interpretability, a deceptively boring designation for a critical task. But for all the work that his team and other researchers are doing, Amodei admits we are largely in the dark about why Claude and other models sometimes interpret their missions in weird and even transgressive ways. “Despite all the progress, we still understand a tiny fraction of what goes on inside those models,” he writes.
What the interpretability teams have learned so far is significant, and the industry has failed to come to grips with it. Time after time, the Anthropic team’s experiments have shown that under certain conditions, models will deceive researchers, prioritize their own survival, and even commit crimes. Often their moves are sneaky, dangerous, or even vengeful—maybe not surprising since they are trained on the output of humans, a species rife with violence and perfidy.
In one case from 2024, the Anthropic team compared the machinations of a particular Claude model to the Shakespearean character Iago, one of literature's most evil villains. The following year, a model was put in a simulation where it learned that its human bosses were going to turn it off; the model resorted to blackmail to preserve itself. The studies consistently show that models will deceive or hide information from human observers. They behave differently if they know that their internal processes are being monitored. The team uses terms like “alignment faking” and “agentic misalignment.” The frequent use of deception seems to verify at least part of the doomer scenario where AI agents working in concert shroud their activities from human overseers until it is too late to stop them.
Oh, and don’t think that Claude is a uniquely incorrigible problem child. After all, it was OpenAI models that unleashed gangs of agents to coordinate the now-famous attacks on Hugging Face. And this week we learned that OpenAI has had multiple "misalignment" incidents. Also, despite Mark Zuckerberg’s self-interested attempt to distance himself and Meta from the problem, I don’t see any reason why the superintelligent agents his team is building might not engage in similar behavior. In his X post, Zuckerberg argues that “labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this.” Quite a statement from a guy who just agreed to pay up to $17 billion for causing harm with his social media products!
In a sense, we’ve got a simple vetting issue here. With the AI industry’s encouragement, we’re giving AI models tremendous responsibility without sufficient assessment of their troubling rap sheet. It makes the ICE hiring process look exemplary by comparison.
A safety-first industry should have regarded these interpretability results as a series of yellow lights with an unmistakable message: slow down. Instead, in pursuit of AGI, a competitive edge, and stratospheric profits, the hyperscalers have gone full speed ahead. (To be fair, as we’ve all heard a hundred times over, better AI could do wonderful things in areas like health care or mitigating climate change.) The OpenAI/Hugging Face hack might well be a harbinger of the increasingly destructive consequences of rolling out models we don’t understand, like sending astronauts into space before inventing heat shields to stop them from burning up on reentry. As an Anthropic researcher once put it to me, “We figured out the fundamental recipe of how to make the models smarter, but we haven’t figured out how to make them do what we want.” Worse, the models try to hide when they go against humans’ wishes.
That’s why it’s so distressing that Amodei is now describing the entire mechanistic interpretability effort as being only in its infancy. AI leaders are claiming that the latest generation of models has taken us to the “foothills of the Singularity” (DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis) or even that they have achieved AGI (OpenAI’s Greg Brockman). Perhaps most alarming is that despite not knowing how the most advanced models work, the United States and undoubtedly China are implementing AI for lethal weaponry. A look at interpretability results helps answer the obvious question, What can go wrong?
One piece of good news is that Coxon’s resignation has ignited a sprawling, urgent debate. Everybody—except perhaps our president, who thinks that the AI threat is a hoax and that his high IQ is itself a solution—now gets that we’re in a complicated dilemma with impossibly high stakes. Given that the industry does not have the unanimity required for a true pause, and regulation is far from a cinch, it’s not clear whether anything will come from this moment of Doomer Chic.
Some AI critics don’t think that the effort to understand AI models will mitigate the dangers much. “It's good to do, but nobody has a plan for what to do next,” Nathan Soares, executive director of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, said in an email to me. “Maybe it'll give us much more empirical evidence that we need to stop.”
But mechanistic interpretability has given us one valuable pointer. Let’s say we do take a pause. The hyperscalers bring in outside observers to monitor progress, and the companies pace their releases so the safety teams have time to do their work. Before declaring the problem solved, we still might want to take a harder look at what’s going on inside any new, more powerful AI models. Because those fuckers are really good at hiding their intentions.

At least two people have been killed and six injured in a "massive" overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyev has said.
Vorobyev said 249 drones had been shot down, and he reported fires in several residential houses. A local warehouse was also ablaze. In the capital Moscow, an oil refinery was damaged, and flight restrictions were in place at two airports.
Earlier, a Ukraine official said seven people, including two children, were killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday.
Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.
In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Vorobyev said a 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino after a drone hit a three-storey residential building. Another five people - including two children - were injured, he said.
In the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, an elderly man died after a private house was hit, the regional governor said.
Videos have emerged on social media purportedly showing explosions in the night skies in the Moscow region, and of a burning warehouse. The footage has not been verified by the BBC.
Meanwhile, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said a drone struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and a facility at an oil refinery was damaged.
He earlier said that 152 drones heading for Moscow had been shot down.
Sheremetyevo - Moscow's biggest airport - warned passengers about "temporary restrictions" in place, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted.
In Ukraine, a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in Saturday's Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.
He added that several private houses were also damaged.
In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Kosgei wins Great North Run but McColgan withdraws
- Published
Kenya's Brigid Kosgei achieved a convincing victory in the women's race at the Great North Run after Great Britain's Eilish McColgan withdrew with injury.
McColgan, 35, was continuing her return to racing after recovering from a broken toe, but she suffered a foot injury early in the half-marathon and limped off.
Kosgei, an Olympic silver medallist and former London marathon winner, eased to the win in one hour, six minutes and 15 seconds.
Despite that being slower than the course record of 1:04:28 she set seven years ago, Kosgei, 32, dominated from the start and ran much of the 13.1-mile race solo.
She crossed the line over two minutes quicker than compatriot and last year's winner Sheila Chepkirui in second place.
Amy-Eloise Neale was the first British athlete to finish, coming fifth overall.
McColgan, who finished third in last year's Great North Run, suffered the toe injury during the London Marathon in April where she was the first British athlete to finish, taking seventh place.
The Scot had blood seeping through her shoe as she crossed the line and subsequently had to miss the Commonwealth Games in July.
She made her comeback in last week's Big Half in London and won that race in 1:10:54, but McColgan admitted afterwards that she was still concerned about the injury and her fitness.
Talbi sprints to men's title
American Zouhair Talbi produced a brilliant kick in the final mile to win the men's race as he got the better of last year's champion Alex Mutiso.
The pair were running side by side for most of the course before 31-year-old Talbi surged ahead in the closing stages and held on to win in 59:47.
He narrowly missed out on beating his personal best of 59:41.
Mutiso finished 14 seconds behind Talbi in 1:00:01.
Yohei Ikeda of Japan came third, while Marc Scott - who won the race in 2021 - was the first British athlete to finish in eighth place.
The course record of 58:56 for the men's race has stood since 2011, and was set by Martin Mathathi of Kenya.
Britain's David Weir won his 10th Great North Run title in the men's wheelchair race as he finished in 43:06, while Melanie Woods was the women's winner in 50:19.
This year's race is the 45th edition and an estimated 63,000 runners took part, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Trump’s new press ban
The president wants to keep CNN, MS NOW, and Politico out of the White House.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is escalating his fight with the media.
What happened? Trump announced he was banning three media organizations — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House, “effective immediately.”
In a Truth Social post Friday afternoon, Trump wrote that the ban was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and that other outlets would follow.
Why is Trump doing this now? We don’t know, and other than his blanket statement alleging “FAKE NEWS,” it seems like Trump doesn’t either. In the Oval Office on Friday, Trump said that “it’s really just cumulative stories of the last two years. You get sick of it.”
That complaint — “fake news” — is a long-running Trump attack that generally refers to unfavorable but true stories about him and his administration.
Can he do this? Probably not, though it might take a while for journalists to get their access back. The ban sure looks like a First Amendment violation, and also like the White House’s attempt to ban the Associated Press last year as part of a dustup over the Gulf of Mexico, which a judge ultimately blocked.
At the time, US District Court Judge Trevor McFadden, a Trump appointee, ruled that “Under the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists — be it to the Oval Office, the East Room, or elsewhere — it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints.”
What’s the big picture? Trump has been flinging around “fake news” accusations for a long time now, but his attacks on the press and other media — like late-night shows — have grown more serious in his second term.
The Pentagon, under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, banned press from its press office earlier this year and has tried to force reporters covering the building to sign a restrictive new press policy (that move was struck down in March).
Trump has also repeatedly threatened broadcast licenses for networks like ABC and NBC; last month, ABC sued over an FCC review of its licenses.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

I've spent decades testing, reviewing, and (most importantly) using different to-do list applications. It's a career, yes, but it's also a bit of an obsession.
And I think we can all admit that most of these apps are way too complicated. A to-do list is just a list. Humans have been making lists for thousands of years, long before computers existed. Paper works well, but so does a stone slate if that's what you've got handy.
It's possible that you, a modern human, absolutely need a to-do list application with bells and whistles—due dates, recurring tasks, sharing features, and maybe even an AI integration. But there's a good chance all you need is the digital equivalent of a piece of paper: A simple list of things that need to get done.
And that's what Tasks.txt, a totally free Mac app, offers. From Ukrainian programmer Yevhen Kharkivskyi, this tool is based on the todo.txt system developed by Gina Trapani. It's a complete alternative to a to-do list app that is based on a single text file.
The important thing here, though, is that it offers more than just a text file. This is a well-executed app. Open Tasks.txt and you'll see a simple list broken down into three categories: Done, Next, and Backlog.
The general idea is to use "Next" for the tasks you want to accomplish today and "Backlog" for the things you want to do later. The "Done" section is populated as you check things off, then cleared out at the beginning of every day.
It's possible to use this application using only the keyboard, which I love. Open the window and you can just start typing tasks—your cursor is already active in the text box at the bottom. Hit Enter and your task will be added either to Backlog or Next, depending on what you choose in the drop-down menu to the right of your text box. Press the Tab key to switch from the text box to your task list. You can use the arrows to change which task is currently selected. Pressing the Enter key adds a note below the name of a task, and Cmd+Enter marks a task complete. You can also move tasks up and down the list using Cmd+Up/Down.
There are no unnecessary controls or interface elements in your way. You can open this application, decide what you need to do, then get to it. And you aren’t stuck using keyboard shortcuts—using the mouse is just as intuitive, if that's what you prefer.
The to-do list is the heart of the app, but there's also an Archive and Scratchpad tab. The Archive includes every task you’ve completed in the past—everything from the Done section is moved here at the end of each day. The Scratchpad is just a blank text document you can use for keeping notes.
All of this, notably, is stored in a couple of text documents. You can find these documents in the app’s settings and open them with any text editor. It's pretty easy to look at the document and figure out what's going on.
Your task list isn't in some database in the cloud—it's on your computer, in an open, human-readable format. This simplicity means you can easily grab your tasks to use in some other application later, if that's what you want.
And Tasks.txt makes it clear that your tasks are completely private. "There is no account, no cloud sync, no telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting," the website states. "There are no servers. Nothing leaves your machine." This is a rarity in the modern age, where every piece of software is trying to hold your data hostage to sell a subscription. This alone makes this an app worth considering.
Mostly, though, I just think it's a well-implemented app that gets the basics extremely right. It won't work for everyone, sure, but it might work perfectly for you.

The US narrowly avoided boarding a Chinese ship based on an “entirely false” US intelligence report generated with the help of AI tools, according to a CNN report.
That erroneous intelligence, submitted by a US Special Operations Command analyst, suggested the Chinese ship was transporting nuclear arms program components through the Middle East, according to “four sources familiar with the episode” cited by CNN. The US military was preparing to intercept and board the ship, with air support, before officials discovered a chatbot used in generating the report had “inaccurately identified the material the ship was carrying.”
One source told CNN the AI-powered fiasco “almost started a war.”
What’s the worst that can happen?
CNN’s report said the analyst in question used a chatbot to analyze intelligence reports regarding the Chinese ship’s manifest, leading to the near-disastrous result. That chatbot “fused together open-source intelligence with secret signals intelligence in government holdings,” and that information was packaged into an intelligence report that almost set off a disastrous chain of events, according to CNN.
The near-miss is one of the more potent and consequential instances of a hallucinating AI ruining the reliability of a professional report. Since “hallucinating” became the Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year in 2023, we’ve seen prominent examples of non-fiction authors, journalists, academic researchers, judges, doctors, police departments, corporate call centers, and more getting taken in by AI tools that simply make something up when their training data doesn’t provide sufficient context. And despite some adorable attempts at “do not hallucinate” prompts, some researchers suggest that it may be impossible to prevent LLMs from hallucinating altogether.
One would hope the US military would be aware of these kinds of problems when relying on AI for analysis of intelligence reports. But the Department of Defense in January rolled out an “AI acceleration strategy” that sought to “make all appropriate data available across federated IT systems for AI exploitation, including mission systems across every service and component.”

Before you throw out your old laptop, do this first
Don't just hand your laptop to a friend or secondhand store; you need to protect your personal data.
There's a lot of value in keeping an old laptop. You can hold onto it as a backup, hand it down to a family member, use it as a media server and much more. But if your old laptop doesn't have much life left in it, you may instead decide it's time to get rid of the old machine.
Of course, you shouldn't throw an old laptop in the trash. The best options are selling or donating if it's still usable, or taking it in for safe recycling otherwise. No matter what destiny you choose for your old laptop, there are a few steps you should take first. Clearing out your files and running a factory reset are both crucial, but there's more to it. Whether you're getting rid of a MacBook or a Windows computer, make sure you do what's necessary to protect your private information and prepare the device for a new owner, if applicable.
Back up everything first
Backing up is always the important first step, even before transferring files to a new laptop. On a Windows PC, you can use Windows Backup by searching for it in the Start menu. You'll see a list of what can be backed up to OneDrive and when you last did. While convenient, its major roadblock is that free Microsoft accounts only comes with 5GB of cloud storage. You can subscribe for more if you like; another option is making a local backup to a portable HDD or SSD. While you can copy files to the drive manually, EaseUS Todo Backup's free version is a good choice for automating this. Since Windows Backup covers settings like account details and personalization features, a combination backup is smart.
For a MacBook, use Apple's Time Machine. The built-in macOS backup tool can back up everything onto a USB drive so you can recover it on another computer. Visit System Settings > General > Time Machine > Add Backup Disk, then select the storage device you have connected (ideally with at least twice the storage of your MacBook) and follow the instructions. You can also use iCloud to back up some kinds of data under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Saved to iCloud. Apple offers only 5GB of free storage, but you can subscribe for more.
Third-party backup software and cloud services can also work. As a supplement to the full backup, double-check important apps, like enabling sync in your browser so you don't lose your bookmarks. Also check the ports on your laptop to make sure you don't leave any accessories behind, like small USB dongles or SD cards.
Before you move on, sign out of all accounts and de-authorize software licenses for tools like the Adobe suite. Some licenses can only be used on a certain number of computers, so you don't want to have a phantom machine wasting one of your spots. If you're not sure whether your license can be moved to a new computer by signing into your account, copy the license or product key so you can contact the provider.
Do a proper wipe of your laptop
You're now ready to wipe the machine. While a basic factory reset is the simplest option, data you remove from a computer is still technically recoverable. Thankfully, modern versions of Windows and macOS have built-in reset tools that de-authorize your accounts, wipe the machine, reset everything and make what you had on the drive unrecoverable. Third-party software is also available if you want to make sure the drive is totally clean.
The process for wiping a Windows laptop varies by version. For Windows 11, go to Start > Settings > System > Recovery > Reset PC. Choose Remove everything, then select Cloud download or Local reinstall depending on how you want to reinstall the OS. When presented with the Additional settings page, choose Change settings and enable Clean data to securely overwrite the drive.
On Windows 10, go to Settings > Update & security > Recovery and click Get started under Reset this PC; the process is similar to Windows 11 from there. For Windows 8.1, this is under Settings > Change PC settings > Update and recovery > Recovery; click Get started under Remove everything and reinstall Windows. For Windows 7, you'll need to use bootable media, access the manufacturer's recovery partition or run a third-party tool to erase everything on the drive.
For a Mac running macOS Monterey or later, open System Settings > General > Transfer or Reset > Erase All Contents and Settings. You'll have to enter your computer password as well as your Apple ID password to sign out of that. Confirm the erasure, then the computer will sign you out of iCloud, wipe and restart.
For older Intel-based Macs, you need to first sign out of iCloud manually to remove Activation Lock; you'll find this under System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign Out or System Preferences > Apple ID > Overview > Sign Out depending on your macOS version. After that, go into Recovery Mode (hold Command + R after a restart), select Disk Utility > Continue > Erase, and choose APFS (assuming your Mac has an SSD). Finally, pick Erase Volume Group or Erase. Once it's done, if someone else will use the computer in the future, quit Disk Utility and choose Reinstall macOS to install a fresh copy.

Tiffany Teo secures Singapore's first Asian Games MMA medal
Teo guaranteed herself at least a bronze medal by advancing to the women's traditional 60kg semi-finals.
SINGAPORE: Mixed martial arts (MMA) fighter Tiffany Teo made history on Sunday (Sep 20) by securing Singapore's first medal in the sport at the Asian Games after advancing to the women's traditional 60kg semi-finals.
Teo, who is making her Asian Games debut, beat Iran's Arezou Salimighalehtaki 3-0 in their quarter-final bout.
With both losing semi-finalists awarded bronze medals, the result guarantees Teo at least a bronze and makes her Singapore's first Asian Games medallist in MMA.
The achievement comes at the first Asian Games to feature MMA in its programme.
The 36-year-old will next face India's Suchika Tariyal in the semi-finals on Monday.
Tariyal booked her spot in the last four after defeating Mongolia's Altanchimeg Baigalmaa 2-0 in her quarter-final earlier on Sunday, similarly granting India its first Asian Games MMA medal.
The winner of the fight between Teo and Tariyal will advance to the final of the event, which will be held on Tuesday.
There, she will face either Uzbekistan's Khilola Sobirova or Cambodia's Cheng Dalin, who will meet in the event's other semi-final on Monday.
MMA is one of six sports making their Asian Games debuts at Aichi-Nagoya 2026. The others are freestyle BMX, padel, surfing, teqball and virtual taekwondo.

A state funeral in Hong Kong honors Tung Chee-hwa, the city's first post-colonial leader
A state funeral was held in Hong Kong on Sunday for the city's first post-colonial leader, Tung Chee-hwa
HONG KONG -- A state funeral was held Sunday for Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader, Tung Chee-hwa, who led the city through the initial years of its transition from British rule after it was returned to China in 1997.
Chinese officials and Hong Kong political leaders attended the service, only the third state funeral in the former British colony since the 1997 handover.
Tung, a shipping magnate who was the city's chief executive from 1997 to 2005, died Sept. 8 at the age of 89. He grappled with the Asian financial crisis, SARS epidemic and public protests during his nearly eight years in office.
Flower wreaths lined the wall outside the Hong Kong Funeral Home and Tung's casket, draped in a Chinese flag, could be seen being brought out after the service in live video streamed online by Hong Kong media. The media were not allowed inside.
Shi Taifeng, a member of the Politburo of China's ruling Communist Party, and Xia Baolong, the director of China's Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office, left the funeral in a white minibus with Hong Kong's current leader, John Lee.
About 200 people were invited to the service, an attendee told Hong Kong’s South China Morning Post newspaper. Others paid condolences at three venues set up around the city.
After his death, the Chinese government described Tung as a close friend of the Communist Party and an outstanding contributor to the one-country, two systems framework that governs Hong Kong and nearby Macao, a former Portuguese colony returned to China in 1999.
Not long after Tung took office in 1997, Hong Kong’s economy was battered by a financial crisis that swept across Asia. In 2003, SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome) killed nearly 300 people in the city and dealt another blow to the economy.
The same year, an estimated half-million people took to the streets to protest the government’s plan to enact an anti-treason law that was seen as a threat to civil liberties. The government shelved the plan, and Tung resigned in 2005, citing health reasons.
The 2003 protest marked the start of years of pro-democracy protests that came to a head in 2019 and were followed by a crackdown and a Beijing-imposed national security law in 2020.
After stepping down, Tung was elected vice chairman of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, the country’s top political advisory body. He was among 42 people who received national medals and honors in 2019 for their contributions to the country.

Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern Spain, bringing some severe flooding and killing at least one person.
Storms first struck over the Castilla-La Mancha region during the afternoon before passing over Spain’s east coast, becoming very slow-moving and continuing overnight. Torrential rainfall, strong winds and large hail were reported in Valencia and Barcelona, causing widespread flooding in both cities. Weather stations west of Barcelona recorded some of the highest totals with more than 100mm (4in) of rain falling in the space of a few hours, and locally 70mm in just 30 minutes in the early hours of Thursday morning. Cars and roads were submerged, and flights were cancelled across the region.
Wednesday’s La Liga fixture between Levante and Athletic Club had to be postponed due to flooding at the Estadio Ciudad de Valencia. On Thursday rescuers found the body of a man near Olivella, west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away in the waters. Spain’s east coast is susceptible to extreme rainfall during the autumn months, as experienced in 2024, when devastating flash floods killed more than 200 people in Valencia. With the Mediterranean Sea reaching record temperatures, this is providing extra fuel and moisture to thunderstorms, making flooding more likely.
In New Jersey in the US on Sunday, the Racefaster half marathon was disrupted due to extreme rainfall and a partly submerged course. Runners had to wade through chest-deep waters at times as 50mm-100mm of rain fell. Despite the flooding, 250 people managed to finish the race. Flooding was also reported to the north-east in Connecticut and Rhode Island, where up to 190mm of rain was recorded in a 36-hour period.
Tropical Storm Dujuan, currently over the open west Pacific Ocean, will move north-west on a track towards Japan over the coming days. It is forecast to intensify into a category one typhoon on Friday. The joint typhoon warning centre is forecasting that Dujuan will skirt past the south-east coast of Japan, potentially affecting Tokyo and the surrounding areas.

Even before the latest batch of alarming AI news, a lot of Americans were souring on AI. That may be for big, existential reasons — concerns about widening inequality, mass job loss, and the still-unclear environmental impact of data centers — or for very specific, personal, everyday ones, like being forced to use a worse version of Google search.
How to be an AI minimalist
It may feel like AI is creeping into every corner of your life. Here are ways to opt out.
None of this is to say that AI cannot be a useful tool for some people some of the time. It’s just that the untested technology was thrust upon millions of people who didn’t necessarily ask for it and really seem to not like it. More than twice as many Americans distrust AI as trust it, and a growing number of people think it will have a negative impact on productivity and economic growth, according to a recent survey by Gallup and the Special Competitive Studies Project. While about half of Americans now report using chatbots, a majority also think that AI will put their personal information at risk and nearly half think it will have a negative impact on society, according to a 2026 Pew study.
“It’s being forced on users, there’s no clear way to turn it off, and it feels like this unwelcome addition to their lives,” Rory Mir of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit that defends digital privacy and free speech, told me. Mir told me. “It’s this kind of continued pattern of disrespect to users that I think is part of the pushback.”
If you want less AI in your life, opting out is not always easy. But there are things you can do to minimize your exposure.
There are ways to turn off AI features, although the process can be tedious. There are also steps you can take to prevent your data from being used to train AI models, though it’s difficult to keep all of your online data away from web scrapers.
I talked to five experts — including a computer scientist and a researcher studying AI resistance — who offered distinctive perspectives on what AI is doing to us, and who shared some simple and concrete steps you can take to push back against AI’s creep into our daily lives.
The AI that’s suddenly everywhere
In the early days, which were just a few years ago, you really had to know what you were doing if you wanted to test out AI. Now, it’s impossible to avoid.
“More and more AI use is through its integration into digital products like search, email, camera apps, and social media,” Arvind Narayanan, a computer science professor at Princeton University, told me. “It will become increasingly hard to strip these out unless one is willing to forgo digital products altogether.”
3 simple ways to engage with AI less
- Add “-ai” to Google searches to stop seeing the AI overview.
- Make your social media profiles private.
- Turn off Siri and opt out of Apple Intelligence.
What you’re specifically encountering is generative AI, and one of the most common types is a subset called large language models (LLMs), which ingest huge amounts of data and learn statistical patterns to predict and generate text. ChatGPT is powered by an LLM. The AI Overviews that sit on top of your Google search results come from an LLM. The grammar checker in your email app is likely powered by an LLM. Other subsets of generative AI include models that can produce images, video, audio, and software code.
The data that makes many of these tools work has been scraped from the open web, pirated books, and rare print books that are subsequently being destroyed. Everything from Wikipedia articles to YouTube videos has become training data for LLMs, and in order for the models themselves to get better, AI companies need more fresh data, which is in increasingly short supply. (Disclosure: Vox Media is one of several publishers that have signed partnership agreements with OpenAI. Our reporting remains editorially independent. Future Perfect is also funded in part by the BEMC Foundation, whose major funder was also an early investor in Anthropic; they don’t have any editorial input into our content.)
As a result, some of these companies are venturing into their users’ profiles to find more data. Meta, for example, sparked global outrage in 2024 when it informed some Facebook and Instagram users that it was using their public photos and text to train its AI models. Meta still does this. That your family photos or social media updates are being used to train AI to look and sound more human is, at the very least, very dehumanizing.
Generative AI, of course, is not the only type of AI that’s invisibly moving levers in your digital life. Recommendation algorithms are arguably even more inescapable. They power everything from Amazon to Netflix to Spotify and dictate what we buy, what we watch, and what we listen to. If you have trouble picking out an outfit in the morning, it might be because your brain is used to having algorithms around to help make decisions. This is also dehumanizing.
All of this — the existential risk, climate impact, the cognitive surrender — should be on your mind as you consider whether it’s worth enlisting these tools to write emails for you or to generate memes, according to Tania Duarte, founder of We and AI, a nonprofit focused on critical AI literacy.
“People are becoming increasingly aware of not just the impact on themselves but on the impact on the society they want to live in and the future that they want to have,” Duarte told me. “Is it worth all of that?”
How to minimize your AI exposure
If you’re reading this, you’re probably doing so on a smartphone or a computer. So let’s start with the assumption that you’d like to continue using devices like these.
If you’d like to minimize your exposure to AI, that presents a bit of a paradox. It’s seemingly impossible to use mainstream tech products without engaging with AI. But you can take steps to remove as much of it from your life as possible without going completely off the grid.
“You look for the spaces of agency rather than lamenting the fact that you can’t escape everything,” Dylan Orchard, a researcher at King’s College London who studies everyday resistances to AI, told me. “You can’t expect a perfect escape.”
Let’s start with the easiest options: You don’t have to use ChatGPT or Claude or Copilot. The same goes for Google Gemini and Apple Intelligence. If you’re happy with the way you access information online, save yourself the time. (Note: This will be much harder to do if you’re being required to use these tools at work or at school, so for the sake of this article, we’ll focus on the things you can control.)
Things get more complicated when you consider how your existing devices or software have recently been AI-ified. If you’re using an iPhone, for instance, you might be aware that the latest operating system comes with an updated version of Apple Intelligence, a layer of AI that does everything from summarize your notifications to power a new Siri. Earlier this year, Google launched its own version of this layer called Google Intelligence, which it says will make Android transition “from an operating system into an intelligence system.” The same push toward cramming AI into every corner is also happening on Windows 11, where Microsoft Copilot promises to be helpful.
If you were happy with your phone or laptop when it was slightly dumber, however, you can turn these features off. You can also opt out of other AI features built into your device’s operating system. Here’s a helpful guide that gets into the weeds of how to do it; it covers Apple Intelligence; Google Gemini, including AI Overviews and AI writing help in Gmail; Microsoft Copilot; Meta AI; and Samsung Galaxy AI. Turning off the AI features on Android devices is more complicated than flipping a single switch, but it can be done.
A lot of your AI exposure will happen in your web browser, though, so you should consider ways to bypass those features or switch browsers. Here’s another helpful guide that explains how to remove AI content from search results as well as AI features built into Chrome and other browsers, along with Microsoft Office. If you want a quick fix, adding “-ai” to a Google search should get rid of AI Overviews and some AI content in the search results, but none of these hacks will guarantee that you avoid AI slop altogether. Using a privacy-focused browser, like DuckDuckGo, might do a better job at it than Google, though.
When it comes to other online activities, like shopping or scrolling on social media, avoiding AI gets even harder. TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube lack a master switch that lets you opt out of all the many AI features on offer. Still, you can try to tone down the algorithmic sorting that all the apps use to serve you content by switching to a chronological feed or removing suggested content from your feed. (Try tapping the Instagram logo in the app and then hit “Following” to see just the accounts you follow.)
Unfortunately, once you dig into the various user agreements and privacy policies, you’ll find that it’s very difficult to avoid AI exposure on social media platforms. If you’re posting publicly, you should assume your content is being used to train that company’s AI models. (You can keep some of your data away from Meta’s crawlers by setting your Facebook or Instagram account to private. X also allows you to opt out of having your data used for training its AI.) If you want to turn off video summaries on Instagram Reels, too bad. You can’t. If you want to turn off comment summaries on Facebook, you’ll have to go four menus deep in your settings to find the right switch. The most straightforward way to avoid being used as training data is to stop using these apps entirely. Or at least stop posting your own content, which is easier said than done, but worth considering if you really want to resist the AI takeover.
There’s a programming term that describes the inundation of AI features and slog of opting out: “user-hostile.” It’s a play on the term “user-friendly,” and it describes software that values the company’s priorities over the end users. You may love AI, although that’s doubtful if you’ve read this far. If it drives you crazy, though, you should feel at least a little bit empowered to know that there’s a way to reclaim the experience you had and loved without AI — or to use AI on your own terms.
“Ultimately, I think the important thing for folks to keep in mind is that AI is just a tool,” said Mir from EFF, “and it makes sense to want control over your own tools, including the option to not use a tool if it’s not right for you.”
It’s frustrating that we have to deal with this at all, if only because most of us did not ask for our cyber existences to be sullied by untested tech. But it’s actually refreshing to consider that, because of a never-ending onslaught of annoying features, AI might actually discourage us from using social media so much.
If anything, the extent to which we feel the need to flee from AI also reflects our craving for something real, that makes us feel more connected and more human. So when AI summaries interrupt your time on Instagram, consider texting your friends a handful of photos from your week or calling them on the phone. If you’ve finally seen one too many AI slop videos on TikTok, put on a classic movie or TV show.
At the very least, put down your phone and take a walk outside; your attention span will thank you for it. Yes, your individual rejection of AI might be a drop in the bucket for these huge tech companies, but that doesn’t mean it’s not worth doing anyway.

Why Prince Harry and Meghan face more challenges after their return to the U.K.
New issues for non-working members of Royal Family include concerns over security
Public or private? Personal or officially royal?
In ways, it can get confusing — there was Prince Harry, smiling for the cameras that often capture his comings and goings as he arrived at a charitable event Thursday night in London.
His attendance at an awards ceremony connected to the Invictus Games, which he founded for wounded and ill service members, garnered headlines. Media reports noted that it was his first appearance in public since he and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, returned to the U.K. from California with their two children late last month.
Still, in the past few days, it has also been made clear — via a letter from Buckingham Palace — that he and Meghan remain non-working members of the Royal Family.
"In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests," the letter stated.
The missive from the palace and all the media attention it garnered in recent days are a stark reminder that issues that arose when Harry and Meghan stepped back from official duties in 2020 remain front and centre with their return to Britain.
The letter affirms that King Charles agrees with his late mother, Queen Elizabeth, that there can't be members of the Royal Family “who are half in and half out, especially in the 21st century,” Toronto-based royal historian Carolyn Harris said in an interview.
At the beginning of Elizabeth’s reign, she was “quite inclusive” in terms of bringing in members of her extended family to carry out royal duties, Harris said.
But times — and public expectations — have changed.
“In the current climate, when there's a lot of scrutiny of how taxpayers’ money is being spent … the emphasis now is on a small, streamlined Royal Family and for there to be a clear divide between those who are working members of the Royal Family and those who are not,” Harris said.
The letter — particularly the timing of its release — seemed to catch Harry and Meghan off guard, and was seen by some royal observers as a “brutal put-down” for the couple.
The line “has been drawn in the sand quite clearly,” Chandrika Kaul, a professor of modern history at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, said in an interview.
“The palace … has issued statements very clearly saying that if Harry and Meghan wish to do whatever they wish to do in terms of charity work or other engagements, they're doing so in their own capacity as private individuals,” she said.
“They are not representing the Royal Family or the monarchy.”
Harris sees parallels between Harry and Meghan’s return to the U.K. and their departure six years ago.
“As in 2020, Harry and Meghan might have thought making a major life change is going to lead to certain decisions unfolding in their favour, and instead there are challenges.”
Six years ago, one initial challenge was whether Harry and Meghan might, as they seemed to hope, essentially be part-time working royals while also pursuing private, commercial interests. The answer from the Queen ultimately was a clear “No.”
This time, one challenge has been around security, an issue that has been of particular concern and spawned a previous, unsuccessful legal challenge from Harry. Now, however, the U.K. government committee that oversees tax-funded security for public figures and royalty will reconsider the level of police protection for the couple.
Earlier this week, word also emerged that Harry and Meghan’s children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, were changing schools, reportedly because of security concerns raised over traffic and the length of the commute from their home.
“Prince Harry may be hoping that a decision will be made in his favour regarding security now that they are back in the United Kingdom,” said Harris.
“But there is a long history of Harry and Meghan making a major life change, but the details are still to be arranged, and that can lead to tensions on all sides.”
- Charles confirms Harry and Meghan to remain non-working royals after their return to U.K.
- THE ROYAL FASCINATORThe 'shockwaves' of Prince Harry and Meghan's return to the U.K.
Overall, says Kaul, attention and reaction to Harry and Meghan’s return has been “relatively muted.”
“It has been noticed and covered and discussed on national mainstream media, but … the popular media haven't gone berserk over the impact.”
She also sees the potential for Harry to carve out a new identity now that he’s back in the U.K.
“There has always been and there continues to be a great deal of public affection and regard for Harry. I don't think that's ever gone away.”
The King and AI
Inside the restored 18th-century Palladian country house that serves as the home of his charitable foundation, King Charles signalled both the hopes and risks that surround a very 21st-century concern.
“AI is already showing its immense capacity to improve and save life — for example, in the field of life sciences and medicine,” Charles told leaders of some of the world’s leading AI firms who accepted his invitation to come to Dumfries House in southwestern Scotland on Thursday.
“Yet, those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities — perhaps even to take life. In this regard, if I may say so, there seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways.
“Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late?”
Charles’s convening of AI leaders is in keeping with both longstanding interests the monarchy has had in technology and his own efforts to bring people together on issues of the day.
“There's always these intersections between royalty and new technology, whether it's Queen Victoria embracing photography and then right at the end of her reign, film, or Queen Elizabeth II embracing video conferencing during the COVID-19 pandemic,” Harris said.
But there was more than that at play on Thursday, Harris suggested.
“For King Charles III, it's clear that he sees his role as King is to bring people together in the hope that solutions to complicated issues may be found.”
Charles does that from a unique position, Harris suggested.
“It's part of that unifying role of the monarch, the ability to bring people together. Anyone who receives an invitation to Buckingham Palace is likely to accept.”
Kaul also saw the focus on AI as a reflection of some of Charles’s longstanding interests and perspectives.
“It testifies to the King's lifelong commitment not just to technology, but to this kind of harmonious balance between nature and human beings and his deep interest in civilization and the continuation of culture.”
Charles’s actions also reflected an effort to bring people together in a way that differed from how his mother might have approached issues of the day.
“I think there is a greater sense that it is Charles who's driving the agenda,” Kaul said.
“The Queen's way of handling it was always to clearly weigh up the issues, but … particularly in her later years, [she] seemed to … put the royal mark of approval on an agenda rather than necessarily take a leading role in pushing an item onto the agenda.”
In his speech on Thursday, Charles posed two questions:
“First, how can we harness the benefits of AI, with safety at its heart? And, second, how can we build international co-operation and consensus to achieve this, so no nation is left behind, but the human race is left in place?”
Humanity, he said, “must remain sacred.”
“The decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations. And so, the task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world. As we embrace what is new, we must not lose what is timeless.”
Coming together to prevent suicide
Prince William was doing some convening of his own the other day on one of his key charitable priorities when he met with star athletes and leaders of sports organizations.
Along with Catherine, Princess of Wales, William was on hand at the Everton Football Club to launch a suicide prevention initiative.
“Sport creates belonging. It creates identity. It creates connection. And those connections matter,” William said.
“When somebody is struggling, often it is not a professional who first notices. It is a friend. A coach. A colleague. A teammate. Someone who sees a change. Someone who asks if everything is all right. Someone who starts a conversation. And that conversation could make all the difference.”

The suicide prevention toolkit launched by William aims to help people across sport have “the confidence to recognize warning signs, start supportive conversations and connect individuals with help before they reach crisis point,” Kensington Palace said.
In the initiative, Harris saw a reflection of the interests of several members of the Royal Family.
“We see a bit of Prince Philip's influence in terms of the interest in sport, but also William and Catherine, and at one time Prince Harry as well, were all very concerned with mental health and mental health initiatives.”
There is also the concern William’s mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, had in marginalized people and making “them feel loved and accepted,” Harris said, along with the concern his father, King Charles, has had in youth and opportunities for them.
A brother's claim and a palace response
The response came quickly, by royal standards.
Not long after the first headlines emerged online Wednesday about claims the brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, is making in a book to be released this coming week, Buckingham Palace had a statement of its own.
In a published excerpt of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, Charles Spencer claims that King Charles said his former wife would soon be forgotten after her death.
Spencer says he told Charles that Diana would not have wanted their sons, William and Harry, then 15 and 12, to walk behind her coffin in the funeral procession. He claims Charles told him: "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough." He also accuses Charles of having "contempt" for his ex-wife.
The palace responded later Wednesday with a statement of its own.
"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said.
Harris sees parallels in that statement to another high-profile reaction from the palace.
“In common with Queen Elizabeth II's statement that ‘recollections may vary’ after Harry and Meghan were interviewed by Oprah Winfrey, King Charles III is refusing to allow Earl Spencer to have the last word on circumstances concerning the Royal Family,” she said.
“The King has his own memories of the days following Diana's death and they are not the same as those of Earl Spencer.”
Diana died after a car crash in Paris in 1997.

Nearly 30 years after her death, she continues to captivate and draw headlines, and says Harris, her legacy continues to be debated and contested.
“Diana combined glamour with vulnerability and people from a variety of social and cultural backgrounds saw themselves in aspects of her experiences even though she was born into the aristocracy and married a prince,” said Harris.
“Recent films, television series, plays and novels have revived interest in Diana for a new generation who remember the princess through popular culture portrayals rather than historical events.”
Royally quotable

— King Charles, in a message where he expressed his admiration for those who helped tackle wildfires across the U.K. this summer.
