Srinagar, Sep 20: PDP president Mehbooba Mufti on Sunday urged Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah to take up with the Centre the issue of converting the Salamabad Trade Facilitation Centre near the Line of Control at Uri into a tourism facility.
“The Salamabad Trade Facilitation Centre was built to bridge divided families, revive trade and heal wounds, not be reduced to a mere tourist site. It came at a heavy price, with many PDP workers losing their lives during the Muzaffarabad Chalo rally. I urge @OmarAbdullah to take this up with the GOI and restore its original purpose,” Mehbooba posted on X.
The former chief minister said there was a need to reopen routes connecting Kashmir to the outside world.
“Kashmir needs more bridges to the outside world, not the shutting of those that connect us,” she added.
The Salamabad Trade Facilitation Centre was built in 2008 after India and Pakistan agreed to a barter system of trade between Jammu and Kashmir and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.
Cross-LoC trade was stopped by the Centre in April 2019 after authorities alleged that the route was being used for terror funding, smuggling of illegal weapons and narcotics, and circulation of counterfeit currency.
Last week, the tourism department took over the trade facilitation centre as the facility had remained idle for the past seven years.

Soon after the news of Hindutva fanatic Swatantra Bhardwaj getting interim bail for three weeks went out, a 1.16-minute video of him got viral, in which he is with another person who boasts about Bhardwaj’s release and compares him with a lion on the hunt. Bhardwaj then threatens those who had attacked his supporters while he was in detention. He says (in Hindi), “You are like insects.. why did you target my brothers? if they wanted they could have beaten you up.. but for some reason, they followed the law… I will not do anything to you.. tell your father Chandrashekhar Azad (Bhim Army chief whom Bhardwaj compares to Ravana), that this Brahmin lion (referring to himself) will avenge the attack. It is an open challenge…”
Bhardwaj faces criminal charges under Sections 115(2), 126(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with provisions of the POCSO Act and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and an attempt-to-murder charge for an alleged assault on the father of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Nishu Azaad. On September 7, he had been sent to 14-day judicial remand.
An X user named Gen-Z of India shared the said video on September 17 and wrote (in Hindi), “As soon as Swatantra Bharadwaj stepped out, he started up again, even though the court had imposed the condition that he would not make any grandstanding statements in the media, but listen to what he is saying.” The post has received close to 1 million views. (Archive)
भारतीय न्याय व्यवस्था एक बार फिर से फ़ैल हो गयी है…
स्वतंत्र भारद्वाज बाहर आते ही फ़िर से शुरू हो गया है, जबकि कोर्ट ने शर्त रखी है कि मीडिया में कोई बयानबाज़ी नहीं करेगा लेकिन यह तो क्या कह रहा है वह सुनिए। pic.twitter.com/pBPNKeQtRs
— Gen-Z of India (@GenZ_of_India_) September 17, 2026
This post was reshared by several influential and verified handles, including Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra, journalist Vir Sanghvi, CJP leader Ratna Singh and others, making it go viral. Others like film writer Darab Farooqi and verified X user @tanmoyofc shared the video as well.
Media outlets Prabhat Khabar and The Mooknayak published reports on the video presenting it as recorded after Bhardwaj’s release on bail in the assault case.
Fact Check
First of all, we found that India Today posted a video on September 17 stating that Bhardwaj came out of Tihar Jail around 9.45 pm on that day (September 17). The caption of India Today’s Instagram post said, “Although he was granted bail two days ago, he was released around 9:45 pm after the remaining procedures were completed. He immediately ran towards a taxi and left without speaking to the media.”
View this post on Instagram
Several other media outlets reported that Bhardwaj walked out of jail late at night on Thursday, September 17, and rushed into a car avoiding media persons.
Next, a reverse image search with some key frames from the viral video led us to a Facebook post and a YouTube video from September 7. This makes it clear that the video was not recorded after Bhardwaj’s release on September 17. Check the screenshots in the gallery below:
By scraping our database of active Right-wing vigilantes, we then identified the other individual in the video as Vaibhaw Kumar alias Vaibhaw Pandey. While going through his Instagram timeline, we found the now-viral video uploaded on June 26.
According to another video posted by Vaibhaw, Bhardwaj was detained on June 22 for threatening CJP leaders at Jantar Mantar.
To sum up, the viral video of Hindutva fanatic and attempt-to-murder accused Swatantra Bhardwaj threatening Chandrashekhar Azad was not recorded after his release on interim bail on September 17. It was shared on social media by another Hindutva vigilante on June 26.

The pros and cons of using wired vs. wireless Xbox controllers
Wired controllers are convenient, but wired gamepads require less maintenance.
I'm an Xbox gamer who battles with dead batteries pretty often. I've stuck with a pair of rechargeable AAs for years, and while I could hook up my standard-issue Xbox controllers to my console via USB, I never do. There's a reason the Xbox (and most consoles of the last few decades) ships with wireless-by-default controllers: convenience.
Now, wired Xbox controllers do have some advantages. There aren't any batteries to worry about, and sync issues aren't a concern either. Next time you're looking to buy a gamepad, think through these pros and cons of wireless and wired Xbox controllers.
Going wired won't guarantee less input lag
Competitive gamers want the fastest response times from a controller, so there's minimal delay between what they do and what happens on-screen. Connecting wirelessly introduces latency, so you'd think this area would be a slam dunk for wired controllers. Surprisingly, it isn't that clear-cut.
Polling Rate Test reports similar polling rates (how often the controller reports its state to the console or PC) for Microsoft's Xbox controllers when used over USB and through the Xbox Wireless Adapter. The latter is an accessory that uses the same proprietary connection protocol of Xbox consoles to connect the controller to a PC. Each polling rate is around 125Hz, which means maximum input delay of about eight milliseconds. In a game running at 60fps, that's roughly half a frame of delay, which is not perceptible to most people.
This isn't a measurement of the entire delay between pressing a button and seeing something happen, though. On the Xbox Series X and Series S, Microsoft uses Dynamic Latency Input to send your latest button presses just before the game needs them, helping it respond sooner.
It's different if you're connecting over Bluetooth (to a PC or phone/tablet). Polling Rate Test estimates you'll see an extra four to eight milliseconds of delay, but this will also depend on your setup (like how many other wireless devices are nearby). If your controller feels slow to respond, it's worth trying a wired connection. A cable won't get rid of input lag completely, but it can help if a wireless connection is unreliable in your situation.
Your display and the game you're playing also matter, as frame rates and game performance can cause a delay with what you're seeing on-screen.
Wired controllers won't leave you scrambling for batteries
As mentioned, I'm always switching out pairs of rechargeable AA batteries when I'm gaming. There's never a good time for your controller to run out of power, unless you've just finished playing. It's a minor inconvenience when playing a single-player title, but can completely interrupt an online match.
A wired controller deals with this problem entirely. You don't need batteries since it receives power over USB. There's no need to think about when to recharge, and there's no ongoing cost to replace your batteries. Any suitable USB data cable should work, so you might want to keep one around in case the batteries run out.
If you prefer to use a wireless controller, this will take a bit more planning. Microsoft estimates you can play with a standard controller for up to 40 hours using AA batteries, but this will depend on the batteries, as well as whether you're using any accessories like a headset or the plug-in keyboard. Keeping a pair of rechargeable AAs on hand to swap in quickly is a good compromise.
Microsoft also has another solution you can try: the Xbox Rechargeable Battery. You place the battery pack where AA batteries normally go, then use the included 9-foot USB-C cable to charge it. The cable is long enough that you can plug it into your console if battery life gets low during a session. It's a good alternative to rechargeable batteries since those need their own charger.
Wireless controllers give you more freedom to move
The impracticalities of a wired controller only pose a problem in certain setups, so think about where you use your Xbox controller most. At a desk, you're probably not expecting people to walk in front of you, so a cable doesn't create a trip hazard or something for children to tug at.
In a living room, a wire has a better chance of becoming an obstacle. Think about cable distance: how much length do you need to sit comfortably with some slack for movement? With too much slack, wires can wrap around furniture or get caught when you get up and forget about them. Running a cable under a rug or along a baseboard can help, but that's not always possible.
With a wireless controller, you don't have to plan around any of these worries. You can sit anywhere in the room where you can comfortably see the screen, and can easily swap your controllers around if you're playing with friends and family.
Wired controllers can be simpler and cheaper
There are plenty of cheaper third-party Xbox controllers that only feature wired support. Basic wired models from brands like PowerA and PDP make sense if you're looking for an affordable spare. The advantages of wired pads can be even more relevant for a controller that you don't use often. For instance, there's no need to worry about dead batteries in a controller that has sat for months when a friend comes over for split-screen a few times per year.
Third-party controllers may also come with tweaks to the official Xbox layout. For instance, they can include extra customizable buttons on the back that handle actions you'd typically use your thumb for. Others, like the GameSir G7 SE, feature upgraded Hall effect thumbsticks, using magnetic sensors instead of conventional sticks that can start to drift over time.
Compatibility isn't guaranteed, even with an Xbox-style button layout, so check that before you buy Xbox accessories. Some models might work wirelessly on a PC, but are limited to USB connections for an Xbox console.
The pros and cons that matter most depend on your setup. For most people, the latency when connected to an Xbox wirelessly isn't noticeable, and the convenience of avoiding wires is great. If you're playing on a PC, opting for a wired connection sidesteps the increased latency of Bluetooth. The key differentiator is whether you want the freedom to move or prefer a wired connection that won't leave you swapping batteries. The only way to know for sure is to try it out and see how well a cabled controller fits your setup.

Inside Somaliland: How Berbera Port is central to the Red Sea's power struggle
Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi"Berbera is the heart of Somaliland," Jama Mohamed Ahmed, the commercial director of DP World in the Horn of Africa, tells me by way of introduction.
We meet outside the glistening, reflective glass office building that is the UAE logistics giant's headquarters in the Horn of Africa, in a country only recognised by Israel and closely aligned with the Emirates.
The building could be any sterile corporate office in middle America or the Gulf; besides that, there is the large sign at the entrance with a wad of green leaves crossed out in red, titled: "No Kat" - the stimulant leaf chewed across the Horn of Africa and Southern Arabia.
Of course, Berbera's importance ripples far beyond Somaliland.
For centuries, the port has been an entry point to Africa and entrepôt between the near and far East. Its importance was documented as early as the 1st century by an unknown Greek-speaking traveller in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a historic account of the region's ancient trading ports.

Malao, as Berbera was then called, was a "peaceable market-town" where copper, cloth, gold coins and glass were imported from India, and frankincense, myrrh, and cinnamon were exported to Arabia, along with some slaves.
Today, Berbera sits at the centre of a raging geopolitical and economic battle to dominate the wider Red Sea. Pick a war, and Berbera could well be one of its flashpoints.
Across the Gulf of Aden, Yemen's Houthis are warily watching Israel and the UAE entrench themselves at a military base here. Meanwhile, to the south, Somalia, flush with new arms from Turkey, sees Berbera typifying the independent ambitions of Somalilanders which need to be stamped out.
But for Ahmed, Berbera is all about jobs. DP World is owned by the Dubai government. Its $45m investment here in 2016 transformed the decaying port, which now employs 1,350 people, he tells me.
Arriving from the West on a desert highway, Berbera announces itself beyond the sandy haze and acacia trees with a bevvy of ship-to-shore gantries rising like phalanxes over dozens of white fuel storage tanks. This is a one-business town.
Ahmed is tall and lean. I see a little of Yemen in his sharp features. They remind me of the mixing and mingling between East Africa and Southern Arabia. He wears pressed grey slacks and a striped button-down, which I find common among Somaliland's growing professional class.
Walking me into his air-conditioned office, Ahmed tells me that Somalis trained by DP World in Berbera are going to Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, to work at the berths that DP World and Abu Dhabi Ports Group took a stake in three years ago.
"We are now exporting knowledge," he says proudly. "Before DP World came, everything at the port was done manually; we even used to carry wheelbarrows of cash in on payday. From software to physical infrastructure, there have been huge improvements."
The port embodies how the UAE is expanding its influence across East Africa - filling the void left by the US, Russia and even China. More than other corners of the Red Sea region, however, Somaliland was ripe for the UAE.
18 days sailing from China
My journey to Berbera started in Jijiga, the growing capital of Ethiopia’s Somali region. From the Ethiopian border to the coast, the drive was smooth as stone along a 250-kilometre highway built by the UAE and guarded casually, but professionally, by Somaliland’s UAE-trained military.
Signs emblazoned with the UAE's flag dotted the highway unobtrusively, but appeared just enough to remind travellers who made this infrastructure possible. Just outside Berbera is a boarding school donated by the Gulf state.
To ensure the quickest journey to the Gulf of Aden possible, the UAE even built a bypass around Hargeisa, Somaliland’s traffic-ridden capital, to accommodate lorries.
Somaliland is a former British protectorate. The empire's colonial legacy here was lighter than in places like Egypt or India. Somaliland was home to the famed Camel Corps, in which a handful of British officers administered tribal law, called Xeer, and ensured the provisioning of Aden - a critical refuelling station across the Gulf-with livestock.
In 1960, Somaliland won its independence, five days before neighbouring Somalia - which had been colonised by Italy.
The two united to form the Somali Republic, but millions of Somalis in Ethiopia, Kenya and Djibouti - a former French colony - were left out of the union.
From the start, the two territories suffered from an uneasy coexistence that culminated in Somali ruler Mohamed Siad Barre overseeing a military onslaught against Somaliland in the late 1980s.
Somaliland declared its independence in 1991 after a decade of war, escaping the civil war and instability that later engulfed Somalia. But until Israel's January 2026 diplomatic deal, the breakaway republic went unrecognised. The UAE's readiness to invest in Somaliland gave it an outsized role here, and with commercial ties have come a military footprint.
In 2017, the UAE established a military base at Berbera.
Recent satellite imagery shared by open-source analysts suggests the UAE has expanded its presence at the city's airport with new surface-to-air-missile sites, radar facilities and hangars. The UAE is also building a naval facility a few kilometres away from the commercial port. The construction has coincided with rising tensions not just between the UAE and Saudi Arabia, but also between Israel and the Houthis.
The US-Israeli war on Iran hangs heavy over Berbera. Ahmed has felt its impact.
"Our transshipment business with Jebel Ali, Salalah and Colombo suffered," he said, listing the big ports of the UAE, Oman and Sri Lanka. "The last port we had going was Jeddah, but that stopped with the Houthi attacks," he said.
But many in East Africa see the war creating new opportunities for Berbera because of the need for alternative trade corridors.
"The Persian Gulf is vulnerable. Ships there are trapped. The logistics aren't dependable. Business will come to the Red Sea," one well-informed businessman in Addis Ababa with port interests told me before I left for Somaliland.
Ahmed agreed. "All the cargo coming from East Asia was transshipped to Gulf ports," he said, using the industry term for when cargo is unloaded at one port before being sent to its final destination. "Now, they can come to Berbera. We are just 18 days sailing from China."
This kind of thinking offers one case for why Dubai diversified its port empire beyond the Gulf. But DP World’s commercial involvement in Berbera emerged alongside shifting security priorities.
'The UAE filled a vacuum'
The year before the UAE and Somaliland inked their port deal, neighbouring Djibouti evicted DP World and Emirati troops stationed in the country. At the time, the UAE was allied with Saudi Arabia, and used Djibouti as a base to wage war against Yemen’s Houthis.
Somaliland and Djibouti are decades-old rivals. The former French colony has been controlled since 1999 by Ismail Omar Guelleh, a wily Somali politician who has used Djibouti's strategic position to rake in rents in return for port access. China and the US both have military bases there. Landlocked Ethiopia pays Djibouti roughly $2bn a year to access the sea.
Somaliland saw a window of opportunity.
"Security and investment would go hand-in-hand," Bashe Omar, Somaliland's former ambassador to the UAE, who negotiated the 2016 port deal, said.
I met Bashe in Hergaisa to better understand Somaliland's motivations. He has a sonorous British accent, a trimmed goatee and a shaved head. He came to our meeting in an elegant ultramarine colored jellabiyad.
"We weren't looking for a one-sided agreement with the UAE. We wanted a partner," he said.
I asked Omar why Somaliland gravitated to the UAE. After all, its closer Gulf neighbour is Saudi Arabia, which purchases most of its livestock - a critical export and source of revenue for the government in Hargeisa.
"Until Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia was very inward. The UAE filled the vacuum," he said, referring to the Saudi Arabian crown prince.
Saudi Arabia joined Egypt, Turkey and other Muslim states condemning Israel's January 2026 recognition of Somaliland. Bashe told me that Somaliland wants good ties to Riyadh.
"Saudi Arabia is discussing their Red Sea security. I don't think their interests are served betting on Mogadishu. The Saudis' historic ties have always been with Berbera," he said.
Saudi Arabia's Hijaz region has centuries-old links to Berbera, but Riyadh reacted quickly to condemn Israel's December 2026 recognition of Somaliland, unlike the UAE.
Riyadh criticised the move for entrenching "unilateral separatist measures". Since the US-Israeli war on Iran, Saudi Arabia has signed a mutual defence pact with Turkey, Somalia's main foreign backer.
Berbera has certainly come in handy for the UAE in its increasingly hot rivalry with Saudi Arabia.
Abu Dhabi has used the airport as a stopover for flights carrying military equipment to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Reuters reported in December 2024. The RSF is battling Sudan’s military, which is backed by Egypt, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Earlier this year, the UAE evacuated its ally and leader of Yemen's Southern separatist movement, Aidarus al-Zubaidi, to Berbera, after Saudi Arabia attacked the group.
Berbera sits at such a strategic intersection that it lends itself as a bargaining chip.
The explorer Richard Francis Burton once came here in 1854 scouting for the East India Company. In his classic travelogue, First Footsteps in East Africa, Burton extolled the virtues of Berbera, which he christened “the emporium of East Africa” over Aden. Burton noted its “salubrious climate, abundance of sweet water…[and] excellent port”, although he would later take a javelin to the face in Berbera during a fight with Somali warriors.
Berbera's Somali rulers saw its appeal, too. As early as 1979, Said Barre offered the US access to the Soviet Union’s former naval and air base at Berbera after Moscow cast him aside as a proxy in favour of Ethiopia. The US came to Berbera in the mid-1980s, revamping its 15,000-foot airport runway - the largest in Africa.
While Berbera’s military value has grown, it’s questionable how much the port is earning its keep in DP World's portfolio.
'Emporium of the East'
For DP World, Berbera is a gateway to the increasingly arable and industrialising southern region of Ethiopia, Africa’s second-largest country.
“Berbera is designed to be the port for southern Ethiopia,” the businessman in Addis Ababa told me.
In January 2024, Somaliland and Ethiopia signed a sweeping deal granting landlocked Ethiopia a 50-year lease on a swath of Somaliland’s coast.
In exchange for a naval base and access to Berbera, Addis Ababa agreed to recognise Somaliland.
The agreement would have been a boon for DP World. Thanks to the UAE’s investments, the port's container capacity is 500,000 TEUs, logistics terminology for half a million twenty-foot containers. Its capacity to handle bulk cargo is two million tonnes.
But the deal was never implemented, and the port is operating at roughly 30 percent capacity, Ahmed told me.
Addis Ababa's move to recognise Somaliland sparked ferocious pushback from Mogadishu, which threatened to expel Ethiopian troops based in Somalia fighting al- Shabab. Egypt also mobilised against a deal that would give its longtime rival access to the Red Sea.
Turkey, which has extensive military and economic ties with Somalia, intervened and negotiated a climbdown for Ethiopia, which it has sold drones to.
Ahmed took me on a tour of the port.
We drove past men in safety vests, muscle shirts, and Macawis, colourful fabrics wrapped around their waists. Despite the sweltering late-summer heat and humidity, the men worked diligently. In 2023, the World Bank ranked Berbera as the most efficient port in sub-Saharan Africa.
Grain from Russia was being bagged from one vessel for a final truck shipment to Ethiopia and South Sudan. Containers from China destined for Egypt were being unloaded before a new vessel arrived to take them onwards. Workers unloaded Indian sugar cane and Malaysian wood for Somaliland's domestic market.
Ethiopia's quest for port access remains unfulfilled. Ahmed is confident the port will live up to its potential.
"All the infrastructure is here. It's only a matter of time," he said.
Meanwhile, the UAE has a new ally in Israel to deepen military cooperation in Berbera.
"That's the base over there," my driver said, after we passed the columned British colonial villas and Ottoman mosque on the city's outskirts - reminders of Berbera's old rulers.
Back in Hergaisa, when I told one Somaliland elder that I visited Berbera, he ruminated wistfully. "Our traders once went all the way to Nairobi from Berbera. Now everything is compartmentalised."
Leaving Berbera, I could feel its untapped potential. Ethiopia is close to the UAE and Israel. It has no qualms about Somaliland's diplomatic deal with the former. But I wondered whether Somaliland's decision to establish diplomatic relations with Israel only made it more isolated in the wider region.
The path is wide open to an Israeli base here. The Somalilanders make no secret of their wish to deepen defence ties.
"I would support a base for both the US and Israel in Berbera because it would make Somalia think twice," Bashe said.
Berbera has seen so many foreign powers come and go. I asked Bashe about the risks of the US or Israel entrenching themselves at the port.
"If America came to Berbera and attacked the Houthis, for example, the Houthis would retaliate. So if they use Berbera for that, it should be in exchange for recognition," he said.
For the foreseeable future, Berbera's commercial prospects will remain subservient to geopolitics.

Rapists could face life sentences and lawyers would be prevented from asking humiliating questions of victim-survivors under a suite of Victorian Labor pre-election commitments designed to reduce violence against women.
The premier, Ben Carroll, on Sunday announced an election commitment to legislate a new form of manslaughter covering cases in which a person takes their own life as a result of family violence, as well as a new offence covering perpetrators abandoning a victim in need of medical care.
The state government also plans to change the law to let courts consider patterns of sexual abuse as evidence at trial and stop barristers using “humiliating and invasive questioning techniques” in court.
“I’m sick of Victoria’s courts and defence barristers putting victims on trial,” Carroll told reporters on Sunday.
The maximum penalty for persistent family violence intervention order breaches would also be doubled to 10 years’ jail under Labor’s pitch.
The government said the two new offences would close “loopholes” that allow perpetrators to “slip through the cracks in the justice system and walk free”.
The government has also committed to increasing the maximum penalty for rape from 25 years to life imprisonment and upping the maximum penalty for every other serious sexual offence by five years. The maximum penalty for persistent breaches of family violence intervention orders would also double from five years’ imprisonment to 10.
It will also make the standard sentence for the murder of a current or former partner 30 years – up from 25.
The proposed offence criminalising the abandonment of victims in need of medical care responds to recommendations made by the coroner after the deaths of Belinda Jones and Narelle Simmons.
Jones, 40, died on the floor of her Maryborough home in July 2023 after her partner left her there overnight and then waited two hours to call an ambulance after waking to find her cold and not breathing.
Jones had succumbed to treatable bacterial infections and sepsis, which a hospital failed to diagnose during an emergency presentation days earlier. Her partner was not charged with any offence in relation to her death.
In her findings published last month, the state coroner, Liberty Sanger, said: “In my view, the act of abandoning a victim of family violence requiring medical attention is an act of family violence, that instils fear in the victim and affirms a perpetrator’s control over the victim.”
Simmons, 42, died in October 2021 after her partner admitted to punching her twice in the face and elbowing her once in the back of the head before leaving her Cranbourne home.
Her body was found nine days later after her daughter requested a welfare check. Sanger was unable to determine whether she died immediately after the assault or hours or days later.
Her partner – whom the coroner said had 18 previous family violence victims – pleaded guilty to common assault and failing to report a reportable death. He was sentenced to five months’ imprisonment and a 12-month community corrections order.
The government’s announcement comes after a week of crime-focused election commitments from Carroll, including creating a new police training facility in Melbourne’s western suburbs and the introduction of Jack’s Law, which would give police and protective services officers the power to stop and search people for knives using handheld metal detectors.
“I’m a tough-on-crime premier – and that means being tough on family and sexual violence,” Carroll said in a statement before Sunday’s announcement.
“We must act on the violence that is killing a Victorian woman every two weeks.”
The Coalition last year committed to Jack’s Law and also have plans to expand adult sentencing for youth offenders, increase police numbers and split the existing court of appeal into two separate entities, if elected in November.

The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas announced on Saturday that Biometric Aadhaar Authentication (BAA) will be mandatory for domestic LPG customers for them to book refills at regulated selling price with applicable subsidy starting 1 October, 2026.
There are 27.43 crore active consumers, out of which around 89.9 per cent have already completed the process, the ministry said.
Those who have completed the authentication process will not need to take any other action and they will continue to receive refills as before.
For consumers who have not completed BAA, subsidised refill booking at the regulated retail selling price will be enabled once authentication is completed.
1. The person who delivers your LPG cylinder can do the BAA on the spot on the OMC phone application.
2. You can also visit the LPG distributor's office where the authentication process can be carried out.
3. Customers can also opt to do the process themselves. Customers of Indane can use the IndianOil ONE app. Bharatgas customers will have to use the HelloBPCL app, HP PAY is the app for HP Gas customers. If you wish to understand what is the process to complete self e-KYC, there are tutorial videos on the PMUY portal.
If someone is unwilling or unable to complete the BAA, they will continue to receive LPG, but the choice for the same will have to be registered through the digital channels of the OMCs, which include consumer portals, mobile apps, WhatsApp chatbots and IVRS.
These customers, however, will not receive any subsidy, and will have to pay as per market prices when it comes to 5 kg or 10 kg cylinders, subject to local availability, the ministry has said.
The government has said that BAA has become essential in order to ensure subsidised LPG reaches those customers who are genuine and eligible. This will also prevent the diversion of domestic LPG for commercial as well as industrial purposes while removing duplicate or ineligible connections.
The ministry said the implicit subsidy on a 14.2 kg domestic LPG cylinder was around ₹210 in September, compared with ₹721 in June. To keep domestic LPG affordable, the government is providing OMC compensation of ₹30,000 crore during FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27.
The initial deadline for authentication was set as 30 June, but was extended several times, with the final deadline being 14 September. Now the government has said it will be mandatory beyond 1 October.

Ghaziabad merchants unwilling to accept UPI from Oct 15 over new 0.4% MDR rule
As per the new rules, Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI payments above ₹2,000 will attract a 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate
Days after the guidelines related to the 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) payments above ₹2,000 were issued, the traders and associations in Ghaziabad are concerned lot and contemplating action starting October 15.
Sanjay Bindal, a grocery shop owner in Vijay Nagar’s sector-9, has put up a poster at his shop that said that he will not accept UPI payments from customers starting October 15.
“I have put up a poster stating that I will not take payment from my customers through UPI from October 15. In such a case, paying cash will be the only option. Since we cannot charge the MDR amount from the customer, we will have to bear the cost. I am also a part of a traders’ association, and our Noida unit has sent a communication to the Union finance minister through the local administration,” Bindal, who is also state president of Rashtriya Vyapari Kalyan Sangh, said.

Also Read:What is Merchant Discount Rate and how MDR will be calculated after revised UPI charges
The members of the fuel pump association also raised concerned.
“The issue has been raised across the state, and MDR will affect the fuel stations. As of now, we have decided that we will not accept payment of over ₹2000 through UPI from October 15,” said Vipin Sharma, president of the Ghaziabad diesel-petrol dealer association.
Also Read:Fuel pump transactions, bill and insurance payments, and more: UPI FAQs as MDR kicks in
Rajnish Bansal, a trader from the city’s prominent Turab Nagar Market, said that the cost of MDR will be borne by the shop owner.
“The MDR will become a cost for us. To compensate for this, we will have to lower our discount or increase the cost. As a result of this, the traders are a worried lot, and many have put up posters that they will not accept UPI payments. We also want more cash flow in the market since we face competition from online trade. But this will be contradictory to the idea of a cashless economy,” Bansal added.
The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) announced on Tuesday that a 0.4% fee will be charged on UPI transactions to certain merchants when the transaction value exceeds ₹2,000. It also clarified that customers will not have to pay any fee for making UPI payments under the revised system.
As per the new rules, Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI payments above ₹2,000 will attract a 0.4% MDR. However, the charge will not exceed ₹300 for a single transaction.
MDR refers to the fee charged to merchants by banks and payment service providers for processing digital payments. The amount depends on factors such as the payment method, the type of merchant, the transaction value, and the agreement between the businesses involved. In a digital payment system, a customer pays a merchant electronically, while the merchant pays a small fee to the company or bank that processes the transaction.

An AI tool is set to start advising air traffic controllers on managing air traffic in the congested airspace above the Washington, DC, area. The expected launch would be the first step toward a planned nationwide rollout covering the 29 million square miles of US national airspace overseen by the Federal Aviation Administration.
The FAA describes the SMART system as using AI models to predict air traffic flows and identify potential conflicts based on operational factors like airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, and airspace conditions. US government and industry officials told The Wall Street Journal that SMART could debut for the three major airports in the Washington, DC, area as soon as Monday, September 21.
The decision to launch SMART in limited scope before going nationwide is the “right call,” said Philip Mann, principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years.
“SMART’s risk was never any single prediction—it is a national-scale system with AI components carrying more unknowns than anything the FAA has fielded,” Mann wrote in an email to Ars. “Every cut in scope shrinks the unknowns.”
The AI-driven forecasts and recommendations are meant to give the FAA, airlines, and aircraft operators the same shared view of operational conditions so that they can agree on the most efficient routes and departure times. The goals of SMART include reducing aircraft fuel burn, improving on-time performance for flights, and speeding up recovery from weather and air traffic congestion events.
However, the airline industry was reportedly confused for weeks about the agency’s plans to deploy the AI tool, according to Politico. Anonymous airline officials told Politico that their concerns only eased after the FAA said the SMART AI tool would not change any procedures for air traffic controllers or airlines, and would instead produce “alternative route information” that is made available through existing FAA systems.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on streaming platforms, FAST channels, and the future of entertainment, follow Charles Pulliam-Moore. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
All roads lead to cable
In their fight to win the war for our attention, streamers are re-creating cable from first principles.
All roads lead to cable
In their fight to win the war for our attention, streamers are re-creating cable from first principles.
How it started
Before Netflix fully committed to becoming a streaming service and leaving DVDs behind, the company experimented with the idea of giving its subscribers a physical box that could access high-resolution digital copies of movies. Films would have been downloaded to the box in the evening and become available to users the next day. But Netflix changed course around 2006 once it saw people were flocking to watch grainy viral videos on YouTube. Though Netflix had already been making waves by disrupting the movie rental business, pivoting to streaming turned the company into a powerhouse that posed a threat to traditional cable services.
People loved being able to instantly access large catalogs of movies from their computers without having to sign up for expensive cable plans. Once the company got into original series in 2012, its binge model helped generate buzz and drive new sign-ups. As Netflix’s user base continued to grow in those early years, other companies, like Amazon, Disney, and NBC, realized there was money to be made by launching (or contributing to) streaming services of their own. And while cable didn’t completely disappear as streaming took off, the number of people subscribed to cable plans began (and has continued) to drop over the past decade.
How it’s going
Streaming is now the most common way that people consume films and television, and many people subscribe to multiple services in order to be able to access all of the things they want to watch. The proliferation of streaming services has led to an explosion of media, but the streaming market’s maturation has also made it much more difficult for companies to find and keep new subscribers.
Platforms have tried to get ahead of that issue and stay on top of their finances with countless price hikes that have made it much more expensive to keep up with shows compared to when streamers first hit the scene. In hopes of courting more price-sensitive customers, many companies have introduced ad-supported tiers to their paid services. But some have also launched free ad-supported television (FAST) services that look and feel a lot like traditional cable.
Unlike regular streamers where constant ads and endless choices have become an annoyance, FAST services like Tubi, Roku, and Pluto TV keep things relatively simple. In exchange for watching a few commercials, users can browse through entertainment libraries or choose to focus on channels that are dedicated to specific series. When you look at the way that most FAST services present their channels in long lists, it’s easy to get the sense that they’ve been intentionally designed to mimic old cable interfaces. That might speak to entertainment executives beginning to think that icon-dense carousels aren’t necessarily the best way to show off a streamer’s offerings. It could also be a sign that viewers have grown weary of the algorithms streamers use to suggest what content to watch. But it also feels like as the streaming wars have carried on, newer companies realized that the old guard got a few things right.
What happens next
Because people still want to keep up with all of the new stuff coming out of the paid streamers without having to individually sign up for every service, we’re probably going to see even more bundling in the future. Bundling gives consumers a way to save money on their entertainment budgets, and almost every single one of the major streaming companies has offered some kind of deal that gives you access to one or more of their competitors. Similar to FAST channels, streaming bundles are reminiscent of the tiered cable packages telecoms sell, and some companies, like Verizon and T-Mobile, include access to streaming bundles as perks for their subscribers.
More individual streaming platforms will likely roll out always-on channels that are designed to give people a way to watch certain series without having to choose a particular episode for themselves. For services like HBO Max, that would be almost like a return to the way HBO’s various channels air on terrestrial television. In addition to helping viewers deal with decision paralysis, always-on channels could also help streaming services ensure that user engagement stays high. And if every streamer in the game decides that paywalled always-on channels, bundles, and even more price increases are the way forward, it’s really going to feel like we’ve come full circle back to cable.
By the way
- More streamers have also begun experimenting with vertical content in an effort to meet mobile users where they are. Some of this is a clear response to platforms like TikTok, but it’s also a sign that Hollywood might be serious about getting into microdramas.

Vijayawada man Sai Krishna beaten to death in police custody, cremated same night: SIT
The SIT officials identified the cement platform No. 16 in the crematorium as the spot where the cremation had taken place
The Special Investigation Team (SIT) of the Andhra Pradesh police probing the mysterious disappearance of 25-year-old Gade Sai Krishna in Vijayawada in May, has confirmed that he was beaten to death by the Krishnalanka police at an abandoned building on May 12, people familiar with the matter said on Saturday.
After confirming that Sai Krishna had died, the police clandestinely took his body to the Swargapuri crematorium near the Krishnalanka police station and cremated it the same night, the SIT authorities told a local court in Vijayawada on Friday.
The SIT officials identified the cement platform No. 16 in the crematorium as the spot where the cremation had taken place. “We collected ash and bone remains from the site for further examination,” the SIT informed the court.
The SIT, headed by inspector general of police M Ravi Prakash and comprised West Godavari superintendent of police Adnan Naveen Asmi, Alluri Sitarama Raju SP Amit Bardar and Bapatla additional SP L Sudhakar as members, was constituted on June 21, after the missing of Sai Krishna triggered a state-wide outrage.
On June 23, the SIT arrested Krishnalanka inspector of police SSV Nagaraju and on June 29, two head constables, Potharlanka Ashok Kumar and Jangam Nani, surrendered before the SIT authorities. All the three were suspended pending investigation.
On Friday, the SIT produced the fourth accused Gulivundala Suresh, a close associate of Nagaraju, before the Second Additional Judicial Magistrate Court, Vijayawada.
The SIT charged Suresh, a real estate broker, with helping Nagaraju and the head constables in shifting Sai Krishna’s body to the crematorium and later bringing pressure on the deceased’s family members to withdraw the complaint as part of a compromise formula.
In the remand report presented before the court, which was reviewed by HT, Nagaraju and the two head constables confined Sai Krishna and subjected him to torture in an abandoned building at Ranigarithota, near the Varadhi area of Vijayawada.
The remand report stated that Suresh had allegedly witnessed Sai Krishna being questioned at the Krishnalanka police station on May 7 by then inspector Nagaraju and head constables Ashok and Nani. Suresh subsequently travelled to Nepal with his friends and returned to Vijayawada on May 11.
“On May 12 at around 10.30 am, Suresh went to the police station to meet Nagaraju. He was allegedly taken by Ashok Kumar to an abandoned building at Ranigarithota, where he found Sai Krishna in a severely weakened condition. The deceased told Suresh that he had been beaten every day since being brought to the building with the intention of killing him,” the SIT said.
Subsequently, Sai Krishna reportedly collapsed and became unconscious and on checking his pulse, the police realised that he had died. “On the night of May 12, the two head constables shifted the body to the crematorium on a motor bike, while Suresh accompanied them. They remained at the crematorium until the body was completely burnt,” the SIT report said.
After Sai Krishna’s family filed a habeas corpus petition in the Andhra Pradesh high court in June, Suresh acting on behalf of Nagaraju, allegedly approached Sai Krishna’s maternal uncle Navarang and pressured him to withdraw the petition.
“After Nagaraju was arrested and two head constables surrendered, Suresh went absconding and on the advice of his lawyers, he surrendered to the SIT on Thursday evening,” the report added.

In March this year, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and the American Heart Association (AHA), both globally recognised premier organisations in cardiovascular medicine, handed down their newest dyslipidemia guideline, and gave universal Lipoprotein(a) screening in every adult a ‘Class I’ recommendation -- the strongest tier there is. The High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP) test got a lighter endorsement: checked selectively, alongside coronary calcium scoring, to sharpen risk estimates when they’re uncertain. These two long-debated biomarkers, were both freshly blessed by the field’s governing societies.
Then arrived the irony. On July 31, pharma major Novo Nordisk’s ziltivekimab — a drug built to block the inflammatory pathway behind elevated C-Reactive Protein (CRP) — fully hit its target in a Phase 3 clinical trial and still didn’t move the needle on heart attacks or strokes. Five weeks later, pelacarsenm, a drug that lowers high levels of Lp(a) failed the same way. Within six months of the guideline telling every clinician to start checking these numbers, the two flagship drugs built to act on them came up empty.
It’s a familiar shape for cardiology. Heart disease mortality fell almost every year through the back half of the last century — statins, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, better acute care — and that decline has visibly slowed this past decade, even as the drug arsenal has never been more sophisticated. LDL (’bad cholesterol’) is already driven remarkably low in anyone on a serious statin; medicine needed a new lever, and reached for the two candidates the guidelines had just endorsed. Neither has delivered yet.
What actually happened
On September 4, Novartis announced pelacarsen missed the primary endpoint of Lp(a)HORIZON, the first cardiovascular outcomes trial ever run for a drug built to lower lipoprotein(a). Pelacarsen is an antisense drug — a short, lab-made strand of genetic material injected monthly, designed to intercept the liver’s instructions for building Lp(a) before it’s ever made, rather than mopping up what’s already circulating. In 8,323 patients with established heart disease, it cut Lp(a) by roughly 80%. And yet, there was no reduction in heart attacks or stroke.
What we were taught
Lp(a) was drilled into me in medical school as one of the ‘unfair’ risk factors — a number you’re essentially born with, indifferent to diet or willpower, and loaded disproportionately onto South Asian patients, who as a population carry some of the highest mean Lp(a) levels of any group studied. It helped explain a pattern every cardiology rotation eventually shows you: South Asian patients with premature, multi-vessel disease and normal LDL numbers. That teaching isn’t wrong, and this trial doesn’t overturn it — Lp(a) is a real, heritable, biologically active risk factor. What it disputes is narrower: whether lowering it, this late and this fast, changes what happens next.
What Lp(a) actually is
Here’s the plain version of how a heart attack builds. LDL particles, commonly known as ‘bad cholesterol’ work their way into the artery wall and get stuck there. Once trapped, immune cells chemically alter them and swallow them up, ballooning into fat-filled ‘foam cells.’ Over years, those dying cells pile up into a fatty core, and the artery seals it off with a cap of scar-like tissue. When that cap eventually cracks or wears thin, a blood clot forms on top of it — that’s the heart attack.
Statins, ezetimibe, and the newer PCSK9-inhibitor injections all lower LDL through different mechanisms, but the trial data lines up the same way every time: about a 22% drop in heart attacks and strokes for every 39-point drop in LDL, no matter how you get there.
Lp(a) is an LDL particle with one extra piece stuck to it — a protein called apolipoprotein(a), built from the same molecular parts as the protein your body uses to break up blood clots. But it’s a decoy, not a copy: it fits into the same docking spots on a forming clot, without carrying the working part that actually gets activated into a clot-dissolving enzyme. So instead of helping to break clots down, it crowds out the real thing and makes clots a little harder to clear. That’s what makes Lp(a) different from LDL: it builds plaque the same way LDL does, but it also nudges the body toward clotting rather than away from it. And unlike LDL, your Lp(a) level is almost entirely set by your genes at birth — diet, exercise, and statins barely move it.
Why did the trial fail?
A floor effect: Mean background LDL in the trial was 66 mg/dL as most patients were already on aggressive therapy. Whatever risk Lp(a) adds on top of that may be smaller than older, less-treated cohorts suggested, offering little room for an 80% reduction to matter.
Too late in the game: Every patient entered with 50-plus years of Lp(a) exposure already built into their arteries. Lowering the level for three or four years in someone’s sixties, after a cardiac event, may be too late to undo a lifetime of exposure the genetic data actually measured.
This isn’t cardiology’s first time at this wall. The CANTOS trial suggested a decade ago that quieting the immune system could work, independent of cholesterol reduction. Hitting the biomarkers still doesn’t seem to be enough: Lp(a) may just be writing the newest chapter of the same story.
Back to basics
The interventions with the deepest trial evidence are still the boring ones: eat well, move, don’t smoke, stay lean. LDL, blood pressure, glucose, and tobacco remain the pillars with decades of reproducible data behind them.
Lp(a) will likely still matter — as a flag for who needs those basics enforced hardest, and maybe eventually as a target that is treated decades earlier than this trial tried. But for now, the fanciest number on the panel failed its biggest test, and the oldest advice in medicine didn’t.
No antisense drug, no anti-inflammatory antibody, has found a way around the same wall. In Greek mythology, Icarus didn’t fall because he was foolish — he flew exactly as high as anyone reasonably could, and the sun turned out to be closer than he’d been told. Despite everything medicine can now measure, alter and silence, the quest for a healthy long life perhaps rests on the same principles it has rested on for centuries: eat well, move well, sleep well.
(Dr. Dinesh Arab is director, interventional and structural cardiology, AdventHealth Daytona Beach and clinical assistant professor of medicine, Florida State University. dinarab@yahoo.com)

Football Sundays are officially back, and my recipe for easy slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip is guaranteed to be the MVP at any party.
Practically every time I entertain friends — be it for game day, the Super Bowl, or any party — I'm always asked if I'll be making my famous Buffalo chicken dip.
Over the years, I've tweaked recipes I've seen online to come up with the easiest, most crowd-pleasing dip. It requires only six main ingredients, plus seasonings you'll probably already have in your pantry.
Here's how to make my easy slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip.
My recipe for slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip requires only six main ingredients.
To make the dip, which feeds about 10 people, you'll need:
- A 6-quart slow cooker or Crock-Pot
- A rotisserie chicken (or 1 lb of cooked chicken)
- 12 fluid ounces Frank's RedHot Buffalo sauce
- ½ cup ranch dressing
- 16-ounce cream cheese
- 1 cup shredded cheddar cheese
- 1 cup shredded mozzarella cheese
- Salt, pepper, garlic powder
I always start by separating the breasts from the rotisserie chicken and removing the skin.
I like to use rotisserie chicken for this recipe because it's often easier and cheaper than buying chicken breasts and boiling them myself. I find that the rotisserie chicken also packs much more flavor, and saves me from having to do any actual cooking.
When it comes to game-day recipes, easiest is usually best.
Then I shred the rotisserie chicken.
I usually do this step by hand, but you can also use two forks to shred your chicken. By the end, you should have about 3 cups of shredded rotisserie chicken.
I put the cream cheese in the slow cooker and cut it into cubes with a knife.
This helps ensure the cream cheese melts evenly and is well-distributed throughout the dip.
You can use full-fat or low-fat cream cheese for this dip, depending on your preference — I've had success using both.
I then add the rotisserie chicken to the slow cooker and season it.
I usually eyeball how much seasoning I use, but typically go for about a tablespoon of garlic powder, a tablespoon of salt, and a few dashes of pepper.
I add the two types of cheese.
I use 1 cup of shredded, low-moisture mozzarella cheese and 1 cup of shredded sharp-cheddar cheese.
Next, my wet ingredients go on top.
I use a whole 12-ounce bottle of Frank's RedHot Buffalo sauce, but you can use whichever brand of Buffalo sauce you prefer. I then add ½ cup of ranch dressing on top.
I mix the ingredients with a wooden spoon until everything is evenly distributed.
You don't need to overmix it — as the dip cooks, the ingredients will melt and combine.
Scoop along the sides to make sure nothing is sticking to the walls, put the lid on the slow cooker, and walk away. It's that easy.
I heat the dip on high for 1 to 2 hours, or on low for 3 hours.
I stir the dip with a wooden spoon a couple of times while it's cooking to prevent any spots from burning on the side and to help it cook evenly.
The dip should be smooth and slightly bubbling when it's done, with all the cream cheese and cheeses fully melted and combined.
I serve the finished Buffalo chicken dip with tortilla chips.
Whether you're making it for the Super Bowl, a last-minute party, or an easy weeknight snack, this six-ingredient slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip shows that crowd-pleasing food doesn't have to be complicated.
Simply toss everything in, let it cook, and you'll end up with a creamy, spicy dip that disappears almost as fast as it comes together.

Herpetologists first discovered in 1933 that rattlesnakes are immune to their own venom. Native to the Americas, rattlesnakes are pit vipers, a family of vipers with a heat-sensing pit organ between each nostril and eye.
Venom resistance in snakes comes in two forms: either the targets in their bodies have evolved such that the venom doesn’t attack them, like in cobras, or they possess specific molecules in their bloodstream that serve as “toxin sponges”, like in vipers, Sean B. Carroll, chair of biology at the University of Maryland, U.S., said.
In 1972, Japanese researchers discovered the first example of a so-called toxin sponge — a serum protein dubbed Fetuin-A — from Okinawa habu (Protobothrops flavoviridis), a pit viper endemic to the Ryukyu Islands. Fetuin-A could inhibit metalloproteinases, a class of venom toxins that could cause haemorrhage, damage tissue, and disrupt the coagulation system.
Metalloproteinases are the most abundant toxin family in rattlesnake venoms, and researchers have studied metalloproteinase inhibitors such as Fetuin-A in great detail. However, only recently did they discover that Fetuin-A belongs to a larger family of FETUA proteins.
In a 2022 paper, Dr. Carroll and his team identified four FETUA proteins from the western diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus atrox).
Curiously, understanding the principles of venom resistance from C. atrox led the researchers to leverage these antitoxins, which had evolved over millions of years, for human benefit.
In a new study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team at Maryland has shown that specific combinations of C. atrox FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality in mice, with roughly 10-times the potency of commercial antivenom.
‘String of surprises’
On discovering metalloproteinase-inhibiting FETUA-2, 3, 4, and 5 proteins from C. atrox, the research team studied their antivenom potency. By injecting various protein combinations preincubated with C. atrox venom into experimental mice, they found that some combinations successfully blocked haemorrhaging, while some even staved off death.
“Rattlesnake venoms have 10-15 different kinds of toxins,” Dr. Carroll said. “So it was entirely unexpected that just blocking metalloproteinases would block the lethality of the venom.”
The test results that followed were a “string of surprises”. Encouraged by the success of FETUA proteins against C. atrox venom, the team tried them against the eastern diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus), which proved successful. Then they tested them against two Asian snakes: the Malayan pit viper (Calloselasma rhodostoma) and the Chinese moccasin (Deinagkistrodon acutus). The proteins could protect against those as well.
The team then moved to candidates outside of pit vipers. Of the two true vipers they tested against, the proteins protected significantly against the Sochurek’s saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus sochureki) — but none against the puff adder (Bitis arietans).
“Our surprises ran out, you could say,” Dr. Carroll said.
According to him, an antivenom needs potency and broad reactivity. And not only could these proteins recognise and neutralise the venom of a spectrum of distant species, when tested against CroFab, a commercial antivenom obtained from animals immunised with four pit viper venoms, including C. atrox, the proteins proved tenfold more potent.
The findings are a “real advance” for antivenom development, according to Kartik Sunagar, an associate professor at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru; he was not involved in the study. “The paper shows convincingly that a combination of naturally evolved FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality by inhibiting metalloproteinases alone.”
However, Dr. Sunagar also pointed out that the study did not exactly measure clinical capacity.
“Every efficacy experiment premixed venom and inhibitor before injection,” he said. “So the study measures neutralising capacity, not treatment of an animal already envenomed, which is the clinically relevant scenario.”
Next-generation antivenom
According to Dr. Carroll, unlike lab-made compounds, FETUA proteins have been tested in nature.
“Rattlesnakes have evolved these proteins for 50 million years, with remarkable specificity and potency to inhibit their own venom, which gives me the sense that it is worth exploring,” he said.
Manufacturability and purity are added advantages, he added: “We can make recombinant FETUA proteins in the lab in unlimited quantities — whereas traditional antivenom requires animals to be immunised, and then the obtained antibodies have to be purified.”
Dr. Sunagar also shared the view that the recombinant and defined nature of FETUA proteins will help sidestep the low purity of animal-derived products.
While the study showed that these proteins can protect experimental mice from venom lethality, toxins other than metalloproteinases will have physiological effects on humans, Dr Carroll said: “What we don’t know is what else we will have to use in conjunction with these proteins to make an antivenom” for humans.
“FETUAs do nothing for the neurotoxins that dominate many medically important venoms,” Dr. Sunagar said. “The honest reading is that these proteins form the metalloproteinase-neutralising component of a next-generation antivenom, but it is not yet a standalone therapy.”
Dr. Carroll also said his team has found a new component that could aid human antivenom development, but did not elaborate on ongoing research.
Implications for India
In countries like India, which host both vipers and elapids such as cobras, FETUA proteins alone cannot provide a complete antivenom solution, Dr. Carroll said.
Although the study revealed partial protection against saw-scaled vipers (Echis carinatus sp.), one of India’s ‘Big Four’ and a major cause of death and disability, partial cross-reactivity need not translate into clinical protection, Dr. Sunagar added.
But India’s bigger takeaway is the strategy: “The logical path for India is to identify and test FETUAs from our own vipers rather than relying on rattlesnake versions, and to pair them with agents covering the neurotoxic elapids the FETUAs cannot touch,” according to Dr. Sunagar.
Nikhil Sreekandan is an independent journalist.

Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan to give firms more long-term certainty: Paul Chan
Finance chief says blueprint’s targets and timelines will help businesses align investment decisions with government goals
Hong Kong’s first five-year plan will give businesses greater certainty to make long-term investment decisions amid a volatile external environment, the city’s finance chief has said.
Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said the plan’s targets and timelines would allow companies to see the city’s direction over the next five years and better align their plans with the government’s.
“The significance of planning lies not only in the document itself, but also in looking at today from the perspective of the future and turning a vision into indicators and action plans that can be reviewed year by year,” Chan wrote in his weekly blog on Sunday.
“The more volatile the external environment becomes, the more the market needs certainty that extends beyond a single year.”

Taobao Instant Commerce, Alibaba’s on-demand delivery service that was revamped last year and is known as Taobao Shangou in Chinese, won a top French Design Award prize on Saturday for its delivery worker uniform, marking the first time the prize was awarded for a design for frontline workers.
“We think the [Taobao Shangou] suit design would transform delivery workwear into a recognisable professional uniform, helping reshape how society sees this essential profession,” said Dario Olivero, chair of the award’s organising committee.

'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
- Published
Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.
"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.
"He used to work out every morning."
Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.
Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.
After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.
That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.
Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.
It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.
In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.
Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.
The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.
It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.
"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.
"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."
In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.
After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.
Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.
"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.
"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"
Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.
Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.
"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."
Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.
All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.
The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.
Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.
At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.
The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.
Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.
Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.
As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."
She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.
On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."
One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.
She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.
Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.
Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.
He was 13 years old at the time
"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC.
He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.
His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.
Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.
Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.
Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.
They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms.
"They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim.
"As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.
Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.
Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down"
Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.
President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.
Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept.
"In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."
Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea.
"Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down.
"Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."
Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us.
"Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.
