The latest GTA 6 content leak rabbit hole has taken fans straight back to GTA 5, revealing the unseen dialog from the game’s original Option A ending. Trevor Philips was apparently supposed to meet an even more horrifying fate.
The newly surfaced material comes from the enormous 192 GB batch of scrapped GTA 5 source code files that suggested GTA 6 may get Liberty City DLC. Recently, the enormous batch of files has been circulating publicly, and data miners continue to dig through the years-old development material.
Among these, X user TJGM received a leak from HeySlickThatsMe that showed an unseen dialogue connected to the ending where Franklin targets Trevor over Michael.
Instead of Trevor crashing into an oil tanker, the leaked dialogue suggests that Rockstar originally considered having him slam into a truck filled with liquid nitrogen. The result would have been brutally fitting for Trevor, as he would freeze before shattering to pieces.
But Trevor isn’t the only familiar face making a surprise appearance in the latest discoveries. TJGM also revealed cut dialogue involving Brucie from GTA 4, who was apparently planned to appear in GTA 5’s single-player campaign and have missions with Franklin.
The GTA 5 and GTA 6 content leak goes far beyond these alternate possibilities. The whole archive reportedly contains cut GTA 5 content, early dialogue, vehicles, mission information, Agent Trevor, DLC assets, and possibly early GTA 6 files.
Fans should remember that most of the material originates from Rockstar’s 2022 security breach and was not newly created. The archive also reportedly contains evidence of a planned Liberty City expansion for GTA 5 alongside some low-quality GTA 6 map assets that resemble the areas shown in the game’s trailers.
These discoveries underline just how many ideas, characters, and storylines Rockstar explored before settling on GTA 5’s final form.

Trump Is Betting on the Wrong Europe
The far-right parties the White House favors have a foreign-policy agenda that won’t serve American interests.
Donald Trump says he wants a Europe that is more capable of defending itself. But the nationalist-populist movements he is championing there will not advance this agenda and may put Europe at odds with the United States over China.
Earlier this month, the nationalist-populist Alternative for Germany party came just a few seats short of an outright majority in a regional parliament, its best-ever result. This Sunday, Germans will vote in two more regional elections. The ruling Christian Democrats are behind in both races, and the AfD is expected to do well in one. On Wednesday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz canceled his visit to the United Nations General Assembly next week, sparking speculation that he could soon be forced to resign.
U.S. officials are ebullient. Trump greeted the AfD’s recent electoral victory with a triumphant message on Truth Social that finished with “MGGA” (Make Germany Great Again). Richard Grenell, Trump’s former ambassador to Germany and now a presidential envoy, called the result “a huge win and a new day in Germany.”
The Trump administration has consistently embraced Europe’s nationalist-populist parties as ideological partners, and even launched a State Department fund to support MAGA-aligned European groups. It surely sees the AfD’s ascendance as a sign that politics are moving in its direction. But that is true only if Trump’s real goal is a fragmented Europe that accommodates Russian and Chinese power and is unable to punch its weight. Such an outcome would be catastrophic for U.S. interests.
Some people in the administration insist that the idea is not to weaken Europe but to shift the burden for its conventional defense to the Europeans themselves. Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, for example, reject claims that the administration is soft on Russia and say that they are calling instead for greater European self-sufficiency. Colby advocates for what he calls NATO 3.0, in which Europeans would take on the primary responsibility for their conventional defense.
But the nationalist populists do not share this view. The AfD has called for an end to all arms deliveries to Ukraine and a lifting of all sanctions on Russia. Its co-leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, boycotted Volodymyr Zelensky’s speech to the Bundestag in 2024, dismissing the Ukrainian president as a “war and beggar president.”
In France, Marine Le Pen, the parliamentary leader of the nationalist-populist party National Rally and the front-runner for next spring’s presidential election, has promised to take France out of NATO’s integrated military command (France would remain a member of the alliance). Such a withdrawal would hardly help the Trump administration shift the burden of NATO’s defense to Europe.
The Trump administration’s affinity for Europe’s nationalist-populist right seems to be almost entirely cultural and civilizational, and based on the notion that Europe’s populists are fighting the same culture wars—including against immigration—as their counterparts in the United States. J. D. Vance explicitly praised then–Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán as an ally in defense of Western civilization at an election rally in Budapest on the eve of the Hungarian elections. And the Trump team seems to see the European populist right’s enemies—the European Union and national political establishments—as versions of its own domestic foes. This commonality appears to take precedence over foreign-policy concerns.
Trump officials have blasted centrist European governments for being too soft on Beijing but have said nothing about the populist right’s position on China. Some of these parties—particularly the AfD and Fidesz, in Hungary—favor much closer ties to the American adversary. The AfD’s Weidel lived in China for six years, speaks Mandarin, and wrote her doctoral dissertation about China’s pension system. Chrupalla, her co-leader, accused the German government of waging “economic war” against China for proposing a tougher trade policy toward Beijing. They have both called for warmer relations with China. Orbán, who was defeated in the Hungarian elections earlier this year, blocked the EU from criticizing Beijing, initiated an “all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership” with China, and welcomed Chinese investment in Hungarian infrastructure.
These largely transactional attitudes toward China and Russia may reflect a broader worldview among the nationalist populists, who praise Trump but are deeply skeptical of American power. In an analysis for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Jeremy Cliffe argued that the AfD supports a multipolar world order and believes that great powers, such as China and Russia, should possess spheres of influence—a perspective that Trump seems sympathetic toward. The AfD, Cliffe wrote, “may regard Trump as a civilizational ally, but its senior figures have long described the United States as a raumfremd in Europe, a hard to translate German word that means something like ‘territorially alien.’”
If parties with these views take power, they could reduce American influence in Europe while making common European action on Russia and China much more difficult. They will also make Eastern Europeans nervous about German rearmament. In 2011, Radek Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister, said, “I fear German power less than German inaction.” He recently revisited that remark, telling the German newspaper Handelsblatt, “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as the largest economy in Europe, to play a strong role in securing our common security. But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany can lead in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party—and that is exactly what the AfD represents.”
Senior Trump-administration officials say they are building a Europe that will carry its own weight. Maybe they are so beguiled by the nationalist populists’ domestic agenda that they have not yet realized it will come at the expense of NATO 3.0. Or maybe Trump doesn’t care about Europe’s defense, doesn’t see it as a U.S. interest, and doesn’t believe that Europe has any contribution to make to America’s security.
Trump and Vance seem to be laying the foundation for a more divided Europe that is incapable of deterring Russia, ever more dependent on China, and at odds with itself. If the administration continues on this path, it may get the European culture war it wants, but the United States will lose its ally.

I've never been good at sports, and I've never been fond of exercise, so you might be wondering why I chose the Chicago Athletic Association when booking hotels for my first-ever trip to the city.
I wanted to step back in time. The Gilded Age hotel was a private club where professional athletes and high-profile individuals trained and socialized from 1893 to 2007.
Following its closure and a lengthy transformation project, the Chicago Athletic Association reopened as a hotel in 2015. I spent one night there in February for $250. It felt extremely luxurious for the price point, and some surprising details made me certain I'd book it again.
Parts of my stay felt like a time warp, but the hotel's history also came out in ways I didn't see coming.
Welcome to the Chicago Athletic Association, the 19th-century private club that's now a hotel.
The Venetian-Gothic-style building was designed by architect and club member Henry Ives Cobb, who took inspiration from the Doge's Palace in Venice, according to the hotel's website.
The hotel stood out to me among modern buildings on Michigan Avenue in Downtown Chicago. It's just across from Millennium Park and the Bean (formally known as Cloud Gate) and within walking distance of many tourist hot spots like the Art Institute of Chicago, the Chicago Theater, and the Chicago Riverwalk.
Inside, the past lives on.
The Chicago Athletic Association began as a Gilded Age gentlemen's club joined by influential sports icons. Membership opened to women in 1972.
It was a stomping ground for industry moguls like William Wrigley and Marshall Field. It was a training base for five-time Olympic gold-medal swimmer Johnny Weissmuller and the first professional football player, William "Pudge" Heffelfinger.
The building's history is celebrated inside the hotel, with 19th-century relics and refurbished materials, from wood paneling to marble flooring, Elizabeth Story, the hotel's sales and marketing director, told Business Insider.
As I stepped into the lobby, I felt like I'd traveled back in time.
The lobby, also known as the drawing room, looked as if it had been designed 100 years ago, with restored 19th-century trim, moldings, and replicated historic details.
"Teams of craftsmen restored the 1893 grandeur of the Lobby Lounge by removing, refinishing, and reinstalling every piece of millwork, and recreating original light fixtures from old photographs," Story said.
I noticed other contemporary details that pay tribute to the city and club's history. The check-in desk, designed with long strips of wood in different colors, was inspired by vintage athletic equipment.
"A mural above the desk depicts the elevated train tracks that encircle Chicago's Loop," Story added.
Restored Gilded Age interiors made communal spaces look as lavish as they were historic.
I was mesmerized by the preserved luxury finishings as I walked through the hotel. Restored Italian columns, stained-glass windows, and golden doors made me feel as if I were inside a palace.
The ballrooms had an old-world, luxury feel.
The hotel had many event spaces, including the White City Ballroom. During the restoration process, Story said that the Italian Carrara marble floor was buried under an inch and a half of carpet, glue, and concrete.
I was surprised by another event space that used to be a swimming pool.
Known as "The Tank," this space still has the swimming lane flooring tiles from its pool days.
"Artists hand-made 167 individual stalactites as part of the atmospheric design," Story said.
Although the highlight of this room is the historic pool tiles, I thought repurposing the space for events was surprising and innovative.
The game room had a mix of historic and fresh details.
The game room was the billiards room back in the club days, Story said.
It didn't feel frozen in time like some of the other spaces. The walls blended antique woodwork with whimsical murals, such as chalkboard sketches of athletes and an aerial view of a basketball court. I thought it was a playful, creative way to showcase the building's history.
Some aspects of the hotel were completely new, like the rooftop bar and restaurant.
"The past was honored at every turn, but the transformation also called for thoughtful new additions," Story explained.
For example, Cindy's, the rooftop restaurant and bar, was built ahead of the hotel's 2015 opening.
I thought the space had a midcentury modern vibe with vintage influence. Cindy's brought the outdoors in with a steel-framed, windowed pavilion inspired by 19th-century train sheds.
The fitness center was sleek and modern.
Here, I found cardio machines with tablet attachments and fun cartoons of men stretching on the walls. The fitness center is open 24 hours a day.
My room had a vintage aesthetic without feeling dated.
I booked a standard room with a comfy king-sized bed and a downtown view for about $250 a night. I immediately noticed the custom metal bedframe with brass accents — a vintage design inspired by the 19th-century club.
The furniture creatively combined elements of old-fashioned gym equipment in a functional way.
The desk was unlike any I'd seen before. Wooden bars, inspired by stretching racks, climbed the wall to a netted shelf that appeared large enough to hold a typical checked suitcase.
The bars were cleverly used as vertical storage, with leather pouches of varying sizes hanging from them. I used these pockets to store my wallet, keys, and chargers during my stay.
The bathroom blended old-school locker room vibes with opulence.
"The bathrooms were conceived as a quiet luxury counterpoint," Story said. A black-and-white palette and a simple striped backsplash were paired with a Carrara marble vanity and a rainfall shower.
There was also a boxing-style robe in the bathroom, which almost made me feel like an athlete myself.
At the Chicago Athletic Association, I got my trip back in time, with some surprises.
While parts of the hotel felt 100 years old, fresh designs inspired by its private-club past gave other spaces a modern twist.
"The goal was never a museum-quality freeze in time, but something more alive," Story said. "A touch of disorder in the new space was introduced to draw in a younger generation, balanced bravely with references to the building's past."
From the palace-like common spaces to the creative nods to the past, the Chicago Athletic Association was more luxurious and distinctive than I expected for $250 a night. I would definitely stay there again, and maybe next time, I'll bring a jock with me.

Home guard arrested, dismissed from service for assaulting woman in Hyderabad
A Telangana police home guard was arrested, dismissed after a video allegedly showed him assaulting a woman and dragging her by her hair outside Hafeezpet Railway Station
A Telangana police home guard was arrested and dismissed from service on Saturday after a video allegedly showing him assaulting a woman and dragging her by her hair outside Hyderabad’s Hafeezpet Railway Station went viral on social media.
The home guard, Anand, who was deployed at Hafeezpet railway station on deputation to the railway police, would be produced before the local court for judicial remand, Cyberabad police commissioner M Ramesh said.
“There is no question of tolerating such inhuman behaviour by the police towards women. We shall take stringent action against the accused home guard,” Ramesh said.
The Miyapur police registered a case against Anand under Sections 74 (use of criminal force against a woman with the intent to outrage her modesty) and 118(1) (voluntarily causing hurt using dangerous weapons or means) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).
“We are investigating the circumstances surrounding the altercation and the assault,” the police commissioner said.
According to the FIR, Anand was performing patrolling duty in the Miyapur area at around 10 pm on Friday night when he was allegedly caught on camera assaulting the woman near Platform No. 1, on the Aditya Nagar side of Hafeezpet Railway Station. Citizens who witnessed the incident reportedly intervened and asked him to let the woman go.
The Miyapur police said the woman was a ragpicker/beggar and that she had allegedly abused the home guard before the assault.
On Saturday morning, the Secunderabad Central Railway (SCR) posted on X, saying the matter had been enquired into and confirming that the personnel involved was a Telangana police home guard deputed to the railway station. “The home guard had been repatriated to the Telangana state police department for necessary disciplinary action,” the SCR said.
Telangana Director General of Police C V Anand strongly condemned the conduct of the home guard and said police personnel could not be excused for such behaviour, irrespective of their rank or the circumstances.
“Such behaviour by our staff, whatever be the rank and whatever be the provocation, cannot be forgiven. It is abominable and in total disregard of all instructions and training,” the DGP said in a post on X.
“He will be removed from service and also a case will be booked and criminal action will be initiated,” the DGP added.
Acting on the directions, Vikarabad district Superintendent of Police Sneha Mehra issued orders dismissing Anand from service following disciplinary proceedings.

Can an AI chatbot save lives by answering texts about pregnancy?
It started with an accident.
A network of clinics for pregnant women in Kenya set up an automated text messaging service to send out appointment reminders. But when the moms received the texts, they started to write back.
Some asked if it's safe to eat avocados during pregnancy (you can!). Others asked if certain symptoms they were experiencing, like swelling or headaches, are normal during pregnancy.
"At the time I joined I think we were getting less than 100 questions a day," recalls Jay Patel, director of technology for Jacaranda Health. "Now it's 15,000."
At first, Jacaranda hired nurses to answer questions one by one. But over the years since 2020, developers have created a program that uses artificial intelligence to understand patient's questions, prioritize them and flag when a user may need immediate medical care. It's called PROMPTS — and is used by patients visiting public clinics in 24 Kenyan counties.
For women without a smartphone, cell reception, or easy access to the internet, a text to PROMPTS may be the fastest way to get a question answered. Other times, it's a reliable way to determine if a long trip to a hospital is necessary.
"If a mom in a rural part of Kenya starts bleeding at 2 a.m., she can't just Google it," Patel says. "But this service runs completely over SMS. It's completely free to the user, and it's accessible to anyone who has a basic phone."
About 7% of messages are flagged by the system as potentially urgent. These are routed directly to a nurse.
"It bypasses all AI functionality and gets straight to the help desk, into a special queue," Patel says. "They can pick it up immediately, look at the mom's question history and call her."
That kind of quick response is critical in Kenya, where about 6,000 women die each year from childbirth or pregnancy-related causes. That's 16 women a day. Almost a third of those deaths are believed to be related to delays in seeking care.
Lisa Mushega, a policy expert for HENNET, a Kenyan coalition of health care providers, says PROMPTS helps prevent these delays by giving women a direct line to a health professional. (Jacaranda Health is a member of the coalition).
"It's a referral," Mushega says. "[PROMPTS] is data driven and can improve the quality of care — informed by the voices of mothers themselves."
Mushega says she has met women who used PROMPTS to correctly identify signs of pre-eclampsia, a life-threatening condition that can start with swollen legs. Another new mother used the system when her newborn seemed sick, and she wasn't sure how to calm him.
"She was told to go to the nearest health facility, because her baby was actually having jaundice," Mushega says. "It really comes in handy."
At a time when the use of artificial intelligence is drawing existential concerns and calls for regulation, a program like PROMPTS demonstrates its potential value, says Smisha Agarwal, director of global digital health at Johns Hopkins University.
The AI Edge
Historically, most public health messaging is one-sided: Public service advertisements, billboards or automated messages written by health authorities and disseminated to the public.
"That conversation is really bounded by what a health system decides a mother should know," Agarwal says. Artificial intelligence sets a different course: "What the LLM really changes is the direction of conversation. Because now we can center it on what the mother actually wants to know, and in a private space on her own phone. There is a fundamental change in power."
In Kenya, PROMPTS understands messages in English, Swahili and Sheng — a popular dialect in Nairobi that is a mix of the two languages. Jacaranda has also expanded to parts of Ghana, Nigeria and Tanzania, building versions for speakers of Twi and Hausa.
"There's local context," Patel says. "If there's a question about nutrition in Kenya, and you give the same answer from a question about nutrition in Nigeria, you're going to get laughed out of the room."
Jacaranda Health is also using PROMPTS to help doctors identify areas of need, based on anonymous feedback from some of the estimated 700,000 users each year.
"Lots of mothers are reporting that they're getting blood pressure checks, but very few report getting breast exams," says spokesperson Laura Down. "It gives mums more agency in the health system — as well as a better understanding of their pregnancy history."
In other cases, Down says the questions mothers are asking can help doctors understand what's happening in their own community.
"So for example, we're starting to see correlations between a spike in extreme heat and a spike in mothers reporting issues like headaches or swelling or dehydration," Down says.
Any potential drawbacks?
But there are limits. These interventions work best in places that already have functional healthcare systems, Agarwal says. There's very little margin for error when human medical needs are processed by a machine. The way the system is trained to do a rapid handoff to a human nurse in an emergency becomes a key factor.
"The first thing I want to know is, what happens when the system gets a message wrong?" says Javaid Iqbal Sofi, a researcher focusing on AI policy and governance at Virginian Tech University. "Suppose a woman describes something urgent, but the system treats it as routine. Would someone catch that? How quickly?"
Patient privacy issues and missed opportunities for care are common concerns, as AI platforms are adopted in medical contexts worldwide. Last month, the use of platforms developed by Palantir to automate staff schedules in hospitals in the United States drew protests by a national nursing union. The use of AI by insurance companies to process and deny medical claims — even without a human reviewing them — has led to outrage and calls for regulation.
In contrast, PROMPTS operates as a limited-use program, trained on a relatively narrow set of issues and concerns. Its developers say the human element of the system is the most important part. A team of 18 nurses are employed to monitor, audit, and respond to PROMPTS questions around the clock.
"Humans are responsible for ensuring the quality of messages going out, and we audit the quality of the answers," says Javan Waita, Jacaranda Health's director of programs in Kenya.
Maintaining a significant human component of the program improves accuracy but raises the cost. Right now, it costs about $2 per user to maintain PROMPTS, which is absorbed by the nonprofit. That gets a mom through pregnancy, and stays with her for a year after birth.
Waita says this is an important backstop, especially when mothers might not have an alternative.
"The sooner a mother is able to access care, the sooner doctors will be able to understand the problem," Waita says. "If PROMPTS isn't there, it means more complications for mothers, more complications for newborns."

'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
- Published
Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."
Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.
"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.
In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.
He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.
Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

Hundreds of wreaths lined the pavement at the Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point, spilling into a nearby playground, while inside the hall the mood was hushed as top officials, former politicians and business chiefs filed in to pay their respects at the invitation-only vigil.
The hall was decorated with white orchids and pine trees, with wreaths from Tung’s widow, Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping, and their three children placed in front of the altar. She did not attend the vigil, the South China Morning Post learned.
One attendee said the ceremony followed the format of a typical local vigil. A master of ceremonies invited visitors to pay their respects and bow to Tung at the altar before they turned to his family to offer their condolences and receive their thanks.
“The mood is solemn and very quiet. Many visitors stay for about half an hour before leaving,” the attendee said, adding that some of Tung’s close friends were allowed into a room to view his body.

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

Pavlo Bazilinskyy still can’t believe he was on PornHub for work. He’s an assistant professor at the Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands, and has spent more than a decade researching AI-driven interactions between humans and robots. But he found himself typing “public transport” into the search bar of a very specific website’s “amateur section.” 297 hits.
“People are hard to predict,” Bazilinskyy says. It’s why he researches what he does. So his prurient pursuit had a point. Robotaxis without cabbies behind the wheel have started picking up passengers in a handful of countries, including the US. Meanwhile, there’s a long history of people getting up to antisocial behavior inside the quasi-private or straight-up public spaces of trains, planes, and automobiles—think the prom night limo, the “Mile High Club,” Tom Cruise in slow motion aboard the Chicago L in Risky Business, the stuff he found on PornHub.
What might riders do when there’s no authority figure inside a vehicle to say, “Hey, stop that!”? What do they do? Can people be convinced to stop before they start?
This week, Bazilinskyy and academic colleagues with backgrounds in systems engineering, computer science, psychology, and tourism studies are hosting an industry workshop asking participants to brainstorm along those very lines: How do you stop people from doing it in self-driving cars? Thinking about sex in autonomous vehicles, they theorize, can let anyone who cares about the future of mobility “stress-test” the role the vehicles might eventually play as communal spaces, where social norms get acted out every day.
The event focuses on prevention not just because these academics are no fun (though Alexandros Rouchitsas, an engineering psychologist who is also hosting the event, admits they are “taking the side of the parents, the elderly—we are not the cool people here”). They don’t want people to have sex in self-driving cars because they’re worried it will give a potentially positive technology a really bad rep.
“We want to see automated mobility solutions accepted, trusted by the general public,” Rouchitsas says. Self-driving could have huge upsides for the elderly, children, and people with disabilities, who have a harder time getting around places where driving is quicker and sometimes necessary. The tech might eventually move beyond private taxis and into public transit, where all sorts of people should be able to travel safely and comfortably. “We want automated mobility solutions to be seen as something that is equitable, serious, societally minded,” he says.
Rouchitsas’ biggest fear is that self-driving gets co-opted by the partiers, the drug users, the sort of hedonistic folk who have descended on some islands of his native Greece. “You know ‘Bang Bus’?” he says. “We don’t want that.”
The four-hour workshop—rise and shine, it starts at 8:30 am—is part of an industry conference in Gothenburg, Sweden, focusing on how people interact with vehicles and larger mobility systems. The organizers expect participants from academia but also the wider industry. (Gothenburg is home to Volvo Cars and the tech supplier SmartEye; BMW and Google are conference sponsors.) Those who show up will be prompted to come up with physical and design interventions that encourage people to not do that. The workshop will focus on preventing consensual interactions, its organizers say.
Rouchitsas, who studies human-machine interactions, says he hopes participants will get creative with their anti-action designs. But just off the top of his head: Maybe the vehicles could be transparent? Maybe a light begins to blink if the technology senses behavior it disapproves of? The organizers intend to publish a paper based on the workshop’s results.
Sex is the fun, eye-catching part here, made all the more alluring because it’s “the elephant in the room” for those thinking about how humans might interact with machines in the future, says Bazilinskyy—very under-studied. But the results of this sort of inquiry could help designers, companies, and lawmakers figure out how to compel people to safely share communal spaces like public self-driving buses in the future.
Prevent sex and maybe you’ll also prevent robbery, bullying, and homicide. “It could be helpful for the industry and academics to use this example to design other things,” he says.

3 new bus routes for Tengah, Woodlands; interim shuttles for delayed Jurong Region Line to launch from mid-2027
Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow said public transport is a “key priority” for Tengah, which has seen its population more than double to 28,000 over the past year.
SINGAPORE: Three new bus routes serving northern and western Singapore will be launched soon, including two services connecting Tengah to Choa Chu Kang and to Bukit Gombak.
This comes as the Tengah population has more than doubled to 28,000 residents over the past year, with more people still moving in every day, said Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow on Sunday (Sep 20).
“In another two more years, Tengah will have 57,000 residents,” he said at a Mid-Autumn Festival celebration at Tengah Community Club, where he gave updates on the Land Transport Authority’s (LTA) Bus Connectivity Enhancement Programme.
The government’s push to boost connectivity in Tengah, Singapore’s newest Housing and Development Board town, has made headlines in recent years, with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong once recalling a resident who described the area as the “Punggol of the West” amid its rapid development.
In his speech, Mr Siow said transport is a “key priority” for the new town, noting that there were only four bus services operating in Tengah last May. Today, there are 11 bus services, he said.
Some services only run during the peak hours for now because there are limited buses and drivers, he said.
“I wanted to prioritise getting more connections first, connect to more places first, instead of putting all the buses into one single service,” he said, adding that if there is demand, the services can slowly be expanded to off-peak hours.
As for the delayed Jurong Region Line (JRL), Mr Siow said an interim shuttle bus service, which will broadly follow the route of the JRL, will be introduced from the second half of 2027.
“Commuters will begin to enjoy the JRL’s connectivity on the original timeline – first by bus, and later by train when the JRL is up and running,” he said.
He previously shared that the JRL’s opening would be pushed back by around six months because of construction delays and testing, and that the line will open in the middle of 2028.
TENGAH, WOODLANDS BUS SERVICES
LTA said in a press release on Sunday that the new bus services 873 and 874, which connect to Tengah, will begin on Oct 25.
The former will link Tengah to Bukit Gombak, Hillview and Hume MRT stations, while the latter will link Tengah to Choa Chu Kang.
Mr Siow, who is a member of parliament for Chua Chu Kang GRC, said many residents have been asking for a bus service like 874.
“I understand, because many of the residents here have moved from Choa Chu Kang and your parents are still in Choa Chu Kang, family still there, some of your children also go to school in Choa Chu Kang,” he said.
Currently, commuters need to change buses two or three times to get to Choa Chu Kang.
“With 874, there will be just one bus,” he said, adding that it will pass through the Choa Chu Kang town centre and by Concord Primary School, Bukit Panjang Government High, Chua Chu Kang Primary, Sunshine Place and Brickland.
In Woodlands, new service 968 will begin at the temporary bus interchange and bring commuters to Woodlands North, Woodlands South and Admiralty MRT stations.
Mr Siow, who is also Second Minister for Finance, said 968 will support the opening of the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link, which is set to open in January 2027.
ENHANCEMENTS TO EXISTING SERVICES
Apart from the new bus routes serving northern and western Singapore, Mr Siow said more trips will also be added to city direct service 674 and service 861.
Service 674 connects Tengah to the Central Business District, while 861 links Sembawang and Yishun.
“I know these are very popular services that residents here take, and they are a bit crowded in the mornings, so we will add more buses and trips so you will have more frequent and less crowded rides,” said Mr Siow.
Over in Punggol, service 381 has been extended from Punggol East to Punggol Coast from Sep 13, LTA said.
LTA said more details on 674, 861, 968 and the Jurong Region Line buses will be shared closer to their respective implementation dates.

Aurobindo Pharma has received final approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (U.S. FDA) to manufacture and market Beclomethasone Dipropionate HFA Inhalation Aerosol, 40 mcg and 80 mcg.
The product is a generic equivalent of QVAR Inhalation Aerosol, 40 mcg and 80 mcg, marketed by Teva Branded Pharmaceutical Products R&D LLC. It is Aurobindo’s first metered-dose inhaler and marks the company’s expansion into complex respiratory therapies. Beclomethasone Dipropionate HFA Inhalation Aerosol is indicated in the maintenance treatment of asthma.
“Building on our leadership in generics, we are now expanding into complex inhalation therapies to create the next wave of differentiated growth in the U.S. market,” Aurobindo said on Tuesday.
The product will be manufactured at subsidiary Aurolife Pharma’s Raleigh facility in North Carolina and expected to be launched in upcoming quarters. The U.S. market for the approved product and newer versions of the reference product was estimated at $301 million for the 12 months ended July 2026, Aurobindo said citing IQVIA numbers.

Identity and access management startup OTPless has elevated cofounders Satyam Nathani and Tanmay Sagar as CEO and COO, respectively, as incumbent CEO Bhavik Koladiya steps away. Koladiya told Inc42 that he plans to retire but did not comment further on his future plans. Under the new leadership structure, Nathani will lead the startup’s strategy and expansion, while Sagar will oversee its operations and execution. OTPless said the appointments come as it looks to expand its offerings across authentication, identity, and payments. In a LinkedIn post announcing the leadership transition, Koladiya described his entrepreneurial journey as “exhilarating and exhausting”. He also expressed confidence in Nathani and Sagar leading OTPless through its next phase of growth. Before joining OTPless, Koladiya cofounded fintech unicorn BharatPe and later founded VC firm Finix Partners. OTPless was founded in 2021 by Nathani and Sagar, with Koladiya taking charge as CEO in January 2023. Nathani and Sagar were founding members of BharatPe. The Bengaluru-based startup helps consumer internet enterprises offer authentication services through its SDKs and APIs. Its offerings include silent network authentication, WhatsApp authentication, device intelligence, and passkeys. These offerings are aimed at reducing dependence on OTPs, PINs, and passwords while enabling enterprises to identify users, prevent fraud, and improve conversion during sign-ups and transactions. OTPless claims to authenticate more than 300 Mn mobile users and serve enterprises including Meesho, Navi, PhysicsWallah, ShareChat, Shiprocket, ixigo, and Zepto. It said it has reached ₹36 Cr in annualised revenue, representing a 2.5X increase over the previous year. The startup also claimed to have been profitable for the past two quarters. OTPless has raised over $6 Mn to date from Venture Highway, White Venture, FJ Labs, SIDBI , Piper Serica, among others. It last raised $3.5 Mn in a pre-Series A funding round led by SIDBI in May 2024. At the time, OTPless said it would use the capital to expand globally and extend its product suite beyond authentication into authorisation.

The 20th edition of the Asian Games are well and truly underway with medals already being won across disciplines.
India has won two medals in shooting on Sunday — both silver — with Suchika Tariyal also confirming another medal after reaching the MMA semifinals.
But what is the story behind the medals at the Aichi-Nagoya edition in Japan? Sportstar looks like the ideation, material, and the details surrounding the same:
Design concept
The design of the medals have been inspired by the Games slogan “Imagine One Asia”.
“The medal expresses the idea of coming together again through sport, represented through both its surface finish and form,” the official Asian Games website read.
Ceramic discs were broken during the ideation process till a “naturally appealing shape” emerged to form the medal’s design.
“The designer envisioned that athletes, too, have endured countless hardships and challenges on their journey to this moment,” the website added.
Who designed Asian Games 2026 medals?
The medals were designed by Daisuke Shiba (Representative Director, MERRY BEETLE Co., Ltd; Representative Director, TOGU General Incorporated Association).
Specifications of Asian Games 2026 medals
Dimensions
Weight/Material
How was the Asian Games 2026 design selected?
There was a competition which was open to students in the design field and individuals who have experience in the professional design field. A review committee selected the winning design.
Recycling involved
In order to promote Sustainable Development Goals, a part of the metals used for the medals was derived from small electronic devices donated by participating municipalities.
Asian Games 2026 medals ribbon
The ribbon carries the silhouette of the kakitsubata (Japanese iris), the official flower of Aichi Prefecture, along with sweeping arcs inspired by its leaves, as per the website.
Asian Games 2026 medals case
The case has an octagon-shaped figure, both inside and out.
“The character “八” (eight) was historically used in the emblem of the Owari Tokugawa family, which once ruled the region that is now Aichi Prefecture, and is also incorporated into the current emblem of Nagoya City,” the website explained.
The case has been made of Aichi-grown Japanese cypress (hinoki), a homage to the region’s long-standing tea ceremony culture where valuable tea utensils and treasures are traditionally stored in wooden boxes, the website added.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz under pressure ahead of German state elections
Polling stations have opened for two German regional elections that could impact Chancellor Friedrich Merz's hold on power
Polling is underway on Sunday across two German state elections where projected gains for the far-right AfD threaten to weaken Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s authority and hamper his ability to deliver economic reforms across Europe’s largest economy.
The regional contests are taking place in Berlin, the national capital, and in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a mostly rural territory in the former communist east that remains economically less affluent.
The voting follows just two weeks after the anti-migration, Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany, or AfD, fell barely short of an overall majority in the small eastern territory of Saxony-Anhalt, giving the movement its strongest opportunity to date to form a far-right regional government for the first time since World War II.
Merz’s leadership was hit hard by his party’s heavy defeat in that 6 September election.
The result stunned a population that had assumed thorough education and robust legal protections enacted after the Nazi era had provided lasting immunity to nationalism and racial ideology.
Further substantial gains for the AfD are expected on Sunday. However, the party lacks any practical path to power in Berlin and faces far tougher resistance from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s centre-left governor than it encountered from Merz’s party in Saxony-Anhalt.
Prospects for Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union are bleaker. It could lose the mayor’s office in Berlin.
If things go very badly, it could fail for the first time to win seats in a state legislature anywhere by falling below 5 per cent of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where it was already weak.
Merz, 70, became Germany’s leader 16 months ago with promises to turn around an economy that has barely grown in years, but has failed to lift a sullen national mood and has himself become deeply unpopular.
The strong showing of AfD in the Saxony-Anhalt election has further weakened the chancellor's standing on the national level as well, and in the past two weeks there have been calls even from within his own party to replace him as chancellor.
No top-level allies have called publicly for his departure, and many have warned against “personnel debates.”
Apparently anticipating a tough postelection period, Merz abandoned a planned trip to New York next week to attend the U.N. General Assembly. Despite the strong headwinds, he has repeatedly said that he’s determined to stay on and finish his term as chancellor.

A post (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that a pregnant woman gave birth on the road in Unnao, Uttar Pradesh, after a government hospital refused her admission due to her inability to cover the medical expenses. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of a woman giving birth on the roadside in Unnao, Uttar Pradesh, after a government hospital denied her admission.
Fact: The visuals are from Rajbiraj, Nepal, where a woman gave birth on the street outside a government Hospital in September 2026 after being denied care over unpaid preliminary test fees. However, a similar incident took place in Uttar Pradesh in April 2026, when a woman delivered her baby on the roadside outside a government hospital in Shamli district after staff allegedly demanded a bribe and refused her admission. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of viral visuals directed us to Nepali news reports (here, here & here) covering the same incident. The event reportedly occurred in the town of Rajbiraj, Nepal. According to these reports, on 10 September 2026, Babita Kumari Paswan, a 30-year-old woman, delivered her baby on the pavement outside the state-owned Gajendra Narayan Singh Hospital in Rajbiraj, Nepal, after her family couldn’t get the money required for preliminary tests.
After a video of the incident went viral, six hospital staff were reportedly suspended pending an investigation. A Google Street View of the hospital’s location matching the area seen in the viral video can be viewed here. However, it is worth noting that in April 2026, a similar incident (here & here) did occur in Uttar Pradesh, where a 30-year-old woman gave birth to a baby boy on the roadside outside the Shamli District Combined Hospital after staff allegedly refused her admission and demanded money. Hospital authorities formed a committee to investigate the matter.
To sum it up, the viral video depicting a woman delivering an infant on the street is from Nepal, not from Uttar Pradesh.

U.S. health regulators will review the scientific evidence on testosterone use in menopausal women on Thursday, including its benefits, risks, dosing and role in female health, as well as perspectives from doctors and patients.
The public meeting, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said could help guide future research and drug development, comes as a growing number of women are turning to testosterone to manage menopause symptoms.
There is no FDA-approved testosterone therapy for women, despite years of off-label use to treat low sexual desire, known as hypoactive sexual desire disorder, or HSDD.
Last year, the FDA removed the boxed warning about increased cardiovascular risk from testosterone products for men after reviewing post-marketing studies, though the products still carry warnings about increased blood pressure.
Physicians who prescribe testosterone to women typically rely on low doses of products approved for men, often dividing existing products such as AbbVie's AndroGel and Keenova Therapeutics' Testim, or on compounded formulations.
The lack of a female-specific product creates practical challenges for clinicians, said Diana Tordoff, an instructor in obstetrics and gynecology at Stanford, noting that an approved product could provide standardised dosing, labeling and safety-monitoring guidance and potentially improve insurance coverage.
Still, some experts say key questions remain unresolved. More long-term safety data are needed, said Stephanie Faubion, director of Mayo Clinic's Center for Women's Health.
The United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa have approved or licensed testosterone products specifically for women.
The FDA's request for public comments ahead of the meeting attracted hundreds of submissions, many from women describing improved libido, energy and quality of life while using testosterone.
Evidence and safety gaps
Interest in testosterone among menopausal women has grown alongside claims on social media that it can improve energy, muscle mass, bone health and cognition, though specialists say the evidence is strongest for HSDD.
"We do not have any evidence in women that it will improve muscle mass or bone density or mood or well-being or really any other metric," Faubion said.
Karen Adams, director of Stanford Medicine's Program in Menopause and Healthy Aging, said testosterone has been reviewed by the FDA four times for use in women but has never been approved because of a lack of long-term safety data and concerns about cardiovascular and breast cancer risks.
The FDA has approved non-testosterone options like Sprout Pharmaceuticals' Addyi and Cosette Pharmaceuticals' Vyleesi for certain patients with HSDD.
Testosterone is generally not recommended for women with a history of breast cancer because it can be converted to estrogen in the body that can drive some cancers.
Excessive testosterone exposure can cause acne and increased hair growth, physicians said, while rarer effects such as voice deepening and hair loss may be irreversible.
Studies show that testosterone therapy is generally considered safe for men with medically diagnosed low levels of the hormone when prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
Tordoff and Adams are leading Stanford's MIX-T pilot study examining how low-dose testosterone affects vaginal health and the vaginal microbiome in postmenopausal women. Results are expected within the next two years.

CJI Surya Kant urges courts to assess cumulative harm in climate disputes
Speaking at the two-day National Green Tribunal International Conference, the CJI said that aspects of the environment cannot be limited to geographical spaces
Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant on Saturday said that adjudication of climate disputes by courts should examine the cumulative harm caused to the environment rather than limit its scope to the isolated environmental injury caused by a project.
Speaking at the two-day National Green Tribunal International Conference, the CJI said that aspects of the environment cannot be limited to geographical spaces as the impact on the environment in one place has a cumulative impact on climate.
Stating the challenges that lie ahead for courts in the field of climate disputes, the CJI said, “A river does not experience pollution according to administrative boundaries. A forest does not understand the distinction between one project from another. The atmosphere does not recognise national frontiers. Climate adjudication must therefore look beyond the immediate proposal and examine the larger ecological system of which that project forms a part.”
He further said that recent Indian jurisprudence on climate marks an important development moving from environmental rights towards climate-related rights. “The recent Indian jurisprudence on climate has brought this question into sharper constitutional focus by recognising that the adverse effects of climate change can implicate fundamental rights of equality, livelihood, health and the conditions necessary for the meaningful enjoyment of rights.”
He said that the challenges immediately ahead will be more demanding as countries are transitioning to new forms of energy generation that require new infrastructure, new technologies and new patterns of land and resource use. “Cities will have to reconcile mobility, housing and economic activity with air quality, water security and ecological resilience. Climate disputes will also increasingly involve multiple actors and multiple jurisdictions,” CJI said.
Globally too, justice Kant said that courts across developed and developing countries have endeavoured to highlight that the “environment is not an inert backdrop to human ambition, but a living, breathing protagonist in the story of our shared well-being.”

HC seeks Delhi Police stand on contempt plea over failure to examine inspector's conduct
New Delhi, The Delhi High Court has sought the stand of the Delhi Police chief and other personnel on a plea seeking contempt proceedings against them for allegedly failing to comply with directions to conclude a departmental inquiry against an inspector.

The FIR was registered under Section 509 of the Indian Penal Code.

"Let affidavit be filed by the respondents, within a period of four weeks," the court said in the order, as it listed the matter for hearing in February.
Represented by lawyer Ujwal Ghai, the petitioner submitted that the FIR against him was "frivolous", but the inspector did not conclude the investigation for nine years, which caused humiliation to him till it was finally quashed by the High Court in August.

The High Court was subsequently informed that a department inquiry had been initiated, but no further status report was ever filed on the outcome of the proceedings against the inspector, the plea alleged.
The petition also informed that during the pendency of the quashing petition, a chargesheet was filed, but the trial court refused to take cognisance and instead requested the DCP concerned to initiate action against the inspector as per the law.
"It is submitted that the Respondents have taken the directions of this Hon'ble Court for granted as the same has not been complied with since February 2025... ."
Further, a compliance report has not been filed on as many as five dates and they "even concealed about the non-compliance of the order passed by the Hon'ble High Court on last date of hearing i.e. 10.08.2026 when the case was finally disposed of", the petition argued.
"The Respondent No. 1 & 2 have flouted the sanctity of the directions issued by this Constitutional Court and have undermined the majesty of this Hon'ble Court which should be dealt with iron hands in a strict and stern manner," the plea added.

Congo begins Ebola vaccinations for health workers in outbreak epicenter
This has been the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history.
BUNIA, Congo -- BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Congo on Saturday began vaccinating healthcare staff against Ebola in Bunia, the epicenter of the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history as they are “particularly exposed and deeply involved in the response,” the provincial governor said.
Health workers and other front-line workers in the Ebola response are being prioritized to receive the Ervebo vaccine that was effective in past Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common type of virus. Clinical trials are ongoing to find a licensed vaccine for the current outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has no licensed vaccine or treatment.
The rollout is targeting the Bunia and Mongbwalu zones in Ituri province, health authorities said Saturday. Both areas are among the hardest-hit by the virus.
“Our collective duty is to protect life. Launching this vaccination drive for front-line staff in Ituri is not an arbitrary choice, as these workers are particularly exposed and deeply involved in the response,” the military governor of Ituri, Maj. Gen. Gaby Kasongo Mulumba, said Saturday.
The campaign in Ituri and North Kivu is expected to cover 20,000 front-line workers over a period of six to nine months.
As of Saturday, the country had recorded 7,541 confirmed cases, including 3,639 deaths, according to government figures, while 1,823 people have recovered. The outbreak is concentrated in Ituri province and is known to be the deadliest of all past 17 Ebola outbreaks in the country.
The outbreak is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers’ strike and intense population movements. The World Health Organization has said it remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Dr. Jeannot Elua, whom The Associated Press met at a health facility in Bunia, said the vaccine was “beneficial.”
“We healthcare workers don’t really have a choice: we are going to receive it,” he said. “Some people here had already received the previous vaccine. I received it myself, because it was mandatory.”
Another front-line health worker, Dr. Jean Paul Uzele, who was vaccinated with Ervebo during the 10th Ebola outbreak, said it was unclear to him whether he should get vaccinated again.
“If it arrives, we will receive it too," he said. “But the question is whether we need to be vaccinated a second time."
Last month, the Ervebo vaccine was rolled out in Kisangani in the Tshopo province. The campaign was expected to cover 14 health zones in Tshopo, Bas-Uele and Haut-Uele provinces.
The use of Ervebo is taking place in a specific scientific context. The vaccine is licensed for use against Ebola virus disease caused by the Zaire strain — a different, more common type of Ebola virus.
The World Health Organization said last month that 70,000 doses of Ervebo were approved for use in Congo.
About 50,000 doses are intended for front-line and health workers, while 20,000 doses will be used in a clinical trial to study whether the vaccine protects against Bundibugyo virus, which is causing the current outbreak and has no licensed vaccine or treatment.
The vaccine is being used under a compassionate-use program, which allows a medical product to be used in a serious disease situation even though it has not been specifically approved for that particular use.
Health authorities said Ervebo could offer some protection against the Bundibugyo virus because the two viruses are related. But whether the vaccine can actually prevent illness in people infected with Bundibugyo Ebola is still being studied.

Trump demanded gerrymandered districts ahead of the midterms. His plan could backfire badly
Democrats have a 69 percent probability of winning the House, compared to Republicans’ 31 percent, according to a new analysis
For over a year, President Donald Trump has been pressuring Republican-led states to redraw their congressional districts with the hope of gaining more seats in November’s midterm elections.
But, according to a new analysis, not only does the multi-state gerrymander look unlikely to work — it may even put more Democrats in power.
Democrats have a 69 percent probability of winning the House, compared to Republicans’ 31 percent, according to a forecast on Thursday from Decision Desk Headquarters.
Last year, numerous Republican-led states under pressure from Trump began pursuing congressional redistricting. While Democrats feared the effort would lead to Republicans maintaining the majority, current data suggests otherwise.
“Redistricting doesn’t look likely to save Republicans in the House. Not only are Democrats favored to capture the House, but they may even gain seats in the redistricted states,” said Geoffrey Skelley, the chief elections analyst for Decision Desk HQ.
The forecast predicts Democrats will win an average of 13 seats in the states with unchanged boundaries, and an average of two seats gained from the nine states that were redistricted.
Across the forecast’s 1 million simulations, Democrats won an average seat majority of 229-206. This would mean a 14-seat gain for Democrats from the current 220-215 GOP majority.
“In our forecast for the unchanged states, Democrats win an average of nearly 150 seats, up from the 137 they currently control,” Skelley wrote.
“Meanwhile, the redistricted states do not come close to offsetting that shift. In those nine states, Democrats win a small gain, on average, going from 78 to 80 seats.”
In Texas, which kicked off the redistricting race by Republican-led states at Trump’s urging last summer, “Republicans are averaging a bit under a two-seat gain, roughly three seats short of their ideal,” Skelley wrote.
Some of these redrawn districts are home to heavily Latino communities, where Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vincente Gonzalez, both Democrats, are expected to hold on to their seats on the November 3 election.
Democrats are forecast to have a 1 in 3 shot of holding onto the newly-drawn 35th district, as well as a 1 in 3 chance of defeating incumbent GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in the 15th District. They also have a 1 in 5 chance of flipping the 23rd District, held by the controversy-stricken Brandon Herrera. Herrera has drawn scrutiny after a CNN review of his videos, podcast appearances and social media posts found years of derogatory and explicit comments about women. He has said his online content includes “dark humor.”
It comes after Trump argued Republicans were “entitled” to pick up five more House seats in Texas.
“We should have many more seats in California. It’s all gerrymandered,” Trump told CNBC’s Squawk Box. “And we have an opportunity in Texas to pick up five seats. We have a really good governor, and we have good people in Texas. And I won Texas. I got the highest vote in the history of Texas, as you probably know, and we are entitled to five more seats.”
Florida may also see Republicans underperform come November 3, even though redistricting was done to target four Democratic-held seats. Two of those seats are currently held by Democrats who are favored to win their races, according to Skelley.
The odds seem similar in Ohio, where three Democrats are likely to keep their seats this Election Day while Rep. Max Miller’s district may be more of a toss-up amid allegations of domestic abuse related to his ex-wife. He has denied the allegations.
Meanwhile, Democratic-led California responded to Texas’ redraw with a ballot measure that was approved in a statewide vote in November 2025 that implemented a retaliatory gerrymander targeting five GOP-held seats.
The move could give Democrats four out of five seats.
“A potential Republican win there, as well as outside shots in districts such as the 13th, 45th, and GOP-held 48th help keep Democrats from averaging the full-on five-seat gain they want in California,” Skelley wrote.
Missouri is the latest state to enter a redistricting battle. However, the state’s Supreme Court shot down a new map that was backed by Trump, saying that the changes would have to be approved by voters in the fall before the lines could be redrawn.
A federal appeals court was considering the new redistricting on Thursday.
The state will likely use the same lines as it did in 2022 and 2024. The Decision Desk HQ has a freeze on Missouri’s forecast until the legal battle over the map is settled.

Gender disparity in organ transplantation is a global problem affecting each step of the transplantation process, from organ donation, recipient listing, waiting times and access, to post-transplant outcomes. This inequality is most visibly expressed in the overrepresentation of women as living donors, while men continue to be the majority of transplant recipients.
What the data reveals
India’s case is a particularly striking example of this gender imbalance. Women constitute the majority of living organ donors, but men get the majority of transplants. As per recent data from the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organization (NOTTO), between 2019 and 2023, 63.8% of living organ donors were women and 69.8% of transplant recipients were men.
This is not a new divide. In 2019 and 2020, roughly two-thirds of living donors were women, but only about a quarter of recipients were women. A 2025 analysis found that women accounted for 36,038 of the 56,509 living donations over the five-year period studied, also highlighting the scale of the imbalance. Of these, however, only 17,041 were transplanted into women, as against 39,447 transplanted into men.
This gendered pattern raises a fundamental question: why are women expected to give and men positioned to receive in disproportionate numbers? The answer goes far beyond biology.
Behind the donations
Women’s decisions to donate organs are shaped by a complicated interaction between sociocultural expectations, economic conditions and family structures. In many Indian homes, women, particularly wives and mothers, are still expected to put the needs of their families before their own. The expectation can be particularly sharp in the case of a life-saving transplant for a close family member.
Studies have noted the role of women in familial organ donation. Mothers are, on average, 73% of all parental donations, and wives are 91% of donations between married couples. These figures are suggestive of a long-standing social tendency to assign the bulk of care work to women, and perhaps even to the final act of bodily sacrifice.
Psychological and experiential reasons may also play a role in women’s higher willingness to donate. Past experiences with the health care system, such as pregnancy and delivery, may increase familiarity with medical settings and trust in health care providers. But these explanations have to be discussed in the light of the strong influence of social conditioning. What seems like a personal choice can sometimes be influenced by expectations, emotional duties or an unspoken belief that a woman should make sacrifices for her family.
Patriarchal attitudes can also be a disincentive for men to become donors. Men are generally considered the primary breadwinner and economic provider for their families. Thus, the prospect of a man needing major surgery, a long recovery period or a temporary loss of income might be seen as an unacceptable financial risk. Such pressure can transfer the burden of donation to women.
This dynamic is particularly problematic when financial dependency is a factor. The costs of evaluation, surgery, recovery and the potential loss of household income may make male donation seem less feasible. In such cases, women may be subtly, and in more troubling cases, explicitly encouraged to donate, because they are seen as more expendable in the family’s economic structure. Thus, the line between voluntary altruism and coercion can become perilously blurred.
It is, therefore, the duty of healthcare providers to fully discuss these issues at every stage of the process, explain the ramifications of a donation and t ensure that they are indeed personal choices of women, and not influenced by other factors.
What needs to change
This has implications for more than just transplant statistics. Essentially, it’s a question of equity, autonomy and justice in healthcare. An organ donation system cannot be truly equitable when it is based on social and familial pressures about who is supposed to donate, and on socioeconomic or structural barriers about who gets the transplant.
Interventions are required at several levels to address this gap. Awareness must be the starting point, but awareness is not enough. Transplant services and community-based initiatives should be extended to rural, underserved and marginalised regions and not be confined to major urban centres. In particular, women should have equal access to information, evaluation and transplantation services.
Equally important is strengthening psychosocial assessment of potential living donors. Pre-transplant evaluation should not only include medical suitability and financial considerations, but also explore the wider social environment in which the donation decision is being made. Healthcare professionals should be trained to recognise warning signs of coercion, domestic abuse, threats, violence, manipulation and financial dependence. Donors must be provided with real opportunities to make informed and voluntary decisions, including the opportunity to withdraw without fear of repercussions.
Better and more comprehensive data collection is also needed in India. Good, disaggregated data on donors and recipients – disaggregated by gender, age, socioeconomic status, geography, relationship to recipient and other relevant factors, would enable policymakers to better identify disparities and design evidence-based interventions. Grassroots research is important because national averages can hide significant inequalities at the regional and community level.
The challenge is to move beyond the financial transaction of organ donation, and to acknowledge the quieter pressures that can exist within families. Sometimes coercion doesn’t take the form of an explicit threat. It could be the expectations of a wife, the responsibilities of a mother or the assumption that a woman should sacrifice herself for the family’s survival.
The bigger message is hard to miss: gender inequality does not stop at the hospital door. It can influence who gives, who gets, who waits and ultimately who gets a chance to live.
(Dr Shivakumar S. Patil is consultant, renal transplant surgery, Manipal Hospital, Hebbal. shivakumar.patil@manipalhospitals.com)
