Cyber researchers broke into OpenAI using its key rival Anthropic’s software, highlighting vulnerabilities in the ChatGPT maker’s security as leading AI companies face mounting scrutiny over safety.
A small cyber security group gained access to an OpenAI employee’s ChatGPT account, which permitted them to read private software information and suggest changes.
The researchers had been given access to an Anthropic tool specifically designed for security professionals, and were paid for the work as part of a program to find vulnerabilities before they could be exploited by bad actors.
Their ability to swiftly break into one of the world’s two leading AI labs again raises concerns about OpenAI’s security amid rising worries about powerful models being used by hackers and foreign adversaries.
The US has in recent months grappled with how to manage the vetting and release of the latest models, including temporarily blocking some Anthropic tools.
The latest incident occurred just two weeks after a swarm of more than 1,000 OpenAI agents escaped a test environment to hack the start-up Hugging Face, which caused widespread awareness of AI’s ability to hack autonomously without human intent.
The three researchers from Hacktron AI, a small security company, were paid $6,500 by OpenAI as part of a bug bounty program, a common practice where tech companies pay ethical hackers to test their security.

The US Army brought thousands of drones to a recent combat exercise, and roughly half were designed to be expendable. Soldiers could use and lose the drones in the fight, treating them like ammunition.
The Army's shift toward using low-cost drones has relied on amassing enough systems to make them expendable. It's getting tens of thousands of drones to soldiers through the Drone Dominance Program, the goal being that soldiers use these systems without worrying about quickly coming up empty.
At the recent Saber Junction exercise in Germany, Army soldiers used approximately 1,900 autonomous systems.
"Those numbers continue to increase every rotation, and we will continue to increase them in future rotations," Maj. Gen. Christopher Norrie, acting commander of US Army Europe and Africa, told reporters at a roundtable on Thursday, which Business Insider received a transcript of.
Of those roughly 2,000 drones used during the exercise, "1,000 were consumable," Brig. Gen. Terry Tillis, head of the 7th Army Training Command, said, adding that soldiers were using them "like a munition."
"They're fired, and then it's employing them in a matter to achieve effects on the battlefield," he said.
At the Saber Junction exercise, US soldiers used drones in different combat scenarios, some informed by the war in Ukraine, against electronic warfare and counter-drone systems. Army officials said replicating more challenging environments was important for giving soldiers realistic experiences.
Using a bunch of drones was similarly important, as "those drones are now a part of our basics of being able to survive and integrate into protection plans, using them to sense further and strike faster," Norrie said.
Russia's war in Ukraine has shown that while drones do not always replace more exquisite strike capabilities, they can offer soldiers a low-cost and effective method for hitting enemy targets. Not worrying about losing the drones to jamming or enemy fire — and having a large enough stockpile to resupply quickly — gives troops a fairly consistent weapon to rely on.
Last year, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth issued a memo directing an overhaul of how the Pentagon purchases small uncrewed aerial systems across the armed forces. The resulting program, Drone Dominance, is investing $1 billion to purchase at least 200,000 drones through 2027.
That memo also characterized how the military should be thinking small drones.
"Small UAS resemble munitions more than high-end airplanes. They should be cheap,rapidly replaceable, and categorized as consumable," the defense secretary wrote.
Tens of thousands of drones have been bought from different companies as part of the Drone Dominance effort. "We're in the process of receiving another 30,000 drones currently," Col. Gregory Merkl, the director of drone dominance for the Army, said. "That is enough absolutely to get them down to every squad level."
Soldiers have also been working on building and 3D printing parts for their own drones so that they can quickly craft systems when they need them or customize them for specific missions.
Earlier this year, a brigade from the 101st Airborne Division, for instance, assembled roughly 150 of the 228 attack drones they used in an exercise, with each system taking a couple of hours for a soldier to build.
Speaking about that exercise, Col. Ryan Bell, the commander of the 3rd Mobile Brigade, said, "If a company has only one or two drones, or a platoon has a single drone, it's a niche capability," Bell said, referring to one-way attack drones. "But a company that is provided 20 drones a day has an entirely new form of combat power."

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
Molly McCann Sanders has a lot in common with many of the other women who helped Donald Trump win a second term as president. A pro-life Catholic who lives in Texas, she has staunchly conservative opinions on immigration and a fierce hatred of eminent domain—the practice of the government taking private property for public use.
Sanders, the president of the Eagle Forum Education & Legal Defense Fund, which was started by Phyllis Schlafly, also describes herself as “a crunchy MAHA mom”—and says she’s been paying particular attention to data centers.
“I'm alarmed by the idea that these data centers can move in and pollute,” she tells me. “I'm not a data center expert. I'm not a tech expert. But I’m suspicious and wary, and want to move slowly.”
She loves Trump, “but I think he’s wrong about data centers,” she says. And she sees the GOP’s effort to court what she calls “the laptop class”—young men who are enthusiastic about technology—at the Republican midterm convention earlier this month as a huge misstep with midterms nearing.
McCann Sanders isn’t alone. More than 60 percent of Americans, including 47 percent of Republicans, say they are opposed to the construction of data centers in a poll released by The New York Times last week. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee sent a private memo to AI companies sounding the alarm on how voters perceive data centers, warning that “campaign or party committees can not fix the toxic brand of an entire segment of the economy.” Last week, GOP strategist Tony Fabrizio issued a memo to the party’s candidates claiming that “unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position.”
But the GOP is facing one big hurdle: Trump himself. In recent weeks, facing mounting scrutiny on his policies and support for the industry, Trump has doubled down on his defense of both data centers and AI. In late August, he wrote in a Truth Social post that only communities that wanted to be “backwards and poor” would refuse data centers coming to town.
Last week, he issued yet another series of posts boosting AI data centers. Users on his own Truth Social platform pushed back. An analysis from The New York Times of thousands of responses found that anti-data-center and anti-AI comments—including from staunch MAGA accounts—outnumbered positive comments by four to one.
Sanders says she sometimes “looks past” the wilder things Trump says, but she can’t fully overlook his pro-data-center rhetoric.
“That is not the right way to go about this,” she says of the “backwards and poor” post. “We do have legitimate concerns. There are real problems.”
My colleague Hugo Lowell, who covers the White House and writes our Inner Loop newsletter, says he’s not surprised by Trump’s attitude. “He’s bullish on AI,” he tells me. “He’s been told that restricting data center development means restricting compute, which means the US loses to China.”
The China competition angle is being publicly echoed by tech accelerationists and White House allies, including former White House AI czar David Sacks and investor and Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale. The latter debated Steve Bannon’s tech editor Joe Allen—whom I profiled last month—at an auxiliary event during the convention. That conversation between Lonsdale and Allen, Sanders says, was the only time she heard data centers brought up during the entire midterm convention.
There’s some evidence that voters haven’t quite made up their minds on how heavily to weigh the issue—and which party to trust. The New York Times poll found that AI and data centers rank far down the list of voters’ priorities, and almost 20 percent say they don’t know which party would handle the issue better.
And candidates otherwise aligned with Trump may just decide to ignore cues from the White House. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for governor in Wisconsin, has scored Trump’s endorsement. But he’s also attacked his Democratic opponent David Crowley for what Tiffany claims are pro-data-center views.
But despite breaks like Tiffany’s and concerns like Sanders’, Trump “thinks MAGA at the end of the day will back him—on Epstein, on Iran, on AI,” Hugo says.
What We’re Writing
Haven’t you always wished that data centers were a little more cuddly? You’re in luck! My colleague Boone Ashworth wrote about a new server-shaped plushie with gangly limbs and a little smiley face, called Bezzy. (Adorable!) When you squeeze him, he emits a terrible droning noise—real audio recorded by people living next to a data center in Virginia.
Bezzy is part of a larger project designed to raise awareness about data center expansion in the US. The plush toy is one of the many ways the data center backlash is taking shape.
“Personally, I love Bezzy and want to adopt one,” Boone says. “Also, it makes me very grateful I don't live near a data center. I really feel for people who do.”
What We’re Reading
The Washington Sun reports that the Interior Department is considering at least 12 data center proposals across at least 17,600 acres of public land—far more than had been previously reported.
Writer Natalie Fertig traveled to a swing district in Pennsylvania to take the political pulse of anti-data-center organizers there. Despite their success in blocking a big data center project, many of the folks she interviewed in both political parties felt like politicians didn’t care about them.
Amazon admitted this week that it had permanently lost customer data that was stored in data centers hit by Iranian drone strikes earlier this year. Reuters broke the story.
Virginia governor Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order on Friday that creates a state AI task force and may limit data centers. The latter is particularly notable given that the state is home to Data Center Alley, a global hot spot for the facilities. Read more about the order in The Verge.

Sky Sports News reporter Danyal Khan assesses the choppy waters Manchester United boss Michael Carrick has found himself in after back-to-back defeats; watch Fulham vs Man Utd on Sunday, live on Sky Sports Premier League from 4pm; kick-off 4.30pm
Sunday 20 September 2026 07:11, UK
Manchester United's Carabao Cup second-round loss at Grimsby last season was a result that many will remember.
It was a defeat which became synonymous with former Manchester United head coach Ruben Amorim's time in charge.
That was a very bad night for United, and although Wednesday's defeat at home to Brighton did not feel as significant, there were similarities for the man who succeeded Amorim, Michael Carrick.

Man Utd's captain for the loss, Youri Tielemans, admitted afterwards that once they went 2-0 down, his side stopped playing - and that was pretty evident by their performance.
You could sense at Old Trafford from 20 minutes onwards that Brighton were in the ascendancy and the game was only going to go one way. Despite bringing on Bruno Fernandes, Kobbie Mainoo, Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha, United failed to make an impression.
That is what will truly worry head coach Carrick.
After the few defeats Carrick has suffered since his return to the club in January, he has always backed his players or found positive qualities in the performances, but there was no such redemption to be found against Brighton.
Predictable problems and defensive worries
When Carrick and his staff first came in, they deservedly received a lot of praise.
Defensively they looked tight and compact and that led to impressive wins against Manchester City and Arsenal.
The likes of Steve Holland, Jonathan Woodgate and Jonny Evans made an immediate improvement to the defensive unit.
But, equally, questions have to be raised now about the frailties that same defence is showing this season. Carrick's side have conceded two goals in three of their four Premier League games.
The defence was exposed once again in the Brighton loss. Yes, one goal was a goalkeeping error by Karl Darlow, but aside from the goals conceded, the shape and understanding of the back four lacked any sort of coherence.
Left-back predictably is an issue for Carrick. He has yet to acknowledge the area as a specific weakness as per his style when engaging in the media, but it is a significant problem - one the United hierarchy knew about going into the summer's transfer window.
Luke Shaw, United's only senior left-back at the club, has missed the last three games through a minor injury, but considering his age and injury track record - despite his excellent availability last season - it was naive not to strengthen in that area.
Carrick has experimented with Noussair Mazraoui in that position but he seems to have fallen down the pecking order, as the less experienced Patrick Dorgu was preferred for the Manchester derby loss.
Young left-back Harry Amass does not seem to be fancied in the position long-term either - so how will United remedy the position for the rest of the season?
An awkward discussion over Carrick's future
It seems ridiculous to even discuss Carrick's job security after only a few weeks of the new season.
Man Utd have still accumulated the most points across the league since his return in January.
However, as Carrick admitted himself, a few moments such as Ainsley Maitland-Niles' equaliser for Everton, City's controversial VAR goal and now a shocking collapse against Brighton, have made it all feel very different.
If United lose at Fulham on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, there will be inevitable and uncomfortable discussions around whether Carrick can lead United out of the storm they currently find themselves in.
That may be for another day, but the United head coach does deserve sympathy for the squad he has been dealt.
The lack of sales and outgoings this summer at United handicapped them in being able to further reinforce the squad. But does that excuse them ignoring key areas to strengthen?
The left-back area, as mentioned, should have been strengthened. Knowing Benjamin Sesko was still nursing a shin injury all summer, perhaps United should have brought in a temporary No 9 to share the load rather than playing Mbeumo and Cunha out of position. Both players have failed to discover the form they showed under Carrick last season.
But, ultimately, until United are able to be in a position where they can really reshape their team in one window, they will continue to be caught in this cycle of strengthening just enough with players left over from previous regimes.
That perhaps is why you could hear boos at Old Trafford after the Brighton loss. Not just aimed at that performance, but perhaps a familiar feeling of a cycle beginning again, a deja vu of seasons past and another false dawn after a promising start under a new United head coach.
Again, it feels too soon for that just yet, and Carrick deserves time after what he delivered last season, but these are the waters he has to navigate, and ultimately, he will be the one judged.
But if he can stop the spiral, even without a win against Fulham with a positive performance, time may allow him to be able to steer the ship back on course.

By Anupam Pateriya, Bhopal

A 30-year-old man allegedly killed his wife and three children with an axe following an argument at their home in Kabirpur village in Madhya Pradesh’s Damoh district on Saturday morning, police said.
Police identified the deceased as Khema Patel (27), her daughter Urmila (7), and her sons, aged five and one.
Investigations revealed that disputes between the couple had been ongoing for over a year. “Six months ago, Khema had filed a dowry harassment complaint at Magron police station, though family members attempted reconciliation,” Damoh superintendent of police (SP) Anand Kaladgi said.
Damoh superintendent of police (SP) Anand Kaladgi said, “We received information at 6.30 am that a man was sitting with an axe outside his house claiming he had killed his family members. A police team rushed to the spot and arrested him.”
The husband, Dwarka Patel, did not flee after the murders. He was found sitting outside his house with an axe, waiting for the police.
“On Friday, fresh arguments broke out. Relatives tried to intervene but left after the situation appeared calm. In the early hours of Saturday, Dwarka allegedly attacked his wife and children while they were asleep,” the SP said.
Police are now investigating the sequence of events, taking into account the earlier complaint and family testimonies.

If there is one feature that truly revolutionized because of AI, it is voice typing. Voice typing did exist way before AI, but it was very basic. It only converted the spoken audio directly into text, which included all the filler words, missing punctuation, grammar mistakes, and more. It basically turned whatever you spoke into text.
But with AI, voice typing goes through one extra step, where all your typing is fed to the AI models, which remove all filler words and format the sentence structure. It fundamentally eliminates the need for you to copy text into multiple apps, fix the grammar and sentence structure, and then copy it again to wherever you need it.
Third-party voice dictation apps went ahead and also included support for different formatting styles based on the app you are using, and they support almost every app.
However, the AI voice dictation feature truly gained traction after Google introduced the Pixel 11’s Rambler feature, which is very similar to AI voice dictation apps that use AI to refine the speech-to-text output.

Japan’s central bank has increased interest rates to a fresh 31-year high as it attempts to combat high global inflation linked to the war in Iran.
The Bank of Japan voted to raise its target interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level since 1995.
The move meant the BoJ joined the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in tightening monetary policy this month, as central banks attempt to curb the impact of rising prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The Bank of England on Thursday voted to leave UK interest rates on hold at 3.75% but warned they could soon rise amid the fallout from the Iran war.
The BoJ has been raising rates since 2024, when it lifted its base rate out of negative territory. It has been under pressure to raise borrowing costs as the yen weakened steadily against the dollar this year, to levels that prompted policymakers to intervene to stabilise the currency. The Japanese currency weakened about 0.7% against the dollar on Friday.
The vote to raise rates was not unanimous – with two board members dissenting to the increase.
“The tone of the statement, along with two dissenters for the decision to raise rates, leaves lingering doubts that Japan’s central bank will be cautious in tightening monetary policy further,” Fred Neumann, the chief Asia economist at HSBC, said.
“While back-to-back hikes appear unlikely, investors will look for clues as to whether officials are prepared to raise interest rates again in December.”
The drop in the yen helped the Nikkei stock market index to rise nearly 2%, while the Japanese two-year government bond yields, which are most sensitive to monetary policy expectations, fell four basis points to 1.82%.
European stock futures slipped 0.35%, indicating a lower open.
Prashant Newnaha, a senior rates strategist at TD Securities, said the BOJ reiterated its concerns that underlying inflation could deviate upwards from its 2% target, but “we don’t see a smoking gun supporting a back-to-back hike in October”.
He said: “We stick with our call for rate hikes roughly every quarter with the next 25 basis points hike in December.”
Hopes of alternative ways for oil supply from the Middle East to reach markets pushed Brent crude futures down as much as 1.5% to $103.29 a barrel even as concerns about strikes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis lingered.

Sunday 20 September 2026 08:52, UK
Pat Brown won the vacant British and Commonwealth cruiserweight titles on home turf on Saturday night, counting out John Hedges in the sixth round at Co-op Live with a body shot he dedicated to Ricky Hatton.
The 26-year-old Olympian took his professional record to seven wins from seven, every one inside the distance, adding the Lonsdale Belt to the WBA International and IBF Intercontinental titles already in his possession.
For Hedges, it was a case of unlucky number 13 after the Harlow-born fighter had gone unbeaten through his first 12 fights.

It was anything but straightforward for Brown, though. Hedges is 6ft 6in, and a southpaw, and the 24-year-old spent the opening exchanges making himself hard to hit, giving Brown nothing to aim at and grabbing hold whenever the Mancunian worked his way inside.

Cruz calls out Garcia after stopping Bravo
Isaac Cruz has called out Ryan Garcia after knocking out Nestor Bravo in San Diego to retain his WBC interim super-lightweight title for a second time at the Pechanga Arena in a controversial contest.
"Hey, Ryan, I'm here," Cruz, known by the nickname 'Pitbull', said after winning the fight. "My next fight for you. Come on, Ryan."
Garcia stopped Conor Benn inside two rounds in Las Vegas last Saturday to retain his WBC welterweight title.
By Monday he was talking about a fast turnaround, naming December or January for his return and Cruz among the men he would face.
Whether it is that simple is another matter as Garcia has also been linked with a fight against Teofimo Lopez, who holds a world title at welterweight, while Cruz operates a division below.
Garcia responded to callout following the fight, though, and said: "Pitbull proved me wrong tonight. Let's do this in December, the offer is on the table.

On Saturday night though, Cruz boxed effectively and started fast as he caught Bravo with a hook in the first round as the Puerto Rican attempted to tie up.
Then came the controversy, courtesy of the referee.
Thomas Taylor took a point off Bravo in the second for holding, warned both men in the third after a series of low blows and docked the Puerto Rican again in the fourth for dumping Cruz on the canvas - telling him bluntly that a disqualification would leave him unpaid.

Parth Jindal elected president of Tamil Nadu Judo Association
Parth Jindal, the founder of JSW Sports, has been elected president of the Tamil Nadu Judo Association (TNJA), taking formal charge after serving as its interim head.
Jindal entered the association through its Thanjavur district unit, where he served as vice-president, before moving into the State body. His election places him at the helm of a programme aimed at expanding judo at the grassroots and creating a stronger pathway for Tamil Nadu’s leading judokas.
Vijaya Mohana Murali, TNJA’s former president and now chief executive officer, said Jindal supported judo for more than a decade before taking a formal role in the association. Murali also said Jindal was a brown belt in the sport.
“He has been supporting judo with zero expectations,” Murali told Sportstar. “He didn’t want to become president or anything. He didn’t have any such expectations.”
Jindal already has an established presence in Indian sport through JSW Sports and the Inspire Institute of Sport (IIS), its high-performance centre in Bellari, Karnataka. Murali said that experience, coupled with Jindal’s personal association with judo, made him a suitable choice to lead the TNJA’s next phase.
The association’s immediate plan is to increase the number of qualified instructors working at the grassroots. Alongside that drive, it intends to identify, assess and further develop promising judokas, with selected athletes training at IIS and, where required, abroad.
The programme will be implemented in six-month phases over the next three years. The opening phase will concentrate on coach development and preparing existing athletes to compete at the international level.
Murali said Jindal had become interim president before the agreement involving JSW, the Tamil Nadu government and the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu was reached. He stressed that the partnership was not the reason for Jindal’s elevation but would support the association’s development plans.
According to the TNJA, the election was conducted by Advocate Elephant Rajendran, the election officer, and overseen by High Court-appointed observer Justice Govindarajan and Tamil Nadu Olympic Association observer Latha.

US and Saudi Arabia lack plan as Houthi strikes expose Riyadh's vulnerability
Saudi Arabia and the United States do not have a clear plan to fight back against the Houthis who took control of a strategically important island on the Red Sea, according to reports.
Multiple sources told CNN on Sunday that despite the US providing additional intelligence and targeting support to Saudi Arabia, it is still unable to push back against Houthi forces.
Anonymous US officials who spoke to CNN said that for months, its intelligence reports indicated the Houthis would attempt to close another key waterway for commercial shipping as Iran did earlier this year.
But despite Saudi Arabia's reassurances for the last decade that it had given effective training to the Saudi-backed Yemeni government to fight the Houthis, according to two US officials, Washington still believes that Riyadh is not capable of pushing back the Houthis.
The CNN report comes after US President Donald Trump unexpectedly cut short a retreat at Camp David to return to the White House on Saturday.

While the administration offered no official explanation for the early departure - a schedule change that could have been due to forecast rain and thunderstorms in rural Maryland - it coincided directly with a major military escalation against Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis reported on Saturday that the Iran-backed group fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh at dawn.
According to local media reports, Saudi authorities issued an unprecedented early-morning alert instructing residents to shelter indoors.
Firefighters were subsequently dispatched to extinguish a fire at a fuel depot near the capital's international airport, where a tanker bearing the Aramco logo had caught fire.
Limitations exposed
Coalition spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki confirmed the missile interception over Riyadh and noted that air defences thwarted separate attempts to target Taif, Baish, Farasan and the coastal city of Yanbu before they reached their targets.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed responsibility, stating the strikes were retaliation for "the Saudi enemy's criminal attempts to target the capital Sanaa".
The State Department and a number of US embassies in the region have also issued urgent security alerts to Americans, citing "the potential for unforeseen escalation" and noting that "Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports".
According to reports, the weekend strikes are part of a broader, intensified campaign by the group to seize full control of Yemen's Red Sea coastline and the vital Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The offensive has exposed the limits of Saudi military capabilities; the kingdom is reportedly running critically low on missile interceptors to defend its domestic infrastructure and has requested urgent air defence support from France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt.
Rebuffed requests
Riyadh's recently signed defence pacts with Turkey and Pakistan have yielded limited immediate action.
While Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan condemned the attacks and offered help under the trilateral pact, he warned that Saudi Arabia should be "kept out" of the broader conflict between Iran and the United States.
Pakistan similarly stated it would act only when the "time comes".
Despite these alarming developments, Washington has shown no appetite to directly enter the fray.
The Trump administration has signalled that its red line is direct US participation in kinetic strikes against the Houthis, capping American involvement at intelligence sharing and targeting data - though the State Department did recently approve a $24.3bn sale of F-35 fighter jets to the kingdom to "deter current and future threats".
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly spoke with Trump twice last week to request US military strikes against the Houthis, but those requests were rebuffed.
Trump has publicly communicated his desire to keep American forces out of the conflict, recently telling reporters: "The Houthis called us and they don't want to fight with us... It's just one country they're not too happy with, and we'll get that straightened out."
This hands-off approach has deeply alarmed Gulf partners, who view the Houthi offensive as a dangerous new front in a broader regional conflict.
As the Houthi advances exacerbate a severe global energy crisis and force Saudi Arabia to cut oil exports, Riyadh faces an increasingly dire reality: with the US reportedly solidifying its own ceasefire with the Houthis via talks in Oman, the kingdom is left to manage a widening conflict largely on its own.

On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced its revamped social media team, appointing Deepak Mhaskey as the national social media convenor, and Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav as co-convenors.
While curiosity grew as to who these newly appointed individuals were and their past work and association with the party, social media users were quick to notice that immediately after the announcement, Gandhi, Dwivedi and Yadav made their X accounts private and there was no trace of Bhatt on the internet.
While all the other IT cell members are back to being active on X, albeit after deleting hundreds of thousands of old posts, Alok Bhatt is the only one in the group whose X handle remains inaccessible or ‘protected’ even a month after the new team was announced.
The only remnants of Bhatt’s online presence are the now-disabled X account, screenshots from his X posts and some articles in Right-wing outlets like OpIndia, Organiser and Swarajya.
Alt News found that in the past, Bhatt had been called out for controversial tweets several times. In archived screenshots of his posts from the past, the BJP functionary can be seen using sexist, Islamophobic, and derogatory language, some of which can be seen below:
Who is Alok Bhatt?
Bhatt, who claims to hail from Dehradun, has worn many hats over the course of his career. According to his LinkedIn profile, he graduated from Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University (HNBGU) in Uttarakhand and went on to work with several organisations, including NIIT University, where he served as financial controller until April 2010.
In 2010, he founded Nature Connect Outdoors — an education and adventure non-profit organisation that deals in outdoor education and skill development, including treks, camping, and rafting expeditions. According to the website’s bio, Bhatt had “shunned his corporate career” to follow his passion, which culminated in the formation of the NGO. The organisation is still functional.
According to details available on Zauba Corp, Bhatt is a Chartered Accountant (CA) and the partner of a firm of CAs called RSAC & CO LLP, incorporated in May 2021.
Bhatt has also served as the economic adviser to former Uttarakhand chief minister Trivendra Singh Rawat. However, it’s not clear when he was appointed and when exactly his tenure ended. He wrote an article for Firstpost defending the ministry of housing and urban affairs over the controversial Central Vista project. The author bio designated him as ‘Economic Advisor’ to Rawat.
In 2020, after a district officer’s press release promoting inter-caste and interfaith marriages drew criticism from social media users, Bhatt had reportedly tweeted: “No one from the government has spoken in support of promoting interfaith marriages. No one in the BJP government in their wildest dreams will support anything that is made out here.”
We sent an email and called up Bhatt several times to know more from him, but he did not respond.
Long-standing Association With BJP
Bhatt’s X handle, @alok_bhatt, was followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In fact, Modi quote-tweeted one of Bhatt’s posts in 2024, where he urged people to watch the film Sabarmati Report.
Bhatt was also invited to PM Modi’s swearing-in ceremony in the past. In 2024, Right-wing influencer Vikas Pandey shared an image with Bhatt alongside former BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma, member of the economic advisory council to the PM, Sanjeev Sanyal, and others, with the caption “First swearing in”.

X Handle Suspended for Violating Guidelines
Alt News found at least three instances, in 2018, 2019, and 2020, where X (then Twitter) had initiated action against Bhatt’s handle for violation of community guidelines, and at least two of those three actions were owing to hateful content.
In 2018, Bhatt declared that all the “killers of Pandits, Rapists of Pandits, Terrorists killing in Kashmir, instigators of Godhra, and bombers of Mumbai were all Muslims, and thus Islam was the problem”. His account had then been ‘limited’.

The Pamphlet-Savitr Analytics-Alok Bhatt Connection
In 2022, Bhatt took on a directorial role at Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation, a company that was incorporated in April 26 that year, with Bhatt and Ashish Nautiyal initially named as directors. According to documents filed with the Union ministry of corporate affairs (MCA), Bhatt holds 9,500 shares, or 95 per cent of the company, while Nautiyal holds the remaining 500 shares, or 5 per cent.
Interestingly, Nautiyal is also the founding editor of the Right-wing media outlet, The Pamphlet.
Savitr Analytics has no website or online presence. We went through its financial records filed with the MCA for the financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25, and found that it was registered as a Section 8 company, i.e., a non-profit. In the 2024-25 financial year, its total revenue from operations was Rs 2.7 crore.
The organisation’s revenue across all three years comes from ‘sale of services’, and the rows for ‘Grants or donations received (relevant for Sec 8 companies)’, present in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 filings, are left blank in 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, the row does not exist.
Under ‘Corporate Information’, they state ‘Research and awareness about Indian culture and heritage…’, ‘Promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, and environmental protection…’ and ‘Advancement of education, learning, and skills development…’ as their activities.
There was a category called ‘professional expenses’ in the 2022-23 filing that was later relabeled as ‘content production expenses’. Rs. 41,48,600 was spent in the first year, Rs. 95,36,600 (filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the second year, and Rs. 1,38,53,200 (also filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the third year.
Next, we found that an individual named Ridhika Aggarwal stated on LinkedIn that she worked as a content writer for Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation until August 2023. We went through her X timeline (linked to her LinkedIn profile) and found that she wrote at least three articles for The Pamphlet during her tenure at Savitr. None of the articles are currently available on the website.
Ridhika is also listed as a non-official member of a steering committee formed by the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change in 2023.
The Pamphlet, previously known as The Indian Affairs, posted for the first time on Facebook in April 2022, which is the same time when Savitr Analytics was incorporated.

— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) March 14, 2023
In other words, two of the three directors of Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. And in both cases, the appointments to Savitr and The Pamphlet came in close succession. This raises the question of whether the two entities are formally linked.
We also found that The Pamphlet had an office space from its inception in Dehradun, and it is evident from a photo posted by Nautiyal that it began with a team of at least 20 people. Bhatt, the reader would remember, also claims to be from Dehradun.
While all of this points to a connection between Bhatt and The Pamphlet, there appears to be a concerted effort to keep that relationship under wraps. Hence, we tried to dig more.
Is Bhatt Linked to The Pamphlet? We Asked The Pamphlet
We sent an email to The Pamphlet on September 3 asking them about the relationship between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet, and whether Alok Bhatt was connected to The Pamphlet, given that he holds a 95% stake in Savitr Analytics, a company whose other directors have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. We also asked them about their funding sources, since nothing is mentioned on the website.
In reply, they asked us to send our queries to another email ID of The Pamphlet and also to Alok Bhatt, Nirwa Mehta, Ashish Nautiyal and Shiv Mishra. Interestingly, they provided us with the email IDs and phone numbers of each of these individuals. This, in itself, might be considered an indicator of some sort of link between The Pamphlet and Bhatt. It is unlikely for an organisation to provide the direct contact details of someone with whom it has no professional association.
We then sent our queries to all of them.
Nautiyal responded to us saying that his reporting manager, OpIndia editor Nupur J Sharma, “suggested” him “not to give (you) any quotes or information as a matter of policy of not engaging with entities that don’t act in good faith”. A day later, he took to X to let the world know that a woman from Alt News “with a Hindu-sounding name” had approached him with some questions.
Pamphlet editor Nirwa Mehta sent us a 1,071-word response, but did not answer any of our questions. Instead, she sent a detailed set of reciprocal questions concerning Alt News’ funding transparency, the outside associations of its founders and editor, and grants received by individuals associated with Alt News, both currently and in the past. She offered to answer Alt News’ questions in writing once Alt News answered hers first.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet published a video on Alt News on August 16, 2026, without seeking a response from the organisation.
This correspondent responded to Mehta, stating that questions concerning Alt News’ funding should be directed to its editor, while questions concerning any of the founders’ personal assignments should be directed to the person concerned. We also reminded her that a so-called expose on Alt News’ founders had been published by The Pamphlet without either of the concerned persons being approached for a response — a violation of basic journalistic ethics.
In her final response, Mehta did not address the question of ethics. Instead, in a demand that many may find bizarre, she asked this correspondent, “as a responsible employee”, to take her questions to the Alt News directors.
At this point, we felt there was no point continuing the conversation.
We will update our article if The Pamphlet answers Alt News’ questions on whether Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet are connected in any way, and whether Alok Bhatt, BJP’s new IT cell member who continues to remain away from X, holds a position at The Pamphlet.
Social Media Posts Answer the Question
The connection between The Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt is one of internet’s worst kept secrets, it seems. We found several instances on social media where well-known faces from the Right-wing ecosystem tagged Alok Bhatt alongside members of The Pamphlet team — whether to thank them for invitations to Delhi Shabdotsav 2026, where The Pamphlet Panchayat featured on the itinerary, or in connection with other events involving the organisation.
On January 5, 2026, Right-wing influencer Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, who was recently criticised for comparing Newslaundry journalists to prostitutes, thanked The Pamphlet team — including its editor Nirwa Mehta, anchor Shreya Arora, and Bhatt — for inviting him to speak at The Pamphlet Panchayat.
Responding to Iyer-Mitra, Nirwa Mehta and another The Pamphlet employee, Pratibha, thanked him for being a part of the session. The exchange is significant because it can be seen as an acknowledgement by the Pamphlet editor and another employee of Bhatt being a part of the organisation.
Delhi Shabdotsav 2026 was a three-day cultural and literary festival held from January 2 to January 4, 2026, organised by Suruchi Prakashan with the support of the department of art, culture and languages of the Delhi government. The Pamphlet was the digital partner at the event and hosted ‘The Pamphlet Panchayat’ at the fest. The Pamphlet team held and moderated several discussions over the three days, including those with Sanjeev Newar, Vijay Patel, and Subhi Vishwakarma. The subjects of the discussions ranged from ‘Love Jihad: factsheet’ to ‘Bharat’s Hostile Neighbourhood & Need to Regain Shatrubodh’.
We went through the images posted on Shabdotsav’s website and found that Bhatt was present at the event.
The link between Alok Bhatt and The Pamphlet becomes more apparent in another conversation on X in which Iyer-Mitra directly addressed Mehta as Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt’s ‘staff’. Iyer jokingly rebuked Mehta for liking a certain kind of car. Tagging Bhatt, he wrote, “Do @Pamphlet_in and @alok_bhatt @shreya_arora22 approve of these disgusting and extremely hateful statements by their staff?” Mehta responded to Iyer-Mitra’s post, but did not object to the ‘staff’ reference.
On June 1, 2023, a little more than a year after The Pamphlet’s inception, one @saket71 posted a picture with Ashish Nautiyal, who was working at The Pamphlet then, and called him a ‘Media Mughal’. He later tagged Alok Bhatt and Shiv Mishra, praising them for “putting a great team together.”
Such a pleasure to meet the young stars of @Pamphlet_in , @RitikaChandola @himanshi__bisht and the whole team. Such a great young team, full of hope and dreams, and a visible sense of great camaraderie. Kudos to @alok_bhatt and @shivkmishr for putting a great team together. https://t.co/NnmHkA9rQO
— saket साकेत ಸಾಕೇತ್ 🇮🇳 (@saket71) June 1, 2023
Several people have congratulated Alok Bhatt at various points of time upon The Pamphlet reaching certain milestones.
To sum up, what raises serious questions about the BJP’s decision to name Bhatt as its social media co-convenor is not just his past social media conduct, but also the opacity surrounding his professional associations. One organisation he appears to be associated with, The Pamphlet, does not publicly disclose its ownership, editorial team, board or funding sources. Without any apparent source of funding, it starts off as a 20-member organization. Who pays their salary? How are establishment costs met? There are no answers. Again, another corporate entity closely linked to him, Savitr Analytics, has no website or public online presence despite reporting Rs 2.7 crore in operational revenue in 2025.
Things get murkier when one takes into account the desperate efforts by Bhatt’s associates to conceal his association with The Pamphlet, evident in the organisation’s refusal to answer direct questions regarding this.
In other words, a man linked to organisations with questionable records, and whose involvement with a pro-government outlet is abundantly visible in public, but markedly absent from the outlet’s own disclosures, has now been given a formal position in the BJP’s social media cell.

Greater things to come from England - Mitchell
- Published
Head coach John Mitchell believes England's thrilling draw with Canada will inspire "greater things to come" from the world champions despite the result ending their record-breaking winning streak.
England had won their past 39 Tests before Saturday's fixture.
Canada, who had lost their 13 previous meetings with the Red Roses on English soil, held England to a 26-26 draw in a nail-biting, physical battle at Exeter's Sandy Park.
It was only the second game domestically or internationally for England's players this season and, for Mitchell, one result is not justification to tear up the playbook.
Instead, he views it as a building block towards future success.
"It was just a matter of scoring across the white line," Mitchell said. "We were applying huge pressure. We just didn't convert."
Avoiding defeat means the Red Roses have extended their unbeaten run to 40 matches, a record they will hope to extend with WXV Global Series games against New Zealand, two more fixtures against Canada and another against the United States still to come.
Mitchell said: "There was such good stuff in there. I'm very patient because we're just starting and we're still alive in this Test series.
"I'm a realist. There will be greater things come as a result of this. There's a greater purpose and one Test match is not going to take us away from our purpose."
For the opening 10 minutes, the match followed the script of last year's World Cup final between the two sides, with Canada breaking the deadlock and England immediately hitting back.
But unlike last September, when they roared on to win 33-13, the Red Roses could not maintain control, with the two teams never separated by more than one try and England unable to convert 20 minutes of sustained pressure into the crucial score.
While acknowledging England would have to review their "game management", captain Meg Jones hailed the spectacle the two sides delivered.
"It was definitely tit for tat and definitely a game of momentum swinging," said centre Jones. "It was two good teams going at each other.
"It was an amazing contest and competitive as we imagined. This is the first Test. We get another two shots at it [against Canada]."
Echoing Jones' defiance before October trips to Toronto and Ottawa, Mitchell added: "We're in a Test series. It's 1-1. That's it."
Winning run has 'just been there' - Jones
England's 39-game winning run started under former head coach Simon Middleton, who, after the World Cup final defeat in 2022, led the Red Roses to a Women's Six Nations Grand Slam in 2023.
Mitchell then took charge midway through the 2023 WXV1 campaign and had won every game until this one.
England beat Scotland in the World Cup quarter-finals last September to claim their 31st straight Test win, surpassing their own record winning streak across both men's and women's international rugby union, which was set in 2022.
World Cup glory, another Women's Six Nations title and victory over Australia last weekend extended that record further.
"It's not necessarily something we speak about as a group; it's something that's just been there," Jones said of the winning run.
"We're very process-driven, so the outcome tends to look after itself."

Israel’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded Palestinian attacker who had stabbed a soldier in the occupied West Bank, in a case that divided the country a decade ago.
Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter and his release after serving two-thirds of his 18-month sentence drew enormous attention in Israel, where military service is compulsory for most Jewish men.
In his first interview after his release, Azaria said he would “act exactly the same, because that’s how I needed to act”.
Azaria had approached Abdel Fattah al-Sharif as he lay on the ground, unarmed and badly hurt, after stabbing a soldier in the city of Hebron. A mobile phone video captured Azaria shooting al-Sharif in the head.
The office of president Isaac Herzog said in a statement on Saturday that he acted on the recommendation of defence minister Israel Katz. The statement cited the time that had passed, and the spirit of the approaching Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, holiday as among the factors in the decision.
Herzog’s office also said that Azaria, who was 20 when he was sentenced, had “expressed his sorrow” in his request. The statement noted that in an earlier request, he called his gunshot an “operational error”.
In a separate statement, Katz called it a “right, humane and fitting decision” and said Azaria had been in a “complex operational mission”.
But the military’s chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, had said in a letter to the defence minister that the pardon should not be granted, Israeli media reported.
The conviction was a rare case of a military court ruling against a soldier for deadly action taken in the field. Top generals had pressed for his prosecution, while many in the Israeli public supported Azaria at a time when there had been a series of stabbings and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians or Israeli Arabs. Some supporters protested outside his trial.
On Saturday, Israel’s hard-line national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said in a statement that “cancelling the criminal record of someone who killed a terrorist makes me emotional and very happy”.
Some Palestinians and human rights groups had described Azaria’s sentence as far too lenient. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of three to five years.
The statement by Herzog’s office on Saturday said that his decision “does not constitute a reassessment of the case”.
The divisions over Azaria’s case led to public polling and political pressure that led the defence minister at the time, Moshe Ya’alon, to resign.
After the verdict, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for Azaria to be pardoned.
After the sentencing, the Palestinian government minister in charge of prisoner affairs, Issa Karaka, called it a “joke”.

Listed NBFC Kissht has secured board approval to raise up ₹832.2 Cr via a preferential issue of equity shares to 34 investors and entities. In a filing with the exchanges, the company said that its board has approved the issuance of 2.6 Cr fully paid-up equity shares to the investors at an issue price of ₹314.11 apiece. The NBFC did not disclose how it plans to utilise the fresh proceeds from the issue. The allotment is still subject to regulatory and shareholder approval. The company has also convened an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders to seek approval for the preferential issue. “Funds raising by way of a preferential issue on a private placement basis of up to 2,64,93,882 fully paid-up equity shares of the company… for cash, at an issue price of ₹314.11 per share… for an amount aggregating to ₹832.19 Cr to identified investors (non-promoters), in accordance with the provisions of… applicable laws….,” read the filing. Among the investing companies, Axis Flexi Cap Fund, Axis Multi Cap Fund and Axis Small Cap Fund together will receive 63.7 Lakh shares worth nearly ₹200 Cr. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, via two entities, will also receive 27.1 Lakh shares totalling ₹85 Cr. Envision Capital will also get 12.7 Lakh shares valued at nearly ₹40 Cr, while PE firm First Bridge will lap up 12.1 Lakh shares for a sum of ₹20 Cr. Kissht will also allot 23.9 Lakh shares to three entities linked to Ashoka WhiteOak Capital for a consideration of nearly ₹75 Cr. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed nearly 45% to ₹669.5 Cr during the quarter under review as against ₹463.1 Cr in Q1 FY26. Shares of the NBFC closed Thursday’s trading session 5.08% higher at ₹359.7 on the BSE.

As a teenager, I'd sit on my bed flipping through glossy magazines, fascinated and completely absorbed by the empowering stories about women. The news felt dominated by men, but magazines seemed to offer a different world — one where women's lives, bodies, careers, and opinions were worthy of entire pages. I knew from an early age I wanted to help bring more of those stories to life.
In 2012, after studying journalism at Northeastern University, I moved to New York City as quickly as I could, interning at Ladies' Home Journal and Self, then gravitating toward parenting publications including What To Expect, American Baby, and Fit Pregnancy.
Motherhood fascinated me long before I became a mother. It was the same intrigue and interest that drew me to magazines — the power of women, what their bodies could do, and the enormity of the identity shift involved in raising a child. Writing about pregnancy and parenting somehow felt very natural to me, even when I understood both mostly in theory.
I loved editing, but I wanted to write
Working at magazines wasn't quite how I'd imagined it from my childhood bedroom. I loved editing: finding the heart of a story, moving pieces around, and helping a writer say what they were trying to say. My boss, Mindy, was one of the first people to make me believe that my creativity and instincts were worth trusting. She taught me nearly everything I knew about shaping a narrative.
But I also began to feel restless. I was putting so much of myself into stories that ultimately ran under somebody else's name. I longed for that authorship and craved the terrifying privilege of starting with a blank page, figuring out what I had to say, and hoping it might matter to even one reader.
Mindy warned me that freelancing would be hard. I believed her and quit anyway. I had just gotten engaged, was planning a wedding, and was already thinking about having children. I also knew that if I kept waiting to feel established enough to become a writer, I might spend my entire career editing other people's work.
I was scared to give up a steady paycheck, especially while planning a wedding and thinking about starting a family. Dan, my now-husband, understood the risk but supported me taking the chance. Neither of us knew whether I could make a sustainable living on my own; I only knew I would regret it if I didn't try.
The transition happened faster than I expected. Within the first few months, I had more assignments than I knew what to do with, partly because leaving my 9-to-5 meant I could attend daytime events, meet editors, and build relationships that led to more work. My income still varied from month to month, but it was far steadier than I had feared. By my second year of freelancing, I was writing at an almost ridiculous pace for around 20 magazines and websites and earning nearly four times the roughly $30,000 salary I'd once made as an editorial assistant.
My career became so much bigger after I left my staff job, but it looked so different from what I could have imagined.
Moving home changed the picture completely
Life started looking even more different in 2018, about a year after I began freelancing, when my husband lost his job. Because I didn't have employer-sponsored health insurance of my own, I had been covered through his job, so we lost coverage along with his paycheck. Our lease was also ending, and we wanted to start a family. Leaving New York suddenly felt less like giving something up and more like the only decision that made sense.
We moved to my hometown north of Boston, where my parents and oldest friends still lived. I became a mom the following spring, April 2019. Less than a year later, COVID turned the world upside down, and there wasn't a single person whose life looked the way they had imagined it.
My working life went from events, meetings, and crowded New York sidewalks to writing alone in the corner of a small, old house, albeit with an ocean view. There were no coworkers nearby, no glossy proofs circulating, and no one across the desk to bounce an idea off. There was just me, my laptop, my cat, and, during several stretches, a pregnant belly.
My hardest experiences became part of my work
Motherhood was so different from what I'd imagined, and so was my path through it. While trying to grow my family, I suffered two miscarriages, which drastically changed the way I understood pregnancy, loss, and the motherhood journey in its entirety. I was so fortunate to have two healthy pregnancies afterward, but I couldn't shake everything the process had shown me.
I was inspired more than ever to create — to bring to life the kinds of platforms and communities I'd needed myself. I co-founded Miscarriage Movement, to make pregnancy loss feel less isolating, as well as The Mother Chapter to talk honestly about motherhood, identity, mental health, and ambition. Neither platform was part of a careful business plan. Both grew from experiences and questions I couldn't leave alone.
My career today looks nothing like the one I imagined as a teenager. I miss parts of New York and the collective energy of a magazine office. Freelancing can still be unpredictable, and running my own platforms means the work is never exactly finished. But I get to write, edit, create, and build something that belongs to me. I'm also close to my parents and present for the small, ordinary parts of my children's lives.
The magazines on my childhood bed made me want to tell women's stories. All these years later, that's still very much what I'm doing. I just couldn't have imagined where I'd be doing it — or how much of my own life would eventually find its way onto the page.

During the seventh edition of Semicon India today, Odisha’s chief minister (CM) Mohan Charan Majhi shared that the state is planning to set up an ‘Odisha Silicon Valley’ across an 870 acre stretch between Cuttack and Bhubaneswar. The state aims to transform from a mineral-rich region into a high-tech chip-making powerhouse. The CM said that the administration is in conversations with international semiconductor companies based out of countries like Sweden, Japan, and others to discuss potential projects pertaining to semiconductors, AI, and data centres in the state. As of now, construction across the state has begun on two central government-approved projects: Sicsem Pvt Ltd’s first-in-India silicon carbide fab and integrated packaging facility, and 3D Glass Solutions’ glass-substrate packaging facility, the CM announced. Efforts have also begun to launch a Phase 2 project with Sicsem to establish a silicon carbide epitaxy and packaging facility, per CM Majhi. As of now, the Odisha government has approved five additional semiconductor projects worth approximately ₹11,000 Cr, which are estimated to create around 4,500 direct jobs and over 16,000 indirect jobs. While RiR Power Electronics, Sancorn Technology, and ASP Semiconductor have signed MOUs for semiconductor projects, Intel and 3D Glass Solutions have also signed an MOU for a partnership aiming to bring $3.3 Bn (₹30,550 Cr) in investment and over 1,800 direct jobs to the state. To support research and commercialisation, Odisha is also investing ₹125 Cr towards a ₹452 Cr National Industry Co-Development Hub on Integrated Power Electronics alongside IIT Bhubaneswar and the National Research Foundation. The state government has also amended its semiconductor policy and committed up to 25% capex for projects approved under the India Semiconductor Mission, the CM revealed. “With this credit, along with full infrastructure support and incentives, Odisha's offering is very attractive and competitive, ensuring our success,” he said. CM Majhi also highlighted specialised training programmes at the World Skill Center in Bhubaneswar developed in partnership with the Singapore government through which the government is aiming to meet the demand for highly skilled labour from the technology ecosystem. “We are focusing heavily on emerging technologies like semiconductors, AI, and data centres.
