Lina Khan on Doomer Panic and Ending AI Exceptionalism
Why the AI-alarmism conversation feels off
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube
As “rogue” AI agents hack systems and leaders warn of catastrophe, who should be held responsible? Former FTC Commissioner Lina Khan argues that the United States already has a lot of the regulatory tools needed. In this live episode from The Atlantic Festival, the Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks with Khan about why the AI-alarmism conversation feels a little off, how money affects politics and regulation, and some of the ways she would be dealing with AI if she were still the head of the FTC.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel. And this is Galaxy Brain, a show where today we’re gonna talk about what on earth to do about the AI companies who are saying their products might kill us all. And I’ve got quite literally the perfect person to talk about this with, the chair of New York City’s Economic Development Corporation and the former chair of the FTC under Joe Biden, Lina Khan. But first, a little bit of background.
A bit more than a week ago, Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic, quit his job and he published a warning: The AI companies, he argued, were not taking safety seriously and they were, quote, “gambling with our lives.” The product that he’d spent the past three years working on was spiraling out of the control of the people who were building it, and it might someday, he said, end humanity. His warning echoed what AI executives, researchers, effective altruists on forums, and Bay Area doomers have been anxiously posting about and writing best-selling books about for more than a decade.
But Coxon’s warning did what all those other warnings failed to do. It broke containment, and it created a national conversation. Concerned lawmakers called for emergency AI meetings; President Obama weighed in; Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind Chair Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk all came to a rare consensus and called for a slowdown of AI development. President Donald Trump responded to all of it by calling AI fears “a hoax.” Things are moving fast. But one thing is clear: The AI-safety conversation is happening at a global scale among insiders and normies alike.
And there are almost unending questions here: How real is this threat? Is this hype and AI-company marketing? But no matter where you land on the actual risk of these companies, there is a question about what we should do about it. The companies themselves are calling for a regulatory framework, including independent auditors of the models. But not everyone’s convinced. Is all of this progress, or are the tech companies simply trying to get favorable, cushy terms that lock them into virtual monopolies? In other words, is all of their talk earnest, or is this a power grab?
What should AI-company regulation look like? Why is nobody holding these companies accountable right now? Do we need new laws? Or should we be using the existing ones better? What are the historical parallels here? Are we in uncharted waters, or is this a normal crisis that is playing out at abnormal speed and abnormal scale?
Lina Khan has spent her career wrestling with a lot of these questions, specifically as they apply to Silicon Valley’s tech giants. As FTC chair, she was part of a genuine shift in antitrust enforcement, arguing that traditional U.S. competition laws were broken and ill-suited for digital platforms.
Now, late last week, as the AI debate was roiling, Khan posted on X that the AI regulation needed to take into account that “law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products.”
So what does enforcement look like in this AI moment? Where do we go from here? I spoke with Lina Khan on Thursday morning in New York at The Atlantic Festival. Here’s our conversation.
[Music]
Warzel: Thank you all for coming. I appreciate it. Thank you, Lina, for coming here.
Lina Khan: Great to be here.
Warzel: I want to just dive in. We have limited time here. And I wanted to start with the news that has been all-consuming in the tech and political spheres over the last week or so, which is the AI-research whistleblowers warning of AI agents spinning out of control that might “kill us all.” Calls from Sam Altman, Dario [Amodei], Elon Musk, others to slow down development, quote “pace the frontier.” You weighed in on the regulatory angle on X recently. But first I just wanted to ask, why do you think this safety panic is breaking through now?
Khan: Well, I think we’ve been seeing it for the last few years, you know, various predictions about what may happen with these tools. And it certainly seems like there have been various inflection points where people within these companies have seen what they would describe potentially as a step change in terms of certain capabilities. It seems like most recently, there have been more instances of agents basically becoming more overtly defective. Some people may call them rogue, really exceeding the parameters of what people and humans had set up them to do. And so that seems to be the latest catalyst.
But I think there’s been, you know, a drumbeat in the background now for several years, including when I was back at the FTC, when we were already starting to confront less these existential questions around, you know, Could we see the eradication of humanity? and more of the bread and butter of How are these tools already impacting people in their day-to-day? I mean, for most Americans, the way they interact with AI is through a chatbot and trying to get customer service, and instead being stuck in some doom loop. Right? So I think there are a lot of ways that this is manifesting, and I think the regulatory-policy conversation can happen across that spectrum.
Warzel: Some of the concern, I think, too, comes from this idea that the models that these companies have trained and, you know, that power a lot of these chatbots, they are themselves very—they’re part of this black box. Right? Like, we don’t really know exactly what’s going into them with the weights, with the training, all of that. When you were at the FTC, when this was all kind of very young and new, what kind of sense did you get about that level of transparency and what we can’t see?
Khan: I mean, there’s a tremendous amount that we can’t see, which is not unique in terms of, you know, the relationship between an enforcer or regulator and a company, but certainly seems to be even more acute in this context. But, you know, we were already encountering black-box algorithms. And what does an enforcer do when it’s really an algorithm that is, you know, resulting in various types of products being shown or not being shown? And what does that mean for our existing laws?
I do think one pattern that we’ve seen across various moments when a new technology hits is that there can be this rush to create some exceptionalism around it, especially vis-à-vis the existing laws and regulations. And so one thing that was very important to me when I was serving in government was to make very clear that there was not any AI exemption from existing laws on the books. And I think we see, even now, a strain in the conversation around new regulation that seems to assume that these current developments are happening in some legal vacuum. And that is just false.
Like, you know, if you’re working on one of these companies, you still have an existing obligation to abide by, you know, consumer-protection laws, antidiscrimination laws, antitrust laws, product-liability regimes. And so part of what I’ve tried to, you know, include in the conversation is this realization that we may want to talk about new rules and regulations. And I think there’s a good case for it. But let’s not forget that existing legal obligations absolutely apply. And some of what we’re hearing from these firms and their executives suggests that the legal care that is already required of these firms is not being taken.
Warzel: Why do you think that everyone in the industry is behaving—and even, you know, some politicians are behaving—like these companies are exempt? What is the reason for that?
Khan: It’s a great question. I mean, I think part of it absolutely stems back to how the firms themselves market their capabilities. And when there is a push for regulation—I mean, we’ve seen this even in, you know, context around crypto, where there was a push to say, Well, existing security laws don’t apply. And, look, sometimes you need to be thoughtful about how new products and services do fit in within the existing legal regime.
But what’s troubling to me is when we see a suggestion that there is some type of blanket immunity or blanket exemption from existing legal requirements because something is so new. I think, you know, we need to have a presumption, a strong presumption, of all existing laws being adequate and applying, and the burden on the newcomers to actually prove why it might be that they may need certain tweaks, as opposed to the defaults being the other way.
Warzel: One response when you posted, I believe it was over the weekend, but sort of talking about this idea, Let’s remember that we have laws on the books, and these companies aren’t exempt—but there’s a feeling, I think, that some people think that just even the discussion of new regulatory frameworks: Is it just a distraction from the moment? And, you know, I do feel like that’s the case, because when the government was trying to regulate the social-media companies, there was a desire for some new paradigms or for, you know, a regulation that fit actually the new thing that these companies were doing. So don’t we need new frameworks for AI as well?
Khan: We absolutely may ultimately decide that we do need something concrete, but I think it’s important to be very precise about, where is it that our existing laws or existing regulatory regimes are falling short? You know, in this case, it seems like there is some activity that happens during the training itself, before these products hit the market, where you see employees saying, you know, This is where we actually need more oversight. You know, it’s been struggling to see that some of those recommendations seem to be more in the vein of, you know, self-regulation or voluntary compliance. Or maybe we have these third-party auditors, but there’s a very cozy relationship. And these specific technologies may be new, but there’s a long history of economic regulation spanning all the way back to the railroads, to telecom. And of course, these are all different tools and technologies. But there are important lessons for what does and doesn’t work.
Even in the blog post that spurred some of these recent conversations, the CEO referenced bank supervision as a potential analog, when you basically have people from the government that are more closely embedded within banks to try to assess certain types of risks. And so I think there is a long history of tools that we should be mining to figure out what makes sense here.
But I do think there’s this basic level in which something about the current conversation has seemed really off, where on the one hand, you have these companies declaring that the technologies and tools that they’re developing may end up having, you know, catastrophic effects alongside getting ready to go public and become billionaires and trillionaires overnight. I mean, if you just take those set of facts and apply it to every other industry, we would think that was ludicrous. And so I think that’s why we need to, you know, look at this AI exceptionalism that seems to be infecting the current conversation with some clear eyes.
Warzel: Yeah. I believe, like, three days after Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, said that there’s a reasonable chance that in six to 12 months, a bot swarm could take over the entire internet. He was at Salesforce, selling B2B software as a service to people, which is kind of an odd thing if you think extinction is coming.
In the in the case of the OpenAI incident where some of its models hacked the website Hugging Face, I wanted to get your perspective on: These are models, that they did behave differently than the trainers wanted them to do, but like, they hacked a website in that specific case. Do you think that OpenAI should face legal ramifications, like, for that instance?
Khan: It’s a very interesting question. And there are a whole set of laws that could potentially apply. But specifically when you’re thinking about the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, which is a criminal statute; criminal penalties apply. People have gone to jail for violating that statute. You know, there usually is an element of intent that you need to find. And so I you know, one thing that people have raised is, Okay, but what does it look like for models to have intent? And can you really ascribe that to the company? I think this also goes back to this basic question of what could have been reasonably known. And I think the more and more we’re getting additional information, it seems that this was not just an outlier incident.
There have actually been a whole set of events where models ended up acting in ways that, you know, the individuals did not want or foresee and may have committed a crime. And so I absolutely think that there is a point at which if you are aware that your technology and the models you’re working on have this capability, because you’re seeing it, and you’re continuing to allow those to act in this way, I think there is a very real question around intent and when that should actually attach.
Warzel: Yeah. Is it intent if you are creating these models to be as collaborative and as crafty and as intelligent and as good of problem solvers as possible?
Khan: I think the other issue here is, you know, a lot of the information that is available here is from this, you know, group called METR that’s comprised of—
Warzel: One of the monitoring groups.
Khan: The monitoring groups. And, you know, they are almost like a civic voluntary group that’s doing this work without any regulatory authority. And so it’s conditional on what information is being made available to them. Oftentimes, their reports are scoped to just look at the models. But I think there is a broader landscape that we need to understand about, What did humans know or should have known, and what, really, the company and should have been in a better position to prohibit or limit? And I think some of that is still pretty murky, because this report was scoped to focus so specifically on, you know, just the models and the agents themselves. So I do think we actually need a much bigger picture outside of the context of some, you know, voluntary inspection and more with the teeth of, you know, law enforcement and real regulation.
[Music]
Warzel: So you posted on X, you know, talking about this, weighing in, as we said: David Sacks whose investors, former Trump AI czar, publicly expressed agreement with your position, which then I saw a bunch of people, you know, doing the eyes emoji at that. But is this also potentially a sign that AI is scrambling some of the traditional political coalitions?
Khan: It’s possible. I mean, that’s not particularly new to this moment. Even when you go back to the broader conversation around how to deal with the concentration of power that we were seeing in firms like Google and Amazon and Facebook, that was already starting to scramble some of that.
I mean, you know, back in 2019, I was working as a staffer for the House Judiciary Committee’s antitrust subcommittee, and we were doing an investigation into Amazon, Facebook, Google, and Apple. And, you know, we had instances where you had the most progressive member of that committee, you know, ask a question that sounded very similar to a question that the most conservative member on that committee was asking, because they were, you know, deeply concerned about concentrations of power. And so you had the House Progressive Caucus and the House Freedom Caucus, you know, actually working closely on some of this.

DOGE, the effort has basically, you know, contributed to the dismantling of the administrative state.
And so, you know, while I will always be encouraged when there is kind of a broader set of people that want to align behind a position that I think is the right one, I think there has been something quite puzzling about people who were all for, you know, tearing down government to now be saying, Actually, the existing laws exist. Warzel: I’ve seen some of the debate around this AI moment framed as extinction versus regulatory capture. And instead, we’ve been seeing their CEO, you know, cast some doubt about what they described as alarmism here.
And so I think the deeply interconnected nature of this industry, where you have an enormous amount of partnerships across investments, interdependencies, where the success of one company is really propping up your balance sheet, I think also is something to be understanding and inspecting.
And one of the investigations we were doing was into these partnerships to try to understand: How are these contracts written? What are companies actually saying that they’re going to be getting in return for their investments? If you see a big investment from, you know, a hyperscaler into one of these model companies, is that also coming with certain rights to shape the business strategy that could, you know, also result in implications to competition? So I think there’s a lot to unpack there.
I think there’s also just a lot to look at in terms of the bread-and-butter effects on people in their everyday lives. And so, you know, we’ve already seen some lawsuits filed privately against chatbots for, you know, engaging in conduct that families have said resulted in their kids taking their own lives. There are various cases that are still under way here. There’s also a question of basic tort law and the questions of negligence. And was there a reckless disregard in terms of certain safeguards that these companies should have put in place that weren’t? So I think there’s a lot to be exploring from a law-enforcement perspective. Some of those cases are being brought privately. But so far, you know, we saw the president tweet, We don’t need any new regulations. We have existing law enforcement, but—
Warzel: Hoax buster.
Khan: The Hoax buster. And instead we’re seeing, you know, an all-time low, effectively, in terms of criminal prosecutions and investigations.
Warzel: So this AI-safety conversation—part of the framing it as, you know, “existential rise of the machines,” “human race will be eliminated” type of thing—I think I fear that it is obscuring a lot of those personal harms to people, like what is happening to workers, like what is happening with the consolidation of the industry, as you said, with companies like Nvidia. Khan: I absolutely think we should be paying more attention to existing harms that are already happening. And, you know, there’s a broader conversation around affordability. And we all know that Americans are really feeling the heat when it comes to a cost-of-living crisis and, you know, under enormous strain in terms of paying rent, buying groceries; health-care costs are skyrocketing. And that sometimes is happening in a totally different space than this conversation.
But there are actually key ways and key places where what we’re seeing with AI could actually be contributing to the cost-of-living crisis. You know, we’ve already seen some firms be engaging in surveillance pricing when they’re using some of these AI tools, to basically serve up prices that are specifically targeted to what they know your pain point is. We’re seeing similar, you know, wage-management algorithms on the worker side. That could also be, basically depressing what workers are making. And so, you know, I think there are a whole set of ways in which these tools are already harming people in a day-to-day sense. And we absolutely need more attention on that.
You know, I think that when it comes to this question of extinction and what is really the harm here, I apply more of a risk-assessment framework. There is a huge information asymmetry between what people working in these companies know and what we, as outsiders or regulators or enforcers, know. And so I think we need to assess that risk, get more information. And if there are things that need to be done to put in place to prevent more of these models being so defective, I think we absolutely need to see that.
Warzel: Some of these AI CEOs have offered some specific ideas, Dario being the one with the—he likes to write really long blog posts. Maybe they’re not specific enough, but they are more specific, it seems, than, like, Mark Zuckerberg and, like, the Web 2 social-media giants who kind of just said, Regulate us, right. There’s the embedded company monitors that are independent, the idea of a slowdown. Like, do you think the things that are being proposed on their face are good ideas?
Khan: I think elements of it should be considered. I mean, I think this question of, you know, We have bank supervision as this long-standing thing should be on the table. Again, I think a lot of the devil’s going to be in the details in terms of: How are you structuring this, how much of this is just voluntary versus you’re actually on the hook for providing information, providing complete information? What are the ramifications if you actually violate some of these procedures?
So I think there are ways to structure this in a way that is relatively meaningless and toothless and just basically a fabrication of any accountability, versus structuring it so that you actually have real teeth and accountability. And so I think where you fall on that spectrum is going to be key. I do think, though, this goes back to who’s driving the conversation and who’s in the driver’s seat. And that’s where I do see a real asymmetry, where so much of the public response and the response from government is in a responsive posture and a reactive posture. And I think that can also have real downsides.
Warzel: The one thing that I think is different about these, or maybe it seems different, rather, the positioning of these AI CEOs, is some of them have, for a really long time, just been obsessively worrying about these issues. It’s not that they’ve devoted their careers to agonizing over, you know, the extinction of humanity, et cetera. I’m just curious, given that there’s always been this kind of safety realm, do you trust that these guys are being earnest about their fears?
Khan: I mean, I don’t see it as my job or really knowable as to, like, What are their internal motives? It certainly seems like, you know, some of the employees that are coming out of these firms, certainly seem to be earnest. I mean, I think there is this question of: At what point does somebody’s financial position line up with what they’re actually saying or not saying? And I think that’s where there’s a real question as to, if you are really committed to the belief that what your company is doing could lead to all of these harms, shouldn’t we be seeing much more extreme actions internally to stop it?
You know, I think one of the responses to the blog post has been: There’s absolutely nothing stopping you from slowing down the pace of these model development, and you don’t actually need an antitrust exemption. Right. And I think it was that call for an antitrust exemption that set off a lot of red flags for people, because it suggested that maybe what is being asked for is some type of regulatory immunity and diverting attention from the fact that these companies do have all the authority and ability to do what they say needs to be done.
[Music]
Warzel: One of the things that you do so well in your writing and in talking about this is drawing historical parallels. And I think in this moment, it feels very odd right now to have all these people talking about, you know, existential stuff. The pace of the news cycle is crazy with all of this. Can you offer some historical parallels for us all to just, like, latch on to here to feel like this is more of a normal type of industrial crisis, than something that is, you know, abnormal, and it’s just maybe playing out at abnormal speed?
Khan: Yeah. I mean, I want to reserve the idea that maybe there is something different here. Similar with, you know, cars. And there were all sorts of car-safety regulations that needed to be put in place.
The idea that you have a new technology that, admittedly, could do a lot of good but also, if not carefully managed and with a lot of safeguards, could do a lot of bad—we’ve encountered that in the past. And we’ve put obligations and requirements on the companies themselves to make sure they are not just letting loose into the wild new technologies that could have disastrous consequences.
And so I think that’s the part of the conversation that we need to go back to in terms of moving away from this AI exceptionalism and thinking in a clear-eyed way about: How is it that we’ve encountered prior technologies? As the Liberal Democrats gather for their annual conference in Brighton this weekend, leader Ed Davey is under pressure to answer a simple question: Why isn’t Britain’s third-largest political party doing better?
Despite winning more than 70 seats at the last general election, a Lib Dem record, the centrist party’s poll ratings have been stagnant in the two years since, while the likes of Nigel Farage’s Reform U.K. and Zack Polanski’s Greens have pulled ahead and increasingly dominate voters’ attention. The new Labour government under Andy Burnham has enjoyed a poll bounce too.
That’s led to grumbling among some Liberal Democrat MPs and activists, who are frustrated at the party’s lack of a national breakthrough and want to see Davey take clearer, bolder stances on the big issues affecting voters. Davey is planning to use the conference to begin detailing the party’s pitch for the next general election, including a focus on the cost of living, economic growth and reforming the political system, according to people familiar with the matter.

One dead and multiple injured after driver, 93, crashes into brunch diners on Jersey Shore
The driver reportedly hit the gas instead of the brake
One person was killed and seven others were injured when a 93-year-old crashed her SUV into a patio teeming with brunch diners on the Jersey Shore over the weekend.
The crash unfolded just after 11 a.m. on Saturday at Meg’s Grill in Lavallette, as a driver of a 2014 Buick Encore was reportedly trying to park — but hit the gas instead of the brake, sending her vehicle speeding into a group of diners, News 12 New Jersey reported.
The Buick plowed through the restaurant’s outdoor patio area and into the building, the Lavallette Police Department said.
Seven restaurant patrons were injured and taken to the hospital with varying degrees of injury.
A 56-year-old woman from Toms River, New Jersey, was killed in the crash, authorities said.
The 93-year-old driver, who was from Lavallette, suffered minor injuries from the crash.
The Lavallette Police Department has not publicly identified the driver, or shared the names of any of the victims.
None of the staff working at Meg’s Grill were injured in the crash, and the building was undamaged, the restaurant wrote on Facebook. Meg’s Grill is located just across the street from the local police department.
“Our building is fine and was undamaged. But I can’t say the same for our hearts. All of our thoughts and prayers are with the people who were hurt. We are closing tomorrow and Monday out of an observance of compassion for my staff and those affected,” the restaurant wrote.
“We plan to reopen Tuesday. If anything changes we will update. Please give an enormous hug to your loved ones tonight.”
Photos published by NJ.com from the scene showed significant damage to the exterior wall of the liquor store next door to the restaurant.

WASHINGTON — Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday named eight new members to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, an influential panel of experts who assess the evidence behind a wide array of preventive medical services.
They include a number of specialists, including in clinical nutrition, gastroenterology, and oncology, as well as a finance professor who has expertise in health insurance. It’s a major departure from the past, when the panel was made up of generalists, as opposed to specialists, to avoid prioritizing one area of medicine over another.
The independent body has more than advisory power because its assessments help determine whether health insurance companies are required to cover preventive services, such as mammograms and drugs to help prevent HIV. The newly appointed chair, Seth Corey, works in pediatric hematology-oncology at the Cleveland Clinic. He replaces Michael Silverstein, who departed from his role last year.
Kennedy has been critical of the 16-person group, which has been left with at least eight vacancies this year after five members rolled off at the end of their terms and the previous chair, Silverstein, departed on his own. Two members — vice chairs John Wong and Esa Davis — were fired in letters sent to them by Kennedy on May 11. The letters, viewed by STAT, said they were terminated due to a review of the current appointments.
The panel hasn’t met in more than a year, after its meetings were canceled by Kennedy. The most recent news on the USPSTF website dates back to August 2025. The group had previously signaled it was working on recommendations related to breast cancer genetic screening, pediatric autism disorder screening, and cervical cancer screening, among others.
Last year Kennedy said he planned to remove panel members, viewing them as too “woke,” but no new members had been named until now. His ability to remove members may be traced to a Supreme Court ruling issued in 2025, in the case Kennedy v. Braidwood Management, which established that the expert task force is under the authority of the health secretary.

College Sports Are Great
The accomplishments of athletes are every bit as impressive and legitimate as those of dancers, debaters, and oboists.
For a decade, I’ve been a member of a faculty committee that works closely with the athletics department at Northwestern University. A fellow professor once complained to me about the special admissions considerations that athletes receive, arguing that we could admit more oboists if athletes didn’t get so many spots. At the time, the university was being sued as part of athletics-department scandals involving sexual harassment and hazing. One case was dropped, and others were settled without the university admitting wrongdoing. During the same period, the university announced the construction of a brand-new football stadium that would be the most expensive ever built for a college team. It was a lot to digest all at once. In answer to my colleague, I nodded in agreement, thinking, Yeah, more oboists.
But as I considered the mission of our university—helping students decide what they want to do after college, cultivating the knowledge and skills they need to achieve their goals, supporting faculty research, and raising capital to ensure that we can continue to do that work—I became less certain that oboists are more desirable, and more qualified for admission, than athletes. Why do we think that, over the course of their life, oboists will make a greater contribution to society than linebackers? (I mean you no offense, kind oboists! The duck is my favorite character in Peter and the Wolf.)
On campus, many people remain doubtful that Northwestern’s athletics and academic missions are aligned, especially as football becomes more and more of a business sheltered by a university. Critics are right to lament the increased professionalization of college sports, but they also believe that most student athletes care more about their sport than their classes. Many academics see sports as frivolous and corrupting, as a distraction from the higher purpose of moral and intellectual formation—and as the most visible sign of the commercialization and corporatization of the modern university. We worry that out-of-control spending on sports could lead us to abandon our commitment to academic achievement.
Many, maybe even most, of these negative views of athletics held by my colleague and others are based on misconceptions. Take the complaint that student athletes are paid. Other students have the opportunity to get paid for work they do for the university and on their own behalf. We have a start-up incubator that has raised more than $1.6 billion in capital. Why shouldn’t athletes profit from the work they do too?
Our college athletes are hardly dumb jocks. As part of my work on the Committee on Athletics and Recreation (now called the Intercollegiate Athletics Committee), I’ve reviewed athletes’ selection of majors, academic performance, and travel schedules. I served on committees that hired our two most recent athletics directors. In my interactions with the athletics department and with student athletes in particular, I’ve been impressed, above all, by the emphasis they place on academic success, and how much effort they put into being students. I wish more of them wanted to major in my discipline, history, but that’s a different story.
Despite the seemingly constant negative attention paid to youth sports, I’m not convinced that parents of athletes put any more pressure on their kids than the parents of kids involved in other pursuits do. Northwestern’s Division I athletes worked as hard to get here as the oboists—or dancers, debaters, and comedians—did. Their accomplishments are every bit as impressive, and their chosen path every bit as legitimate.
Yet student athletes have told me that they sometimes feel like they don’t deserve to be here; that nonathletes don’t want to do group projects with them, either because they think that their practice and travel schedules will make them unreliable partners or that they are intellectual lightweights.
In fact, athletes do as well as nonathletes in their classes, and they typically get better grades during their active season of play compared with the offseason. As the director of our American Studies program, I met frequently with majors, one of whom was a runner on our varsity cross-country team. In addition to talking about her thesis or the classes she needed to graduate, we talked about the discipline necessary for her to maintain her 3.9 GPA. Her answers combined behaviors she learned from sports and from academics: physical activity, nutrition, sleep, good study habits. I learned a lot from her about a life well lived.
Student athletes do get support from tutors and advisers whom they’re required to meet with regularly. But nonathletes also have access to advisers, tutors, and other academic-support services. They aren’t required to use them, although it would benefit them if they did.
Athletes do miss a lot of classes, which grates on professors. On average, they miss maybe five days of class per quarter. In a nine- or 10-week quarter, that could amount to 15 or 25 percent of all class meetings. When athletes arrive on campus, their advisers tell them they can major in anything they want. That’s not entirely true, because some majors have requirements, such as lab time in the natural sciences, that conflict with practice or competition schedules. I wish they really could major in anything, but all students and not just athletes decide which classes to take and which subjects to major in based on their other curricular and extracurricular commitments, including work and family obligations. They’re also the only students who have to announce at the beginning of each quarter how many classes they’ll skip.
Football and, to a lesser degree, men’s basketball are fundamentally different from our 19 other varsity teams. These two sports spend and earn the majority of athletics-department revenue, are responsible for the most controversial changes to how college sports work, and receive almost all of the negative press. They make the system run and are inextricable from it. They, too, can add academic value.
To be transparent, I’m a fan. I’ve traveled to football bowl games in Nashville and Las Vegas, and March Madness basketball games in Sacramento, where I met recent and older alumni. To demonstrate how big-time college sports can help an entire university to prosper, a trustee pointed me to the example of Vanderbilt University, whose chancellor, Daniel Diermeier—previously on the faculty at Northwestern and the University of Chicago—has invested heavily in sports (especially football and basketball), written about the benefits to the university, and seen applications skyrocket and admissions rates dip. (There are also counterexamples; Northeastern University dropped its football program in 2009 and has still shot up the rankings.)
Over the past decade or so, applications from high-school students in the Northeast to schools in the Southeastern Conference—the Big Ten’s primary rival in athletics, in terms of prestige and television dollars—have increased by more than 90 percent. Perhaps it’s a coincidence, but most SEC schools have climbed in the academic rankings over the same period. Maybe they’ve ridden the wave of social-media posts of outdoor parties in February, or Bama Rush. But maybe a good football team, along with fancy dorms and good food, is considered by many incoming students to be an essential part of university life. Meal plans and residence halls aren’t core to our academic mission, either.
This fall, we’re debuting our new $875 million stadium. Our roster of college-football players will earn $21 million to $25 million to play this year, and our quarterback will make $1 million to $2 million. We’ve lured Chip Kelly to Evanston; as the former head coach of the NFL’s Philadelphia Eagles, he will be as much of a campus celebrity as an offensive coordinator can be. We’ve also landed a $35 million gift from the Uihlein family specifically for football. Mac Uihlein was a captain of the team last year. That donation has upset some of my peers not only because of the family’s politics—they’ve donated to pro–Donald Trump super PACs and national efforts to limit abortion rights—but also because it’s further evidence of our investment in sports at a moment of austerity for much of the university. It’s a big bet that spending so much on football will lead the team to victory and that competitive success will boost the whole university.
The dramatic transformation of college sports makes it harder for me to justify my fandom—to myself and others. Conference expansion has shattered pretenses to regional coherence. Athletes now sometimes attend three, four, or five schools during their college career. Federal courts have held that student athletes can be paid directly by universities and simultaneously earn additional income from sponsorships and advertisers. Amateurism as the model on which college sports are based has always been a half truth, but today it’s basically dead. These facts are enough to make one wonder what the college half of college sports even means.
As a faculty member, I’m fine with most of this, but with many reservations. When I taught a large lecture course on the history of college sports, I learned about a tackle named James Hogan, who played for Yale University from 1901 to 1904. He was in his mid-to-late 20s and didn’t pay tuition, and the university paid for his spring breaks in Havana. His story is a reminder that money has infected college sports for a long time.
Even so, I’m concerned that the money our athletes receive will affect my interactions with them as students in my classes. Instead of learning history, will they be focused on how to invest or spend the dollars the athletics department is paying them? Their labor for the university is more valuable than mine, so will they wonder why they should have to listen to me at all?
Yet I continue to believe that a university’s athletic and academic successes are complementary, if not connected. I still disagree with my colleague’s claim that sports drag down the more elevated intellectual and creative purpose of our institution. Football games and other sports connect generations of students, faculty, and alumni. Investments in athletics can boost a university’s academic reputation, along with our roster of poet laureates, Nobel Prize winners, and Marshall Scholars, and can also be a source of financial stability or even prosperity.
Even now, I think college sports, on balance, do more good than harm. It has been a rough period at Northwestern and other institutions of higher learning. I see sports as part of what holds us together as a community at the same time that they’re one more source of tension for others, such as my oboist-loving colleague. Yes, there’s too much money in the system, and that money can invite corruption that goes against our values. But there’s also too little attention paid to what college athletes gain from a university education, and what the rest of the university gains from having first-rate athletes here, in the classroom as well as on the field. The value of big-time college sports is real—for players, for fans, for professors—although you do have to work harder than ever to see it.

On dinner timing, weight management, emerging research, pain, disease prevention, healthcare gaps and more
(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Athira Elssa Johnson writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
What we eat, when we eat and how we manage our weight remain important questions in health, even as advice often runs ahead of the evidence. This week,I examine one deceptively simple question: is there a right time to have dinner?
Does eating late really affect our health? Is the time at which we eat more important than what we eat? And how should dinner timing be considered alongside sleep, work schedules, physical activity and the overall quality of the diet? Doctors explain what we know about meal timing, and what it can and cannot tell us about maintaining good health.
Close on the nutrition and weight-management front is a study from the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, which looks at what works better for lasting weight loss. The study finds that combining diet and exercise is more effective for sustained weight loss than either approach alone. The findings are a useful reminder that weight management cannot be reduced to one food, one nutrient or one short-term intervention.
Meanwhile, the focus on protein continues to grow, particularly on social media. But increasing protein intake is not, by itself, a definition of a healthy diet. Ramya Kannan looks at what constitutes a wholesome meal and the importance of considering the overall dietary pattern rather than focusing on individual nutrients or products.
Emerging research
From everyday nutrition, we move to some interesting areas of emerging research.
Researchers are exploring whether material derived from menstrual blood could have applications in the treatment of osteoarthritis. A recent study as reported by Manjeera Gowravaram examined extracellular vesicles derived from menstrual blood stromal cells and their effects on processes involved in cartilage formation. The findings are from laboratory research and do not establish a treatment for osteoarthritis, but they add to growing interest in regenerative approaches to cartilage damage.
Another study reported by Anirban Mukhopadhyay takes a closer look at the genetic basis of cerebral palsy. Researchers found that far fewer genes may have a clear and reproducible association with the condition than some earlier studies had suggested. Understanding which genetic findings hold up is important not only for research but also for how clinicians interpret genetic information in people with cerebral palsy.
Diagnosis and care
There are also important questions about what happens within the healthcare system after patients seek care.
Dr. Suvira Jain writes about why one in three donated corneas is wasted. Eye donation does not automatically translate into transplantation. The cornea has to be retrieved, assessed, preserved and transplanted within the appropriate window. Gaps at different stages can mean that donated tissue is ultimately not used, even as many people continue to wait for corneal transplants.
Pain, too, can persist long after the original injury or illness has apparently healed. Persistent pain may require specialised assessment rather than being dismissed as something a patient simply has to live with. Afshan Yasmeen looks at why persistent pain can be complex and why appropriate pain management needs to go beyond treating the original condition.
Prevention and public health
On the disease prevention front, rabies remains an important public-health concern. Maya C. reports a study from Keralam that looks at the potential impact of dog vaccination in preventing rabies, underlining the importance of controlling the disease in its animal reservoirs alongside ensuring timely post-exposure care for people. Rabies prevention cannot depend on treating people after exposure alone; sustained vaccination and surveillance of dogs are central to controlling transmission.
The issue of counterfeit medicines also highlights why the quality and safety of healthcare products matter. A large stock of suspected counterfeit medicines was seized from a private facility in Bengaluru. Such cases raise concerns that go beyond regulation: a medicine that does not contain what it claims to contain, or does not meet required quality standards, can result in treatment failure and expose patients to further harm.
Air pollution remains another persistent health concern. A study examining winter pollution in north India finds that western disturbances explain a substantial share of the year-to-year variation in winter pollution. Weather systems are only one part of the pollution story, but understanding their role can improve forecasting and help strengthen public-health responses during periods when pollution levels are expected to rise.
Muscle metabolism, healthy ageing
For this month’s Nobel feature we look back at the work of Archibald V. Hill and Otto Meyerhof, whose Nobel-winning research helped establish how muscles generate and use energy. Their independent work helped explain fundamental aspects of muscle metabolism and the relationship between oxygen use, energy production and muscular activity.
And Health Wrap, Episode 50 looks at longevity and the role of racquet sports in healthy ageing, Navin Gnanasekaran, longevity physician and head of radiology, Apollo Hospitals, talk about healthspan, nutrition, sleep, muscle strength, stress, metabolism, inflammation and cognition. The conversation also looks at how racquet sports can bring together physical activity, social interaction and cognitive engagement, making them an interesting part of a broader discussion on maintaining health as we age.
And more:
Shanthi Dass looks at why physiotherapy matters, and the role rehabilitation can play in helping people recover function and manage health conditions.
Dr. Jyoti Bajpai writes about melanoma in India, and why the messaging around this potentially serious skin cancer needs to change to encourage earlier recognition.
Dr. Shivika Gupta looks at what to eat in the weeks before egg retrieval, addressing nutrition in the period leading up to an IVF procedure.
Bindu Shajan Perappadan reports on a WHO-linked study examining smoking and infertility, including the evidence on how quitting smoking can make a meaningful difference.
And in Keralam, health officials have sounded a caution as rising temperatures coincide with a fresh wave of fever cases in Ernakulam, another reminder of how seasonal and environmental changes can intersect with public health.

Messi in Argentina squad for farewell friendly
- Published
Argentina have named Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.
Messi announced his retirement from Argentina duty in August in the wake of his country's defeat by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final and after saying he was considering his future in football following the death of his father, Jorge.
The 39-year-old, who captained Argentina when they won the 2022 World Cup, said the decision to stop playing for La Albiceleste hurt him "deeply" but that he had "given it my all" and had "nothing left to give".
Messi, an eight-time Ballon d'Or winner who currently plays for Inter Miami, is Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player, having scored 125 goals in 207 appearances.
"We made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the symbol of our national team, our captain, Lionel Andres Messi, so that he can have the farewell he truly deserves on 6 October here in Argentina," said Argentine FA president Claudio Tapia.
River Plate's Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, which has an 85,000 capacity, will host the game against Benin.
Argentina's 2022 World Cup winners have also been invited to the match, which Tapia said would be an "unforgettable" occasion.

In September 2026, Snopes readers searched this website for information about a video allegedly showing a 104-year-old woman named Mabel Rose Thompson chiding U.S. President Donald Trump.
A search located a Threads post (archived) from Sept. 15 displaying the clip with the onscreen caption, "At 104, I've Seen 18 Presidents. Trump Was the Most Unforgettable." That Threads post featured the TikTok watermark for a user who previously posted (archived) the video and garnered more than 2 million views.
The video begins with the elderly woman saying she's seen 18 presidents during her lifetime — a number that would mean, given her age, that Warren G. Harding would have been her first president:
Mabel Rose Thompson here. I'm 104 years old. I've seen 18 presidents sit in that office. And I'm going to tell you something that will make half of you furious and the other half want to buy me a drink.
Donald Trump was the worst man I have ever watched lead this country. Not because of taxes, not because of tariffs, not because of any policy you want to argue about at Thanksgiving. Because of character, because of what he did to the American heart. Because in 104 years, I have never seen a president who worked harder to make good people hate each other.
Now before you start typing, let me establish my credentials. I was born in 1922. I was 9 years old when Herbert Hoover was still in office. And I remember my father cursing his name at our kitchen table because the man couldn't stop the hunger. I was 20 when Franklin Roosevelt died. My mother wept at the radio. I was 41 when they shot Kennedy in Dallas. I was folding laundry when the news came on. I dropped a towel and didn't pick it up for an hour. I was 53 when Nixon got on that helicopter, waving that ridiculous double peace sign, flying away in shame.
I have voted in every single presidential election since 1944. I have lived under Democrats and Republicans and men so boring you forgot they were there. I have watched them all. And I am telling you plain, none of them, not Nixon, not Johnson, not anyone, none of them damaged the soul of this country the way that man did.
Further searches for the "At 104, I've Seen 18 Presidents" caption, as well as a reverse image search, yielded what appeared to be the original video (archived) posted on the Real Talk With Time YouTube channel (archived). That clip displayed the same title, "At 104, I've Seen 18 Presidents … Trump Was the Worst." It also displayed YouTube's user-enabled label for artificial-intelligence content — a descriptor creators can select when they upload a video.
In sum, the video is fake and was generated using AI. "Mabel Rose Thompson" is a fake name. An AI tool generated the elderly woman, the room in which she supposedly sat and all of the visible objects in it.
Snopes emailed the YouTube channel's owner to ask what tools were used to make the videos, what inspired the clips and whether the channel's content is created simply to make money. The channel's only members-only video (watchable with a free trial that becomes a $9.99 recurring payment in the second month) showed a thumbnail image of a purported 112-year-old woman promising to tell how she avoided the diseases that killed her friends. We'll update this article if we receive further information.
Detecting signs of AI
Beyond the YouTube video's AI label, the elderly woman's waxy-looking skin (another common tell in AI-generated images) confirms its artificiality.
Readers can spot another of the more common signs of AI content by examining the area behind the old woman. The bookshelf is filled with books, none of which appear to have legible letters and numerals on their spines. According to Northwestern University's Kellogg Insight blog, illegible text is often an indicator of AI-generated images and videos.
A scan of one of the video's still frames by the Pangram AI-detection tool displayed a "Fully AI" result: "We believe that this image is fully AI-generated." A separate Pangram scan of the video's spoken text displayed concluded: "100% of this text is AI" and "We believe that this entire text is AI."
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. For Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as criticisms of the tool.
For further reading, we previously debunked an AI-generated image supposedly showing quadruplet sisters posing with a cake on their 90th birthday.

This past summer, Samsung launched the Galaxy Watch9 alongside the Galaxy Watch Ultra2, its more rugged, shock-resistant smartwatch for outdoor adventures.
The Watch9 is the everyday option, and it’s a solid smartwatch and fitness tracker with a plethora of health features. It’s available in a 40-mm size in cream and graphite, and a 44-mm size in graphite and silver, starting at $80. Compared with last year’s Galaxy Watch8, it’s a modest update, though. There’s a faster processor, a slightly larger battery capacity, and an expanded suite of wellness metrics.
After two weeks of testing the 40-mm model, I wouldn’t necessarily upgrade to the Watch9 from the Watch8. But if you have an older Galaxy Watch or you’re invested in Samsung’s ecosystem and are looking for a smartwatch, the Watch9 is the best choice.
A Familiar (Squircle) Face
The Galaxy Watch’s main hardware update is its new processor. It now utilizes Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform, which Samsung claims enhances CPU and GPU performance along with efficiency. In testing, the watch responded smoothly when scrolling menus, launching apps, and dismissing notifications.
Wear OS 7 also adds more customizable widgets and live updates from compatible apps. One of the more exciting new additions is raise-to-talk for Gemini. Lift your wrist toward your mouth, and you can start talking to Google’s AI assistant. The Google Pixel Watch has had this feature for two generations now, so I’m happy to see Samsung finally catch up.
Samsung has also slightly increased the battery capacity. The 40-mm model has a 390-mAh battery (up from 325 mAh), while the 44-mm models get a 445-mAh cell (up from 435 mAh). Unfortunately, that doesn’t translate to an improvement in battery life, which is probably because it’s being used to power the watch’s expanded suite of health features (more on that later). Samsung still estimates up to 30 hours of battery life, but I averaged closer to 25 hours with Always-On Display enabled. That’s enough to get through a full day and night, but not enough to make charging something you can forget about. A full recharge also took me about 100 minutes on average, which is significantly longer than the 45 minutes it takes the Pixel Watch 5 to reach a full charge.

In Summary
- New Apple CEO, John Ternus, announced a range of products at the Surprise and Shine event.
- While most of the focus was on the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, there was much more to the event than just devices and a CEO debut.
- We bring you eight takeaways that were buried in the buzz around the new devices, which might have escaped your attention.
It might not have surprised too many people – the leaks messed that up – but Apple did a fair bit of shining at its recent Surprise and Shine event. The event, which also marked John Ternus’ debut as Apple CEO at a launch, went on expected lines, with Apple revealing new AirPods, Apple Watches, new iPhone Pros and, of course, the iPhone Duo, which has grabbed the most attention. There was, however, much more to the event than just the launches. Here are our eight biggest takeaways from the day on which the world saw Apple’s new foldable and the CEO on stage:
Table of Contents
New Era? Presentation-wise, Apple is still Cook-ing (Pun intended)
Yes, it was John Ternus who held the reins at Surprise and Shine. But in terms of presentation style, the template that was followed was still from the menu of the preceding chef, Tim Cook. We had multiple speakers, elaborate backdrops, and a similar race through a number of products, leaving the most time for the star of the show (it was the Air last time around, the Duo this time). Yes, in terms of presentation style, Apple remains well ahead of the competition, although we miss the wit and humor of the past; this launch was more from the Cook manual than the Ternus one.
No surprises (Sigh)…
It’s been a while since Apple surprised the Dickens out of us at a launch, but in recent years, the brand’s product announcements have often been leaked out well in advance. And that was pretty much true this time around. From the iPhone Duo to the shades of Burgundy to the fact that there would be no suffix-less iPhone at the event, the leak community got a lot of things right, which, as we have said in the past, takes some of the mystique and surprise out of the event. Mind you, Apple did pull one rabbit out of its hat.
…except for the AirPods 5
There were no suffix-less iPhones at Surprise and Shine, but there sure were suffix-less AirPods. And while most of the noise was about Apple’s first foldable, the AirPods 5 might have emerged as the silent, value-for-money heroes of the show. While most people had been expecting new AirPods Pro with perhaps a camera built into them, Apple brought in a new version of the classic AirPods, complete with better ANC and battery life, even while retaining the “open” fit and, surprise, surprise, the same price tag as its predecessors. Not too many noticed…until the price of the Duo was announced, and suddenly a device with no price increase became the belle of the tech ball.
Hooray, we will now have TWO iPhone launches every year
Surprise and Shine marked the beginning of a new iPhone era, in which Apple will release its iPhones in two tranches over a twelve-month period. While Apple has released iPhones at two different times of the year in the past, the second launch has generally been a relatively low-profile and soft one (of the SE and ‘e’ mainly). That is set to change now. Even if Apple does a soft launch for the iPhone 18, the iPhone Air 2 and the iPhone 18e, rather than a full-fledged event, the fact is that close to half of the iPhone portfolio will be launched in the second half of the year, and the remainder in the first half of the next year. The iPhone schedules just got tweaked.
Apple is getting REALLY serious about AI (no, really, this time)
Two years ago, Apple launched the iPhone 16 series, saying it had been designed from the ground up for Apple’s avatar of AI, Apple Intelligence. However, AI is one area where the Cupertino brand has been found trailing the competition. So it was not surprising that the brand was clearly out to write a new chapter at Surprise and Shine. Every device it announced – iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods – had a strong element of AI, which different presenters stressed would work wonderfully well, even while preserving the users’ security. Well, we have heard that a few times in the past, but never in such a comprehensive manner. Is Apple finally going to crack the AI puzzle? Based on what we saw, it would be no Surprise if it went on to Shine in that department in the coming months.
Whoop, Whoop, the Apple Watch is now a full-fledged fitness and health device, and is targeting Whoop
It started out trying to be a computer on your wrist, complete with apps, notifications and alerts, but the Apple Watch has of late graduated (or been demoted, depending on your perspective) to being mainly a health and fitness tracking device. And Surprise and Shine saw this trend continuing, with most of the talk about the Apple Watch 4 Ultra and Apple Watch Series 12 revolving around better sensors and measurement. The highlighting of features like Readiness Scores and Health Age seems to indicate that the Cupertino brand now has the screenless Whoop, which popularised these features, in its sights.
The narrative is unmatched, but is now very hardware-driven!
Processors, camera apertures, health sensors, ANC, battery life…these formed the major part of the narrative around Surprise and Shine, showing how Apple’s has shifted from storytelling to specs at its launches in recent times. This might be fine for some, but we do miss the time when an announcer would walk us through nuances of design and amazing (or they called amazing, and often, unbelievable) features on devices.
Yes, Apple remains the lord, master, and commander of product launches, but we prefer tales to tech, and a live presenter on stage to edited videos, no matter how sleekly edited. The fact that the Duo section stood out from the others because of its stress on design and UI only reinforces our belief that Apple might perhaps reconsider going back to its storytelling roots, and leave the specs on the spec sheet, rather than on the speech notes. Everyone else talks specs anyway.
Cosmic orange is out of the Apple cosmos… and Black is back!
This was so typically Apple. After making orange the color of the last twelve months, courtesy of the Cosmic Orange variant of the iPhone 17 Pro series, and making a number of brands come out with orange phones and other devices (JBL even had a pair of headphones in orange), the Cupertino giant pushed the shade out of its color palette. It also brought back the one color that everyone had missed in the Pro series – Black. Henry “Any Color As Long As It Is Black” Ford and AC/DC would approve of the return of the color, and so do we. We are not shedding any tears for orange, although we suspect those orange Pros are going to have great antique value some day.
And one more thing…
Craig Federighi’s hair looks as awesome as ever!

How an Aston Villa fringe player became Europe's most prolific scorer
- Published
Just eight months ago, Donyell Malen was struggling to make a significant impact at Aston Villa.
Today, no player in Europe's top five leagues has scored more goals since his Roma debut on 18 January.
The Netherlands international has enjoyed a remarkable turnaround since joining Roma, transforming from a player who struggled to establish himself in the Premier League into one of the continent's most productive forwards.
Europe's hottest scorer
Since his Roma debut, Malen has scored 20 goals, more than Harry Kane (16), Lamine Yamal (15) and anyone else in the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 during the same period.
He also leads the way for combined goals and assists with 22, ahead of Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes (20), Barcelona's teenage sensation Lamine Yamal (19) and Bayern striker Kane (18).
No player across Europe's top five leagues has made a greater contribution in front of goal.
Why Roma's system suits him?
The contrast with his time at Villa could hardly be greater.
In 46 appearances for the Premier League club, the 27-year-old scored 10 goals and registered two assists. Since joining Roma, he has scored 21 goals and provided three assists in just 25 matches.
His scoring rate has improved from one goal every 149.8 minutes at Villa to one every 96.7 minutes in Rome.
On the surface, the figures suggest two very different versions of the same player. But Roma's success with Malen may owe as much to how he is being used as to any change in confidence or form.
The Dutchman arrived in Italy with a proven goalscoring pedigree and the data suggests Roma have found a role that maximises his attacking instincts.
While confidence and form may have played a part, a change in position appears to be a major factor behind the resurgence.
At Villa, Malen was often used across the frontline and spent only 52% of his league minutes as a central striker. At Roma, 99% of his Serie A minutes have come through the middle under manager Gian Piero Gasperini, making him the focal point of the attack and placing him where he can do the most damage.
The stats are backed up by the eye test. After Roma's 1-1 Champions League draw with Fenerbahce last Thursday, when Malen set up his side's goal, French football journalist Julien Laurens told Match of the Day the Dutchman had become central to Gasperini's plans.
"He has been incredible since January," said Laurens.
"He has been really efficient, super clinical. Malen is at the heart of everything they do with the ball."
Following a familiar Serie A trend
Malen is not the only former Premier League player to have flourished in Italy.
Former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay has thrived since swapping Old Trafford for Naples. Since joining Napoli in August 2024, only five players have scored more Serie A goals than the Scotland international's 22.
His impact has been such that Napoli supporters have even erected a street shrine in his honour.
Former Manchester United striker Rasmus Hojlund has also enjoyed an upturn in fortunes. His time in north west England divided opinion among supporters and pundits alike.
But since his Napoli debut, only Federico Dimarco, Lautaro Martinez and Malen have recorded more goal involvements than the Denmark international (19).
Their success highlights how a move to Serie A can provide players with the opportunity to thrive in a different environment and role.
For Malen, however, the transformation has been particularly dramatic.
Rather than changing Malen's game, Roma appear to have found a role that gets the best out of him. Used almost exclusively as a striker, the Dutchman has responded by producing the kind of form that first brought him to the attention of Europe's biggest clubs.
For a player whose Premier League spell failed to meet expectations, his resurgence in Italy's capital ranks among the most notable revivals in European football this year.

Protection for women who defy the Mafia is changing in Italy. Does it go far enough?
Practical, emotional toll can be tougher for women who speak out against the Mafia
"Take a map of Italy, tear Sicily from it and throw it away."
That was the advice the late anti-Mafia prosecutor Paolo Borsellino gave a young Piera Aiello in 1991, when she came to him to say she was ready to tell all about the Sicilian Mafia family she had married into.
Aiello's husband had been gunned down in front of her in the pizzeria they ran together. He was the abusive son of the local Mafia boss, and Aiello had been coerced into marrying him as a teen. Still, she wanted his killers caught.
"I have already decided," she recalls telling Borsellino about her decision to testify. "I just need to pack my bags."
Three days later, Aiello left Sicily with two suitcases — one filled with clothes, the other with toys for her three-year-old daughter.
The following year, Borsellino was killed, along with five members of his police escort, in a Mafia car bombing in the Sicilian capital of Palermo.
Aiello would spend most of the next three decades living under another identity, which kept her safe from the Mafia.
But cut off from her Sicily and her old life, building a new one was lonely and arduous.
"I couldn't find work, and I had to support my daughter," she said, explaining how she found work in the countryside harvesting olives, eventually saving enough to open a small business.
Aiello's early years in protection reveal a less visible aspect to Italy's long fight against organized crime: what happens after someone speaks out. For women, the rupture can be both practically and emotionally tougher.
A new Italian law extending protection from organized crime — and providing social, economic, educational and psychological help — to children and the adults caring for them, often their mothers, is designed to address some of those gaps.
Limits of protection
Liberi di scegliere — the "Free to Choose" bill — became law in July and entered into force on Aug. 9.
Sen. Vincenza Rando spent years pushing for the law and working with women who wanted to break away from Mafia families. Many of them, she says, fall outside the categories around which Italy's traditional protection system had been built.
"Women who are neither justice witnesses nor co-operating witnesses, I call them 'cultural collaborators.' They leave that environment and build a culture of legality," Rando said.
They may not be informants or have any useful intel about a murder, a drug shipment or an extortion racket. Their act of rebellion, she says, may simply be deciding that their children will not grow up inside a Mafia family and culture.
Rando says some leave homes flush with cash, only to end up with nothing. Others need a new identity just to sign an employment contract without being traced. Their children are forced to change schools and friends, thrust into a life with entirely different moral codes.
"If you move somewhere where nobody knows you and you cannot even say who you are, who can you talk to?" Rando asked. "Who can you safely tell your story to?"
Under the new legislation, people under the age of 25 and relatives who care for them may be relocated outside their home region, provided with education and psychological support and, where necessary, given new identities.
Critics say the law gives the state too much power over family life, allowing for the separation of children from parents, which could be seen as punishing children for their parents' crime.
But Rando and supporters say the law prioritizes keeping mothers and children together when the mother breaks with the criminal group.
Aiello supports its aims, but worries short-term intervention will not be enough to permanently break the cycle. She says longer-term support through education and job training is essential.
"What does it mean for the State to take responsibility for them for two years?" Aiello asked. "It means nothing."
For Aiello, the lesson from her own experience is that protection has to mean more than physical safety: it also has to provide the tools to build an independent life.
The 'privilege' of never walking alone
Anti-Mafia prosecutor Nino Di Matteo has spent most of his career seeing the cost of protection from the inside.
He has lived under police escort since 1993, at times under Italy's highest level of security. His two children were born while he was already under protection; within days of leaving hospital, he recalls, they too were travelling in an escort car.
Now based in Rome, he says people outside Sicily sometimes perceive police protection as a mark of status, which he says irritates him.
"People can tend to see the protected person as privileged," Di Matteo said. "From that point of view, I would rather not be 'privileged.' People should perhaps think about the sacrifice involved in never being able to take a walk alone."
Di Matteo is equally wary of a lot of the mythology surrounding the Mafia itself. He points to the media's focus on its most cinematic elements of violence and overt criminality — "the so-called military Mafia" — rather than the white-collar Mafiosi who appear to be part of legitimate businesses and cultivate relationships with political and institutional power.
And he says women's roles in that world have also frequently been misunderstood.
"Women have always played a fundamental role, for both good and bad," Di Matteo said.
Some wives and mothers are the family enforcers of the Mafia identity of husbands and sons. Others have rebelled against it — often painfully breaking away — to become justice witnesses and campaigners.
"For a woman I imagine it may be even harder," Di Matteo said of criminal organizations built heavily around kinship. "Especially when speaking out means accusing your own son, your own blood."
When Mafia threats reach your family
Federica Angeli came to protection by a very different route.
An investigative journalist in Ostia, Rome's gritty seaside district, Angeli spent years reporting on local criminal clans and their grip on parts of Ostia's lucrative beachfront economy.
In 2013, during one investigation, Mafia boss Armando Spada discovered the hidden camera she was carrying. Angeli says he detained her upstairs in a room, placed a gun between them and made clear that he knew where she was most vulnerable.
"You have three children. What shall we do?" Angeli remembers him saying to another man. "Shall we start with the youngest one, the one with the pretty eyes?"
A month later she witnessed an attempted double murder near her home. She testified and was placed under police protection.
For 13 years, armed escorts have followed Angeli through ordinary life: work, dinner out with friends, a day at the beach, family outings. She says friends stopped inviting her over because security officers first had to inspect their homes. Restaurants meant being seated according to security requirements. Spontaneity vanished.
Angeli chronicled her ordeal in the memoir A mano disarmata (Unarmed), later adapted into a feature film. In 2016, Italian President Sergio Mattarella made her a Knight of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic.
But despite the public recognition, the beachfront clean-up in Ostia has sometimes generated resentment: Angeli says she hears residents complain that some establishments worked better under Mafia-linked operators. Other criticism aimed at her is more gendered.
"As a woman, and as a mother, I was heavily criticized for my choice," she said. "Everyone said, 'You put your children in danger,'" who for five years were placed under protection, too, due to threats.
But she rejects the idea that there is one correct maternal response.
"There is no handbook for being the right mother," she said of the decision to denounce organized crime. "But I wanted to free my children from having to bow to the Mafia."
Piera Aiello wanted the same thing for her daughter when she left Sicily.
She built a new life near Rome, and in 2018, she was elected to parliament — Italy's first sitting justice witness — after a long battle to regain her real name. She sat on the Antimafia and Justice committees, where she pushed for stronger witness protections.
And, this summer, more than three decades after Borsellino told her to tear Sicily from the map, she moved back to her beloved island.
"I kept that crumpled piece of Sicily in a drawer," she said, "And I picked it up and glued it back on."

Merz faces key test as 2 German states hold elections with eyes on the far-right AfD
Polling stations have opened for two German regional elections that could impact Chancellor Friedrich Merz's hold on power
BERLIN -- Polling stations opened Sunday in two German state elections in which the far-right AfD party is expected to make further gains that could determine whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz can hold on to power and push ahead with reforms in Europe’s biggest economy.
The state elections are taking place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural region in the formerly communist and less prosperous east, and in the capital, Berlin.
The vote comes two weeks after the anti-migration, Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany, or AfD, finished just short of a majority in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, and has its best chance yet of forming the country’s first far-right regional government since World War II.
Merz’s authority was severely damaged by his party’s stinging defeat in the Sept. 6 election by AfD — a result that shocked many Germans who had believed their country had developed an immunity to nationalism and assertions of racial superiority after confronting the horrors of its Nazi past through education and laws to outlaw persecution.
The AfD is expected to make significant gains in Sunday's elections as well, but has no realistic path to power in Berlin and faces a much stronger challenge from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s center-left governor than it did from Merz’s party in Saxony-Anhalt.
Prospects for Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union are bleaker. It could lose the mayor’s office in Berlin. If things go very badly, it could fail for the first time to win seats in a state legislature anywhere by falling below 5% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where it was already weak.
Merz, 70, became Germany’s leader 16 months ago with promises to turn around an economy that has barely grown in years, but has failed to lift a sullen national mood and has himself become deeply unpopular.
The strong showing of AfD in the Saxony-Anhalt election has further weakened the chancellor's standing on the national level as well, and in the past two weeks there have been calls even from within his own party to replace him as chancellor. No top-level allies have called publicly for his departure, and many have warned against “personnel debates.”
Apparently anticipating a tough postelection period, Merz abandoned a planned trip to New York next week to attend the U.N. General Assembly. Despite the strong headwinds, he has repeatedly said that he’s determined to stay on and finish his term as chancellor.
