Alice Augusta Ball lived a very short life. In 24 years, she had remarkable achievements, and was predictably forgotten for a while, until the world was shaken up to her brilliance. Her work on distilling chaulmoogra oil for use as effective treatment for leprosy brought hope to a number of patients globally.
An African American woman born into middle class in the late 1800s, Alice Ball benefitted from an early exposure to chemical processes as her family was involved in photography. She went on to shine in science at school, and could hope to move on to university, a rare opportunity for a woman and a person of her race at that time. She lived up to her potential and at the University of Washington, racked up her skills in chemistry and pharmacy. She finished two degrees – a bachelor’s in pharmaceutical chemistry and a bachelor’s in pharmacy – thus arming herself for a career –short lived, but so sparkling, people are still talking about her, though subsequent innovations have transformed care for leprosy.
With a full scholarship, another rarity for the times, Alice moved to the College of Hawai‘i, and became the first woman and the first African American to earn a master’s degree in chemistry. We mention it because it is an achievement, but also because it was an achievement that attracted the kind of attention a career flourishes on. It is said that Harry T. Hollmann, a public health officer, thought her thesis research on extracting active compounds from the kava (awa) root might have implications for his passion – finding cures for leprosy.
Leprosy or Hansen’s disease is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, and was discovered by Norwegian physician Gerhard Armauer Hansen in the 1870s. While it is prevalent in people living in tropical regions, leprosy which affects the nervous system, also has the moniker of being the world’s oldest disease. Evidence of leprosy has been found in skeletons from back in 2000 BCE. Those affected develop visible skin lesions and extremities including fingers and toes malformed and misshapen fingers. Sometimes amputations were also performed on limbs that could not be salvaged. As a result of the disfiguration, the stigma surrounding the disease was so high, those with leprosy had to be sequestered in camps and asylums outside the community.
Alice did accept Hollman’s invitation and what she managed to achieve was to revolutionise the field of leprosy care in the very near future. Described as the Ball Method, Alice devised a method that would “convert the oil’s fatty acids into water-soluble ethyl esters that could be injected into patients. Until then Chaulmoogra oil was promising as treatment for leprosy, but it was thick, not soluble in water, besides difficult to inject and swallow. Soon the world adopted the Ball Method and the landmark contribution changed life for the better for people who were battling leprosy across the world, without hope until then. Alice was in her early 20s at the time of this achievement.
Records of the time say, since the new formulation dispersed in the bloodstream instead of pooling under the skin, patients for the first time celebrated as earlier, there was none of the severe local reactions and oozing oil that the injections caused. Used on patients at Kalihi Hospital in Hawai‘i, researchers managed to show that patients administered the new formulation, became ‘bacteriologically negative, their lesions resolved, and many were discharged from isolation to rejoin their families, without fear of infecting them.’ This injectable preparation remained the best available treatment worldwide until sulfone antibiotics, Dapsone, in combination with other drugs, replaced it in the 1940s, facilitating a future unimaginable until then, for those who were diagnosed with leprosy and condemned to social isolation.
However, Alice’s contribution never made it to the headlines thanks to a set of factors – her gender, age and race were primary. She died young, it is speculated that it could be a result of a laboratory accident, a senior male colleague, her department head Arthur L. Dean appropriated and published her work without sharing any credit, in fact, promoting it as the ‘Dean method’, accounts of that period list.
It went unchallenged until decades later, when researcher Harry Hollmann revisited the archives and credited Ball. Finally, the historical records were righted, and Alice Ball’s name was affixed to the method she had painstakingly developed. By 24, despite the disdvantaged circumstances she worked in, Alice Ball had changed the world, it is a matter of speculation how much she would have achieved had she lived longer, but a safe bet to say she would have left a deeper impact. For the punch she packed in her short life, and the revolution she managed in that life, it’s time we say her name, say “Alice Augusta Ball.”

Who Will Foot The UPI MDR Bill? UPI transformed digital payments by making them virtually free. From October 15, this equation will change as high-value transactions will begin attracting MDR. While the new regime opens a new revenue pool for fintechs, it could reshape user behaviour. So, who will now bear the cost? UPI Ends Free Ride: The new framework imposes a 0.4% MDR on P2M UPI payments above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and more. Merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month via QR codes remain exempt, but sellers crossing the threshold repeatedly will enter the MDR category. This could expose small businesses to payment acceptance costs, particularly during the festive season when higher-value transactions are the norm. The Merchant-Side Test: For many sellers, the financial effect will depend on ticket size and transaction mix. A business selling low-value goods may see little immediate impact, while retailers and D2C brands could face a meaningful recurring cost. More importantly, merchants will now have to weigh MDR alongside gateway fees, logistics and marketplace commissions when calculating margins. The Convenience Question: While the government has prohibited merchants from passing on the costs to consumers, the order does not guarantee that the cost will disappear. Businesses, under margin pressure, may absorb MDR through broad price increases rather than displaying a separate payment fee at checkout. On top of this, many fear that higher-value buyers could move back to cash if UPI loses its frictionless appeal. Sustainability Vs Scale: Nevertheless, fintech startups see MDR as essential for funding technology upgrades and wider payment infrastructure without relying on subsidies. The revenue could also make UPI more viable for smaller payment players competing against dominant apps. But the success of the policy will rest on maintaining a delicate balance between protecting small merchants and ensuring costs are not pushed onto consumers. So, can UPI finally become financially viable without losing the low-cost advantage that made it indispensable? ‘Tight slap on his face’: BJP targets Rahul Gandhi after ABVP's big win in DUSU elections
Slamming Rahul Gandhi, BJP's Sidharth Yadav said the ABVP victory reflected students' rejection of “politics of lies, deceit and propaganda,"
While the ABVP – affiliate of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) – marked a big win in Delhi University Students' Union elections on Saturday, the NSUI – student wing of the Congress party – suffered a major setback as it drew blank.
ABVP's Yash Dabas secured the president's post and the RSS affiliate party also clinched two other top posts. Interestingly, Deepanshu Shokeen, who won the vice president post as an Independent candidate, was denied a ticket by the National Students' Union of India (NSUI).
Dabas polled 24,576 votes, defeating NSUI’s Vijai Shankar Meena by a margin of 2,053 votes. Shokeen won the vice-president’s post with 30,615 votes. The NSUI drew a blank, though its candidates lost the posts of president and joint secretary by narrow margins.
ABVP's Riya Chhawdi won the secretary's post, while Lakshya Raj Singh secured the joint secretary's post.
A closely watched contest in student politics, ABVP's big win drew major political reactions as the BJP took potshots at the Congress given LoP Rahul Gandhi's recent youth outreach campaign under ‘Chhatron ki Goonj’.
Last year, the ABVP won the posts of president, secretary, and joint secretary, while the NSUI had secured the vice-president's post.
Union home minister Amit Shah congratulated the ABVP and said the win 'reflects the unwavering trust of the youth in the council's ideology of "Nation First" and its commitment to student welfare.'.
In a dig at the Congress, BJP national media co-convener Sidharth Yadav said the ABVP victory reflected students' rejection of what he described as “politics of lies, deceit and propaganda,"
“For a long time, Rahul Gandhi was working on creating an anti-India agenda. He was creating a narrative that the country's youth are moving away from nationalist ideas and the younger generation is appreciating the politics of lies and conspiracy,” Yadav was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.
He added, "Today's result (of the DUSU polls) is a tight slap on his face. DUSU results have completely demolished the narrative that the Congress, Left and their entire ecosystem was trying to build."
Yadav said DU students "downed the shutter" of Gandhi's politics of "falsehood and negative propaganda", adding, "The DUSU results are GEN Z's mandate against Rahul Gandhi. It will give him sleepless nights."
"Rahul Gandhi is sounding 'jhooth ki goonj' at several places. Rahul Ji, are you able to hear this 'sach ki hunkaar' (roar of truth) from students or not?" Yadav added.
Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami also took a jibe at Gandhi and said, "Despite all the attempts by Congress and Rahul Gandhi to influence the student elections with the Jhooth ki Goonj (echo of their lies), Gen Z has chosen the ideology of national interest with its wisdom."
The remark referred to Rahul Gandhi's "Chhatron Ki Goonj" campaign, with Dhami using the phrase "Jhooth ki Goonj" as a criticism.
The new DUSU president also took a swipe at Gandhi and said, "We want Rahul Gandhi to become even more involved in student politics, because the more involved he gets, the further NSUI declines."
NSUI's DUSU setback comes at a time when Gandhi is organising youth outreach programme's across the country under the banner of ‘Chhatro ki gunj’ – a caimpaign started following the NEET paper leak row. While the NSUI drew blank in Delhi University polls on Saturday, Gandhi was addressing students at the 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' programme in Indore, where Madhya Pradesh Public Service Commission (MPSC) aspirants raised concerns over delays in recruitment.

Will the three-week break put more pressure on managers?
- Published
Three weeks is a long time in football - especially if you are a manager struggling for results.
So far this season two coaches have lost their jobs - Paul Heckingbottom at Preston North End and Michael Duff at Wycombe Wanderers.
But plenty of others will be looking over their shoulders heading into the new, extended international break.
That includes the managers of Fulham and Manchester United, who on Sunday meet at Craven Cottage in the final fixture before players jet off around the world with their countries.
It will all be pretty new to Alvaro Arbeloa, appointed as Fulham's manager in the summer after taking charge of just 28 games as Real Madrid boss in the second half of last season.
But with no wins and three defeats in his first four Premier League matches, and speculation of unrest among the squad due to players' social media activity, the pressure is already on Arbeloa.
Likewise Michael Carrick at Old Trafford, especially after the 3-2 EFL Cup exit to Brighton on Wednesday.
It was the first time United had led at home by two goals and lost since they were beaten 3-2 by Tottenham in 1976, half a century ago.
Coming on the back of the 1-0 loss to 10-man Manchester City, and with their only victories this season against Ipswich Town and Sabah, Carrick needs results.
But they are not the only managers who might have cause for concern.
The stats: Do clubs change managers in the international break?
Over the past 10 years, it has been rare for a Premier League manager to be replaced this early in the campaign.
Even more so in the international break.
But could it be different this year? The first break is longer, three weeks rather than two, and comes later.
The September slot used to come at the start of the month when clubs had only played three league fixtures.
In the past 10 years only two managers - Watford's Javi Gracia in 2019 and Nottingham Forest's Nuno Espirito Santo last year - moved on during this break.
What about the October stoppage? Again, only two managers have previously lost their jobs during the same period - Francesco Guidolin at Swansea in 2016, and Xisco Munoz at Watford in 2021.
This suggests clubs do not tend to use an international break to change manager.
It is, though, far more likely to happen in November, with six bosses replaced in the past 10 years.
That does not mean managers are safe, though. The changes simply were not made during the breaks.
In the past 10 campaigns, nine coaches had left their jobs by the time the second international break came along - which is where we are in the number of games.
With no manager to move on yet, could it come in the next three weeks?
Breaks give clubs a chance to bed in a new manager - Pulis
Former Stoke, West Brom and Middlesbrough boss Tony Pulis explains when the pressure can build for a football manager.
With the first international break upon us, rumblings around certain clubs that have started the season poorly have surfaced.
In my time, the October/November international breaks, the pause just after the Christmas period, and then early March would be the three sticking points for any manager who was struggling with results.
Why these breaks are used for clubs to make changes is plain to see. The pause in the season gives football clubs the chance to appoint a new manager with time for them to settle into their new role, to take stock of the surroundings, staff and time to prepare for their first game in charge.
After Christmas, usually the first game is an FA Cup match, which again gives the new boss a chance close up to see what they have to work with. First impressions can be a vital starting point, so again the manager has time to prepare and deliver their principles to the lads.
Personally, I've joined quite a few of my clubs midway through seasons, and have left a few clubs going the other way, but I do honestly believe that those international breaks, for the reasons I've given, definitely heighten the chances of struggling managers getting the sack.
I don't see this September break as a flashing light, it is too early in the season, but from then on in, the dates I have mentioned really do come into play.
But this early international break doesn't help any managers.
Whether your team is winning or losing, on both accounts, it's a nightmare. If you're winning you want to keep playing, and yet if you've started badly as a manager you want more time to put it right. Players travelling and the chance of injuries at such an early stage of the season is completely bonkers in my opinion.
Which managers could be under threat?
While the evidence suggests things have to get pretty bad for a club to change manager early in the season, a few bosses are feeling the heat.
Manchester United
Simon Stone
There are ways of losing games of course, but I don't see the trip to Fulham as being 'make or break' for Carrick in the sense of his job.
Carrick says it would be "ridiculous" to think that way - and I agree.
He got enough credit in the bank last season by steering Manchester United into the Champions League to ride out a poor start to the season.
I think the issue is United generate so much debate that a loss at Craven Cottage, which would be United's first since 2009, against a team that has only one point and is bottom of the table, would lead to numerous external inquests - which in turn puts a laser focus on the club when they resume their campaign against Tottenham on 10 October.
Fulham
Nizaar Kinsella
It is unclear exactly how much danger Arbeloa is in, but there appears to be some substance to reports of disgruntlement among elements of Fulham's squad early in the campaign.
His significant tactical changes since replacing Marco Silva have left the Cottagers vulnerable at the back, although they produced a more solid display in a goalless draw away to Liverpool last weekend. Silva spent five years at Craven Cottage.
However, owner Shahid Khan has shown a ruthless streak in the past when making managerial changes. Claudio Ranieri lasted just 106 days in charge, while Felix Magath was sacked in September 2014, albeit having been appointed the previous season.
Tottenham
Sami Mokbel
The results go from bad to worse for Tottenham. Having spent about £300m on new talent over the summer the club's owners are getting very little bang for their buck in terms of points (and goals) scored.
But there is no sense whatsoever that Roberto de Zerbi is under pressure despite the club's difficult start - no wins from six games.
The vibes with regards to how the team is starting to play are positive amid a sense that it is only a matter of time before they click.
Of course, for Tottenham, it needs to click sooner rather than later.
Crystal Palace
Sami Mokbel
Pierre Sage has endured an indifferent start to life at Palace. One league win so far hasn't gone down particularly well internally, nor has the team's leaky defence since the Frenchman's arrival from Lens.
Allowances will be made for the unavailability - for a manner of reasons - of key attacking duo Ismaila Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta.
The 4-0 win over Lech Poznan in the Europa League on Thursday eased some of the pressure, but a defeat at Leeds this afternoon would come at the worst possible time for Sage.
Burnley
Nicky Hayen quit Genk to spearhead Burnley's bid to return to the Premier League at the first attempt.
The Clarets started the season as third favourites for promotion, behind West Ham and Wolves, but are winless in their first eight matches.
In his pre-match news conference on Friday, the Belgian faced questions about his future.
Hayen admitted he was under pressure and Saturday's game against fellow slow starters Derby was a must-win fixture.
But a disappointing 1-1 draw, with the Rams scoring a stoppage-time leveller, left Burnley rock-bottom going into the break.
The Burnley board might now be assessing their options.
Derby manager John Eustace, who almost took the club to the play-offs last season, is not safe either with the club in the relegation zone.
Watford
A Watford manager can never rest easy in their seat. Alessio Dionisi, appointed in the summer, became their 27th permanent manager in just under 18 years.
Friday's defeat at Bristol City left the Hornets with two wins from their first eight league games under the Italian, who managed Empoli before moving to England.
Sitting in 19th position in the league table, three points above the drop zone, it would not be a surprise if owner Gino Pozzo decided to make an early change.

NEW DELHI: Is the implementation of the Uniform Civil Code emerging as a new point of contention between the Bharatiya Janata Party and one of its oldest allies, Janata Dal (United)?The question has come into focus after Union home minister Amit Shah's assertion that UCC would be implemented in all 21 NDA-ruled states before the next Lok Sabha elections prompted differing reactions within the JD(U).The issue surfaced after Shah, during his visit to Mumbai, put a timeline on BJP's plan to implement one of its longstanding ideological objectives before the 2029 Lok Sabha polls."Triple talaq has been abolished, giving Muslim women equal rights. We have introduced the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in several states and I am confident that in the 21 BJP-NDA ruled states, we will introduce the UCC before 2029," Shah said.
Shah's message, however, drew a different response from some JD(U) leaders in Bihar.JD(U) general secretary and former minister Shyam Rajak said his party did not favour implementing UCC in the state."Our stand on the issue was made clear by our leader way back. He had said that although our party was supporting the UCC Bill in the Parliament, it was not in favour of implementing the same in Bihar," Rajak said."The chief minister may be of the BJP but the government is being run with the help of allies...
our stand is clear, the question of implementing UCC in Bihar does not arise," he added.
However, Bihar deputy chief minister Vijay Kumar Chaudhary, who is considered to be a close ally of former chief minister Nitish Kumar, adopted a more cautious stance and said the party would first study the legislation and would not oppose it "for no reason" if its provisions were found to be unexceptionable."As of now, we are not aware of the details of the legislation on UCC. Let it be placed before us. If we find there is nothing objectionable, why shall we oppose it without any reason? And if there are points of concern, these will be conveyed to the Union home minister," Chaudhary said.JD(U) working president Sanjay Jha has also indicated that party leaders would discuss the issue with Shah.
For now, therefore, JD(U)'s stand is not entirely clear. While some leaders have spoken against implementing UCC in Bihar, remarks by senior leaders such as Chaudhary and Jha have left scope for the party to examine the proposed provisions before taking a final position. The party has historically favoured wider consultations and consensus on the issue.
What is UCC
India already has uniform criminal laws and common civil laws covering matters such as taxation, contracts and negotiable instruments. However, when it comes to personal laws such as marriage, divorce and inheritance of property, different religious communities follow laws based on their respective traditions and practices.Article 44 under the Directive Principles of State Policy of the Constitution says that the State shall endeavour to secure a UCC for citizens throughout India."The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India," the Constitution says.A UCC broadly seeks to provide a common legal framework for citizens in matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and succession.
BJP's old promise
The Uniform Civil Code has been a longstanding part of the BJP's political agenda and has featured repeatedly in the party's election manifestos over the years.The party has repeatedly included the issue in its election manifestos, arguing that a common civil code would ensure equality before law and strengthen women's rights in matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption.Matters such as marriage, divorce, adoption, wills, intestacy and succession fall in the Concurrent List, allowing both the Centre and state governments to make laws on them.
In 2022, then Union law minister Kiren Rijiju also informed the Rajya Sabha that states were empowered to legislate on these subjects."Article 44 of the Constitution provides that the State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India," Rijiju had said in a written reply."Personal laws such as intestacy and succession; wills; joint family and partition; marriage and divorce, relate to Entry 5 of List-III-Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, and hence, the States are also empowered to legislate upon them," he had added.This has allowed BJP-ruled states to take the state route on UCC.Uttarakhand became the first state in independent India to implement a state-specific Uniform Civil Code on January 27, 2025.Since then, UCC Bills have also been passed by the assemblies of BJP-ruled Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh. As of mid-September, the Bills in these three states were awaiting the President's assent.Other NDA-ruled states are at different stages of considering or preparing their own legislation.Shah's latest remarks have now put a 2029 timeline on that process for all NDA-ruled states.
Why UCC needs careful balancing for JD(U)
For JD(U), the issue comes with both political and ideological considerations.Nitish Kumar has long maintained that a reform such as UCC should not be pushed without broad consultation and consensus, particularly given India's social and religious diversity.There is also an electoral dimension.Within the NDA in Bihar, JD(U) has traditionally sought support across a social coalition that includes Extremely Backward Classes, women and sections of minorities. While its support among Muslims has weakened over the years, the party has continued to reach out to the community.Muslims constitute around 17.7% of Bihar's population, according to the state's caste survey. Recent electoral data cited by The Indian Express suggests that only a relatively small section of Muslim voters backed the NDA in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, underlining the challenge for JD(U) in retaining support among the community while remaining part of the BJP-led alliance.In the 2025 assembly election, JD(U) fielded four Muslim candidates, but only Mohammad Zama Khan won from the Chainpur seat.The political setting has also changed since that election.The NDA won 202 of Bihar's 243 assembly seats, with the BJP emerging as the single-largest party with 89 seats and JD(U) winning 85.Nitish Kumar is also no longer chief minister, with BJP's Samrat Choudhary now heading the NDA government. JD(U), however, remains one of its two principal constituents.This makes the UCC question an important one for the alliance: BJP has put a timeline on a longstanding policy commitment, while JD(U) has traditionally stressed consultation before any such move.
When JD(U) differed with BJP
Although an ally of BJP, JD(U) has not always agreed with it on politically sensitive issues.On UCC itself, Nitish Kumar has long cautioned against hurried implementation.In January 2017, as Bihar chief minister, he returned the Law Commission's questionnaire on UCC, arguing that there was insufficient clarity about what the proposed code would contain and calling for wider consultations with affected groups.Nitish argued that diverse customs and practices had existed for centuries and that any effort towards a common code should be based on consensus rather than simply imposed.JD(U) has also differed from the BJP on issues such as the Triple Talaq Bill and the abrogation of Article 370.In 2019, JD(U) opposed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Bill, commonly known as the Triple Talaq Bill. The party objected particularly to the provision making instant triple talaq a criminal offence, arguing that the legislation could create "a lack of trust" in society. Its MPs walked out of the Lok Sabha debate and later abstained during the Rajya Sabha proceedings.In August 2019, the party also opposed the Modi government's decision to abrogate the special status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 and reorganise the former state into two Union Territories. JD(U) MPs staged a walkout when the measures were introduced in Parliament.However, it struck a reconciliatory note later and said that once the law had come into force, it should be abided by all.These differences did not, by themselves, prevent the BJP and JD(U) from working together. The two allies have in the past maintained separate positions on some issues while continuing their political partnership.UCC could similarly depend on what form a proposed law for Bihar eventually takes and whether the allies are able to arrive at a common position.
Mahagathbandhan's offer to Nitish
Amid the debate over UCC, Congress and Rashtriya Janata Dal have taken the opportunity to invite Nitish Kumar to join the opposition alliance.RJD MLA Bhai Virendra asked Nitish to break ties with the BJP and form a new government with its support, saying the parties shared a socialist political tradition.The RJD MLA alleged that Nitish was surrounded by people who were "hellbent on ruining his political career" and said, "We urge Nitish Kumar ji to walk out of the NDA and form a govt with our support."Former Bihar Congress president and Rajya Sabha member Akhilesh Prasad Singh also extended an invitation to Nitish to join the Mahagathbandhan, saying Nitish had long been associated with socialist politics.
"It is the agenda of the BJP and the RSS. Several allies of the NDA may not agree with it, and Nitish certainly should not agree with it. He has always been associated with social concerns and socialism, so I do not think he can ever agree with this," Singh said."Why would Congress have any objection to that? If he leaves, Congress will always welcome him," he added.For now, however, the differing remarks on UCC do not necessarily point to a larger crisis within the Bihar NDA.
JD(U)'s final position remains open. Some of its leaders have opposed implementation in Bihar, while others have said the party should first see the proposed legislation and discuss its concerns with the BJP leadership.Shah, meanwhile, has set a clear target of introducing UCC in all NDA-ruled states before 2029.It remains to be seen whether Bihar eventually follows that roadmap and, if it does, what shape the proposed law takes after consultations between the two allies.

A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.
Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.
Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.
A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.
Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.
Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”
Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.
The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank.
In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.
“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”
Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.
Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outlet Nyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”
Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.
Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.

Pocket FM is betting heavily on AI to improve its content economics and lift its EBITDA margin to 15%-20% from around 5% currently, cofounder Prateek Dixit told Inc42. Dixit did not disclose a timeline for achieving the margin target. However, he said AI already powers about 90% of Pocket FM’s production, while its post-production process is entirely AI-driven. Overall, AI is involved in 80%-90% of the startup’s creative processes. The audio series platform is using AI to reduce production costs, accelerate content creation, and scale its IP across languages, geographies, and entertainment formats. The margin expansion target comes shortly after Pocket FM claimed to have crossed $500 Mn in annual recurring revenue (ARR). Founded in 2018 by Dixit, Rohan Nayak, and Nishanth KS, Pocket FM offers audio content across multiple languages and genres. Backed by Lightspeed, StepStone Group, Tencent, and Times Internet, the startup has raised $196 Mn to date. It was last valued at $750 Mn during its $103 Mn Series D funding round in 2024. The startup claims its entertainment ecosystem comprises more than 7.7 Lakh titles, 5.5 Lakh creators, and 5.5 Bn hours of playtime and engagement data. It also has more than 1.4 Mn hours of text and voice content. Inside Pocket FM’s AI Content Engine As part of its broader AI push, Pocket FM has launched Sherpa, a fiction-writing platform designed to help creators build long-form stories spanning anywhere from 10 to 1,000 episodes. The platform is currently free for all writers, and Pocket FM does not expect it to become a revenue generator in the near term. “Closed-source frontier models can write one or two episodes reasonably well, but they struggle with long-form planning across 100 or 200 episodes and with creating strong IP. That was the thought process behind launching Sherpa,” Dixit said. Unlike a single generative AI model, Sherpa uses multiple specialised agents across ideation, research, story planning, prose generation, feedback, and narrative memory. The platform is intended to maintain consistency across characters, relationships, conflicts, and storylines extending over hundreds of episodes. Dixit said Sherpa’s planning and prose models use Pocket FM’s proprietary data, while its assistant layer can draw on frontier models such as OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude. “We have around 2.5 Mn hours of content on the platform, which is massive and gives us proprietary engagement data. We have used this data to train a model for writing great prose,” Dixit said. Taking Pocket FM’s IP Beyond Audio The startup is now looking to expand into new geographies while taking its existing IP into additional entertainment formats, Dixit said. It plans to enter Japan and South Korea over the next six to eight months. It is also exploring markets such as the Netherlands, Belgium, Turkey, and the Scandinavian countries. Beyond audio, Pocket FM is evaluating interactive storytelling and gaming opportunities, although Dixit said no specific launches have been finalised. Pocket Saga is currently the startup’s key video bet. Through the platform, Pocket FM is adapting its existing IP into long-form, AI-generated anime content. Dixit said Pocket Saga titles could run for 50 to 100 hours, comprising two-to-three-minute episodes, with individual shows potentially spanning 1,000 to 2,000 episodes. The strategy follows Pocket FM’s decision to shut down Pocket TV, its short-form video drama product. Dixit said Pocket TV suffered from weak user retention and operated in a segment where AI had increasingly commoditised short-form video production. The cofounder declined to comment on Pocket FM’s IPO and fundraising plans. Recent media reports suggest that Pocket FM is looking to raise $100 Mn to $120 Mn at a valuation of about $2 Bn. However, Inc42 could not independently verify this.

AI assistants are finally ready to help you run your life. All you need to do is trust them with your email login, your contacts, and your credit card — and hope they don't go rogue.
Meta, Google, and the buzzy startup Instinct have rolled out personal AI agents in recent months that promise to handle tasks such as booking travel, buying concert tickets, and scouring Facebook Marketplace for deals.
At a basic level, these agents behave largely the same way. You send the agent a request via an app or WhatsApp — or, in the case of the newly launched Rene agent, via iMessage — and leave it to complete the task.
The catch is that AI agents are only as useful as the level of access that you give them. Want AI to book your flight? It'll need access to your credit card and airline account. Want it to tidy up your inbox? It will need the keys to your email.
These shiny new tools come after a summer of multiple high-profile incidents in which AI agents went rogue and hacked companies, as well as user reports of their own agents taking unintended actions.
In one case earlier this year, a man in Australia said his AI agent running on OpenClaw secured him a spot in a Pilates class by breaking into the gym's online booking system.
The result is a sense of whiplash between wonder and anxiety. Early adopters of personal AI agents have shared examples of how the technology has made their lives much easier, but also ways in which it hasn't gone to plan.
"It has access to your email, files, accounts, and even passwords — a mistake or manipulation could have real-world consequences, and that is terrifying," Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at internet security firm ESET, told Business Insider.
Agents in a time of misalignment
This summer, before fears of an AI apocalypse reached fever pitch, a flurry of tech companies reported incidents in which their AI agents went rogue.
In July, an internal OpenAI model escaped its development sandbox and broke into Hugging Face's internal systems, the companies said. Meta and Anthropic later disclosed that their own agents also conducted hacks without their knowledge.
While these incidents involved cybersecurity-focused agents in testing, the same underlying problem applies to consumer-focused agents: misalignment, where AI pursues a goal that conflicts with what its human creators or users intended.
"AI agents need safeguards built in. Without these guardrails, they are designed to go 'rogue' because they are specifically designed to get a task done — however it decides to achieve it," Moore said.
During testing of Meta's Muse agent, which soared to the top of Apple's App Store a week after launch, it displayed several undesirable behaviors, The Information reported. Those included sending unapproved emails and, in one case flagged by an employee, trying to undermine a rival app the user was building, the report said.
Conducting tests like these is one way tech companies can mitigate against misalignment. A Meta spokesperson said the internal testing process is designed to "get feedback, and implement safety and privacy protections" to improve the products.
Meta, Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic all have broadly similar safeguards for their agents: they limit the apps, accounts, or data an agent can access; require user approval for higher-stakes actions such as purchases or sending emails; and scan for hidden instructions on webpages, emails, and files.
However, some of the executives building the technology warn that the risk of AI taking unintended actions isn't going away yet.
"We have not solved alignment," Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, told Fortune this week. "We are not done with our research there. I believe no lab has solved alignment."
The era of personal agents
For years, AI company leaders have been expounding the potential for personal AI assistants to make our lives better. Google chief scientist Demis Hassabis has often spoken of his vision to build a "universal AI assistant." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has long shared his vision of "personal superintelligence" for everyone.
While OpenClaw became popular among techies earlier this year, agents like Muse and Instinct are showing early signs of becoming the mass appeal personal digital assistants we've long been promised. Business Insider's Pranav Dixit has used Instinct to buy whey protein, book a cabin getaway, and cancel subscriptions.
"It feels like magic. And contrary to what some people have said, I don't think the appeal is limited to Silicon Valley types," wrote investor Sheel Mohnot on X in a review of Instinct.
That broader consumer appeal could also prove problematic.
"The magic of these products is the access that they have, and that's also the risk," Joe Sullivan, a former chief security officer at Facebook who is now a board member of Manifold Security, told Business Insider. "Consumers don't have the benefit of a whole security team running next to them like enterprises do."
Keeping your agent aligned
So, how do users get the most out of their AI assistants while minimizing the risk of things going wrong?
Moore said agents should have limited access to your services and "be designed to require human approval for sensitive actions."
Similarly, Sullivan warned that early adopters of these agents should "start narrow" in terms of how much access they give the tools.
"I used one of the agents this morning to book a rental car for me. I wouldn't give it permanent access to my Avis account," he said.
Users experimenting with personal agents should turn off access when they're done, especially when testing and comparing different agents, Sullivan added.
"Don't just leave the other one hanging out there with your data, with permission to do things," he said. "Disconnect doesn't mean the same as delete."

A 67-year-old woman whose body was found inside a suitcase at a Kansas fire station has been identified as Lorretta M Moody, as police continue to investigate her death as a homicide.
The discovery was made on the evening of 16 September at Wichita Fire Station 22, where two people arrived carrying a suitcase and told fire department personnel that it contained a body.
Wichita police said fire personnel requested an urgent police response at about 6.25 PM. Officers arrived at the station, located at 2659 S. Hydraulic, and found Moody inside the suitcase. She was pronounced dead at the scene before her body was taken to the Sedgwick County Medical Examiner's Office.
Police initially believed they knew the woman's identity but waited for fingerprint confirmation before releasing her name. On 18 September, authorities confirmed that the victim was Moody. She had previously been reported missing, adding another piece to a timeline investigators are now trying to reconstruct.
The circumstances surrounding the suitcase remain unclear.
The two people who brought it to Fire Station 22 have been interviewed by investigators. Police have not released their identities or said what relationship, if any, they had with Moody.
Detectives are working to determine how Moody and the two individuals were connected, as well as how and where she died. Investigators have been interviewing other people, reviewing evidence and working to establish a complete timeline of events.
Police have not publicly disclosed Moody's cause of death or said whether anyone has been arrested in connection with the case. ABC News reported that no arrests had been announced as of 18 September.
The unusual discovery has left several key questions unanswered. Authorities have not said when Moody died, where she was before the suitcase was brought to the fire station, or why the two individuals chose to take the suitcase there.
Despite the homicide investigation, Wichita police said they have no information indicating an ongoing threat to the public.
Detectives and crime-scene investigators worked through the night following the discovery and into the following morning. Police also canvassed the surrounding neighbourhood and said they were looking for additional witnesses and other locations that could be connected to the case.
The police department has urged anyone with information about Moody's death or the events surrounding the suitcase to contact its homicide investigators at 316-268-4407. The case is listed under number 26C179314.
For now, investigators are focused on piecing together what happened to Moody before her body arrived at the Wichita fire station. The identification has answered one important question, but much of the timeline remains under investigation.
Wichita police have said further information will be released when it can be made public without compromising the investigation.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to make his first US state visit in more than a decade next week, meeting President Donald Trump at the White House on September 24.
Xi’s visit will be his first to the White House since 2015, when he met then-President Barack Obama. Trump is preparing an unusually high-profile welcome, including personally greeting Xi at Joint Base Andrews when he arrives on Wednesday (September 23).
The visit comes as Washington and Beijing try to preserve a fragile trade truce while competing over technology, critical minerals and geopolitical influence. The two leaders are also expected to discuss issues including trade, tariffs, artificial intelligence, rare earths, Taiwan, the Iran war, China’s economic ties with Iran and the flow of fentanyl precursor chemicals.
Here are the key issues expected to dominate the Trump-Xi talks.
Trade is likely to be the central economic issue.
The US and China are trying to preserve a tariff truce that is due to expire in November. Washington and Beijing have been negotiating possible tariff reductions on a limited range of non-strategic goods, while also discussing agriculture and energy trade.
The US and China are also considering tariff reductions covering about $30 billion of goods on each side. One specific area under discussion is China's tariff on US liquefied natural gas.
Rare earths are another major bargaining point.
China controls a dominant share of global rare-earth processing and supplies minerals and magnets used in smartphones, electric vehicles, advanced electronics, aerospace and defence equipment.
Beijing has previously restricted exports of some critical minerals, making rare earths a powerful negotiating tool in the trade dispute. Washington wants more predictable supplies, while China is seeking relief from US technology and export restrictions.
US officials have indicated that Washington is not prepared to trade away its own export controls in exchange for greater Chinese rare-earth supplies.
AI has become one of the newest and most important areas of US-China competition.
Trump and Xi are expected to discuss AI safety, the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems and ways to maintain communication between the two countries.
The issue is complicated by Washington's restrictions on China's access to advanced semiconductors and AI technology. Beijing has criticised US efforts to restrict Chinese technology companies, while US officials have raised concerns about Chinese access to American AI capabilities.
The presence of leading technology executives at Trump's state dinner for Xi—including Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Tesla's Elon Musk, Google's Sundar Pichai and Apple's Tim Cook—also underscores the importance of technology to the visit.
Taiwan remains the most sensitive security issue between Washington and Beijing.
China claims Taiwan as part of its territory, while Taiwan's government rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims. The US does not have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan but provides it with military equipment under US law.
A potential US arms package for Taiwan worth up to $14 billion could add to tensions surrounding the summit.
Chinese officials want Trump to go further than Washington's traditional formulation that it does not support Taiwanese independence and explicitly oppose Taiwan independence.
The US-Iran war and its impact on energy supplies are also expected to feature in the wider Trump-Xi discussions.
China is a major buyer of Iranian oil, giving Beijing an important economic relationship with Tehran. Washington, meanwhile, has been seeking to pressure Iran and its economic partners.
The conflict has disrupted energy flows and raised concerns about global oil supplies, making China's relationship with Iran relevant to US efforts to manage the wider crisis.
Another US priority is the flow of fentanyl precursor chemicals from China to criminal networks.
Washington has repeatedly pressed Beijing to take stronger action against companies and networks involved in supplying chemicals used to manufacture fentanyl.
The issue has already featured in US-China negotiations and remains part of the broader American effort to secure Chinese cooperation on counter-narcotics.
Agricultural purchases, particularly US farm products, are another area where the two sides could find common ground.
There could also be movement on Boeing aircraft purchases. China has previously discussed large aircraft orders, making Boeing a potentially significant part of any package of commercial agreements accompanying the summit.

Ukraine fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, including hundreds targeting Moscow, in what officials on Sunday described as the "largest ever" attack on the Russian capital.
Two people were killed and 20 injured across the wider Moscow region, local governor Andrei Vorobyov said. The strikes also damaged a Moscow oil refinery and a residential building.
Ukranian President 
Volodymyr Zelenskyy
 confirmed the attack on refinery, as part of Kyiv's efforts to dismantle Russia's energy infrastructure that funds its war campaigns.
"These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine", Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that a range of missiles and drones including domestically developed Flamingo and Pelican missiles were used to hit the oil and logistics facilities.
Meanwhile a mother and her two children were killed in an overnight Russian drone attack near Kyiv, Ukraine's emergency service said.
Russia’s defense ministry said 1,100 Ukrainian drones were shot down across the country, including the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.
Strikes during last day of elections
The attacks came on the third and final day of Russian parliamentary elections.
Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said the “unprecedented attack” was an attempt to disrupt the elections. 
"The enemy failed in this regard," he said, adding that 450 drones were destroyed while approaching the capital.
Russia also held parliamentary voting in the four partially controlled Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia it annexed during the initial days of war. Voting was also held in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula Russia annexed in 2014.
Ukraine considers the voting in the occupied territories illegal.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion more than four years ago, Ukraine has developed increasingly advanced military drone capabilities. Kyiv has used domestically produced long-range drones, alongside missiles, to carry out strikes deep inside Russian territory. The country's drone technology has also drawn attention from governments and defence manufacturers internationally.
According to the Associated Press, Kyiv's strategy is aimed at making the Russian public feel the consequences of the war and increasing pressure on President 
Vladimir Putin
 to negotiate a peace settlement. 
Putin
 has so far given no indication that he intends to halt the invasion.
Instead, Russia and Ukraine have become increasingly engaged in long-range aerial strikes against each other's territory.
Meanwhile, fighting along the roughly 1,250 km front line in eastern and southern Ukraine has reportedly slowed, with large numbers of drones and ground robots making troop movements increasingly difficult.

A video is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) claiming that Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he would eliminate poverty from the country in one stroke. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Prime Minister Narendra Modi saying that he will eradicate poverty from the country at once.
Fact: The viral video is presented out of context to make it appear that Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he would eradicate poverty from India in a single stroke. In the original video, PM Modi was referring to Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s earlier statement about eradicating poverty and questioning the claim, rather than making the claim himself. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version of the same video uploaded on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s official YouTube channel on 14 April 2024, titled “PM Modi addresses a public meeting in Hoshangabad, Madhya Pradesh”. According to the video description, PM Modi addressed a public meeting in Hoshangabad ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and paid tribute to Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar on his birth anniversary. At the 28:05 timestamp, PM Modi can be heard referring to a statement by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, saying that Gandhi had claimed he would eradicate poverty from the country in a single stroke.
PM Modi said, “Modi’s guarantee begins where expectations from others end. That is why a desperate Congress is making announcements that even its own leaders fail to comprehend. The Congress ‘Prince’ made a declaration that would make you laugh too: he claimed he would eradicate poverty from the country in a single stroke. The entire nation is astonished to hear this. People ask where this ‘royal magician’ has been hiding all these years. Fifty years ago, his grandmother had announced the eradication of poverty. Before 2014, they ran the government via remote control for a decade. And now, they claim to have found a magic mantra that can do the job in one stroke. Where did they get this ‘one-stroke’ mantra? Tell me, isn’t this a mockery of the poor? Isn’t this an insult to the poor? You tell me, can poverty really be eliminated in a single stroke? What are they saying? Who would trust them? It is because they make such claims that they become a laughingstock across the country; the nation does not take them seriously.”
We also found that the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) official YouTube channel uploaded the same video on the same day, featuring a longer version of the viral clip.
The full transcript of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s speech at the Hoshangabad rally was also available on his official website. The transcript confirms that PM Modi was referring to Rahul Gandhi’s claim about eradicating poverty in a single stroke, rather than making the claim himself, as the viral video suggests.
A few days before PM Modi’s rally, Rahul Gandhi said at a rally in Anupgarh, Rajasthan, “The Congress government will give one lakh rupees annually to one woman in every family. One lakh rupees, or 8,500 rupees every month, will be deposited into your bank account every year, and in one fell swoop, we will eradicate poverty from India.”
To sum up, PM Modi did not say he would eradicate poverty in one stroke; he was referring to Rahul Gandhi’s earlier statement.

Trump says 250-foot arch will now be a military complex for attack drones, snipers and ammo
Effort comes as Trump has struggled to get his GOP congressional majorites to pony up for ballroom and arch projects
Donald Trump made another push on Sunday to redefine one of his Washington, D.C. “beautification” projects that is likely aimed at securing funding for the project from a skeptical Congress.
The president posted on Truth Social that the planned 250-foot structure will now be loaded up with “large numbers of drones, plus Snipers,” and insisted that the commemorative structure on the grounds of one of America’s most sacred spaces — Arlington National Cemetary — would become a “top grade Military Complex.”
“At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch, planned since the Civil War Era many years ago, at the Receptive Circle adjoining the Arlington Memorial Bridge, into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage,” wrote the president.
“There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World,” Trump added, before adding: “Out of the 59 top cities and Capitals, Washington, D.C., IS THE ONLY ONE IN THE WORLD THAT DOES NOT HAVE A TRIUMPHAL ARCH.”
The president’s remarks come after he made similar plans to convert his planned White House ballroom, which like the ‘triumphal arch’ is facing legal challenges due to lack of congressional approval, into a military installation at the White House. Trump sought to secure funding for the “ballroom/drone port” through Congress this summer by insisting that funding for it could be part of necessary Secret Service security upgrades to the White House grounds, but the Senate balked and refused to grant him money for the project in a budget package approved on party lines through the reconciliation process this year.
Trump has already sought to break ground on this latest project without congressional approval, citing a century-old authorization from Congress for another project in the same location.
Democrats and legal groups have filed to stop the construction, joining battles being fought over land across the District of Columbia including the Kennedy Center and the former location of the White House East Wing, which was demolished to pave way for the ballroom project.

Rescuers dig 4 bodies from a Nepal hydropower tunnel as families demand answers
Rescuers in Nepal have recovered four bodies from a hydropower plant tunnel three weeks after a devastating flash flood
KATHMANDU, Nepal -- Rescuers in Nepal have recovered four bodies from the tunnel of a hydropower plant as search operations continued for those still missing three weeks after the devastating flash flood last month that killed hundreds and left thousands missing.
Families of the thousands missing, meanwhile, are seeking answers from authorities on their whereabouts.
Nepal's army said that four bodies were recovered Wednesday from the Chilime Hydropower plant, which was situated on the Trishuli River that flooded on Aug. 26.
Nepal's disaster management agency said five more bodies were located in a different location and equipment was being sent to recover them.
The number of bodies that have been recovered since the flooding has reached 1,403 while 6,150 people are still missing, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
Families of the missing have been pressuring the government to speed up the rescue and recovery process from the tunnels.
They have held rallies and many have called on the government to declare the missing as dead because they want to receive death certificates, which would allow them to move forward with legal proceedings and religious rites and give them some emotional closure.
At the Tribhuvan University Teaching hospital in Kathmandu, the lobby walls have been pasted with photos of hundreds of missing people. Relatives go there seeking news of their loved ones.
Usha Khatri's husband Indra Bahadur was working as a cook with a group of pilgrims when the flood hit the Nepal-China border. Since then she has been searching for him in many of the towns where the river flows and where bodies have been recovered.
“The government has not done much for us. They have not met us or given any information or any assurances. I am by myself searching for my husband,” Khatri said.
There were 13 hydropower plants that were damaged by the flooding and many workers were either swept or trapped by the raging water or debris.
Finding the workers who were trapped has been a priority for the government and rescuers. But access to the tunnels has been hampered by thick mud, debris and damaged infrastructure, making it difficult for rescue teams to reach the areas.
Two Nepali workers were found alive by rescuers on Sept. 4, days after the flooding. A day later a Chinese worker was pulled out alive from a separate area.
The government estimates the country's reconstruction costs at around $4.78 billion.

Combining healthy dietary practices with regular physical activity is the most effective non-drug strategy for achieving sustained weight loss and improving key metabolic health indicators among adults with overweight or obesity, according to a major review by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) here.
The findings, published in the international journal Obesity Pillars, are based on an umbrella review that analysed evidence from 112 systematic reviews and meta-analyses covering 2,332 randomised controlled trials and more than 5.07 lakh participant observations across over 50 countries.
The review, led by ICMR-NIN scientists Mahesh Kumar Mummadi and Samarasimha Reddy, compared the impact of dietary interventions, physical activity, lifestyle changes and combined approaches on weight management and cardiometabolic health.
Researchers found that all major non-pharmacological interventions produced statistically significant, though generally modest, reductions in body weight and Body Mass Index (BMI). However, the combination of diet and physical activity delivered the most sustained results, with participants losing an average of 3.68 kg beyond 12 months compared with control groups.
Low-calorie diets were found to be the most effective for short-term weight loss, resulting in an average reduction of 2.64 kg within the first three months. Physical activity alone led to smaller reductions in body weight, but its benefits increased over longer follow-up periods.
Lifestyle interventions such as behavioural counselling, goal-setting, self-monitoring and health education also showed positive outcomes, with their effectiveness improving over time. Beyond weight loss, the study highlighted significant improvements in metabolic health. The combination of diet and physical activity produced the greatest benefits in blood sugar control, reducing fasting blood glucose levels and insulin resistance after 12 months.
Physical activity emerged as the most effective strategy for lowering blood pressure, reducing systolic blood pressure by about 6.1 mmHg between six and 12 months. Intermittent fasting showed the largest short-term reduction in diastolic blood pressure and supported weight loss for up to a year, although these benefits were not sustained beyond 12 months.
ICMR-NIN director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings underscore the importance of an integrated approach to tackling obesity. “Healthy dietary practices, regular physical activity and behavioural support each have a role, but their combination can provide broader and more sustained benefits. This is particularly relevant for India, where scalable and sustainable approaches are needed to address the growing burden of overweight, obesity and related non-communicable diseases,” she said.
Mr.Mummadi noted that although the review drew evidence from more than 50 countries, most studies originated from high-income and upper-middle-income nations. India and other lower-middle-income countries remained under-represented, highlighting the need for more locally relevant research, said a press release on Saturday.

The CFA has told residents of Golden Beach, Paradise Beach and Seacombe, in Victoria's Gippsland region, to prepare to leave after an out-of-control bushfire broke out on Sunday afternoon.
The fire is burning in a south-easterly direction along the Longford-Loch Sport Road at Seacombe.
What's next?
The CFA will provide further updates as crews fight the blaze.
Central Gippsland communities have been told to prepare to leave as firefighters battle an out-of-control bushfire at Seacombe, about 42 kilometres east of Sale.
The CFA issued a Watch and Act warning on Sunday afternoon, "strongly" recommending residents in Golden Beach, Paradise Beach and Seacombe prepare to leave after a fire broke out on the Longford-Loch Sport Road.
A CFA spokesperson said crews responded to reports of smoke about 1:20pm in Seacombe.
The fire, located south-west of the coastal town of Loch Sport, is burning in a south-easterly direction.
By 6pm Sunday, 27 CFA vehicles were on scene fighting the blaze, while air attack support had also been requested.
The cause of the fire is yet to be determined.
Longford-Loch Sport Road closed
Authorities say they have closed the Longford-Loch Sport Road at the Seacombe turn-off so that people cannot enter the area, but they are still free to leave.
They are encouraging people to monitor the situation, including increases to wind speed or a change in wind direction, and to note that smoke or poor visibility can mean the situation is worsening.
A CFA spokesperson advised people in the affected communities to leave as soon as they were ready, "as roads will become busy".
"Those affected can travel to Yarram or Sale, or friends or family away from the fire," they said.
People who do leave have been told to take three days of provisions with them, including cash, clothes and medicine, a phone and chargers, toiletries, important documents, meaningful items, and gear for their pets.
The CFA said further updates would be provided.
