Jenee Gragston dropped to the ground and held on to the grass as if it could save her life. She yelled to her family members to get down. She later told me that she didn’t know where the bullets were coming from, but she knew they were close. When the firing stopped, the cries began. She could hear her 4-year-old nephew howling: “Get it off me! Get it off me!” She wasn’t close enough to see what had happened, but it looked like he had blood on his chest. A teenage boy was lying near the child. The teenager “never screamed or anything,” she said. “I can still see all of it.”
It was a Saturday afternoon, mid-August in Lexington, Kentucky. Hundreds of people had gathered in Charles Young Park to celebrate what’s called East End Day—a combination of family reunions, live music, and lots of food. I grew up going to festivals in that park, though I lived on the west side of town, in the Charlotte Court housing projects.
Kentucky isn’t the most dangerous place in America, but it’s up there, with the 14th-highest rate of gun deaths. Twelve years ago, my uncle was murdered in Lexington. Three years ago, my sister’s husband was shot and killed there. I worry about my brother, who still lives there. He had gotten himself off the streets for a while, but is now back living in the city. Lexington had recently seen a hard-won drop in gun deaths—last year was the fourth straight year of declines in gun violence among young people. This spring and summer set a record of 190 straight days without a homicide. Then came the East End Day shooting, which killed that teenager, 16-year-old Di’Zhon Robertson, and wounded four others—including the 4-year-old, who was shot in the leg. The next weekend, another person was killed. The weekend after that, four separate shootings left two more dead.
Gragston was selling Polish sausages in the park. She’d paid more than $300 for the grill, $300 for the sausages, more than $1,000 in fees, $75 for the booth. Business was good; some people returned for seconds. Her husband, her kids, and other family members had come to help her set up her tent. Her 4-year-old nephew was handing customers sodas and water bottles. On the basketball court nearby, Devine Carama was talking with a group of young people. Carama is the director of ONE Lexington, a city-funded program that tries to prevent gun violence by mentoring at-risk boys. He, too, threw himself down when he heard gunfire. “I almost got shot that day,” he told me. Two people near him were hit—a man and his girlfriend. Carama and others tried to bandage the man’s leg; he told me he could see a glimmer of bullet or bone through the blood.
A day later, 18-year-old Jametrius Griffin turned himself in and was charged with murder. According to court testimony, Griffin’s younger brother had gotten into an argument; punches were thrown, and the younger brother fell or was pushed. When Griffin saw that, he yanked out a gun and started firing.
For the past three years, Robertson had participated in ONE Lexington’s summer youth program, which offers workshops on building emotional and social skills, as well as college-campus visits. “He wasn’t a street kid,” Carama said. Griffin’s younger brother was in ONE Lexington, too—in its school mentoring program. The organization had also helped Griffin get a job at UPS. The group’s work seemed to be making a difference. And then a fight left one young man dead, one wounded, and one in prison.
In many ways, Lexington feels like a small town, where everyone knows everyone. I went to middle school with Griffin’s lawyer, Daniel Whitley, who has a big reputation locally for representing people accused of murder—and for winning their cases. The week after the shooting, I spoke with Whitley and with Griffin’s mother, Jay-Me Baxter, on a video call.
“A bunch of bullshit” was how Baxter described the park shooting, “because everybody’s friends and everybody’s family.” She said her youngest son told her he had been bullied by Di’Zhon Robertson and others. The day after the shooting, she made the same argument in a video she posted on Facebook that outraged many in the community. She suggested that her older son had had no choice and said she didn’t care “who makes it home as long as mine do.” (I tried to reach Robertson’s mother through family members to see if she would talk with me about what happened to her son; her sister replied that the family didn’t want to relive it. But friends and family members described the teenager as quiet, observant, and “very respectful.”)
“I’m like, Shit, I know Di’Zhon’s mama,’” Baxter told me—the other mother was close friends with her own sister. Baxter said she had had a conversation with her about the beef between the boys, and assumed the issue had been settled. Griffin loved football, and he had started college at Kentucky State University. “But you know them kids,” she said. “They be doing stuff in silence.” Her son must have been simmering with fury.
I knew Baxter’s family growing up—she’s a year older than me, and they, too, lived in the Charlotte Court housing projects. She didn’t remember me, but she knew my brother. Her mother was white, and had nine children. Baxter, the third-oldest, is half Black, like her younger siblings. But the oldest two are white. Her mother used to cry, Baxter told me, because “the white kids didn’t ever live with us.” In our majority-Black neighborhood, a white mother with mixed-race kids stood out. Baxter remembers people throwing rocks through their windows and a lot of name-calling—“white bitch.” Her family was poorer than many others, but people in the neighborhood assumed that she was privileged, and tormented her for it. “That white mama, man,” she said. “You know what I’m saying?”
That kind of bullying is part of the pain of being impoverished. You feel so low, you desperately want to make someone else feel lower.
Baxter is a single mother, and Griffin is the oldest of her five children. Like my own mother, she lost custody of her kids because of drugs—she signed over her parental rights to her mom. She told me the story as if she was discussing a character in a book: “Jay-Me got in trouble. Jay-Me started using drugs, cocaine specifically.” Like my mother, Baxter was a victim of sexual abuse. She grew up watching her mother “get beat by men. I done been touched by men, and I never told my mama until a couple months before she died.”
It took Baxter seven years to stop using drugs and get her kids back. Those kids needed her, yet she kept choosing drugs over them, she said, as her voice cracked and tears hit her cheeks. “That hurts, because I can’t believe I did that.” I’ve heard those same words from my own mother and watched her cry for the same reason.
Before Baxter signed over her rights, she said, she asked her mother to promise that what she’d experienced as a little girl wouldn’t happen to her kids. She wanted to break the cycle of violence, poverty, and dysfunction that is the inheritance of so many children. “I’m not a gun mama,” Baxter told me, but she believes in “stepping in the street” to fight. “I’ve been fighting all my life,” she said.
Backgrounds like these are so common in Whitley’s line of work that he seemed to tune out our conversation. At one point on the video call, we heard the sound of snoring. Baxter joked about it: “Listen to him. My lawyer tiiiiiired.” We continued talking for a few more minutes and never heard from him again. “Night night, Daniel,” she said before we hung up. He called me back later, apologized for not saying goodbye, and said he hadn’t been asleep.
Despite the pity I felt for Baxter and her family, I felt more for those shot by her son, and their families.
Di’Zhon Robertson’s uncle Tyrone Johnson officiated his funeral, and told me that the church was full of people “struggling with their emotions.” I was told by attendees that the teenager’s grieving mother had to be pulled off the coffin. Damon Williams Jr., a 14-year-old wounded in the shooting, was hit in the thigh. He had been planning on joining his middle school’s football team this season. Lakeisha Martin was shot in the stomach and the sternum. East End Day, her older brother Isaiah Barron told me, “is a day for our community that we look forward to every year.” Martin was in the hospital for 21 days and will be unable to work for months.
The day of the shooting, Jenee Gragston rushed to the hospital as her nephew went into surgery. She told me the police said she should leave her tent, and could return later to retrieve everything. But when her husband went back to the park, almost everything was gone. The cooler with the meat. The grill, the propane tank, even her prescription eyeglasses. Other tents had been robbed as well. Gragston told me that she was grateful her nephew was okay, but that she would never go to one of the park festivals again.
Lexington is trying hard to reduce this kind of gun violence. Mayor Linda Gorton told me the city has handed out free gun locks and offered to buy back guns from residents, among other interventions. Through ONE Lexington, it offers groceries, hotel stays, and educational funds to people affected by gun violence. The city relocated a family whose house had been shot up, Gorton said. Still, she conceded, “there are times when we cannot control every human being’s behavior.”
It doesn’t help that Kentucky has such lax gun laws. Just this year, state legislators dropped the age required to carry a concealed firearm from 21 to 18. When I was growing up in Lexington, gun violence was even worse. Whenever you have a community of young men who feel powerless and disrespected, who have been raised to protect themselves and their families from perceived threats, and who believe words can’t save them but a gun might, then death will follow. The story of what happened in Lexington this summer is particularly tragic because so many had worked so long and so carefully to make a difference. But a gun changes everything in a moment.
Carama, of ONE Lexington, told me he has more friends who are dead than alive. He, too, said that “a lot of it is out of our control,” and that there’s only so much someone from outside a young person’s family can do. You can monitor a kid all you like, but if he has a gun, “you got a split second to react.” Ultimately, he said, “you can’t prevent everything. It’s just not possible.”
In Jay-Me Baxter’s account, she tried, in her way, to intervene. “The mamas grew up together,” she told me. “This could’ve been prevented.” But it wasn’t.

When we think about the stakes in healthcare, we tend to think of them in terms of life and death, being sick or being healthy. The conversation is about your physical well-being and maybe your mental health — and it pretty much stops there.
How bad healthcare can derail a woman’s entire life
Exclusive: Melinda French Gates on the ways the US health system fails American women — and how to turn it around.
But health affects so much more than your body’s biology or even just you personally, as a new survey from Gallup and Pivotal, a philanthropic group founded by Melinda French Gates, shows. That’s especially true for women, who frequently report negative experiences with the health system and ongoing struggles to get their concerns taken seriously; poor health affects the trajectory of their careers and their ability to be engaged with their families, friends, and wider community.
It starts at the doctor’s office or hospital: 51 percent of women say they have had a negative healthcare experience in the past five years, versus 39 percent of men. About 1 in 3 said that a doctor did not take them seriously when they said they were feeling pain or other symptoms, versus 21 percent of men, and 33 percent said that they either were misdiagnosed or did not receive a diagnosis. The cost of paying for care is another deterrent: 32 percent of women said they have skipped or delayed care in the past year because of the cost, compared to 25 percent of men.
“To see that half of women in the United States who sought care in the last five years came out feeling like they hadn’t gotten the help or care they needed, that’s frankly staggering,” French Gates told me in an email. “It says a lot about how little we’ve invested in women’s health and how much we expect them to just push through pain or accept uncertainty.”
And the effects of those experiences, the failure to receive proper treatment, ripples out into the rest of the women’s lives. More than half of US women, 54 percent, said they had experienced at least one health-related impact on their family life or relationships; 42 percent said their health had led to a negative effect on their career or work. It also affects their community: 32 percent said their health had affected their ability to participate in civic life.
The toll is not only physical but mental: 48 percent of women said they’d dealt with a mental health condition like depression or anxiety. And socioeconomic disparities abound. Black and Hispanic women are more likely to report being in poor or fair health. Women who have lower incomes are more likely to face career struggles because of their health than those who make more.
I had the opportunity to interview French Gates, who has made women’s health a priority in her work, over email about the survey; its findings on community engagement, menopause, caregiving, and more; and what could be done to address the problems that it reveals. Our exchange is below, lightly edited for clarity and length.
Which of these survey findings surprised you most and why?
The number of women [54 percent] who said they experienced a mental health challenge during or after pregnancy should stop us all in our tracks. And the fact that less than one in three women who sought care found it helpful is really concerning. It’s why I feel so strongly about integrating women’s mental and physical healthcare, especially during pregnancy and postpartum. Mental and physical health are so linked together.
Too much of the burden is placed on women to get answers. All of us deserve so much better.
Other findings from the Gallup/Pivotal survey:
- 28 percent of women said menopause had affected how much effort they could give at work, while 22 percent said it had led to them being less involved in their community
- 56 percent of women say they have to do their own research in order to make an informed decision about their contraception
- 64 percent of women reported finding misleading or inaccurate information about contraception on social media when doing their own research
- 37 percent of women who have been through menopause said they first learned about menopause when they started to experience symptoms themselves
Nearly one-third of women said in the survey that health problems limited their ability to be involved in their community. What does that look like in practice, and what do communities lose when women can’t fully participate?
Women are so often the backbones of their communities, whether they’re rallying their neighbors around a cause, leading the PTA, or serving in elected office. Without having women — and their ideas and voices — in those roles, we’re missing half of the conversation. Issues that affect women and families are less likely to get on the agenda. They’re less likely to be solved.
When a woman has a health challenge, and she has to spend so much of her time and resources chasing down answers, that makes it harder for her to show up in those spaces. We saw that in the survey: 30 percent of women said their health limited their ability to be involved in their communities. And when women couldn’t get the care they needed, that percentage doubled.
Women’s health is often talked about as a personal issue, but this data is helping us prove that it’s also an economic issue, a family issue, a community issue — it affects all of society.
Caregiving and family responsibilities prevent many women from getting medical care, in particular Hispanic and Black women. That seems to create a vicious cycle: Women are often so busy being the caregivers in their families that they neglect their own health. Eventually, they are the ones who will need care. What do you think can be done to break that pattern? Is there a philanthropic solution? What public policy changes could be made?
Women are often taught to put themselves last and minimize their own needs. They don’t always have time to care for themselves because they’re so busy caring for others. And they might not be able to afford childcare or home health support for their aging parents. Our survey showed one in six women delayed healthcare because of their responsibilities caring for their family members. For Black women it’s one in five, and Hispanic women one in four. Too many women are facing an uphill road to even just get to a doctor’s office.
It’s possible to make it easier for people to balance healthcare and family responsibilities — but it’s going to take action from many angles. That’s exactly why I invest in both women’s health and in caregiving, and I’d encourage more philanthropists to do the same. Businesses can also support employees with good paid leave policies and reliable but flexible schedules.
But for women everywhere to benefit, we need government leaders to prioritize increasing access to affordable childcare, home health supports, and paid family medical leave. These are policies that have the support of large majorities of Americans because these are issues that affect everyone. So there’s a real opportunity here to offer meaningful help to families.
I am struck by our collective failure on menopause: Women report that they aren’t aware of menopause symptoms until they experience them on their own, that they struggle to get their doctor to take menopause symptoms seriously, and that their menopause experience has held them back in their career. What are some short-term and long-term steps we can take to address those problems?
If more than a third of women only learn about menopause symptoms when they go through them, the system is clearly not working. Women need to learn about menopause from their doctors before they experience it. But doctors aren’t getting the education and training they need on menopause while they are in school. One doctor told me she got just one lecture on menopause across all her years in medical school. One said it was mentioned one time. They are seeking out better training but it can be hard to find. That’s why Pivotal is partnering with the Menopause Society to expand physician training on menopause so doctors, nurses, and other health care providers can access the information they’re looking for to better help their patients.
Because menopause isn’t just about being uncomfortable; it can also bring anxiety, heart palpitations, insomnia — significant symptoms that can really hold women back. More than a quarter of women who’ve experienced menopause or perimenopause said it made it harder to live up to their full potential at work. One in 10 had to take leave or leave their jobs entirely. That just shouldn’t be. Women shouldn’t have to step back right at the moment when they could be stepping into leadership roles.
The most immediate steps can come from policymakers, especially at the state level. They can include menopause care in insurance and Medicaid coverage and offer workplace protections to women in menopause the way they do for pregnancy, so women can get the care they need without losing their jobs. I’m also focused on longer-term solutions, like expanding training for healthcare providers and investing in research to accelerate treatment options.
Women are at the forefront of a lot of wellness trends these days and yet, as the survey reveals, women also report encountering a ton of health misinformation on social media. Why do you think women are so often the targets of this kind of content? What can be done to point women toward and build their trust in sound medical information?
One in three women said she left an appointment without a diagnosis, with her pain being dismissed, or with no answers or next steps. You can understand why those women would start looking for information online. And because women’s health has been underfunded and under-researched, there just isn’t as much reliable information out there as there should be, which leaves a lot of room for people to come in with misinformation. Investing in credible scientific research to fill that vacuum will give both women and their doctors more information going into their appointments.
In terms of your own organization’s work, which investments are you making that you think can make progress on the underlying problems revealed in this survey?
We need to address the right now and we need to address the longer term. Right now, women need better care at critical moments in their lives.
One way we’re investing in that at Pivotal is by making it easier for women to get the mental health care they need during and after pregnancy. So we are investing in integrated models that put mental and physical healthcare under one roof. I visited a health clinic in Alabama earlier this year where they identify issues like depression and anxiety right at the outset and then help the mom all the way through her pregnancy care, all in the same place. That model is something we strongly believe in.
Better care for menopause will require better training, which we are thinking about in both the immediate and long term. I mentioned that we’re making more menopause training available to doctors who are currently practicing. That is something I’m really excited about because I’ve heard from physicians who really want to better support their patients and are looking for better information so they can do that. And longer-term, menopause needs to be a much bigger part of the curriculum at medical schools moving forward.
Another longer-term focus of ours is trying to make up for decades of lost time in research. We are funding medical research focused on how diseases specifically impact women, in partnership with an innovative organization called Wellcome Leap. They are working to accelerate progress in women’s health on everything from autoimmune diseases to cardiovascular disease in years, not decades, which is how long health breakthroughs usually take. That’s the kind of urgency women need and deserve.

- Social media users alleged in September 2026 that U.S. truckers planned to strike over high fuel costs beginning on Oct. 1, leading to food and supply chain shortages.
- There was no evidence to support this unfounded rumor.
- Searches indicated the claim largely spread because of a video one social media user originally posted on Sept. 15. Other users then reposted his clip without first looking for credible evidence.
- A spokesperson for the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association said they had no knowledge of an upcoming strike. We also emailed the International Brotherhood of Teamsters and the man from the video, and will update this article if we receive more information.
In mid-September 2026, social media users alleged U.S. truckers had announced a plan to strike beginning on Oct. 1 to protest record-high diesel fuel costs of more than $6 a gallon. The posts claimed the stoppage of transportation would lead to nationwide food and supply chain shortages.
There was no evidence to support this unfounded rumor. Queries of DuckDuckGo, Google and other search engines found no news media outlets or other authoritative sources reporting about truckers planning to strike. Reddit's r/Truckers subreddit, a forum with hundreds of thousands of weekly visitors, featured a post with commenters saying they had heard nothing of a strike.
We emailed the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association to ask about this rumor. The organization's website says it has over 150,000 members in the U.S. and Canada operating more than 240,000 trucks and truck fleets. A spokesperson responded, "Our awareness is consistent with yours in that it seems to be social media chatter at this point in time."
We also emailed the International Brotherhood of Teamsters to ask about the rumor. The labor union has a freight division it says is made up of tens of thousands of Teamsters. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Where the unfounded rumor spread
Searches of social media websites indicated a video, first posted on Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived) on Sept. 15, was potentially the most-popular content promoting the rumor. Users have since reposted the same video across platforms, including Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and X (archived). Others also generally shared the rumor of a trucker strike.
In the video, which ends with a request for users to buy paid subscriptions, a man tells viewers about the purported strike and subsequent food shortages:
In the trucking world, they put out a deal to strike until the fuel prices drop. Shut down Oct. 1. Park it. Stand together. Make their voices heard. Truckers are done.
You know what that means if they do that? Food shortages. Food's not getting to grocery stores. Nothing's getting anywhere.
What have I been telling you? Make sure you've got enough f***ing food for a month to three months, even six months. S***'s gonna hit the fan. S*** is hitting the fan, currently. And with this deal, this is huge.
A lot of people don't understand if trucks aren't moving, you're not getting anything. Grocery stores aren't getting a f***ing thing. Nobody's getting a thing. Just FYI.
That should probably freak you out a little bit because that happened basically during COVID. Remember when you couldn't find anything in the f***ing stores. This'll be a lot worse, if it comes to fruition. Just FYI. 
Please like, share, follow. Share my s***. Subscribe for a buck. 
We messaged the man in the video on Facebook and Instagram to ask for evidence, and will update this story if we receive more information.
A TikTok user's video (archived) also promoted the rumor with the caption "50,000 Truckers Threaten Strike: What It Means For America." In the video, the user claims, without evidence, that 50,000 truckers "are reportedly said to" no longer drive as of Oct. 1.
The unfounded rumor potentially originated out of a previous strike claim (archived) appearing to pertain to the dates of Oct. 1-10, 2025.
For further reading, we previously reported the truth of a story regarding truckers banding together to save someone from jumping off an overpass.

‘Hyperzionism’: How Germany’s conflation of antisemitism and anti-Zionism allowed a far-right return
In the week leading up to Germany's historic elections, a supporter of pro-Israel politician Karoline Preisler wrote that they had “experienced antisemitism up close” after being confronted by a pro-Palestine activist on the U-Bahn in Berlin.
Preisler, a Free Democratic Party (FDP) politician and lawyer known for her provocative one-woman counter-protests at pro-Palestine demonstrations, posted the video to X.
In it, she is seen brandishing an English sign reading “Intifada is a call to violence” at two men she called “racist white terror supporters”.
There was a problem, though. While neither Preisler nor her supporter are Jewish, the heckler they accused of antisemitism is, and was wearing a shirt reading “Another Jew for a free Palestine”.
In response, Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories, commented: “Feeling threatened by Jews who oppose genocide defies epistemology. Time to patent misplaced victimhood.”

The incident came just before Germany’s far-right Alternative fur Deutschland (AfD) won a decisive election in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, the strongest result for a far right party since the Second World War.
The far-right accounts for by far the largest share of antisemitic hate crimes in Germany, making up 84 percent of perpetrators’ political motivation.
Despite this, the majority of public discourse in Germany equates antisemitism with anti-Zionism and critique of Israel, even among Jews, repressing pro-Palestinian speech and protest with extraordinary violence.
Externalisation of guilt
In 2019, the AfD put forward a motion to completely ban the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement.
This led the way for the German government to pass a non-binding anti-BDS resolution calling on institutions not to platform anyone remotely associated with the movement to boycott Israel, and has caused several public figures to be cancelled or disinvited from events for signing BDS petitions.
'Even though the AfD downplays its antisemitism and emphasizes its Zionism, it still follows the same playbook with its fascist predecessors'
- Esra Ozyurek, University of Cambridge
AfD MP Jurgen Braun said at the time that his party was a true friend of Israel in the German parliament, claiming “antisemitism comes from the left and Islam”.
The AfD even made Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s son Yair their poster-boy after he called the EU an “evil globalist organisation”.
“As antisemitism has been equated with the critique of Israel, far right actors have been able to hide their antisemitism and present themselves as transformed,” Esra Ozyurek, an expert on Holocaust memory at the University of Cambridge, told Middle East Eye.
“Even though the AfD downplays its antisemitism and emphasizes its Zionism, it still follows the same playbook with its fascist predecessors in demonizing a religious/ethnic minority,” she explained, “scapegoating them for problems in society which have nothing to do with them, and trying to unite a ‘nation’ through the exclusion of a minoritised group.”
Staatsrason
Though Germany's ties to Israel date from not long after its founding, the sense of Israel as a fundamental part of German national identity is more recent phenomenon, with the externalisation of Holocaust guilt onto Muslims only emerging after 9/11.
In 2008, then-German chancellor Angela Merkel gave a speech in the Israeli Knesset proclaiming that Germany’s unequivocal support for Israeli security was part of the country’s Staatsrason, or “reason of state”.
For Hans Kundnani, editor of the book Hyper-Zionism, this marked a shift where “Germany went from a universalist understanding of the lessons of the Nazi past to a more particularist one”, moving the meaning of “Never Again” from “Never Again for everybody” to specifically protecting not even Jews, but the nation state of Israel.
'Support for Israel has less to do with love for Zionism, but mostly the necessity at all costs to protect the redemption of Germany'
- Daniel Cohen, Rice University
“Merkel wanted to take support for Israel out of democratic contestation, to kind of lock it in…before it is too late”, Kundnani explained.
Indeed, loyalty to Israel now spans the political spectrum, with nominally left-wing parties like the German Greens and Die Linke routinely conflating pro-Palestinian sentiment with Nazism.
This attitude is not reflected in the wider German public: in 2025, polling found almost 80 percent of German voters believe Israel’s actions in Gaza are unjustified, while 62 percent believe they constitute genocide.
Meanwhile, only 10 percent fully support the idea that Israel’s security should be Germany’s raison d’etat. This holds true across political divides.
Partially, the shift is down to generational and demographic changes, with younger and immigrant Germans more likely to oppose Israel and support Palestine. Berlin is also home to the largest Palestinian diaspora outside the Middle East.
Preisler is a kind of “moral crusader” who goes around looking to get into these confrontations with the public, Kundnani said, explaining that he believes her posture of moral superiority is typical among German elites who defend Israel.
“The way Germans think about it,” he said, is that “we did our exemplary engagement with the Nazi past, we have this exemplary memory culture, better than anyone else,” and thus feel “morally superior to the whole world.”
Antisemitism is therefore considered to be an “external problem because it has been solved internally”, blaming immigrants for “reimporting antisemitism” back into Germany, since other countries, especially Muslim ones, haven’t dealt with it as well as Germany.
It has “become a matter of national identity,” Daniel Cohen, historian at Rice University, told MEE, where “anybody who is defending Palestinian rights” is labelled “unGerman” or “non-German” in the interest of protecting a certain German identity - “a German white identity, since the fear of antisemitism is also the fear of immigrants”.
“Support for Israel has less to do with love for Zionism, but mostly the necessity at all costs to protect the redemption of Germany,” Cohen said, referencing the German idea that the country has managed to deal with the shame of its antisemitic past to create a "nirvana" free of anti-Jewish hate.
‘Philosemitic McCarthyism’
Key to this is the role of Germany’s army of Antisemitism Commissioners, who regularly weigh into public discourse to “cancel” figures associated with the pro-Palestine movement.
Most commissioners are not Jewish, but self-identifying Christians who have pointed fingers at everyone from German Israeli academics to Jewish South African photographers.
One such commissioner, Michael Blume, prompted backlash when he called Judische Stimme (Jewish Voice for a Just Peace in the Middle East), a network of German Jews who support Palestinian rights, “ostensibly Jewish”, drawing an official complaint from the organisation.
Blume has a history of making strange comments about Judaism: during a 2015 conference, he told the audience Jews are not a race but part of an ancient school that brought literacy to the world and the origins of antisemitism lie in a resentment towards Jews for their special gift of literacy.
Cohen explains that this philosemitic admiration emerged immediately after the Second World War, preserving Germany’s problematic mythologisation of Jews by opportunistically co-opting their identity.
Despite the country’s tiny Jewish population, Jewish baby names are the most popular among German parents, while the trend of Germans converting to Judaism has drawn criticism as an attempt to atone for their family’s Nazi past.
Susan Neiman, who wrote a book in 2019 celebrating Germany’s model memory culture, has since acknowledged that the process has gone “haywire”, contributing to what Kundnani calls “hyper-zionism”.
Neiman termed this “philosemitic McCarthyism”, where “the determination to root out antisemitism has shifted from vigilance to hysteria”, particularly after the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
Amid this witchhunt, Judische Stimme was categorised by Germany’s domestic intelligence service as a “foreign extremist organisation” – although this has since been overturned in a Berlin court.
“For Germany’s governing policymakers, Zionism is the answer to Nazism,” Udi Raz, board member of Judische Stimme, and author of upcoming book JEW. DESPITE GERMANY, told MEE.
However, “these are…continuations of the same supremacist ideology put into practice by Nazism,” he said. But while Nazism placed Jews “outside the category of the superior, Zionism places us within it.”
“The unconditional support of Germany’s government for Israel suggests that Germany has never fully de-Nazified,” Raz said.

Mum's viral barefoot race sparks debate over India's education crisis
- Published
Despite having no training, or even a pair of running shoes, Ramabai Ranveer sprinted barefoot to victory in her first-ever race in August.
The 47-year-old widow had entered a 3km (1.86-mile) community run with a single goal: winning the prize money to help pay for her two daughters' education.
When she crossed the finish line first, Ramabai from Maharashtra in western India was delighted. The 3,000-rupee ($31; £23) prize would help her buy books and study materials for her daughters.
It was not much money. It would not come close to covering the cost of higher education in India, or even a course at the coaching centre where one of her daughters is preparing for a government recruitment examination.
But videos of her barefoot run spread rapidly on social media and in newspapers, striking a nerve as India's education system faces unusual scrutiny.
"Is it glory or a source of shame for us as a society?" one social media user remarked.
Soon, a woman who had never imagined becoming a runner was being held up as a symbol of something much bigger: the extraordinary lengths some Indian families go to in the hope that education will give their children a better life.
For Ramabai, the decision to run was simple.
"My elder daughter came to me early in the morning and said, 'Mummy, I want to take part in a running race'," she told BBC News Marathi from her home in Beed district.
"I asked her where it was and she said it was nearby. She told me that if she won the prize money, it would help with her education."
Her younger daughter, Arati, lives in Nanded and was struggling to afford books.
"I couldn't send her money to buy books and because of that she didn't speak to me on the phone for eight days," Ramabai said. "So I decided I had to run and win the race."
When her slippers kept slipping off, she removed them, gathered her sari and ran barefoot, pulling ahead to win the women's 30-60 category.
Her elder daughter, Pooja, also won a prize after finishing second in her age group. But she reserved her praise for her mother, describing her as courageous.
Ramabai has been the family's sole provider since her husband died in 2012.
"I did whatever work I could find," she said. "I picked soybeans and chickpeas in other people's fields. I also collected turmeric, processed it and sold it."
She left school when she was 13. Her daughters, she says, should have the opportunities she never had.
"I believe that as long as I am alive, I should do everything I can to give my daughters a good education."
That aspiration is shared by millions of Indian families. But getting a child through the education system and into a secure career can involve years of preparation, intense competition and, for many families, considerable expense.
One of Ramabai's daughters is preparing for police recruitment and the other for the civil services - two fiercely competitive routes into the security and social status associated with a coveted and secure government job.
Millions of young Indians spend years preparing for such examinations, often paying for coaching and study materials. But faith in the system has been shaken by repeated allegations of question-paper leaks and other irregularities.
The controversies have fed a wider sense of frustration among young Indians over education, jobs and the increasingly uncertain promise of a secure future. That frustration has also fuelled student-led protests and youth movements demanding changes to India's education system.
For families such as Ramabai's, education is something they make sacrifices for every day.
After her husband's death, she took whatever work she could find. She now cooks at the coaching centre where one of her daughters prepares for police recruitment.
Ramabai's run also drew the attention of authorities. Earlier this month, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant directed local officials to provide her with financial assistance of 50,000 rupees.
But Sukhadeo Thorat, a former chairman of the University Grants Commission, says the family's story points to broader structural challenges.
"If a woman is compelled to struggle so hard for her daughters' education, it shows that government education schemes are not reaching people adequately," he said. "Both the central and state governments run a variety of schemes. The problem is that implementation remains weak."
For Ramabai, though, the debate is secondary. What matters most is ensuring her daughters have a better future.
"I don't want them to go through the hardships I have faced," she said. "I don't want them to struggle through mud or travel under the scorching sun and rain. Whatever I have suffered, I don't want my daughters to suffer the same."

I was 8 years old, sitting at dinner with my grandparents, watching Gong Gong’s face turn bright red after a few sips of yellow wine. He loved making me laugh, and though he enjoyed his drinks, I think he liked my reaction even more.
Over a decade later, I would recognize the same alcohol flush reaction at parties and happy hours in some of my East Asian friends, and in myself. A few of these friends took histamine blockers like Pepcid AC before going out, hoping to hide the anticipated redness. Once, I watched someone keep drinking through the flush to prove they had a higher tolerance than what their body was communicating.
Most of us knew the reaction by its colloquial name: “Asian glow.” The phrase makes the phenomenon sound harmless, even playful.
It was not until I started medical school and attended an Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month event that I understood the science behind the reaction. After taking an ethanol patch test that turned positive, I learned that flushing is a common marker of reduced activity in mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2, or ALDH2, an enzyme involved in breaking down alcohol. This inherited deficiency affects an estimated one-third of people of East Asian descent and is exceedingly rare in other ethnicities. (Its associated redness may be mistaken for rosacea, which some studies suggest that drinking can raise the risk of developing, but rosacea is a separate condition involving chronic inflammation that affects all skin tones and types.)
There is no safe or healthy level of alcohol consumption for any given person. However, people with ALDH2 deficiency face both immediate discomfort and long-term cell damage and susceptibility to developing cancers of the upper digestive tract. Every clinician with East Asian patients should dedicate time to explaining the biological consequence behind what has long been dismissed as an aesthetic quirk.
When ALDH2 activity is reduced, acetaldehyde, a toxic intermediate in alcohol metabolism, accumulates in the body, dilating blood vessels, promoting histamine release, and causing facial redness, nausea, and rapid heartbeat. Acetaldehyde is also a DNA-damaging mutagen with implications in cell death pathways.
Not every person with deficiency presents the same way. People heterozygous for the most common ALDH2 reduced-function mutation, or ALDH2*2, have one active copy of the gene inherited from one parent and one variant copy inherited from the other. Their symptoms are not severe enough to discourage continued drinking, so they often keep going, even though their alcohol consumption is associated with a greater risk of cardiovascular disease, brain disorders, pancreatitis, and malignancies, particularly esophageal cancer. Homozygotes, who inherit two inactive copies of the gene, are less likely to develop cancer because they get such severe reactions to drinking that they avoid alcohol.
Although many East Asians recognize that they flush after drinking, they might not understand the associated risks. Health care providers should identify patients who experience alcohol flushing and counsel them on what it means for their health. Simple questionnaires about past flushing reactions, and in some settings ethanol patch testing like the one I took in medical school, have been shown to reveal ALDH2 deficiency with relatively high sensitivity and specificity. These tools can be incorporated into routine social history taking, alongside questions about alcohol use and family history.
For some groups of people, alcohol may hold special social and cultural meaning. For them, education should be widespread and, importantly, tailored and considerate.
Teenagers and young adults like me, for example, navigate significant peer pressure around drinking. My East Asian college friends deserved to know that taking antihistamines to hide flushing might reduce visible redness, but it would not lower acetaldehyde levels in their blood. They deserved to know that masking their body’s warning signals can make it easier to drink more than they otherwise would.
Recently, Nectar, a canned hard seltzer and cocktail brand, launched an AAPI Heritage Month campaign urging people to reframe the alcohol flush reaction as an “Asian Glow Up.” Though the intention may have been to turn a source of embarrassment into a viral beauty moment, the company’s failure to include a disclaimer mentioning the health indications pushes a narrative that encourages more drinking within an already vulnerable, under-informed population. An Instagram caption for the promo said: “Sharing drinks with friends before so you can share your glow with everyone after.”
Of course, young people, the target audience for ads like these, deserve to receive information about the reality behind “Asian glow” not as a reprimand, but as knowledge that preserves their agency and could help them make more informed choices.
On my medical school campus, many of the events promoting alcohol intolerance awareness are small focus groups led by my own peers, where attendees are more willing to trust and ask questions. A 2010 randomized study found that personalized ALDH2 genetic feedback reduced 30-day drinking frequency and quantity among Asian American young adults with one inactive ALDH2 allele; future studies may want to consider seeing what the results are if such feedback were given by peers.
A similar principle applies to counseling older adults and immigrant families. Telling an entire subset of the population simply to stop drinking risks being dismissive of the worlds that patients hail from. Alcohol serves as a social lubricant in certain East Asian cultures. To ignore that reality may deepen mistrust and gaps in culturally responsive care for Asians.
Providers can bridge this gap by partnering with trusted community centers and leaning on hospital advisory boards to host events that reinforce clinical counseling within familiar spaces. This year, I plan to host a service event inviting a Stanford physician to speak on ALDH2 deficiency after service one day at a nearby Chinese Baptist church.
When immigrant families like mine moved to the United States, they had to decide what to carry with them and what to leave behind. Some things were obvious: loved ones, places, languages. Others were quieter: recipes, rituals, and everyday habits, including drinks poured at mealtime, for guests, or before making a business deal. I grew up at the crossroads of their world and my American one, where blame or exclusion rarely led anywhere useful.
When I first learned about ALDH2 deficiency, I itched to call family and friends back home, some of whom do not have access to health insurance or a regular primary care provider, to tell them about it. But I had to approach it carefully: I’m not a doctor yet.
My father ended up having an ethanol patch test performed at a free clinic visit, while I was on FaceTime with him. Since hearing about ALDH2 deficiency, he has been drinking significantly less. He probably would not have responded as well to an order for him to abstain completely from alcohol or a lecture about acetaldehyde-induced DNA adducts and cross-linking in white blood cells.
My mother, too, may not need to know every molecular pathway by which acetaldehyde-induced oxidative stress impacts bone formation. But she deserves to know, in language that is accessible to her, that ALDH2 deficiency increases the risk of osteoporosis that she may already be more vulnerable to as a post-menopausal East Asian woman.
In my family, roles reverse as I grow older. Gong Gong, now 91, is the one I try to make laugh. Medicine, I am learning, is not only what I know. It is how gently and truthfully I offer what I know to the people I love, and to the strangers who one day trust me with their care.
Brian Zhang is a second-year M.D. student at the Stanford University School of Medicine, where he currently serves as student body president.

Large Typhoon Dujuan advanced northward over waters south of the Tokai region on Sunday morning and is expected to reach the Izu Islands and the Kanto region between Monday afternoon and early Tuesday morning before moving east, off the coast of the Tohoku region.
The Japan Meteorological Agency urged residents in the Izu Islands and Kanto, as well as Pacific coastal areas of Tokai and Tohoku, to remain on high alert for torrential rain, violent winds and high waves.
As of 9:00 a.m. Sunday, the year’s 25th named storm was moving northwest over waters south of the Tokai region at 10 kilometers per hour. It had an atmospheric pressure of 970 hectopascals at its center, with maximum sustained winds of 35 meters per second (126 kph) and maximum gusts of up to 50 meters per second.
The storm zone had wind speeds of at least 25 meters per second within a 110-kilometer radius, as well as a gale-force zone with winds of 15 meters per second or higher extending up to 800 kilometers to the northeast and 440 kilometers to the southwest.
In the 24 hours through 6:00 a.m. Monday, up to 250 millimeters of rainfall was forecast for the Izu Islands, 200 mm for Kanto and 150 mm for Tokai.
In the subsequent 24 hours through 6:00 a.m. Tuesday, rainfall could reach up to 400 mm in Kanto and the Izu Islands, 300 mm in the Tokai region and 200 mm in Tohoku.
With the typhoon coinciding with Japan’s Silver Week holidays through Wednesday, the storm is likely to disrupt transport networks and wreak havoc on cultural events.
The Tokyo Game Show, which began Thursday, announced the cancellation of Monday’s program, shortening the five-day video game extravaganza by a day.

Middle powers don’t have to wait for a Trump-Xi-Putin summit
Rather than waiting for great powers to reshape the world, middle powers can find agency by deepening connections between hubs of cooperation
3-MIN READ3-MIN
Hao Nan is a Susan Strange Associate Fellow with the Helsinki Geoeconomics Society, and a Nuclear Futures Fellow with Ploughshares Fund & Horizon 2045. 
The prospect of United States, Chinese and Russian leaders meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen this November has revived the Yalta analogy. Talk of a Trump-Xi-Putin summit – echoing the 1945 meeting that reshaped the world – surfaced during the first Trump term, and speculation returned last year with the 80th anniversary of the second world war.
No such meeting occurred. However, Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted the two presidents back-to-back in Beijing this May, and Moscow now says a three-way meeting in Shenzhen is possible. The symbolism would be potent: the three leaders around one table as the international order fragments. It would also evoke an enduring instinct – the belief that disorder is ultimately managed by a handful of great powers.
A literal 21st century Yalta remains improbable. Yet its underlying logic is increasingly visible as trade, technology, finance, infrastructure and development are organised through great-power bargains and rivalries.

US Rep. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) has proposed a law that would require Internet service providers and other network operators to block foreign piracy websites. Issa’s bill would help copyright holders obtain judicial blocking orders to be served to ISPs, domain name resolution services, and virtual private networks.
Issa, who is retiring from the House at the end of this year, is the latest in a string of Republican and Democratic lawmakers to propose a site-blocking regime that’s been sought by the Motion Picture Association (MPA). He submitted the bill this week, after indicating in a June 30 hearing that he planned to introduce site-blocking legislation.
“While millions of listings for copyright-infringing content are removed every day under [the] notice-and-takedown process set forth in the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, right-holders have raised concerns with the speed,” Issa said at the hearing. Issa asked, “Can we do it at the speed of sound? Can we do it at the speed of light? More importantly, in a 45-minute or sometimes a fraction of that live sports broadcast, can we do it soon enough to make it no longer profitable for those who pop up and sell their clandestine wares?”
Issa argued that online piracy helps fund terrorist groups and other criminal networks. Advocacy groups opposing his bill say it would impose a broad censorship regime and disrupt small businesses falsely accused of piracy.
“Rather than attacking the problem at its source by bringing the people running overseas piracy websites to court, Congress and its entertainment industry allies have decided to build out a sweeping infrastructure for censorship,” said Meredith Rose, senior policy counsel at Public Knowledge. “Site-blocking orders force any service provider, from residential broadband providers to global DNS resolvers, to disrupt traffic from targeted websites simply accused of copyright infringement.”

In mid-August, I moved out of the home I shared with my husband. My new temporary home is my parents' converted single-car garage, a roughly 150-square-foot casita.
I have asked for a divorce, although we haven't filed anything yet, so I'm still getting used to saying that word. My marriage had reached a point where I knew I needed to leave.
Friends offered me places to stay, but my parents are both in their early 70s, and I wanted to spend time with them. However, the idea of living together still scared me. Our relationship was especially rocky around the time I left home as a teenager, when I vowed I would never live with them again.
We've all changed and grown in the 20 years since. I've matured and gained perspective with age, and they've softened and become more introspective. The casita also offers more privacy than living in my old bedroom would. Still, I worried moving back home would return us to those old dynamics, but it's only been a gift.
Living in such a small space has challenges
The casita is about 10 feet by 15 feet, and an adult life does not fit neatly into that square footage. But in reality, it's enough. It holds a bunk bed, a sofa, a kitchenette, a dresser, and a small bathroom. There's even a little portable island for me to sit at, though I use it to hold books and paperwork at the moment. Laundry and cleaning supplies are accessible in the main house, but my trips over are most often to spend time with my parents rather than for practical reasons.
I'm still moving belongings out of my house and deciding what deserves a spot here. I've downsized my clothes and cleared out makeup and skincare products I wasn't using. My book collection is harder to cull; I love my books, and haven't figured out what to do about that yet.
The room was already furnished when I moved in, and we swapped a wardrobe for a more practical clothing rack; my mom donated the former, along with some shelves, to make space. I didn't even have to ask. My parents haven't imposed a laundry schedule, and they've made room for me without making me feel like an inconvenience.
I was especially worried about my chronic migraines during the move. I had arranged my previous home around them, including installing blackout curtains for days when the light is painful. Thankfully, my mother's decor already included blackout curtains, too. Sound and food smells can also be difficult during an attack, but the casita has an outside entrance and is separate enough that neither has been an issue. I'm only steps from my parents, but I still have privacy.
They aren't charging for rent or utilities while I figure out my finances during these transitional months. Hearing how much they love having me here is a balm as I go through this season.
My parents have supported me in ways I didn't expect
Most nights, we eat dinner together. I also sit with my dad while he feeds the neighborhood kittens that appear each day. They seem a little feral, but they love him. As soon as they hear his high-pitched call of "Kitty, kitty, kitty," they come running because they know it means food. I wouldn't see these ordinary moments if I had accepted a friend's spare room.
My parents are softer and more easygoing than I remember. They listen when I need to talk about my marriage. Recently, I saw that my husband had taken off his wedding ring when I came to visit our dog. I was still wearing mine out of respect for the fact that we are legally married and are only beginning this process. I asked for the divorce, but seeing his bare hand still hurt.
When I came home and cried, my parents listened. Growing up, they took care of all of my physical needs. Somehow, I feel more supported by them now. Their willingness to sit with me in the sadness means more than anything they could buy or fix.
The casita is giving me time to figure out what I want next
I see this as a transitional space. I don't know where I will live next or exactly how the divorce process will unfold. Moving to my childhood home has become one of the kindest parts of an extremely painful time.
I had stopped expecting my relationship with my parents to feel this different. Living here has shown me that people can change, on both sides, even after you've given up imagining another version of the relationship. That means so much more to me than square footage.

A survivor from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week has recounted his panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths.
Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) – a paramilitary group that works with police – initially blamed the deaths in Minna, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger, on a disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report seen by Agence France-Presse said preliminary information suggested that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible.
Dauda Shehu, a survivor from the cell, told journalists at a hospital on Friday: “We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well. All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.”
A video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men clad only in shorts, most of whom appeared to be teenagers, sprawled on the ground out in the open. Volunteers wearing gloves can be seen standing over the dead, while veiled women try to identify the bodies of their relatives. Voices shouting curses on those responsible can be heard in the background.
Protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in Minna. On Friday dozens of young people, including miners and their relatives, gathered near the NSCDC’s office in the city. Police cordoned off the area and attempted to disperse the protesters by firing teargas.
A Reuters witness saw security forces fire live rounds as protesters – some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles – called for justice. Some protesters tried to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighbourhood. “We are not thieves – we are simply seeking a way to make a living by mining,” Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters. At least one body lay on the streets. Soldiers and police officers patrolled Minna to try to restore order.
The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. Nigeria’s interior minister, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, ordered the immediate suspension of Niger state’s NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of a full investigation.
Niger state, which is Nigeria’s largest and more than twice the size of Belgium, is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most lured by gold.
Police and the NSCDC did not initially provide a precise number of deaths but the state governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago, later confirmed 37 people had died.
“It’s so sad, it’s so tragic,” he said, adding an inquiry into the deaths had already started work. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections due in January. The men were buried on Thursday, according to Islamic tradition, without any forensic investigations.
The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state is fuelling violence by criminal gangs, according to officials and experts. The gangs tax the miners and demand a cut from the extracted ore as a levy to allow them access to the pits.
Most of the illegally mined gold is smuggled to the United Arab Emirates, where it is laundered into the global supply chain in Europe, the US, Asia and South Africa, according to a 2024 Swissaid report.
Apart from gold, the state of Niger sits on deposits of other minerals including tantalite, copper and lithium, which are in strong demand for use in electric vehicles and clean energy technology.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

MUMBAI: A CCTV footage showed a speeding BMW crashing through the barrier on Mumbai's Coastal Road and plunging off a bridge into an under-construction parking site early on Sunday, killing three students and critically injuring another.
The luxury car was seen travelling at high speed before it fell from the bridge and crash-landed at the construction site. The vehicle was heavily damaged.
Police suspect the driver allegedly failed to negotiate a turn near Lotus Jetty, opposite Lala Lajpatrai College.
"The car was at a high speed. The driver couldn't understand the turn and crashed into the outer railing, following which the car plunged from the bridge," police said.
The incident occurred at around 5.20am when the BMW was travelling from Marine Drive towards Haji Ali.
All four occupants were rushed to the nearby civic-run Nair Hospital, where three were declared dead.
The deceased were identified as Shanaya Gajjal, 21, Aditya Jakasania, 20, and Dhirya Seth, 17.
The fourth occupant, an unidentified man aged around 20, sustained severe injuries and was admitted to the hospital's trauma ward in critical condition, police said.
Image Credit: Sanjay Hadkar/TNN
Shanaya Gajjal and Aditya Jakasania were students of a management college in Juhu, while Dhirya Seth studied at a college in Kurla, police said.
All four students were originally from Ahmedabad, according to police. Police said the BMW belonged to Gajjal's family.
Image Credit: Sanjay Hadkar/TNN
The Mumbai Coastal Road is a 10.58-km high-speed freeway connecting Marine Drive in south Mumbai to the Worli end of the Bandra-Worli Sea Link.

We recently shared a detailed guide on how to build Android apps using Google Antigravity. That approach is best for someone who wants an affordable way to build AI apps that work.
Current Google models in Antigravity offer way better rate limits than models from ChatGPT or Claude. However, Gemini isn’t the best for building advanced AI apps or if you want to include any other advanced features in your app.
For advanced apps, using Claude or ChatGPT Codex is the most reliable option. In this guide, you will learn how to build Android apps using Codex. OpenAI’s ChatGPT models in Codex are not free; you need a minimum ChatGPT Plus subscription to access top models. Also, the rate limits are very poor, which you can easily exhaust if you play with them for some time.
However, these models are way more powerful and currently among the leading frontier models. Also, thanks to the different connections, plugins, and MCP servers, the process of building Android apps using Codex is more convenient and takes fewer steps compared to Google Antigravity. In this guide, you will learn how to build Android apps using OpenAI Codex.
Table of Contents
Prerequisites
To build an Android app in Codex, you need:
- ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription (which you can get from here)
- An Android app with Expo Go installed – Download the Expo Go app
- An Android phone
- A free account on supabase.com – Sign up here
- A free account on expo.dev
Once done, you can follow the process below to build Android apps using OpenAI Codex.
Set Up Codex
Step 1: First, download and install the ChatGPT app on your Mac or Windows. It is also available for Linux.
Step 2: Once installed, sign up with your ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription account.
Step 3: Once done, switch to Codex.
Step 4: Now tap on New chat, and from here, tap on Choose Folder.
Step 5: Now, you can create a new folder or use the existing folder, which stores all your app files.
Create Your App
Step 1: Now, enter the following prompt. You can edit the prompt to include your own prompt. For this guide, iam building a simple Pomorodo app.
Build a simple Pomodoro timer app using Expo and TypeScript.
The app should let users start, pause, resume, reset, and skip Pomodoro sessions. Include focus, short break, and long break modes. Show the remaining time clearly, track completed focus sessions, and save the timer settings and session history locally using SQLite.
Create a clean, polished mobile UI that works well on Android. Do not create an Android build yet. First, implement the app, check for errors, and explain how I can preview it using Expo Go.
Step 2: Now, in the model selector, select GPT-5.6 Sol or GPT-6 Astra.
In this guide, we are building a simple Pomodoro timer application that keeps track of your focus and how much time you have been distracted.
The latest Codex GPT-6 Astra model is very good at frontend development. Even if you haven’t included reference images of the app UI, since it is a simple app, it can generate a very reliable UI based on the prompt.
However, if you want something unique that is personalized to yourself, I highly recommend submitting UI references. It will generate exactly what you are looking for, including the font options that you used while designing the app. You can use Google Stitch to generate UI.
Design the UI With Google Stitch (Optional)
You can use Google Stitch for designing the UI. It is very similar to Figma, but more AI-focused: it lets you generate UI through AI prompts and also lets you customize with basic tools.
We created a detailed course on how you can create UI designs using Google Stitch, with 12+ videos guiding you through all the core features of Google Stitch.
If you want to quickly create UI designs using Google Stitch, you can go to stitch.withgoogle.com and follow these steps:
Step 1: Paste your prompt (for whatever your app is) into the prompt area.
Step 2: Wait for Google Stitch to generate your UI designs.
Step 3: Tap on the prototype icon at the top to check the preview.
Step 4: Export and save it as a zip file.
Step 5: To upload the references to the Codex file in the entry box, after entering the prompt, you can click on the plus icon and select Files and folders. From here, you can attach the UI reference images (Remember you need to extract the folder).
You can attach up to 10 images, which is more than enough for a basic or even a medium-level app with all those screens.
Preview the App on Your Phone
Step 1: Wait for Codex to generate the full design in the Expo app, and then you can enter the prompt so that it can show you a preview of the app. You can install the Expo Go app on your Android phone. Open the app and scan the QR code generated by Codex after following these steps.
Step 2: Carefully review everything and ensure that everything works.
Step 3: Once finished, enter this prompt to preview the app on your mobile. If it asks you to run the terminal code, you can ask GPT to run the code for you.
GPT models are often known for lying: even though something isn’t finished, it confidently mentions that it has finished or fixed the issue. I highly recommend you verify each and every output.
Build the Android App

Thousands of patients in India are diagnosed with melanoma, a type of skin cancer, each year. While melanoma is far less common here than in Western populations, it is far from rare and the way it presents in our patient population makes it uniquely difficult to detect early. Too many patients come to us when the disease is already advanced, precisely at a time when treatment options have never been more powerful or more personalised. This contrast between available therapies and the stage at which patients are diagnosed defines one of the most pressing challenges in melanoma care in India today.
Why melanoma gets missed
The warning signs most people associate with skin cancer come from research developed for fairer-skinned populations, where melanoma tends to appear on sun-exposed areas as an irregular or darkening mole. That picture does not reflect what clinicians see in India.
Melanoma here, most commonly presents on the soles of the feet or beneath the nails, sites that are rarely examined and even more rarely associated with cancer. This condition is called acral lentiginous melanoma, a subtype that accounts for 35 to 60% of cases in dark-skinned individuals. Such lesions are frequently mistaken for bruises, fungal infections, or diabetic ulcers, and by the time a biopsy is taken, the disease has often progressed.
Mucosal melanomas, a rare type of cancer that starts in the mucous membranes, are highly aggressive with a very low chance of recovery and produce few early warning signs. Most are diagnosed only after spread has occurred.
Any pigmented lesion that changes or persists, wherever it appears on the body, deserves investigation rather than reassurance.
A decade of transformation
When I began my oncology career, managing advanced melanoma meant offering patients limited and rarely durable options. That has fortunately changed significantly.
The foundational shift came from James Allison and Tasuku Honjo, whose discoveries on CTLA-4 and PD-1 earned them the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Their research established the principle of immune-checkpoint blockade: rather than attacking a tumour directly, we can sometimes release the biological brakes that stop the patient’s own immune system from doing so. The results can be extraordinary. Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter was diagnosed at 91 with melanoma that had spread to his liver and brain. Surgical resection of liver disease, stereotactic radiation for the brain, and immunotherapy with the checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab produced a durable remission, and he lived to 100.
Precision medicine has reshaped the approach in parallel. Some melanomas carry specific mutations, particularly in the BRAF pathway, that can be directly targeted with molecularly designed therapies. This is where next-generation sequencing, or NGS, becomes critical. In simple terms, it reads the genetic blueprint of a patient’s tumour and identifies the alterations that should guide treatment, turning what was once a single clinical decision into a detailed, individualised process.
The melanoma story is not over; it is only becoming more exciting. TIL therapy takes tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, expands them in the laboratory, and reinfuses them in far greater numbers, a step toward truly personalised cellular treatment. In August 2026, intismeran, a personalised mRNA vaccine built from the patient’s own tumour sequence, was combined with pembrolizumab in high-risk melanoma patients after surgery. The results were striking: a significant reduction in recurrence compared with pembrolizumab alone, making it the first positive late-stage trial of a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine, though survival data remain pending.
What still needs to change
All of these advances deliver their best results when treatment begins early. The more sophisticated our therapies become, the more clearly we see that they work best before the disease has spread. In India, awareness and referral gaps continue to push diagnosis toward advanced stages.
Recalibrating public health messaging to reflect how melanoma actually presents in Indian patients is a start. Faster pathways from primary care to specialist centres matter equally. More fundamentally, India needs a national melanoma registry, stronger epidemiological and genomic data, more clinical trials in Indian patients, and deeper international collaboration. The advances of the past decade are genuinely extraordinary. Whether they reach the patients who need them comes down to one thing: a diagnosis early enough to act on.
(Prof. Jyoti Bajpai is director – medical precision immuno-oncology, Apollo Hospitals, Mumbai & Western Zone. drjyoti_ba@apollohospitals.com)

Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
- Published
US President Donald Trump has announced that he will form an "AI Force" and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar amid warnings about the emergent technology.
In a social media post on Saturday, he said his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth" of the industry, and pushed back against calls to slow down the development of AI until better safeguards are put in place.
His post came as a slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action on the technology's development.
Trump offered no details or a timeline for his plan.
- Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings 
  - Published3 days ago
"AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP," he said on social media, adding that he wants the US to continue leading China in AI.
AI now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech, and it is expected to be discussed when Trump meets President Xi Jinping next week.
Meanwhile, Trump said his administration would use the existing criminal and civil justice system to target any bad actors using the AI.
He also repeated comments that criticism and concerns around the potential dangers of AI are a "hoax".
Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells in recent weeks.
Major AI companies have been racing to develop better systems, including creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans.
AI titans Anthropic, OpenAI and Google - the tech companies behind Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, respectively - have also disclosed instances of security breaches or incidents in which their chatbots were used for "malicious activity".
Anthropic head Dario Amodei recently called for AI development to slow down and proposed industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.
Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI have both said they agree with his recommendations.
Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told BBC that a "kill switch" that can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry.
The warnings have prompted US lawmakers to propose legislation around the technology but Altman suggested this week that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the new tech and how to regulate it. He said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep it safe.
"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman told a conference in San Francisco.
In the UK, MPs across parties and peers have identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence and have argued that existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth.
The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) has published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.

White House bars CNN, MS Now and Politico reporters after Trump ban
All three news outlets separately said their teams’ press passes were confiscated on Saturday morning
The White House on Saturday denied access to journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico, following through with US President Donald Trump’s announcement that he would ban them from the building’s grounds.
All three news outlets separately said their teams’ press passes were confiscated on Saturday morning when their journalists went to the White House.
They have signalled that they may contest the ban on the grounds that it conflicts with the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press.
A CNN statement on Saturday called the ban “an illegal assault” on its constitutional right to do journalism without interference from the government. In separate statements, MS Now and Politico said they would “defend our First Amendment rights”.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.
