West Bank families led by women face greater displacement risks, OCHA says
Due to surging Israeli settler violence, West Bank families headed by women are more likely to be displaced and more likely to have chronic illness among household members compared with those headed by men, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
The agency estimates that some 83,000 households (one in eight families in the West Bank) are headed by women.
Nearly nine in 10 women interviewed who are heads of their households stated that checkpoints make travel feel unsafe, and more than half said movement restrictions are blocking access to their livelihoods.
A UN Women’s analysis of a survey, among women who are formally recognised as household heads, notes that 82 per cent are responsible for managing household income, 77 per cent are responsible for childcare 75 per cent make all decisions about household members’ safety and 65 per cent handle aid registration alone.

Quick Answer
Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, could give the stagnant foldable market a much-needed push. It may not reinvent the category, but Apple’s reach, software focus, and mainstream appeal could make foldables far more popular.
September is here and so are the new iPhones. This year at Apple’s Surprise and Shine event, the Cupertino tech giant came with a number of changes, not just in terms of devices but in terms of management too. There was a new CEO – it was John Ternus’ first event as CEO – as well as new Apple Watches, AirPods and, of course, new iPhones too.
The Duo dominates the new iPhones
Even though Apple showcases a number of products during its September event, it is mainly the iPhones that the world waits for. And even in iPhones, it is usually the Pro and Pro Max iPhones that make the headlines (barring the odd occasion when the Air popped up). The plain iPhones are usually pushed to the sidelines and launched as the more “economical”, “affordable” iPhones whose price tags and generally minor upgrades in specs and design are the only things that get them any attention.
For the longest time, we have been feeling for the plain iPhones because they are quite capable and bring in big sales numbers (especially in markets like India, where they are bestsellers) and yet do not get the hype they deserve. Well, this time around, the iPhone Pro and the Pro Max got the taste of this bitter medicine. The two smartphones had to fold (pun intended) and give up all their headline space for the more expensive, exclusive, and most different iPhone since the inception of the original iPhone: the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone.
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has finally marked its official entry in the world of foldables. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 299,900 in India ($1,999 in the US), which has naturally inspired a tsunami of reinvented kidney jokes and all sorts of comparisons about all that you can buy for that price. It has also got many competing brands scoffing at Apple’s very late attempt at foldables, calling the Duo a “copy”. While some of the criticism and cynicism around the Duo is valid, we think a foldable phone from Apple is just what the foldable market needed to make foldables mainstream. Not because the Duo is an out-of-the-tech-world, never-seen-before, and extraordinary folding smartphone (hey, we haven’t reviewed it yet), but for much simpler reasons.
Ghost of foldables past: A story mainly of Samsung
Samsung is considered by many to be the modern foldable phone pioneer. It was the trailblazer that was responsible for actually bringing in foldable phones that not only landed on the tech moon but also managed to stick around for seven2 years – Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold arrived in 2019, followed by the Galaxy Z Flip in 2020. The brand did not really have a working blueprint that they could have used back then to have perfected their foldables and technology around it, but it enjoyed an early mover’s advantage in the segment and managed to create a very strong reputation for itself. They built a strong rapport with the consumers that none of the other brands could develop, even after launching just as good, just as powerful foldable smartphones.
Following Samsung’s start, many leading tech brands have been surfing the foldable wave for a while now. The OG flip phone master, Motorola; the Android originator Google; the flagship killer OnePlus; the Chinese Apple, Xiaomi; Vivo, Oppo, and others have created foldables with their own touches and twists. Huawei has gone one step further and has launched a tri-fold – a smartphone that folds twice. But even after all this effort, none of them could really be a standout foldable smartphone brand. Only Samsung did.
But in spite of Samsung’s consistency and the efforts of other brands, foldable smartphones have not become mainstream. They have never really made impressive numbers or become popular/common devices. Yes, most of them come with premium price tags, but even those that are relatively affordable – mostly flips or budget foldables (yes, there are some) – have not gained the kind of traction that had been expected. The foldable revolution that many had predicted seemed to have stalled, and apart from a few devices (mainly from Samsung), growth was largely limited.
Apple and the tech snowball effect… could it come to foldables?
Now Apple has stepped into the foldable ring, and while there are many contenders in it already, we think the Cupertino tech giant might get the buzz around foldables going. It has been quite a trend setter in the tech world, and is identified with premium innovation. Features, functions, and devices that existed long before Apple “reinvented” them suddenly became popular once they started shipping with an Apple logo and Apple’s own unique take on them. They not only became mainstream but also often became a common sight on products from other brands as well. Touchscreen phones, apps and app stores, music stores, portrait mode, notches (Dynamic Island), are just some of the products that Apple did not invent, but made a part of
everyday technology.
Of course, every time this happens, the Internet is flooded with techies pointing out how the particular feature or product has been around for years and how Apple is not really innovating or, rather, thinking differently (Apple’s very tagline). Despite all the chatter and gossip around this topic, somehow the feature picks up momentum, and soon enough the world gets interested in knowing how it works and then owning a device that lets them use it. This initiates a snowball effect of sorts, which leads to that feature or device becoming extremely popular.
We will keep it simple: quite often, it basically takes an Apple device or feature to grab mainstream attention. It happened with GUI, MP3 players, ultra-portable notebooks, touchscreen phones, tablets, TWS, smartwatches, and we think it could happen with foldables too. The Duo has the potential to put the seemingly jammed foldable wheels in motion.
It is important to remember that it is not like whatever Apple does just becomes a hit automatically. The brand has a loyal following, but it has released many features, devices, and functions that did not strike a chord with consumers and have faded away. The Apple Vision Pro, HomePod, iPhone Mini and iPhone Plus, the Touch Bar on the Mac…Apple’s failure list is quite long. It may be one of the most successful tech brands in history, but Apple is no tech Midas – there is no real guarantee that the iPhone Duo would be an absolute hit. The stakes are quite high for the Duo, especially given its price tag (which is even higher in India).
It has got the hype, but what would make the Duo click?
Unlike Samsung, Apple has not had to reinvent the foldable wheel. It has had time to read, research, develop, try, and make mistakes, and fix them all, even while observing the efforts of other tech brands. And while the Duo’s design and specs, and indeed, many of its features, are nothing we have not seen before, these are not areas where Apple differentiates itself from the regular crowd. The iPhone Duo needs to bring Apple’s attention to detail when it comes to user experience, and software tuned exactly to suit the needs and capabilities of the device it supports.
We have not yet had the pleasure (or pain) to experience the device but so far, from the looks and the videos on the Internet, we can tell you there are a few things we love about the iPhone Duo – the TouchID on the side (yes, we actually love it), the vertical tool bar for easy access, the matte display layer which makes the crease largely invisible, and yes, of course, the animation that blurs out the side/front screen when the phone is being opened or folded. But it’s not all pink skies and red roses. We are not very convinced by the asymmetrical shape of the device, the insanely high price tag, and, well, even the name. Duo? Really, Apple? We are also really curious about how Apple has worked on apps for the cover display as well as the inner ones.
But these are early days. The iPhone Duo is more than a month away, and we are sure Apple will fine-tune it even further before releasing it. In the meantime, we expect the kidney jokes to continue and even gather momentum, but on the flip side, curiosity will also grow, as we are sure more will be revealed about the device and its features and functions.
The iPhone Duo has generated more buzz about the foldables in a few months than other players in the field got in years, but it is all going to boil down to how well and how differently it works from other foldables. Given the interest levels around it, it might just prove to be the elixir that foldables need.

Dr. Reddy's Laboratories on Friday (September 18, 2026) entered into an exclusive distribution agreement with Takeda Pharmaceutical Company to promote and distribute its dengue vaccine, QDENGA, in India's private market for pediatric and adult vaccination.
Subject to local regulatory processes, the vaccine is expected to be available in the first half of 2027. The vaccine received marketing authorisation by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) in July 2026 for individuals aged 4-60 years, Dr. Reddy's said in a press release.
QDENGA, a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine, aims to strengthen dengue prevention and management by providing broad immune coverage across all four circulating dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4). Administered as a two-dose regimen given three months apart, it is India's first approved dengue vaccine, according to the release.
While Dr. Reddy's will exclusively manage private-market distribution, disease awareness, and healthcare professional engagement, Takeda will retain rights for the public market, legal ownership, and overall medical and brand oversight, it said.
"As the second-largest vaccine player in India, we believe the introduction of India's first approved dengue vaccine is an important development for the country's healthcare landscape," said M. V. Ramana, CEO, Global Generics, Dr. Reddy's Laboratories.
"Through our collaboration with Takeda, we look forward to making QDENGA available to eligible individuals and contributing to efforts aimed at addressing the country's dengue burden," Mr. Ramana said.
Dr. Mahender Nayak, Head of Intercontinental Markets, International Business Unit, Takeda, noted, "In parallel, our private-market collaboration with Dr. Reddy's will help enable timely private-market access for eligible individuals once QDENGA becomes available in India." Approved in 43 countries, QDENGA has seen over 32 million doses distributed globally.

Canadian language school files for bankruptcy, leaving students stranded
Canada's largest language school cancelled classes abruptly Friday, leaving 1,300 students in limbo
Canada's largest private language school filed for bankruptcy on Friday, leaving current and incoming students in limbo.
A notice posted to the International Language Academy of Canada's (ILAC) website says it has ceased operations effective immediately, noting it "no longer has the financial resources necessary to continue operating."
ILAC operated in Vancouver and Toronto, offering a variety of programs including short-term English-language courses, a high school program, and college programs lasting up to two years.
"I’m just really confused and lost," said incoming student José Carlos Chavez, speaking from Guadalajara, Mexico, on Saturday.
Chavez, who works in Mexico as a professional photographer, was supposed to be starting a two-year-long marketing program at ILAC in mid-October.
His flight to Vancouver is booked for next week.
Chavez says he found out the news from social media. Despite reaching out to the school, he says he has not yet heard back from ILAC directly.
According to receipts Chavez provided to CBC News, he has paid the school almost $14,000 in tuition fees.
He will also have to pay a penalty if he cancels his Vancouver apartment lease now — which will cost him around $1,800.
"Stressed, confused, I don’t know what’s going to happen," said Chavez.
Chavez worries he may have to go into debt and won’t be able to afford studying elsewhere if he doesn’t receive a refund.
"I just hope that the school can ... help me in any possible way," he said.
The school's notice says it has faced financial challenges over the past three years due to "significant regulatory changes affecting the sector."
Since the federal government started tightening the intake cap on international student permit applications, education providers have been challenged by funding issues.
The number of new students arriving in Canada with study permits has dropped from roughly 293,000 in 2024 to 115,000 in 2025. Between January and July this year, only about 28,000 new students came to Canada with study permits.
Languages Canada, the national language education association that represents and accredits language programs, said the school has 1,362 students.
"The sudden and disorderly closure of Canada’s largest language school is a shock to everyone," said a Saturday statement from the organization’s executive director Gonzalo Peralta.
The statement said Languages Canada will work over the weekend to place current students in alternate equivalent programs.
Incoming students face the unknown
Beatriz Gil runs Truly Canadian Education, a company based in Metro Vancouver that connects international students to Canadian schooling.
She has dozens of clients currently enrolled in ILAC programs in Vancouver and Toronto. For both students and staff, she says Friday was a confusing and upsetting day.
"We were in shock," Gil said, noting she got a call from an ILAC staff member in tears.
Gil said those who were studying at the ILAC high school in Vancouver were asked to take their items and leave the building on Friday.
"They were outside the school with all their belongings asking what’s going on?" she said.
She said their team is working with Languages Canada to transfer current students to other institutions in Vancouver and Toronto.
But for incoming students like Chavez, Gil says she does not know what will happen.
Gil said she is working with one incoming student who had just made her tuition payment to the institution on Thursday — the day before it declared bankruptcy.
"It’s very, very sad for all of them," she said.
ILAC's closure comes just five days after the closure of EC English, a major international English-language school that had operations in Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal.
"Indeed, there have been closures of many language programs around the world in the last few years," said Language Canada's statement on the ILAC closure.

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.
The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America. It was found in Bolivia’s lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 18in (46cm) long and weighs about 3lbs (1.4kg), making it smaller than the average domestic cat.
Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.
“Its fur is light brown ... with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.
Little is yet known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
Tiger cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.
Referring to the new species, Lescroart said: “Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.”
One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives in the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.
Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?”
The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.
“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said.
Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4m years ago.
“The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.
The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas, naming it Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca empire that included the area it inhabits.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) red list tracking the status of species currently treats tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species with declining populations.
The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could be considered endangered when assessed on their own.
The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute in the Yungas, one of the region’s most threatened ecosystems.
The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales-Ascarrunz added.
“Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats ... there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”

After Donald Trump signed the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026” into law, Union Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh on Saturday said India considers the tariffs being imposed “unfair” and asserted that New Delhi is making its decisions independently, without pressure from any other country. Singh asserted that energy security remains a key priority for India and that the country will source energy from locations offering commercially viable and economical options for its people. The legislation, signed by Trump on September 18, gives the US president powers to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries such as India and China that continue to purchase Russian oil and gas. Quick answers to key questions The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 is a US law that authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries, including India and China, that purchase Russian oil and gas, aiming to penalize Moscow for its ongoing war in Ukraine. India considers the US tariffs unfair because they impose pressure on its energy sourcing decisions. The Indian government asserts that it prioritizes energy security and will seek commercially viable sources independently of foreign influence. The US tariffs could significantly impact India's energy imports by increasing costs and disrupting supply, particularly since Russian oil accounts for a large portion of India's crude imports amid reduced alternatives due to issues in other regions. India is not obligated to comply with US sanctions and has indicated it will continue sourcing Russian oil as necessary for its energy security, depending on market dynamics and the need to maintain stable supplies for its population. India is diversifying its energy sources and has committed to sourcing energy from economically viable locations, while also planning to continue importing Russian crude despite potential US tariffs that may increase costs. "We always say that these tariffs that are being imposed are very unfair. And we are not under the pressure of any country. Energy is a very primary concern of ours. And wherever we find commercially viable, economical energy sources for our country and our people, we will take energy from there," Singh told ANI. He said the government's foremost concern is the welfare of India's 140 crore people and that it will take all necessary measures to safeguard their interests while maintaining the country's strength and stability. "The priority of the country of India and our government is our people, our people of 140 crores. We will take every step which is necessary for the convenience of our people. We will take every strong step for the strength and stability of our country, our population of 140 crores. We have our own independent foreign policy. We will not follow any country based on what our country is doing. We will do whatever is good for our country," Singh said. The new US law expands measures against Russian officials, financial institutions, defence-linked networks and the country's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships accused of transporting energy while bypassing Western restrictions. It also extends the Iran Sanctions Act for another five years. The legislation cleared the US Senate in August with an 86-11 vote before passing the House of Representatives 262-159 earlier this week. It was named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who had been a prominent supporter of the measure. “On Friday, September 18, 2026, the President signed into law:H.R. 5334, the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” which authorizes and expands statutory sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions on Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran,” the White House mentioned. One of the key provisions gives the US President authority to impose targeted tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, along with countries accused of helping Moscow evade oil-related sanctions. The provision could have implications for India and China, both major purchasers of Russian crude. It establishes a legal mechanism for imposing tariffs on imports from countries that continue certain purchases of Russian energy. The President can also waive the measures under specified circumstances, including by certifying to Congress that granting a waiver is in the national interest. When a woman has difficulty conceiving or experiences repeated pregnancy loss, the focus often turns to the uterus, the quality of the embryos or ovarian reserve. However, hormones, too, can play an important role, and one hormone that deserves attention is prolactin.
Prolactin is produced by the pituitary gland and is best known for its role in breast milk production. Its levels naturally rise during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Outside these periods, however, persistently elevated prolactin, a condition known as hyperprolactinaemia, can interfere with normal reproductive function.
The symptoms are not always obvious. Some women may have irregular or absent periods, difficulty conceiving or an unexpected milky discharge from the breasts. Others may have no noticeable symptoms at all.
Prolactin and fertility
Reproductive hormones work as a closely connected system. Prolactin is part of this system, and when its levels remain elevated, it can interfere with the hormonal signals required for ovulation.
High prolactin can suppress the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the brain. This can subsequently affect Luteinising Hormone (LH) and Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH), which are involved in follicle development and ovulation. As a result, some women may ovulate irregularly or stop ovulating altogether. Their periods may become longer, unpredictable or absent, making conception more difficult.
Prolactin also interacts with reproductive hormones after ovulation. This is one reason why its possible role in the early stages of pregnancy has attracted clinical attention, although the relationship is more complex than simply linking one abnormal hormone level to pregnancy loss.
The link to repeated pregnancy loss
The relationship between elevated prolactin and recurrent pregnancy loss is documented in clinical literature but described with appropriate caution. A 2025 guideline published in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada found that elevated prolactin is associated with pregnancy loss and may contribute to luteal phase deficiency. The guideline recommends prolactin testing in women with recurrent pregnancy loss who also present with irregular periods or unexplained breast discharge.
The clinical nuance here is important. Hyperprolactinaemia is one contributing factor among several more established causes of recurrent pregnancy loss, such as chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo, uterine structural issues, antiphospholipid syndrome, and thyroid dysfunction. This does not reduce the clinical relevance of elevated prolactin, but it does mean that a single elevated test result should not be treated as the explanation before other causes have been assessed. The 2025 guideline is explicit on this: elevated prolactin should be confirmed through repeat testing before any treatment is initiated, and thyroid function should be checked first, as hypothyroidism can independently raise prolactin levels.
The connection with PMOS
Among women with PMOS, earlier known as PCOS, mildly elevated prolactin levels are occasionally found alongside the more typical hormonal pattern of the condition. Some research has found a mean hyperprolactinaemia prevalence of 11.9% in women with PMOS, though the range across studies is wide, reflecting how variable the relationship is across different populations and diagnostic thresholds. Hyperprolactinaemia is not considered a clinical manifestation of PMOS, and the two conditions are assessed and managed independently.
Why the elevation
The causes of elevated prolactin are varied. A benign, prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour called a prolactinoma is among the more significant causes and is identified through an MRI when prolactin levels are substantially elevated. Hypothyroidism, certain medications including antipsychotics and some antihypertensives, and occasionally stress or intensive exercise can also raise prolactin levels transiently. This is why repeat testing under standardised conditions such as fasting and avoiding physical stress before the blood draw, is important before a diagnosis of hyperprolactinaemia is established.
When true hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed, dopamine agonist medications such as cabergoline or bromocriptine are effective at normalising prolactin levels in most cases. Research has demonstrated successful restoration of ovulation and term pregnancy outcomes in women with hyperprolactinaemia following dopamine agonist therapy, including in cases involving pituitary tumours. The condition, when properly identified and treated, is one of the more manageable contributors to fertility challenges.
What women should know
For women experiencing recurrent pregnancy loss or difficulty conceiving, prolactin testing is a reasonable part of a comprehensive hormonal evaluation. The results need to be interpreted alongside thyroid function, ovarian reserve, and a full assessment of both partners, because the factors that influence reproductive outcomes are rarely operating in isolation.
(Dr. Prachi Benara is a fertility specialist at Birla Fertility and IVF, Gurgaon. prachi.benara@birlafertility.com)

Hot dogs feel the economic bite during Chile’s cost of living crisis
Workers also say wages aren’t keeping pace with inflation
Around the Plaza de Armas in central Santiago, lunchtime businesses are serving up the "completo", long considered one of Chile’s most egalitarian dishes.
For decades, this local variation of the hot dog offered affordable food to people of all social backgrounds. Yet as economic stagnation deepens and living costs climb, even this staple street snack is becoming significantly more expensive.
"Not long ago, I used to pay 2,500 pesos ($2.60) for a completo," said Antonia Bravo, a 21-year-old student. "Now, they cost 3,500 or 4,000 pesos ($3.60 or $4.10)."
Official figures published this month show the country stands on the verge of recession after experiencing two consecutive quarters of negative growth. Unemployment has reached 9.5 per cent — its highest point in five years — while annual inflation accelerated to 4.1 per cent over the past year, fuelled by rising food and transport costs.
This subdued economic performance led Chile's Central Bank to lower its 2026 GDP growth estimate from 1 per cent –1.75 per cent to between 0.25 per cent–0.75 per cent.
Addressing a media briefing last week, Central Bank President Rosanna Costa cautioned: "We cannot rule out the possibility that the current weakness may prove more persistent than anticipated."
Eating out has become a luxury for many
The completo was born in one of those small shops in downtown Santiago in the early 1930s. Chile’s take on the hot dog features a sausage topped with sauerkraut, tomato and homemade potato-based mayonnaise. Avocado and other ingredients were added over time, turning it into a complete meal. Hence its name, “completo.”
“Back then, people weren’t well-off; they didn’t have many resources and would come here for completos,” said Guillermo Cid, manager of the restaurant credited with creating the dish. “It is the same today. Instead of sitting down for a full meal, many people just stop by for a completo."
Chile's monthly basic food basket cost just under $100 in August, up 5 per cent from a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Social Development. The country's monthly minimum wage is about $580. Chile has also faced rising fuel prices resulting from the U.S.-Iran war.
Together, these pressures "feed into inflation and erode household purchasing power,” creating a scenario where “confidence... deteriorates,” the Central Bank president said.
As the cost of living rises and household budgets tighten, Chileans are looking for ways to stretch their incomes by cutting spending on key areas, including food.
“The price of basic products just keeps going up and up,” said Mauricio Aravena, a 30-year-old teacher. “Eating out has always been somewhat of a luxury, but now even more so.”
Even a get-together with friends has become synonymous with extravagance.
“Compared to last year, when my friends and I could plan more outings, these days it’s more about staying in and cooking at home,” said Tabata Martinich, 31, also a teacher. “You have to watch your spending more closely; everything is way more expensive.”
Workers also say wages aren’t keeping pace with inflation.
“Bills are more expensive overall, and pay raises aren’t keeping up with those costs,” Aravena added. “We are lagging about five years behind.”
Frustration is on the rise
Since taking office in March, President José Antonio Kast has pursued an economic recovery agenda aimed at boosting investment and employment, as Chile's economy and labor market weaken. His challenge is ensuring that these reforms not only translate into stronger economic indicators but also reach citizens’ pockets.
“Expectations are turning into frustration,” analyst Guillermo Holzmann said. “Despite progress in approving major projects, the investments have not materialized at the pace needed.”
Kast recently acknowledged the situation, saying Chile is “facing higher inflation than expected and lower growth than projected.”
At a meeting Tuesday with ministers and leaders of parties in the ruling coalition, Kast instructed his team to draft a “labor emergency plan” that should be presented in the coming weeks — although he did not provide details.
The plan follows several other measures announced recently — including the economic and tax overhaul, which was approved by Congress but has yet to be ratified as the Constitutional Court reviews complaints filed by opposition parties.
The proposed reform includes initiatives such as tax cuts for large corporations, the elimination of double taxation to encourage more private investment, and the implementation of financial compensation for companies whose projects are rejected due to environmental concerns. It also establishes the “right to financial oblivion” for old debts in new credit assessments and bans the charging of interest on interest.
Holzmann said the worsening economic conditions are pushing the Kast administration to race against the clock to translate medium- and long-term initiatives into concrete actions that have a direct impact on citizens’ pockets. “Making ends meet is becoming increasingly difficult,” he said.
“There is a disconnect between consumers’ income levels and the prices of products in stores,” he added. “Social frustration is the primary breeding ground for unrest in a country.”

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.
Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”
The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”
Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.
Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.
Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

As Europe warms, Italy sees West Nile virus spread
Italian health authorities see evidence that rising temperatures and longer warm seasons are helping mosquitoes spread West Nile virus across a wider area, during more months of the year.
More than 650 infections have been reported in Italy so far this year, accounting for roughly half of all cases recorded in Europe, according to local health authorities.
"Higher temperatures linked to climate change help mosquitoes reproduce and extend the transmission season, increasing the chances that infected mosquitoes will spread the virus to people," said Antonino Bella, researcher at Italy's National Institute of Health, or ISS.
West Nile has been considered endemic in Italy since 2020, when cases started to surge, and is now reported every summer and early fall. About 80% of infected people develop no symptoms, while most others experience a mild flu-like illness. Severe neurological complications occur in a small minority of cases, mainly among older adults and people with underlying health conditions.
Experts say this year's case numbers are broadly in line with recent seasons.
But warmer temperatures favor mosquito reproduction and can mean the transmission season sometimes lasts as late as November, Bella explained. Areas once largely unaffected are increasingly reporting infections, reflecting a gradual expansion of the virus across the country.
Italy's experience with the virus is drawing attention from European countries located farther north. A Belgian research team visited the ISS last May to study Italy's research and surveillance system after the country began recording locally acquired West Nile cases.
The Netherlands this year has reported more than two dozen West Nile cases, the first since 2020, as well as several deaths, according to its public health institute.
"There's no doubt that warming weather will expand the period of replication for the virus and the vector in more countries," said Marc-Alain Widdowson, who leads the Pandemic Threats, Communicable Diseases, and AMR Division at the World Health Organization's Europe office.
"You've got to be careful not to say that climate change is all of it, but certainly a warming climate means that we have a longer mosquito season, so that the vectors can survive for longer. Warm temperatures also mean that the virus itself will survive better," he added.
Experts note that Italy's extensive monitoring network, which tracks mosquitoes, birds, blood donors and human infections, also helps explain why the country detects so many cases.
"There are definitely trends which we think are contributing to increased activity," Widdowson said, citing a warming climate, loss of biodiversity and changes in land use. A longer mosquito season creates more opportunities for transmission, he added, while declines in bird diversity may favor species that are efficient reservoirs of the virus.
In June, the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control, or ECDC, warned that because Europe is experiencing a warming trend — with heat waves and flooding becoming more frequent and severe, and summers getting longer and warmer — the conditions are more favorable for invasive mosquito species such as Aedes albopictus and Aedes aegypti.
Aedes aegypti — known to transmit dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya, zika and West Nile viruses — has been established in Cyprus since 2022 and may spread to other European countries.
A decade ago, the Aedes albopictus mosquito was established in eight European countries, with 114 regions affected. This year, the mosquito is established in 13 countries and 337 regions, the ECDC said.

Months after a fractured wrist had healed, a 42-year-old homemaker from Mysuru was still unable to cook or even tolerate the touch of clothing on her hand. Despite repeated investigations confirming that the fracture had healed, she continued to have severe burning pain, swelling, stiffness and changes in skin colour.
She was eventually referred to pain specialists and diagnosed with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), in which the nervous system continues to generate pain long after the original injury has healed. With specialised pain management, she gradually regained function and independence.
Pain specialists say such cases highlight the need to recognise chronic pain as a condition that may require specialised care.
At Victoria Hospital, attached to the Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI), more than 1,200 patients have undergone specialised pain-relieving procedures since its pain clinic was established in June 2023. The clinic, run by the Department of Anaesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine, has also provided outpatient consultation to over 4,000 patients.
Public awareness campaign
As September is observed as Pain Awareness month, the Karnataka Chapter of the Indian Society for Study of Pain (ISSP) has launched a public awareness campaign urging people not to accept chronic pain as an unavoidable part of life, but to seek specialised care when it persists beyond the normal healing period.
“Our team led by our head of the department Nethra S.S. has performed over 1,200 advanced pain intervention procedures and has seen over 4,000 patients in the outpatient department,” said Satish Kumar M.N., associate professor, Department of Anaesthesia and Pain Medicine, BMCRI, and treasurer of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
The clinical team, comprising associate professor Nethra H.N., assistant professor Harshavardhan H.S., Satish Kumar and Dr. Nethra, treats patients with cancer pain, neuropathic pain, musculoskeletal disorders, spine-related pain, knee and shoulder pain, trigeminal neuralgia and other chronic pain conditions.
Besides image-guided nerve blocks and joint injections, the clinic performs advanced procedures such as radiofrequency ablation, which interrupts pain signals from affected nerves.
Dr. Kumar said the acquisition of a radiofrequency ablation machine had enabled the BMCRI to offer procedures that were previously available largely in corporate hospitals.
Pain is more than a symptom
Sadasivan S. Iyer, consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, and vice-president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP, said a common misconception was that patients should simply learn to live with chronic pain.
“Many patients are told to simply live with pain because investigations do not reveal an obvious cause. But persistent pain can itself be a medical condition requiring specialised evaluation and treatment,” he said.
While acute pain serves as the body’s warning signal after an injury or illness, pain lasting beyond three months can become a condition in itself, he said. The nervous system can continue to transmit pain signals even after tissues have healed. Therefore, normal scans do not necessarily mean that the pain is imaginary, while abnormalities on imaging do not always explain the severity of symptoms.
Beyond painkillers
Pain medicine is not limited to prescribing stronger painkillers. Depending on the condition, treatment may include medication optimisation, physical rehabilitation, psychological support, lifestyle modification and minimally invasive, image-guided procedures such as nerve blocks, epidural injections and radiofrequency ablation.
“The goal is not simply to reduce a patient’s pain score. It is to help them sleep better, return to work, perform daily activities and regain independence. Pain relief is ultimately about restoring quality of life,” said Murali T.S., consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Apollo Hospitals, Bengaluru, and president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
When should patients seek help?
According to the ISSP, millions of Indians live with persistent back and neck pain, sciatica, diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, cancer pain and pain that continues after surgery.
Specialists advise people to seek evaluation if pain lasts for more than three months, repeatedly returns, interferes with sleep or daily activities, persists despite treatment of the original illness, or is accompanied by burning, shooting or electric shock-like sensations.

The day after Rob Waters learned of his layoff from Google last year, he was encouraged to apply for a new role there as an AI sales specialist. Google soon offered him the position, with a six-figure salary.
Waters wasn't sure he wanted to return. He'd grown frustrated with the bureaucracy at Google and how the reorganization that eliminated his team had been handled.
But walking away meant giving up about a few hundred thousand dollars in unvested equity.
"I killed myself working and dedicating myself, and then all I got to show for it was getting let go," said the 42-year-old, who lives in San Francisco.
He'd also dreamed of starting his own company. The layoff, he said, "ripped the bandaid off." Waters decided to bet on himself and pursue Kanawai AI, a startup he cofounded.
"All the equity that was unvested was gone," he said. "I went from making very high six figures to zero."
Stock compensation has long given Big Tech workers a powerful incentive to stay put. Since the end of 2022, shares of Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft have all at least doubled.
But years of Big Tech layoffs have reminded some workers that their stock compensation isn't guaranteed. Meanwhile, the AI boom has created another path to potential equity riches. And for some workers, years of gains on vested stock have given them the financial security to leave Big Tech on their own terms.
When Big Tech stock makes leaving easier
Julie Zhu, 29, had wanted to become a founder since she was 18 and said she'd developed a "love-hate relationship" with Apple, where she worked as a product designer. She was grateful for what she'd learned at the company but said it was a high-pressure, high-stress environment. She wanted more control over her work.
Still, Zhu wanted to make sure she could afford the risk of leaving. Her goal was to have three to five years of runway. Her Apple stock came in handy.
"I didn't sell anything during my time at Apple, and Apple has been doing really well," she said.
Last year, after nearly four years at Apple, Zhu resigned to focus on Odd One In, the artist collectible company she'd been building on the side. She said it felt like the right time, though leaving meant forfeiting the remaining quarter of her Apple stock grant that hadn't yet vested.
Yousuf Imran also built up a financial cushion during roughly six years at Google, where his compensation included company stock. He set aside $350,000 for business and personal expenses before leaving in April to start an AI sales tools company. Imran said the potentially "life-changing" equity packages at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic shaped his decision.
"If the only way to get real upside in this AI moment is equity, at some point, you ask yourself whether the equity should be in your own company," he said.
Dave Lewis also credited stock compensation for giving him the flexibility to consider career options outside Big Tech. Lewis, who spent more than a decade working at Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, said the wealth he'd accumulated from stock compensation gave him enough of a financial cushion to be selective after he was laid off by Microsoft last October.
With AI reshaping the tech industry, Lewis said he wanted his next role to position him for where he thought the industry was headed. In May, he joined Emberos, an AI startup, as head of partnerships.
With stock compensation, timing can be everything
For all its potential upside, stock compensation can leave workers' finances exposed to luck and timing: of when they join the company, vesting schedule, stock performance, and their decisions to sell or hold. One former Meta employee got lucky: Meta's shares had fallen sharply when he joined in 2022 and received a "boatload" of restricted stock units on the cheap. The stock then surged over the next few years.
Not everyone is as fortunate. A former Microsoft employee in her 60s said she still held a large amount of company stock when she lost her job last year after more than a decade there. She initially thought her savings and stock holdings might allow her to retire, but after Microsoft shares fell sharply, she began to question whether she could afford to.
The golden handcuffs only go so far
For all its complications, stock compensation remains one reason Big Tech is so appealing. A former Amazon employee said the company's salary-and-stock compensation was lucrative and also felt more predictable than the bonus-heavy pay structure she had at her previous employer.
But even a predictable compensation package depends on keeping the job. After a few years at Amazon, she was laid off last year.
Even for workers who do retain their jobs, the financial incentives to stay only go so far. As Bushra Amiwala weighed whether to leave her sales associate role to run for Congress, she said she felt the pull of Big Tech's so-called "golden handcuffs." Staying at Google offered the salary, stock, and stability that could help her continue supporting her immigrant parents financially.
For Amiwala, the deciding question wasn't whether she'd win the race — she ultimately left Google but lost the election — or what she'd give up financially by leaving Google. It was whether, five or 10 years later, she'd regret not taking the chance.
"For me, it was a no-brainer," she said. "I knew I'd regret not doing it."

The Food and Drug Administration on Thursday approved a new gene therapy for Sanfilippo syndrome type A, an ultra-rare disease sometimes known as childhood Alzheimer’s.
The therapy, called Fayuvi, was developed by Ultragenyx. It is the first drug specifically approved to treat Sanfilippo. Ultragenyx did not immediately release a price.
“It’s hard to overstate what this approval would mean for everybody who is living with this really horrific disease and watching their children suffer and pass away early, and all the rest that it brings,” said Cara O’Neill, chief science officer of the Cure Sanfilippo Foundation, in an interview earlier this week. “This, gosh, would just finally mean when patients and families receive this shocking diagnosis, they wouldn’t be told to… take their kids home and love them. They would be given hope and an action plan for treatment.”

The 18th BRICS Summit was held on 12 and 13 September 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, bringing together leaders from BRICS member countries and several partner nations. Against this backdrop, a video showing police personnel allegedly dragging a woman by her hair on a road is being widely shared (here, here), with the claim that police used force against young protesters in Delhi, dragging female protesters onto the streets while the BRICS Summit was being held nearby. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows police taking action against protesters in Delhi while the BRICS Summit 2026 was going on.
Fact: The viral video does not show police action against protesters in Delhi during the BRICS Summit. The video is from Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh, where paramedical students were protesting over unpaid stipends and mandatory 12-hour hospital shifts. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a video published by Deccan Herald on 13 September 2026, featuring similar visuals. According to its description, the video shows police action against paramedical students protesting in Tirupati over unpaid stipends, including footage of a male police officer allegedly dragging a female student by her hair.
Further, a relevant keyword search led us to several media reports indicating that this incident took place in Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh (here, here, here, here). According to the reports, BSc MLT and other allied health students, along with student union representatives, protested at Garuda Circle in Alipiri on 12 September 2026 over mandatory 12-hour shifts and pending monthly stipends of ₹15,000. ASI Lakshmi Kumari was accused of dragging a woman protester towards a police van and was reportedly moved to vacancy reserve (VR). Tirupati Additional SP Ravi Manoharachary clarified that the woman was pulled by her hand, while her hair covering the hand made it appear as though she was dragged by her hair.
Moreover, we found no reports of police action near the venue of the BRICS Summit.
To sum up, a video showing police action against protesters in Tirupati is being shared as visuals from Delhi during the BRICS Summit.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

Ominousness permeates Darkling. In Titas Halder’s dramatic monologue, we witness a young girl’s coming of age set against the backdrop of the 1984 toxic gas leak in the Indian city of Bhopal, an environmental catastrophe that remains one of the worst industrial disasters in global history, leading to thousands of deaths.
Actor Linnea Berthelsen – best known for her role as Kali in Netflix series Stranger Things – makes her UK stage debut and gamely takes on the singular role in a tightly wound, physical performance. Leaping across Simon Kenny’s artful, soil-filled set, Berthelsen embodies childlike wonder as she recounts her early years playing in the rain, savouring bowlfuls of plain rice and idolising her older sister.
So far so good. Except, alongside her emotional growth, the silhouette of a new factory rises in the background – effectively portrayed by lighting designer Rajiv Pattani’s projection – foreshadowing the calamity to come. When it eventually arrives, we hear of the horrors she witnesses, stepping over maimed bodies, facing blinded relatives and breathing in toxic fumes, all relayed through increasingly frenzied description.
Herein lies the main issue with Darkling. By using a monologue format – especially one where our narrator is never dramatically questioned – all the audience receives are streams of poetic description, a barrage of words that never feel emphatic or adequate enough to match the gruesome scale of such a tragedy. Coupled with Halder’s uneven pacing, which lingers in childhood for too long before alighting on trauma and then descending into a hectoring denouement that places the blame for the disaster on individual shoulders, Berthelsen is faced with a gargantuan task to maintain a sense of dramatic tension.
As Matthew Xia’s production draws to a close, with a strangely repeated narrative beat that equates female worth to motherhood, you are ultimately left feeling that this is a tragedy told without the requisite horror. Darkling is a worthy reminder of an often-overlooked disaster – but one that may well fail to take root in the mind.

Littler could boycott Dutch events over booing
- Published
World champion Luke Littler has threatened to stop playing in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled at during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.
The referee stopped the match during his narrow win against Nathan Aspinall in the last eight on Saturday to warn the hostile crowd about its behaviour, before play resumed.
It followed Littler also being booed during his win against home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday.
Littler has faced similar treatment in Germany and has stopped playing in European Tour events in the country.
Asked if he was prepared to take a similar stance for Dutch events, the 19-year-old told Online Darts: "100%."
Littler, who is expected to play at the European Championship in Dortmund in October, added: "With the Germans, I haven't been for a long time, we will have to see in Dortmund whether it changes or stays the same.
"If the Dutch stay like this, then I'm not going to do any Euro tours over there. There's just no point in me travelling, wasting my time whilst I'm getting booed.
"I just want to play my darts, obviously sign autographs.
"The past two nights, I've done nothing, I've just walked off stage and not thanked anyone. There's no point thanking everyone when they are booing me."
Littler was also booed during a win over Rob Cross at the PDC World Championship in December.
After the match, he said: "I'm not bothered [by the booing]. Really not bothered. You guys pay for tickets and you pay for my prize so thanks for booing me."
